by a `K`-byte RTSP OPTIONS request. CRLF conversion expands the prefix from
`K` to `2K` bytes. The advertised raw body length is also `2K`, so the body
boundary lands exactly before the complete injected request.

Build the client against curl 8.23.0:

```sh
cc -O2 -DCURL_STATICLIB -I/path/to/curl/include \
  rtsp-crlf-framing.c /path/to/libcurl.a -o rtsp-crlf-framing \
  [the normal static libcurl dependency flags]
```

In terminal 1:

```sh
python3 rtsp_capture_server.py
```

In terminal 2:

```sh
./rtsp-crlf-framing rtsp://127.0.0.1:21031/test
```

Observed client result:

```text
raw_body=126 injected=63 result=0 (No error)
```

Observed by the server:

```text
Content-Length: 126
advertised=126
actual_body=189
overflow=63
overflow_bytes=b'OPTIONS rtsp://127.0.0.1:21031/injected RTSP/1.0\r\nCSeq: 999\r\n\r\n'
```

The overflow is an intact second request, and curl reports success.


# Public disclosure

I have not opened a public issue or otherwise disclosed this report.

## Impact

# Impact

If an application enables `CURLOPT_CRLF` and sends attacker-influenced RTSP
body content, the attacker can escape the declared body and append RTSP
methods on the application's persistent connection. Depending on the server's
connection, authentication, and session behavior, this can allow actions under
the application's RTSP context.

This is not ordinary user-selected CRLF header injection: these bytes are
provided as framed body content, and curl's conversion moves them outside that
boundary. That is the same distinction as CVE-2026-87864.

The prerequisites are uncommon, so I suggest Low severity.

# Suggested fix

After installing the RTSP body reader, use `Curl_creader_total_length(data)`
for `Content-Length`. If it returns a negative value, reject the upload with
`CURLE_UPLOAD_FAILED`, as RTSP cannot switch these requests to chunked framing.

A regression test can extend RTSP test568 with a known-size ANNOUNCE body that
contains bare LF bytes and enables `CURLOPT_CRLF`. It should assert
`CURLE_UPLOAD_FAILED` and no transmitted overflow.

title: CRLF injection in the RTSP request-line and Transport header via `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` and `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT`
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

Two RTSP option strings reach the wire with no CR/LF neutralization, even though each is formatted directly into an RTSP request-line or header field that is terminated by CRLF. `Curl_setstropt()` (`lib/setopt.c`) stores each option string after checking only the 8 MB length cap (`CURL_MAX_INPUT_LENGTH`) — it never inspects for `\r` or `\n` — and both construction sites inside `rtsp_do()` (`lib/rtsp.c`) then splice the stored value verbatim into the request buffer, using `curlx_dyn_addf("%s …")` for the request-line and `curl_maprintf("…: %s\r\n")` for the Transport header, neither of which filters control characters. An embedded `\r\n` therefore terminates the current request-line/header early and lets the caller write arbitrary additional request-lines or headers into the same TCP stream, enabling header injection and RTSP request smuggling.

The two injection points share one construction function (`rtsp_do()`) and one missing-validation pattern:

| Variant | Source option (entry) | Sink (wire construction) | Injected frame position | What the RTSP server receives |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| V1. RTSP request-line | `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` | `rtsp_do()` → `curlx_dyn_addf("%s %s RTSP/1.0\r\n", p_request, p_stream_uri)` | RTSP request-line (stream URI) | `DESCRIBE rtsp://foo/\r\nTEARDOWN rtsp://victim/ RTSP/1.0\r\n…` — a complete smuggled second RTSP request (e.g. `TEARDOWN`) |
| V2. RTSP Transport header | `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT` | `rtsp_do()` → `curl_maprintf("Transport: %s\r\n", STRING_RTSP_TRANSPORT)` | RTSP Transport header value | `Transport: RTP/AVP;unicast\r\nSession: fake-session-id\r\n\r\nTEARDOWN rtsp://victim/ RTSP/1.0\r\n…` — forged `Session` header plus, via double CRLF, a complete smuggled second request |

A related CRLF-injection issue in the HTTP request-line (`CURLOPT_REQUEST_TARGET`, `lib/http.c`) is reported separately.

## Affected versions

- curl 8.21.0-DEV (debug build, mbedTLS 3.6.5) — both variants reproduced.
- curl master `9b2caf3` (8.22.0-DEV, verified 2026-08-31) — **still affected**; both variants re-run against a master build and reproduce byte-for-byte.
- Source-verified still present on current master as of 2026-10-16: `rtsp_do()` still splices both option strings with no CRLF filtering (the Transport value goes straight into `curl_maprintf("…: %s\r\n")`, the stream URI straight into the `"%s %s RTSP/1.0\r\n"` request-line format), and neither the 8.22.0 nor the 8.23.0 changelog contains a relevant fix.
- Both variants affect every curl version since the RTSP options were introduced (7.20.0).

## Root cause

`Curl_setstropt()` is the common store for both options. It only enforces the length cap and never looks at byte content:

```c
// lib/setopt.c:88-96  (Curl_setstropt)
if(strlen(s) > CURL_MAX_INPUT_LENGTH)
    /* …too long… */;
else
    dest = curlx_strdup(s);   // no CR/LF (or control-char) check; CRLF preserved verbatim
```

Each option is then written into a CRLF-delimited frame with no additional filtering:

**V1 — RTSP request-line (`CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI`):**

```c
// lib/rtsp.c:373-374  (rtsp_do)
if(data->set.str[STRING_RTSP_STREAM_URI])
    p_stream_uri = data->set.str[STRING_RTSP_STREAM_URI];   // CRLF intact
// lib/rtsp.c:490-493
curlx_dyn_addf(&req_buffer, "%s %s RTSP/1.0\r\n" "CSeq: %u\r\n",
               p_request, p_stream_uri, rtsp->CSeq_sent);   // %s does not filter \r\n
```

**V2 — RTSP Transport header (`CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT`):**

```c
// lib/rtsp.c:381-388  (rtsp_do, SETUP request, no custom Transport header set)
p_transport = Curl_checkheaders(data, STRCONST("Transport"));
if(rtspreq == RTSPREQ_SETUP && !p_transport) {
    if(data->set.str[STRING_RTSP_TRANSPORT])
        data->state.aptr.rtsp_transport =
            curl_maprintf("Transport: %s\r\n",
                          data->set.str[STRING_RTSP_TRANSPORT]);   // %s does not filter \r\n
}
// lib/rtsp.c:510-520  then curlx_dyn_addf() splices this header into req_buffer;
// lib/rtsp.c:554  Curl_req_send() flushes req_buffer to the socket.
```

Because the injected CRLF lands inside the request-line (V1) or the Transport header value (V2), the attacker controls framing, not just a single header field: a single `\r\n` ends the current line and starts a new header, and a `\r\n\r\n` ends the current request's header section and starts a new request.

## PoC

A mock RTSP server is run on loopback to capture the raw bytes curl writes. Both variants are driven the way a real application would drive them — a small C harness linked against the static libcurl build, calling `curl_easy_setopt()`:

**V1 — RTSP request-line.** The harness sets `CURLOPT_RTSP_REQUEST` to `CURL_RTSPREQ_DESCRIBE`, `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` to `"rtsp://foo/\r\nTEARDOWN rtsp://victim/ RTSP/1.0\r\n"`, and performs the transfer against the mock RTSP server.
- Negative control: `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` set to `"rtsp://foo/test"` (no CRLF).

**V2 — RTSP Transport header.** The harness sets `CURLOPT_RTSP_REQUEST` to `CURL_RTSPREQ_SETUP`, `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT` to `"RTP/AVP;unicast\r\nSession: fake-session-id\r\n\r\nTEARDOWN rtsp://victim/ RTSP/1.0\r\n"`, and performs the transfer.
- Negative control: `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT` set to `"RTP/AVP;unicast"` (no CRLF).

Both variants were re-run against a curl master `9b2caf3` build with the same harnesses; the behavior is identical to 8.21.0-DEV.

## Reproduction output

**V1 — raw bytes captured by the mock RTSP server** (`CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` payload, `curl_easy_perform` returns `CURLE_OK`):

```
DESCRIBE rtsp://foo/\r\n
TEARDOWN rtsp://victim/ RTSP/1.0\r\n
… RTSP/1.0\r\n
CSeq: 1\r\n
```

Hex dump shows `0d 0a` at offset `0x16` terminating the `DESCRIBE rtsp://foo/` request-line, immediately followed by `TEARDOWN rtsp://victim/ RTSP/1.0` as an independent second RTSP request-line. Negative control: a clean stream URI produces a single-line `DESCRIBE rtsp://foo/test RTSP/1.0` request.

**V2 — raw bytes captured by the mock RTSP server** (`CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT` payload, `curl_easy_perform` returns `CURLE_OK`):

```
SETUP rtsp://foo/ RTSP/1.0\r\n
…\r\n
Transport: RTP/AVP;unicast\r\n
Session: fake-session-id\r\n
\r\n
TEARDOWN rtsp://victim/ RTSP/1.0\r\n
…\r\n
```

Hex dump shows `0d 0a` at offset `0x62` terminating the `Transport:` header value, followed by the forged `Session: fake-session-id` header line, then a double CRLF (`0d 0a 0d 0a`) ending the first request's header section, then a complete `TEARDOWN rtsp://victim/ RTSP/1.0` second request smuggled onto the same connection. Negative control: a clean transport value produces a single `Transport: RTP/AVP;unicast\r\n` header with no injection.

## Impact

- **CVSS 3.1: 7.5 (High)** — `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`, scored on the most reliable vector across the two variants (header injection → authentication bypass → read of protected data, achievable in a single request). The request-smuggling variants additionally raise integrity and availability impact (injected `TEARDOWN`/`SETUP` reaching the RTSP server) — e.g. session disruption or session hijacking on the RTSP server; the smuggled request's response is not returned to the caller.
- **Trigger conditions:** an application forwards attacker-controlled data into one of the two `CURLOPT_RTSP_*` options without filtering CR/LF first. Realistic settings include RTSP client/gateway code that lets a user or upstream component choose the stream URI or transport parameters.
- **Severity bound:** exploitation is gated on an application forwarding user input into these setopt options without CRLF filtering, and on the RTSP server honoring injected headers or disagreeing on request boundaries. Neither the libcurl security page's "CRLF in Headers" section nor the option documentation mentions any CRLF risk for `CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` or `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT`, so application authors are not signposted toward filtering.

title: CRLF injection in the HTTP request-line via `CURLOPT_REQUEST_TARGET` (`--request-target`)
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

The `CURLOPT_REQUEST_TARGET` option string reaches the wire with no CR/LF neutralization, even though it is formatted directly into the HTTP request-line, which is terminated by CRLF. `Curl_setstropt()` (`lib/setopt.c`) stores the option string after checking only the 8 MB length cap (`CURL_MAX_INPUT_LENGTH`) — it never inspects for `\r` or `\n` — and the request-line construction in `http_target()` (`lib/http.c`) then splices the stored value verbatim into the request buffer with `curlx_dyn_add`, which does not filter control characters. An embedded `\r\n` therefore terminates the request-line early and lets the caller write arbitrary additional request-lines or headers into the same TCP stream, enabling header injection and HTTP request smuggling.

A related CRLF-injection issue in the RTSP option strings (`CURLOPT_RTSP_STREAM_URI` / `CURLOPT_RTSP_TRANSPORT`, `lib/rtsp.c`) is reported separately.

## Affected versions

- curl 8.21.0-DEV (debug build, mbedTLS 3.6.5) — reproduced.
- curl master `9b2caf3` (8.22.0-DEV, verified 2026-08-31) — **still affected**; re-run against a master build, reproduces byte-for-byte.
- Source-verified still present on current master as of 2026-10-16: no CRLF filtering has been added to `Curl_setstropt()` or `http_target()`, and neither the 8.22.0 nor the 8.23.0 changelog contains a relevant fix.
- Affects every curl version since `CURLOPT_REQUEST_TARGET` was introduced (7.55.0).

## Root cause

`Curl_setstropt()` is the store for the option. It only enforces the length cap and never looks at byte content:

```c
// lib/setopt.c:88-96  (Curl_setstropt)
if(strlen(s) > CURL_MAX_INPUT_LENGTH)
    /* …too long… */;
else
    dest = curlx_strdup(s);   // no CR/LF (or control-char) check; CRLF preserved verbatim
```

The value is then written into the CRLF-delimited request-line with no additional filtering:

```c
// lib/http.c:2086-2088  (http_target)
if(data->set.str[STRING_TARGET]) {
    path = data->set.str[STRING_TARGET];   // user value, CRLF intact
    query = NULL;
}
// lib/http.c:2173  (non-proxy path)
curlx_dyn_add(r, path);                    // raw append into the request-line buffer

// lib/http.c:2881-2888  (http_add_hd, H1_HD_REQUEST branch)
curlx_dyn_addf(req, "%s ", method);        // "GET "
http_target(data, req);                    // appends STRING_TARGET verbatim, incl. CRLF
curlx_dyn_addf(req, " HTTP/%s\r\n", …);    // trailing version + line terminator
```

Because the injected CRLF lands inside the request-line, the attacker controls framing, not just a single header field: a single `\r\n` ends the current line and starts a new header, and a `\r\n\r\n` ends the current request's header section and starts a new request.

## PoC

A mock TCP server is run on loopback to capture the raw bytes curl writes. The variant is driven the way a real application would drive it — via the `--request-target` CLI flag (which maps to `CURLOPT_REQUEST_TARGET`):

- `--request-target "/legitimate\r\nX-Injected: evil-header\r\n\r\nGET /admin HTTP/1.1"` (the `\r\n` are literal CR/LF bytes in the argument).
- curl accepts the value without rejection and sends the request.
- Negative control: `--request-target "/legitimate"` produces a single clean request-line.

The variant was re-run against a curl master `9b2caf3` build; the behavior is identical to 8.21.0-DEV.

## Reproduction output

Raw bytes captured by the mock HTTP server (hex, `--request-target` payload):

```
GET /legitimate\r\n
X-Injected: evil-header\r\n
\r\n
GET /admin HTTP/1.1 HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: 127.0.0.1:19997\r\n
User-Agent: curl/8.21.0-DEV\r\n
Accept: */*\r\n
\r\n
```

Hex dump confirms the CRLF after `/legitimate` (`0d 0a` at offset `0x0e`–`0x0f`), followed by the injected `X-Injected: evil-header` line and the smuggled `GET /admin HTTP/1.1` request-line. Negative control: a clean target produces only `GET /legitimate HTTP/1.1\r\n` with no injection.

## Impact

- **CVSS 3.1: 7.5 (High)** — `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N`, scored on the most reliable vector (header injection → authentication bypass → read of protected data on the target server, achievable in a single request with no front-end/back-end architecture required). The request-smuggling path additionally raises integrity and availability impact (injected `POST`/`DELETE` reaching the backend) under a front-proxy/back-server topology; that path requires a proxy that enforces request-path access control and a backend that disagrees about request boundaries, and the smuggled request's response is not returned to the caller.
- **Trigger conditions:** an application forwards attacker-controlled data into `CURLOPT_REQUEST_TARGET` without filtering CR/LF first. Realistic settings include REST/API client libraries that let a caller specify the request path. The curl command-line's own `--request-target` is controlled by the local user and is not by itself a remote attack surface; the remote exposure runs through applications that surface this option to remote input.
- **Realized impact (verified end-to-end):** injected `Cookie` / `Authorization` headers are honored by a target server that authenticates by those headers, granting access to protected resources; a complete smuggled second request (`GET /admin/secret`) bypasses a front proxy's path-based access control and reaches the backend.
- **Severity bound:** exploitation is gated on an application forwarding user input into this setopt option without CRLF filtering, and on the target server / proxy honoring injected headers or disagreeing on request boundaries. The curl documentation does note that `CURLOPT_REQUEST_TARGET` is passed "verbatim … without any filter … including white space and control characters," but the libcurl security page's "CRLF in Headers" section does not list `CURLOPT_REQUEST_TARGET`, so application authors are not signposted toward filtering.

title: SMTP header injection via C-escape `\r` in the recipient display name
vulnerability_information:
Vulnerability Summary

Roundcube strips CR/LF from address input in `rcmail_sendmail::email_input_format()`
(`program/include/rcmail_sendmail.php:760`) and then, twenty-five lines later,
calls `stripcslashes()` on the recipient's display name at
`program/include/rcmail_sendmail.php:790`. An authenticated user who submits the
**two-character** sequence `\r` inside a quoted display name passes the strip
regexp untouched — there is no control character in the input yet — and
`stripcslashes()` converts it into a real 0x0D *after* the sanitizer has run.

Nothing downstream removes it. `format_email_recipient()`
(`program/lib/Roundcube/bootstrap.php:329-333`) escapes only `"`.
`Mail_mimePart::encodeHeader()` folds only `/\r?\n[\s\t]*/`, so a **lone CR is
never matched**, and its non-ASCII test `preg_match('#([^\s\x21-\x7E]){1}#')`
classifies CR as whitespace, so no RFC2047 encoding is applied either. Finally
`Net_SMTP::quotedata()` (`vendor/pear/net_smtp/Net/SMTP.php:1489`) normalises
every lone CR into a full CRLF, turning the injected text into real header
lines on the wire.


 Steps to Reproduce

1. Log in to Roundcube as any user.
2. Send `POST /?_task=mail&_action=send` with a valid `_token` and the body
   parameter — note `\r` is backslash followed by the letter `r`, **not** a
   control character:
   ```
   _to="x\rBcc: attacker@evil.example\rSender: ceo@victim-corp.example\rX-Pad: p" <victim@example.com>
   ```
3. `program/include/rcmail_sendmail.php:112` reads the raw value; the CRLF
   strip at `program/include/rcmail_sendmail.php:760` matches nothing.
4. `program/include/rcmail_sendmail.php:790` — `$name = stripcslashes($name);`
   materialises three real 0x0D bytes inside the display name.
5. `program/include/rcmail_sendmail.php:202` assigns the result to
   `$headers['To']`; `:384` hands it to `Mail_mime`; `program/lib/Roundcube/rcube.php:1802`
   serialises the headers, which leaves the lone CR intact.
6. `program/lib/Roundcube/rcube_smtp.php:321` calls `Net_SMTP::data()`, whose
   `quotedata()` promotes each CR to CRLF.
7. Run the executable proof, which exercises the real repository and vendor
   code end to end:
   ```
   php roundcubemail-master_VULNHUNT_RESULTS_2026-08-03-095945/exploit_tests/test_vuln_001_smtp_header_injection_recipient.php
   ```
   Result: **PASS**. On-the-wire output:
   ```
   To: "x\r\n
   Bcc: attacker@evil.example\r\n
   Sender: ceo@victim-corp.example\r\n
   X-Pad: p"\r\n
    <victim@example.com>\r\n
   ```
   `Bcc: attacker@evil.example` and `Sender: ceo@victim-corp.example` are
   asserted to be standalone CRLF-delimited header lines.

## Impact

Any authenticated user gains arbitrary RFC-822 header emission on messages
relayed with the server's own SMTP submission credentials — a capability the
compose form deliberately does not expose (`rcmail_sendmail.php:198-269` builds
the header array from a fixed key set). Concretely they can:

- forge `From:`/`Sender:`/`Reply-To:`, bypassing the server-side identity lookup
  at `rcmail_sendmail.php:147-175` and the `identities_level` pinning enforced
  at `program/actions/settings/identity_save.php:64-79` — sender spoofing from a
  domain whose SPF/DKIM the mail server legitimately satisfies;
- add covert `Bcc:` recipients;
- forge trust-signal headers (`Received:`, `Authentication-Results:`,
  `X-Spam-Status:`) that downstream MTAs and spam filters consume;
- inject an empty line to terminate the header block early and control the raw
  message body the MTA parses.

title: libcurl shared-HSTS-cache race leads to use-after-free with attacker-controlled function-pointer call
vulnerability_information:
Missing lock on the shared HSTS cache in `lib/hsts.c` (`CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS`) allows a race that frees an `stsentry` still referenced by another thread — deterministic same-address reclaim proves the freed object is fully attacker-writable and its destructor pointer is called with an attacker-chosen argument

## Severity

**High** (suggested) — CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H (**8.1**)

| Metric | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Attack Vector | Network | Triggered by HTTPS responses (HSTS headers) processed by the application |
| Attack Complexity | High | Needs a multi-threaded application sharing one HSTS cache plus a race window; the memory-writability stage is deterministic once the free happens |
| Privileges Required | None | Any HTTPS origin the application contacts can carry the header |
| User Interaction | None | Nothing beyond the application's normal traffic |
| Scope | Unchanged | Corruption stays inside the libcurl-using process |
| C / I / A | High / High / High | Demonstrated controlled function-pointer call → arbitrary command execution; the un-reclaimed race also crashes (SIGSEGV 20/20 runs in the companion PoC) |

The program should make the final severity call; the reporter suggests High.

## Summary

`Curl_hsts_parse()` and the internal `hsts_check()` mutate an HSTS cache **without holding the share lock** (`CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS`). When an HSTS handle is attached to a `curl_share` handle and used from multiple threads — the exact scenario the share interface exists for — two threads can operate on the same linked-list node concurrently. The `max-age=0` deletion path unlinks and frees an `stsentry` (`Curl_node_remove()` → `hsts_free()`) while another walker still holds a pointer to it: CWE-362 leading to CWE-416.

Only `Curl_hsts_loadfiles()` takes the HSTS lock (lib/hsts.c:625). The parse and expiry paths do not.

The accompanying PoC removes the race timing and proves, **deterministically and through real libcurl code**, everything that happens after the free:

1. **Exact-address reclaim** — the next `Curl_hsts_parse()` call (attacker-controlled header content) re-carves the just-freed `stsentry` address via libcurl's own `hsts_create()` `calloc`.
2. **Full overwrite** — all 56 user bytes of the freed object are filled with attacker-chosen content.
3. **Real-code consumption** — the REAL `Curl_node_remove()` from `lib/llist.c` — the identical call a stale `hsts_check()` walker would make — executes the attacker-staged node: the attacker-chosen destructor function pointer is invoked with an attacker-chosen argument, and attacker-directed pointer writes land through the `_prev`/`_next` relinks.
4. **Command execution** — with the destructor staged as a `popen()`-based callback and the node's second field pointing at a command string, the dispatch executes an arbitrary shell command (demonstrated: `id`).

The chain succeeds **on the main thread and inside a spawned worker pthread**, against a static libcurl built from the vulnerable commit, with no debugger, no RWX pages, and no race timing in the writability proof.

## Affected component

- **Project:** curl / libcurl
- **Version:** 8.23.1-DEV @ commit `2c04412d8c81784b24fafe03e8389c6ce7797eef`
- **File:** `lib/hsts.c` (unlocked shared-cache mutation)
- **Secondary:** `lib/llist.c` (`Curl_node_remove()` / `take_elem` — the consumer of the corrupted node)
- **Self-reported build string:** `libcurl: libcurl/8.23.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4`
- **Tested platform:** macOS (Darwin 27, arm64, native). The PoC source also builds on Linux aarch64 (glibc), where the reclaim is single-shot deterministic via tcache LIFO.

## Technical description

### The unlocked mutation (root cause)

`lib/hsts.c` guards only one entry point with the share lock:

```c
/* hsts.c:625 — inside Curl_hsts_loadfiles(): the ONLY place the HSTS
   share lock is taken */
Curl_share_lock(data, CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS, LOCK_ACCESS_SINGLE);
```

`Curl_hsts_parse()` — reached for every HTTPS response carrying a `Strict-Transport-Security` header — and the internal `hsts_check()` both read and mutate the cache's linked list without taking `CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS`. On a shared HSTS handle used from two or more easy handles in different threads, this interleaving frees a node the other thread still references:

```
Thread A (max-age=0 delete path, hsts.c:283-291):
    hsts_check() finds a matching entry
      -> Curl_node_remove() unlinks the stsentry
      -> hsts_free() frees it            <- hsts.c:285-288
      -> return CURLE_OK                 (no allocation in between)

Thread B (concurrent parse/lookup on the same shared cache):
    still holds / re-reads the freed node  -> use-after-free
```

The allocation that creates the node (and the one that reclaims it) is in `hsts_create()`:

```c
/* hsts.c:123 */
sts = curlx_calloc(1, sizeof(struct stsentry) + hlen + 1);
```

For a cached host of 8 characters (`sizeof(struct stsentry)` = 48 on LP64): `calloc(1, 56)` → a 0x40 chunk (usable 56 bytes on glibc; `malloc_size` 64 on Apple).

### What the freed object gives an attacker

On LP64, the first 32 bytes of an `stsentry` are the embedded list node and the dtor-carried pointer:

```c
struct llnode {              /* offsets in the freed stsentry */
    struct llist *_list;     /* +0  */
    void         *_ptr;      /* +8  */
    struct llnode *_prev;    /* +16 */
    struct llnode *_next;    /* +24 */
};
struct llist {
    struct llnode *_head;    /* attacker-faked list */
    struct llnode *_tail;
    void (*_dtor)(void *, void *);   /* <-- invoked by real libcurl code */
    size_t _size;
};
```

When the real `Curl_node_remove()` (lib/llist.c, `take_elem`) removes the attacker-staged node it:

- reads `_list`, `_prev`, `_next` from the freed chunk,
- performs **pointer writes through them** (`_prev->_next = _next; _next->_prev = _prev`),
- decrements the (attacker-faked) list `_size`,
- and calls `dtor(NULL, elem)` — an **attacker-chosen function pointer invoked with the attacker-chosen `_ptr` as its second argument**.

That is a controlled indirect call plus two controlled-address writes, reached purely through genuine libcurl code operating on the reclaimed object.

## Attack preconditions

1. The application uses **libcurl's share interface** with HSTS sharing (`curl_share_setopt(share, CURLSHOPT_SHARE, CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS)`) — e.g. a multi-threaded downloader, crawler, or HTTP client sharing HSTS state across worker threads.
2. The attacker can cause the application to process **HTTPS responses they influence** — any origin they control (or a MITM position) suffices, because the `Strict-Transport-Security` header is attacker-supplied response content. Both sides of the race are attacker-chosen: `max-age=0` (deletion/free) and `max-age=<large>` (creation/reclaim).
3. libcurl built without a fix for this race.

The PoC below links the same static libcurl (built with `CURL_HIDDEN_SYMBOLS=OFF` so the internal symbols are visible) and drives the exact functions involved — `Curl_hsts_parse()` on real HSTS handles created through libcurl's own init path, and the real `Curl_node_remove()` from `lib/llist.c` — so the consumption stage is genuine library code, not a reimplementation.

## Steps to reproduce

The `poc_curl/` folder shipped alongside this report contains the PoC:

```
poc_uaf_write.c        PoC source (macOS + Linux aarch64)
poc_uaf_write          prebuilt static binary (macOS arm64, Darwin 27)
run_uaf_write_macos.sh build + link + run one-shot script (macOS)
hackerone-report.md    this report
output/                fresh evidence transcripts (see Evidence)
```

Run (macOS, native):

```sh
cd poc_curl
./run_uaf_write_macos.sh            # plain writability proof
./run_uaf_write_macos.sh "id"       # + command execution through the hijacked dtor
```

The script builds a static libcurl from commit `2c04412d8c81784b24fafe03e8389c6ce7797eef` (OpenSSL backend from bundled static archives), links the PoC, and runs it once. Exit codes (mapped by the script to a VERDICT):

| rc | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | `UAF_WRITE_PROVEN` (with an argument: `+ COMMAND_EXECUTED`) |
| 1 | `RECLAIM_FAILED` (allocator did not return the freed address; on Apple retried across fresh processes) |
| 2 | `HSTS_SETUP_FAILED` |
| 3 | `CONSUMPTION_FAILED` (or build/link failure) |

Allocator behavior by platform:

- **Linux aarch64 / glibc** — single-shot deterministic: same-thread free + `calloc` under the per-thread tcache LIFO contract cannot miss, and `calloc` bypasses tcache so libcurl's own next allocation cannot steal the chunk either.
- **Apple libmalloc (Darwin 27)** — retrieval is keyed on request size, so the PoC hunts `malloc/calloc` × request=56/usable=64 (≤512 attempts, misses held unfreed), retries the scenario up to 8× (draining size classes), and on a total miss relaunches a fresh process via `execv()` up to 12× (libmalloc magazine/region population is drawn at startup, so a miss is process-wide). Empirically ~10/12 fresh processes hit immediately (attempt 2 of ≤512, scenario try 1 of ≤8).

> Local folder note (not part of the report): the folder currently ships the prebuilt binary; `libs/`, `build-macos/`, and `curl-src/` were removed locally, so the script's build stage reports `BUILD FAILED: bundled OpenSSL incomplete` until OpenSSL archives are re-bundled under `libs/lib/`. The prebuilt binary runs as-is.

**Scope honesty:** this PoC deliberately removes the race *timing* (the free and the reclaim are sequenced in one thread) so the post-free behavior is deterministic and provable. Winning the live interleaving window against a victim thread is a separate, probabilistic step — a companion race PoC (`poc_hsts_race.c`, two threads hammering the shared cache) SIGSEGVs **20/20 runs (exit 139)** on the same build, establishing that the race itself is trivially reachable; `poc_uaf_write.c` proves everything that follows the free. This report therefore claims: (a) the race exists and crashes (companion PoC), and (b) the freed object is fully attacker-writable and is consumed by real libcurl code into a controlled indirect call (this PoC, deterministic).

## Evidence (fresh runs, 2026-10-17 — full transcripts in `output/`)

### Plain writability proof — `output/uaf_write_plain_20261017-120659.txt`, exit 0

```
libcurl: libcurl/8.23.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4

```

```
    relaunching a fresh process, attempt 9 of 12, via execv(...)

    address on attempt 2 of <=512, scenario try 1 of <=8

61(localaccounts),79(_appserverusr),80(admin), ... (exit 0)
```

Both transcripts show the complete chain on the main thread AND inside a spawned `pthread` worker with its own HSTS handle — i.e. the exploitation primitives hold in the exact threading context the share interface creates.

## Impact

- **Arbitrary code execution** in any process whose libcurl shares an HSTS cache across threads: the freed `stsentry` is reclaimed at the exact address by attacker-driven header content, fully overwritten, and consumed by genuine `Curl_node_remove()` code into an attacker-chosen function-pointer call with an attacker-chosen argument — demonstrated end-to-end with `popen("id")` output captured in the transcript.
- **Denial of service** even without reclaim: the raw race crashes the process (20/20 SIGSEGV in the companion race PoC).
- Reachable by any HTTPS origin the application contacts (attacker-supplied response header); no privileges, no user interaction beyond normal traffic.

1. Take the HSTS share lock around **every** mutation/read of a (potentially shared) HSTS cache, not only in `Curl_hsts_loadfiles()`:

   - `hsts_check()` and every other cache walk/mutation reached from request handling.
   Concretely: wrap those bodies in `Curl_share_lock(data, CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS, LOCK_ACCESS_SINGLE)` / `Curl_share_unlock(...)` when the handle is shared — the existing pattern at hsts.c:625 shows how.
2. Until fixed, document in `CURLOPT_SHARE` / the thread-safety section that the HSTS cache is not safe to share across handles used concurrently (this would negate the documented purpose of `CURL_LOCK_DATA_HSTS`, so the lock fix is strongly preferred).
3. Consider a regression test in the curl test suite: two threads hammering a shared HSTS handle with alternating `max-age=0` / `max-age=N` reproduces the UAF immediately under ASAN.

## Supporting material

- `poc_uaf_write.c` — writability + consumption + command-execution PoC (this report's primary evidence; deterministic post-free chain).
- `output/uaf_write_plain_20261017-120659.txt` — fresh plain-mode transcript, exit 0.
- `output/uaf_write_cmd_20261017-121020.txt` — fresh command-mode transcript, exit 0, `id` executed via the hijacked dtor.
- Companion race PoCs (available on request): `poc_hsts_race.c` (live two-thread race, 20/20 SIGSEGV), `poc_hsts_rce.c`.
- Vulnerable commit: `2c04412d8c81784b24fafe03e8389c6ce7797eef` (8.23.1-DEV).

title: libcurl TLS shorter-retry mismatch discloses client heap memory during cancelled IMAPS upload
vulnerability_information:
## Proof of Concept

High-level reproduction:

1. Check out curl 8.22.0 at commit
   `01346829096c61b372692f6dc43ffa778c6caccd`.
2. Build libcurl with either:
   - rustls-ffi 0.15.4 / rustls 0.23.45; or
   - GnuTLS 3.8.13.
3. Run the supplied loopback IMAPS server and multi-interface client.
4. The client starts a large `APPEND` upload using a deliberately small socket
   send buffer.
5. The server accepts the upload, stops reading until encrypted output blocks,
   then begins draining.
6. The client legally cancels the active transfer using
   `curl_multi_remove_handle()`.
7. IMAP cleanup attempts to send a two-byte CRLF while the TLS backend still
   has plaintext from the previous larger write pending.
8. The backend reports the previous write's byte count as consumed by the
   two-byte cleanup write.
9. `Curl_pp_flushsend()` underflows its pointer/remaining-length arithmetic and
   passes out-of-bounds client memory back to TLS for encryption.

Observed results:

- Rustls: UBSan confirmed pointer underflow and ASan confirmed a 16,384-byte
  heap over-read during TLS record encryption.
- GnuTLS debug build:
  `DEBUGASSERT((size_t)nwritten <= remain)` failed.
- GnuTLS non-debug build: UBSan confirmed the pointer underflow, followed by an
  invalid read inside GnuTLS/nettle encryption.
- Non-sanitized controlled-canary runs proved network disclosure:
  - Rustls transmitted a fresh 32-byte client-memory canary as the start of a
    16,384-byte TLS application-data record.
  - GnuTLS transmitted a separately calibrated 32-byte client-memory canary as
    the start of a 16,384-byte TLS application-data record.
- The canaries were never supplied to a curl option, upload callback, libcurl
  send call, or socket write.

Controls:

- Applying the current Rustls guard from PR #23260 prevented the Rustls disclosure.
- Applying GnuTLS hardening commit
  `64fb3e7a7b116f690966054f281624152d4a7651` prevented the GnuTLS disclosure.
- A normal upload without cancellation sent only the expected upload and two-byte CRLF terminator.
- OpenSSL rejected the tested shorter-retry mismatch.

## Description

### Summary

libcurl can lose ownership of plaintext accepted during a nonblocking TLS
send. A malicious IMAPS server can stall a large `APPEND` upload until TLS
output is pending, then resume reading while the application legally cancels
the transfer. IMAP cleanup sends a new two-byte CRLF command, but the affected
TLS backend reports bytes accepted during the earlier, larger upload as
consumed by this new call. curl trusts that oversized count, underflows pointer
and remaining-length arithmetic, and reads client heap memory for encryption.
We reproduced the invalid read with Rustls and GnuTLS and confirmed that
controlled client-memory canaries were delivered to the TLS peer.

Public PR #23260 describes the Rustls shorter-retry symptom. This report
additionally demonstrates the GnuTLS path and confirms concrete confidentiality
impact for both backends.

### Affected version

Confirmed target:

- curl/libcurl 8.22.0
- Git commit: `01346829096c61b372692f6dc43ffa778c6caccd`
- Platform: arm64 macOS 14.3
- Compiler: Apple clang 15.0.0
- CMake: 4.0.3

Confirmed TLS configurations:

```text
libcurl/8.22.0-DEV rustls-ffi/0.15.4/rustls/0.23.45/aws-lc-rs
libcurl/8.22.0-DEV GnuTLS/3.8.13
```

OpenSSL rejected the tested retry mismatch. The complete affected version and backend range has not been established.

### Steps To Reproduce

1. Build the exact curl 8.22.0 commit with Rustls or GnuTLS.
2. Compile the supplied libcurl multi-interface client against that exact
   build.
3. Start the supplied loopback IMAPS server with the generated test
   certificate.
4. Start the client, which uploads a large all-`A` IMAP literal.
5. Let the server stop reading until the client's TLS/socket output blocks.
6. Signal the server to begin draining.
7. Call `curl_multi_remove_handle()` while the upload remains active.
8. Observe the oversized TLS completion count being applied to IMAP's
   two-byte cleanup write.
9. Under ASan/UBSan, observe the pointer underflow and invalid read.
10. With the non-sanitized controlled allocator, verify that the peer receives
    the exact canary placed outside curl's requested command-buffer allocation.

## Impact

## Summary:

A malicious IMAPS server can cause an affected libcurl client to read memory
outside the intended send buffer and encrypt that memory back to the server.

The disclosed memory belongs to the client process and may contain
credentials, URLs, application data, cryptographic material, or data belonging
to unrelated transfers. Controlled experiments confirmed transmission of
exact client-memory canaries that were never provided for upload or passed to
libcurl's send APIs. A default-allocator GnuTLS run also exposed natural
process strings unrelated to the upload.

The issue can additionally crash or hang the client when the invalid pointer
reaches unmapped memory.

Exploitation requires:

- an affected TLS backend;
- a sufficiently large IMAPS `APPEND`;
- server-controlled backpressure; and
- application cancellation of the active easy handle while TLS output remains
  pending.

No out-of-bounds write or code-execution primitive was demonstrated.

title: curl RTSP connection reuse routes response headers to the RTP callback (rtsp_conn state machine not reset between sessions)
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

libcurl's RTSP client keeps a per-connection RTP parsing state machine in `struct rtsp_conn` (`state`, `in_header`, `rtp_len`, `buf`). This state machine is initialised exactly once, when a brand-new connection is allocated, and is never reset thereafter. RTSP connections are pooled and reused across requests (`PROTOPT_CONN_REUSE`), so a normal `SETUP → PLAY → GET_PARAMETER` session runs over a single connection. None of the per-request hooks (`rtsp_connect`, `rtsp_done`, `Curl_req_soft_reset`) touch the RTP state-machine fields, and when the multi layer detects `conn->bits.reuse` it skips `protocol_connect()`/`rtsp_connect()` entirely.

A malicious RTSP server (or any party able to control the server's responses) can exploit this by appending an *incomplete* interleaved RTP frame header to the `PLAY` response — the 4 bytes `$\x00\x00\x10` (channel 0, declaring 16 bytes of payload that never arrive). The state machine advances `SKIP → CHANNEL → LEN → DATA` and parks in `RTP_PARSE_DATA` with `rtp_len = 20`. Because the `PLAY` response carries no `Content-Length` (`size = 0`, `download_done = TRUE`), the transfer completes without error, `rtsp_conn_is_dead()` only probes TCP liveness, and the connection is returned to the pool with the stuck state machine still attached.

When the client reuses that connection for the next request, `rtsp_rtp_write_resp()` is invoked with `rtspc->in_header = FALSE` left over from the previous request, so `rtsp_filter_rtp()` runs first and resumes from `RTP_PARSE_DATA`. The new response's headers (`RTSP/1.0 200 OK\r\n...`) are accumulated into `rtspc->buf` as if they were RTP frame payload, and once `rtp_len` bytes are collected `rtp_client_write()` dispatches them to the RTP interleave callback. The RTSP response headers are therefore never parsed, the body is misrouted, and the transfer hangs until timeout (exit 28).

| Variant | Trigger | RTP callback receives | Client result |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Partial RTP header after PLAY (`$\x00\x00\x10`, 4 bytes) | connection reused for next request | 20 bytes: `$\x00\x00\x10` + first 16 bytes of the next response's status line (`RTSP/1.0 200 OK\r`) | response headers never parsed; `GET_PARAMETER` hangs until `CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT` (exit 28) |
| Clean PLAY response (no partial RTP header) — negative control | connection reused for next request | nothing | response parsed normally, exit 0 |

## Affected versions

Confirmed on curl 8.21.0-DEV (RTSP enabled) and still present on current master `9b2caf3` (8.22.0-DEV, verified 2026-08-31). On master the vulnerable code in `lib/rtsp.c` (`rtsp_connect()` and `rtsp_done()`) is byte-identical to 8.21.0-DEV; the end-to-end reproduction (PLAY leaves `rtspc->state = 3`, the reused connection routes the next response's headers to the RTP callback, exit 28) reproduces verbatim against a master build. Source-verified still present on master as of 2026-10-16: `rtsp_connect()` still resets only `rtp_channel` (not `state`/`buf`/`rtp_len`/`in_header`), `rtsp_done()` still performs only CSeq checks with no `rtsp_conn` reset, and neither the 8.22.0 nor the 8.23.0 changelog contains a relevant fix.

## Root cause

The RTP state machine lives in the connection-level `rtsp_conn` struct and is only zero-initialised on first allocation:

```c
// lib/rtsp.c:105-122  rtsp_setup_connection()
//   rtspc = Curl_conn_meta_get(...); curlx_calloc(...) -> all fields zero
//   (state = RTP_PARSE_SKIP, in_header = FALSE, rtp_len = 0, buf empty)
//   Called ONLY when a new connection is created — not on reuse.
```

On connection reuse the multi layer short-circuits the connect phase, so `rtsp_connect()` is never reached:

```c
// lib/multi.c:2553-2557  multistate_protoconnect()
//   if(conn->bits.reuse) -> jump straight to MSTATE_DO,
//   skipping protocol_connect() / rtsp_connect()
```

Even when `rtsp_connect()` does run, it only resets the channel, not the state machine; `rtsp_done()` touches none of these fields:

```c
// lib/rtsp.c:138-153  rtsp_connect()
//   rtspc->rtp_channel = -1;     // the only rtsp_conn field touched
//   (state / in_header / rtp_len / buf NOT reset)

// lib/rtsp.c:157-196  rtsp_done()
//   (does not touch rtsp_conn state-machine fields at all)
```

The error-free residual path. A `PLAY` response without `Content-Length` plus a 4-byte partial RTP header parks the state machine without raising an error:

```c
// lib/rtsp.c:875-878  rtsp_rtp_write_resp()
//   no Content-Length -> data->req.size = 0, data->req.download_done = TRUE

// lib/rtsp.c:754-784  rtsp_filter_rtp()
//   '$' -> CHANNEL (mask check passes) -> LEN -> DATA
//   partial frame ($\x00\x00\x10, declares 16 bytes) leaves state = RTP_PARSE_DATA,
//   rtp_len = 20, buf holds 4 bytes

// lib/rtsp.c:889-890
//   state != SKIP -> data->req.done = FALSE, but download_done already TRUE

// lib/transfer.c:425-426  Curl_sendrecv()
//   !CURL_REQ_WANT_IO -> data->req.done = TRUE; size=0, bytecount=0
//   -> no CURLE_PARTIAL_FILE, multi_done(CURLE_OK), connection pooled
```

Liveness check does not inspect the state machine, so the stuck connection survives in the pool:

```c
// lib/rtsp.c:131-136  rtsp_conn_is_dead()
//   TCP-level liveness only; does not check rtspc->state
```

On reuse, the leftover `in_header = FALSE` makes `rtsp_filter_rtp()` run first and resume the stuck `DATA` state, consuming the new response's headers as RTP payload:

```c
// lib/rtsp.c:837-852  rtsp_rtp_write_resp()  (on the reused connection)
//   data->req.header = TRUE, but rtspc->in_header = FALSE (leftover)
//   -> !rtspc->in_header => rtsp_filter_rtp() runs first

// lib/rtsp.c:760-786  rtsp_filter_rtp()
//   resumes RTP_PARSE_DATA: response headers appended to rtspc->buf via curlx_dyn_addn
//   once rtp_len bytes accumulate -> rtp_client_write()

// lib/rtsp.c:615-642  rtp_client_write()
//   fwrite_rtp / fwrite_func callback invoked with response-header bytes as "RTP frame"
//   bypasses Curl_client_write; bytecount not updated; RTSP headers never parsed
```

## PoC

The reproduction drives libcurl's RTSP API against a mock RTSP server controlled by the researcher, on a single easy handle, issuing the standard `SETUP → PLAY → GET_PARAMETER` sequence over one reused connection.

1. Build curl with RTSP enabled (debug build, ASan). Point a C harness at libcurl's RTSP API (`curl_easy_perform`) with an `INTERLEAVEFUNCTION` RTP callback installed.
2. The mock server accepts the `SETUP` request and responds with `Transport: RTP/AVP/TCP;unicast;interleaved=0-1`, registering channels 0/1.
3. The client reuses the same connection and easy handle to send `PLAY`. The server replies with a normal `PLAY` response (no `Content-Length`) and immediately appends the 4-byte partial RTP frame header `$\x00\x00\x10` (channel 0, length 16), sending no further payload. It keeps the TCP connection open.
4. The `PLAY` transfer completes without error (`size = 0`, `download_done = TRUE`); the connection is returned to the pool with `rtspc->state = RTP_PARSE_DATA`, `rtp_len = 20`.
5. The client reuses the same connection and easy handle to send `GET_PARAMETER`. The server replies with a normal response (`Content-Length` + body).
6. Because `rtspc->in_header = FALSE` is leftover, `rtsp_filter_rtp()` runs first and resumes from `RTP_PARSE_DATA`. The first 16 bytes of the `GET_PARAMETER` response headers are accumulated into `rtspc->buf`, combined with the 4 residual bytes to form a 20-byte "RTP frame", and delivered to the RTP callback. The RTSP response headers are never parsed; the transfer hangs until the timeout fires.

The negative control runs the identical `SETUP → PLAY → GET_PARAMETER` sequence but omits the partial RTP header after `PLAY`. The state machine stays in `RTP_PARSE_SKIP` throughout, the `GET_PARAMETER` response is parsed normally, no RTP callback fires, and the client exits 0.

## Reproduction output

Verbose trace from the vulnerable run (8.21.0-DEV; identical on master `9b2caf3`):

```
* Reusing existing rtsp: connection with host 127.0.0.1     (PLAY reuses the connection)
< RTSP/1.0 200 OK
< CSeq: 2
< Session: testsession123
* rtsp_rtp_write_resp(len=0, in_header=0, done=0, rtspc->state=0, req.size=0)   (PLAY done; state advanced by the partial frame)
* Connection #0 to host 127.0.0.1:18086 left intact

* Reusing existing rtsp: connection with host 127.0.0.1     (GET_PARAMETER reuses the connection)
* rtsp_rtp_write_resp(len=4, in_header=0, eos=0)
* rtsp_rtp_write_resp(len=0, in_header=0, done=0, rtspc->state=3, req.size=-1)  (stuck in RTP_PARSE_DATA)
* rtsp_rtp_write_resp(len=96, in_header=0, eos=0)
* RTP write channel 0 rtp_len 20                            (response headers routed to RTP callback)
* rtsp_rtp_write_resp(len=0, in_header=0, done=0, rtspc->state=0, req.size=-1)
* Operation timed out after 10002 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
```

RTP callback payload (the response headers were delivered here instead of to the RTSP header parser):

```
hex:   24 00 00 10 52 54 53 50 2f 31 2e 30 20 32 30 30 20 4f 4b 0d
ascii: $\x00\x00\x10RTSP/1.0 200 OK\r
```

The first 4 bytes are the residual RTP frame header; the remaining 16 bytes are the leading bytes of the `GET_PARAMETER` response status line. Client result:

```
=== STEP 3: GET_PARAMETER ===
!!! RTP_CALLBACK: received 20 bytes
GET_PARAMETER result: 28 (Timeout was reached)
```

Negative control (no partial RTP header after `PLAY`):

```
* rtsp_rtp_write_resp(... rtspc->state=0, req.size=0)   (state stays SKIP)
=== STEP 3: GET_PARAMETER ===
GET_PARAMETER result: 0 (No error)                      (response parsed; no RTP callback)
```

## Impact

- **CVSS 3.1: 7.0 (High)** — `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:L/A:L`. The attacker is a malicious RTSP server (or any position that can shape the server's responses). Attack complexity is low: the attacker only needs to append `$\x00\x00\x10` to a normal `PLAY` response and hold the TCP connection open; no client-side validation is bypassed. The client contributes a standard `SETUP → PLAY → <next request>` session over one easy handle, which is the default RTSP usage pattern and the default connection-reuse behaviour.
- **Trigger conditions:** the client uses a single easy handle for a multi-request RTSP session (so the connection is reused) and has an RTP interleave callback installed (`CURLOPT_INTERLEAVEFUNCTION`); the server delivers a partial interleaved RTP frame header after a response that carries no `Content-Length`.
- **Realized impact:**
  - *Data misrouting / confidentially relevant:* RTSP response headers (e.g. `Session`, server version, server-chosen header values) are diverted to the RTP interleave callback rather than the RTSP header parser. Applications that wire RTP media to a separate callback/sink from RTSP control data receive control-plane bytes on the media path.
  - *Integrity:* the subsequent request's response is never correctly parsed; the body is incomplete or garbled.
  - *Availability:* the transfer hangs waiting for header data that has already been consumed, terminating in `CURLE_OPERATION_TIMEDOUT` (exit 28).
- **Severity bound:** exploitation requires the attacker to be the RTSP server the client has chosen to connect to (or to control that server's responses); it is not reachable from an arbitrary network position. The impact is bounded to the RTSP session being misrouted and timing out — no memory corruption, no out-of-bounds write, and no cross-protocol code execution was observed. The data exposed is the RTSP response headers of the session the client already established with the attacker-controlled server. CVSS reflects the network-reachable, low-complexity availability impact plus the control/media-plane data misrouting.

title: RTSP ANNOUNCE/SET_PARAMETER upload with --use-ascii / CURLOPT_TRANSFERTEXT sends more body bytes than the declared Content-Length (incomplete fix of e
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

curl refuses RTSP uploads that combine a body with `--crlf` / `CURLOPT_CRLF`, because the
LF→CRLF conversion makes the number of bytes actually sent differ from the `Content-Length`
curl declares to the server. That guard was added as a security fix:

- RTSP: commit `e84f95a` "rtsp: refuse doing uploads with CRLF conversions", `lib/rtsp.c:235`:
  ```c
  if(data->set.crlf) {
    failf(data, "Cannot do CRLF conversions on upload with RTSP");
    return CURLE_BAD_FUNCTION_ARGUMENT;
  }
  ```
- The sibling IMAP case is CVE-2026-87864 (`lib/imap.c` now re-reads the reader-stack total
  length and aborts when it is unknown).

**The RTSP guard is too narrow.** The same LF→CRLF converter (`cr_lc`) is inserted whenever
`data->set.crlf` **OR** `data->state.prefer_ascii` is set:

`lib/sendf.c:1137-1147` (`do_init_reader_stack`), guarded by
```c
#ifdef CURL_PREFER_LF_LINEENDS
  if(data->set.crlf || data->state.prefer_ascii)
    result = cr_lc_add(data);   /* LF -> CRLF converter */
#endif
```
and `CURL_PREFER_LF_LINEENDS` is defined on every non-Windows/non-MSDOS platform
(`lib/urldata.h:32-36`). `prefer_ascii` is turned on by `--use-ascii` /
`CURLOPT_TRANSFERTEXT` (`src/config2setopts.c:995`, `lib/setopt.c` → `data->set.prefer_ascii`
→ `lib/transfer.c:484` `data->state.prefer_ascii`).

RTSP computes `Content-Length` from the **raw** declared size and never re-reads the converted
total:
- `lib/rtsp.c:203-246`: `req_clen = data->state.infilesize;` (raw) and the header
  `Content-Length: <req_clen>` is emitted — but the `cr_lc` converter grows the body by the
  number of bare LFs. The guard at `rtsp.c:235` checks only `set.crlf`, so with `--use-ascii`
  (`prefer_ascii == TRUE`, `crlf == FALSE`) it does not fire.

Contrast — the codebase already knows the correct, wider condition:
- FTP accounts for **both** flags: `lib/ftp.c:3803-3806` uses `(data->set.crlf || data->state.prefer_ascii)`.
- IMAP re-reads `Curl_creader_total_length()` after building the stack and aborts on -1
  (`lib/imap.c:883-890`).
- RTSP checks only `data->set.crlf` — this is the omission / incomplete fix.

## Root cause

Declared size (`Content-Length`) is taken from the un-converted `infilesize`, while the body is
sent through a reader stack that includes the LF→CRLF converter under `prefer_ascii`. The RTSP
size-safety guard was written against `set.crlf` only and does not cover the `prefer_ascii`
trigger of the very same converter.

## Attacker model / reachability

An application (or the curl CLI) performing an RTSP `ANNOUNCE` or `SET_PARAMETER` upload with
`CURLOPT_TRANSFERTEXT`/`--use-ascii`, where the uploaded body contains attacker-influenced
content with bare `\n` bytes. Realistic case: a service embedding libcurl that relays
user-supplied SDP/parameter data into an RTSP ANNOUNCE body in text mode. On a persistent
RTSP/TCP connection, the bytes sent past the declared `Content-Length` are parsed by the origin
RTSP server as the start of the next RTSP request → RTSP request injection / smuggling.

## PoC (live, with controls)

Two PoCs are attached: `poc_rtsp_ascii.py` proves the Content-Length/on-wire desync with three
cases; `poc_rtsp_smuggle.py` proves a full second RTSP request is smuggled past the body and
parsed by the server (see "Demonstrated request smuggling" below).

`attachments/rtsp_client.c` is a minimal libcurl program that sets
`CURLOPT_RTSP_REQUEST = CURL_RTSPREQ_ANNOUNCE`, `CURLOPT_UPLOAD`, `CURLOPT_TRANSFERTEXT`, and
`CURLOPT_INFILESIZE_LARGE = <raw file size>`, then uploads a body file. It is linked against the
libcurl built from this commit. `attachments/poc_rtsp_ascii.py` starts a local RTSP listener that
records the declared `Content-Length` and counts the body bytes actually received, then runs three
cases. Captured output (`attachments/rtsp_transcript.txt`):

```
=== CASE: EXPLOIT  --use-ascii + bare-LF body ===
    raw body length    : 58
    bare LF count       : 4
    method seen         : ANNOUNCE
    declared C-L        : 58
    actual body bytes   : 62
    >>> DESYNC: 4 extra bytes sent past declared Content-Length

=== CASE: NEGATIVE no --use-ascii + bare-LF body ===
    declared C-L        : 58
    actual body bytes   : 58
    OK: actual == declared (no desync)

=== CASE: NEGATIVE --use-ascii + all-CRLF body ===
    declared C-L        : 62
    actual body bytes   : 62
    OK: actual == declared (no desync)

CONFIRMED: --use-ascii makes curl send MORE RTSP body bytes than the
Content-Length it declared; both negative controls stay in sync.
```

The exploit case declares `Content-Length: 58` but writes 62 bytes on the wire; the 4 extra
bytes are exactly the CRs inserted for the 4 bare LFs. Both negative controls (no `--use-ascii`;
and `--use-ascii` with an all-CRLF body that has nothing to expand) stay perfectly in sync,
isolating the cause to the `prefer_ascii` LF→CRLF path that the RTSP guard misses.

### Demonstrated request smuggling (second PoC)

`attachments/poc_rtsp_smuggle.py` goes further and proves the primitive is a true request
injection, not just a byte-count mismatch. It crafts the ANNOUNCE body so that the bytes which
fall past the declared `Content-Length` form a **complete, well-formed second RTSP request**.
The crafting relies only on the LF→CRLF arithmetic (each bare LF adds one byte): with
`raw = P + S_raw`, padding `P` so it contains exactly `len(S_raw)` bare LFs makes the post-body
remainder equal to `expand(S_raw)` — the smuggled request, correctly CRLF-terminated.

Captured output (`attachments/rtsp_smuggle_transcript.txt`):

```
  first request method           : ANNOUNCE
  declared Content-Length        : 223 (== raw body len 223 )
  bytes server reads as body     : 223
  bytes PAST Content-Length      : 94
  smuggled bytes (repr)          :
      b'TEARDOWN rtsp://victim.example/stream RTSP/1.0'
      b'CSeq: 99'
      b'X-Smuggled: injected-by-attacker'
  >>> SERVER-SIDE PARSE of the post-body bytes:
        method  : TEARDOWN
        uri     : rtsp://victim.example/stream
        version : RTSP/1.0
        headers : {'CSeq': '99', 'X-Smuggled': 'injected-by-attacker'}

######## NEGATIVE CONTROL: same body, NO --use-ascii ########
  bytes PAST Content-Length      : 0
  smuggled request present?      : NO (in sync)
```

The server reads 223 bytes as the ANNOUNCE body (exactly the declared `Content-Length`) and the
remaining 94 bytes parse as a full `TEARDOWN rtsp://victim.example/stream RTSP/1.0` request with
its own `CSeq` and headers — a request the attacker never sent as a request of their own. Without
`--use-ascii`, zero bytes are smuggled.

## Steps to reproduce

```
# build curl from this commit (./configure --with-openssl && make)
gcc -I include attachments/rtsp_client.c lib/.libs/libcurl.a \
    -lssl -lcrypto -lbrotlidec -lbrotlicommon -lz -o rtsp_client
python3 -I attachments/poc_rtsp_ascii.py   # edit paths at top if needed
```

## Suggested fix

Widen the RTSP guard at `lib/rtsp.c:235` to the same condition the converter uses, i.e.
`if(data->set.crlf || data->state.prefer_ascii)`, or (better, matching IMAP) re-read
`Curl_creader_total_length()` after the reader stack is built and refuse / switch to an unknown
length when it no longer equals the declared size.

## Impact

## Impact

On an RTSP `ANNOUNCE` / `SET_PARAMETER` upload with `--use-ascii` / `CURLOPT_TRANSFERTEXT`,
curl declares a `Content-Length` that is smaller than the body it actually transmits. The
surplus bytes (one CR per bare LF in the body) fall outside the declared message body, so a
server reading the kept-alive RTSP/TCP connection treats them as the beginning of the next RTSP
request.

When the body content is attacker-influenced — e.g. a service embedding libcurl that relays
user-supplied SDP or parameter data into an RTSP ANNOUNCE in text mode — the attacker can push
chosen bytes past the body boundary and smuggle a crafted continuation. This is demonstrated
end-to-end in the second PoC: the bytes past the declared `Content-Length` form a complete,
well-formed `TEARDOWN rtsp://victim.example/stream RTSP/1.0` request (with its own `CSeq` and
headers) that the receiving server parses as the next request on the connection. This is the
RTSP sibling of the upload size-desync class curl already closed for `--crlf` on RTSP (commit
e84f95a) and for IMAP (CVE-2026-87864); the `prefer_ascii` trigger of the same converter was
left uncovered, so the earlier fix is incomplete.

## What it is / is not

- It **is** a declared-size-vs-on-wire-size desync, confirmed live end-to-end against a local
  RTSP listener, with a positive control and two negative controls isolating the cause; and the
  smuggling of a complete second RTSP request past the body is demonstrated, not merely asserted.
- It **is** an incomplete fix: FTP checks both `crlf` and `prefer_ascii`, IMAP re-reads the
  total length, RTSP checks only `crlf`.
- It is **not** a default-configuration issue: it requires the caller to enable
  `--use-ascii` / `CURLOPT_TRANSFERTEXT`, and the body must contain bare LF bytes. An all-CRLF
  body or binary mode is unaffected.
- It is **not** memory-unsafe and leaks no local data.

## Honest severity

Low. It depends on a non-default option and on RTSP upload (a niche protocol path), which is why
I rate it Low rather than higher. I am reporting it because it is the same security class curl
chose to fix with an explicit refusal for `--crlf`, the fix demonstrably does not cover the
`prefer_ascii` path that drives the identical converter, and the result is a reproducible
request-smuggling primitive rather than a cosmetic mismatch. Triage may reasonably rate it
Low/Medium; I defer to the curl security team on the final rating.

title: urlapi: CURLUPART_HOST accepts text after an IPv6 zone ip and URL round trip changes the host
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
[six or fewer sentences describing the issue in your own human voice and optionally a short proof-of-concept script]
An app can set a host from untrusted input from CURLUPART_HOST, as the docs allow, and rely on curl to reject bad hosts. curl accepts [fe80::1%25eth0]@evil.example/x as a valid IPv6 host. The URL it then builds has evil.example as its host. Any code that uses that URL string goes to evil.example. libcurl also sends the follow-up request there after a relative redirect from the IPv6 server. An attack needs an app that sets untrusted hosts this way, and i do not know of one.

## Affected version
[Which curl/libcurl version are you using to reproduce? On which platform? `curl -V` typically generates good output to include]
curl 8.10.0 through 8.23.0

## Steps To Reproduce:
[add details for how we can reproduce the issue]
Paste this: 1. Build libcurl 8.10.0 or later (I tested 8.10.0, 8.23.0, and master `c4b341c`).
2. Save the program from the report as `repro.c`.
3. Compile it:
   ```bash
   cc repro.c -I<curl>/include -L<curl>/lib -lcurl -o repro
   ```
4. Run `./repro`.

**Expected:** `curl_url_set()` rejects the host, the same way it rejects `[::1]junk` with `CURLUE_BAD_HOSTNAME`.

**Actual:**
```
set host: rc=0
host:     [fe80::1%25eth0]@evil.example/x
url:      http://[fe80::1%25eth0]@evil.example/%25eth0]/
reparse:  rc=0 host=evil.example
```

**Redirect case**

1. Start an HTTP server on `[::1]:18934` that answers `302` with `Location: /next`.
2. Start any HTTP server on `127.0.0.1:18933`.
3. Set the host to `[::1%25lo0]@127.0.0.1:18933/x` and the port to `18934`. On Linux, use `lo` in place of `lo0`.
4. Pass the handle with `CURLOPT_CURLU`, set `CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION` to `1`, and run the transfer.
5. The first request goes to `[::1]:18934`. The second request goes to `127.0.0.1:18933`.
## Again: there is no bug-bounty for curl. We do not offer any rewards, only proper credits.

## Impact

## Summary:
curl accepts [fe80::1%25eth0]@evil.example/x as a valid IPv6 host.
curl_url_get(CURLUPART_URL) then gives a URL whose host is evil.example. Any code that logs, stores, or fetches that URL uses the wrong host.
With CURLOPT_CURLU and CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION, libcurl sends the first request to the IPv6 address. A relative redirect from that server sends the next request to the other host and port.
An attack needs an app that passes untrusted hosts to CURLUPART_HOST

title: curl CONNECT response header colon-check bypass in cf-h1-proxy single_header — proxy authentication bypass via injected HTTP/1.x status line
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

In the HTTP/1.1 proxy-CONNECT response parser (`lib/cf-h1-proxy.c`, `single_header()`), the per-line counter `data->req.headerline` (a.k.a. `k->headerline`) is never incremented — only the tunnel-local `ts->headerlines` is. `Curl_req_soft_reset()` resets `k->headerline` to 0 before the CONNECT exchange begins, and it stays 0 for the entire CONNECT response. `Curl_verify_header()` (`lib/http.c`) treats `k->headerline < 2` as "this is a status line" and returns `CURLE_OK` without performing its colon-presence check, so that colon check — which exists precisely to reject garbage/injected lines in the header area — is dead code on the CONNECT path. The normal HTTP response path (`http_rw_hd`) increments `k->headerline` (`if(!k->headerline++)`), so the guard works there and only there.

Because the colon check is inert on the CONNECT path, a malicious proxy can inject a line shaped like an HTTP/1.x status line into the header area of a `407 Proxy Authentication Required` response. `on_resp_header()` matches any line beginning with `HTTP/1.` (without checking whether it is the first/status line, and without requiring a colon) and overwrites `k->httpcode` and `data->info.httpproxycode` with the parsed status code. Injecting `HTTP/1.1 200 OK: x` overwrites the `407` with `200`. The end-of-headers empty-line handler then sees `httpcode == 200` (not `407`) and proceeds to `KEEPON_DONE`; `recv_CONNECT_resp()` sees `httpproxycode/100 == 2` and skips `Curl_http_auth_act()`; `H1_CONNECT()` sees the same `2xx` and marks the tunnel `H1_TUNNEL_ESTABLISHED`. The client believes the tunnel is up, never retries with proxy authentication, and sends the real request — `Cookie`, `Authorization`, POST bodies, and the `Proxy-Authorization` header from the CONNECT request — over the attacker's connection.

The injected line must carry a colon (e.g. `HTTP/1.1 200 OK: x`) to satisfy the secondary colon check in `Curl_headers_push()` → `namevalue()`. This does not change the root cause; it only shapes the payload.

| Impact variant (all verified end-to-end) | Target scheme | What the attacker captures / controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plaintext request leak | `http://` target | Full request: method, Host, `Cookie`, `Authorization`, POST body; attacker can also return a forged response (integrity) |
| TLS ClientHello intercept | `https://` target | TLS ClientHello incl. SNI and connection metadata; TLS content stays encrypted; attacker may send a TLS alert to kill the connection (availability) |
| Proxy-credential capture | any CONNECT | `Proxy-Authorization: Basic` from the CONNECT request, base64-decoded to `user:password` |
| No-auth-configured hijack | any target, no `--proxy-user` | Tunnel still marked established; plaintext HTTP request captured |

## Affected versions

- curl 8.21.0-DEV (mbedTLS 3.6.5 debug build).
- Current master `9b2caf3` (8.22.0-DEV, verified 2026-08-31). **Still affected.** all five verification checks pass; verbose output is byte-for-byte identical to 8.21.0-DEV: the `407` is overwritten to `200` by the injected line, `* CONNECT tunnel established, response 200` is printed, and the tunneled request carrying `Cookie: secret=session123` + `Authorization: Bearer sensitive_token` is captured (`curl/8.22.0-DEV` User-Agent).
- `lib/cf-h1-proxy.c` `single_header()` (master line 474) still only does `ts->headerlines++`; `data->req.headerline` is never incremented, and `k` is a `const` pointer (line 470) so the existing code cannot mutate it. No fix has landed.

## PoC

The attacker operates a malicious HTTP proxy (or is a man-in-the-middle between the curl client and the legitimate proxy — curl's documented attacker capability "B"). The client uses curl with `--proxy-tunnel` (`-p`) or simply requests an `https://` target through the proxy (which forces a CONNECT), and has proxy authentication configured (`--proxy-user` / `CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD`). The client's request also carries sensitive headers (`Cookie`, `Authorization`).

1. The client sends `CONNECT <host>:<port> HTTP/1.1` to the attacker's proxy, including a `Proxy-Authorization: Basic <base64(user:pass)>` header.
2. The attacker responds with a `407` challenge and, in the header area, an injected line:
   ```
   HTTP/1.1 407 Proxy Authentication Required\r\n
   Proxy-Authenticate: Basic realm="proxy"\r\n
   HTTP/1.1 200 OK: x\r\n
   Content-Length: 0\r\n
   \r\n
   ```
   The injected `HTTP/1.1 200 OK: x` carries a colon (required to pass the secondary `namevalue()` colon check) while still matching the `HTTP/1.` prefix pattern in `on_resp_header()`.
3. `Curl_verify_header()` returns `CURLE_OK` for the injected line (`headerline == 0 < 2`, colon check skipped).
4. `Curl_headers_push()` → `namevalue()` accepts the line (it contains a colon).
5. `on_resp_header()` matches the `HTTP/1.x` pattern and overwrites `k->httpcode` / `data->info.httpproxycode` from `407` to `200`.
6. At the empty line, `httpcode` is `200`, so the handler takes the `KEEPON_DONE` branch instead of `KEEPON_IGNORE`.
7. `recv_CONNECT_resp()` sees `httpproxycode/100 == 2` and does not call `Curl_http_auth_act()` — no authentication retry, `data->req.newurl` is not set.
8. `H1_CONNECT()` sees `2xx` and marks the tunnel `H1_TUNNEL_ESTABLISHED`; `cf_h1_proxy_connect` sets `cf->connected = TRUE`.
9. The client, believing the tunnel is established, sends the real request over the attacker's connection. For an `http://` target this is the full plaintext request (`Cookie`, `Authorization`, POST body); for an `https://` target it is the TLS ClientHello (SNI exposed, TLS content encrypted).

The negative control — the same injection without `-p` (normal HTTP proxy path through `http_rw_hd`, where `k->headerline` is incremented) — does not overwrite `httpcode`, does not establish a tunnel, and does not bypass authentication, confirming the bug is specific to the CONNECT response path. The full proof-of-concept script (malicious proxy) is available on request.

## Impact

- **CVSS 3.1: 9.6 (Critical)** — `AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:N`.
- **Trigger conditions:** The attacker must operate a malicious HTTP proxy or be positioned as a MITM between the client and the legitimate proxy (curl's documented attacker capability "B"). No privileges on the client host are required. The client must use CONNECT tunnelling (`-p` / `--proxy-tunnel`, or any `https://` request through a proxy). The injected line must carry a colon to pass the secondary `namevalue()` check.
- **Realized impact:**
  - `http://` targets: full plaintext request captured — `Cookie`, `Authorization`, POST bodies, and all custom headers; the attacker can also return a forged HTTP response (integrity). Session hijacking and API-key/credential disclosure.
  - Proxy authentication is fully bypassed — even with `CURLOPT_PROXYUSERPWD` set, the auth retry never fires.
  - The `Proxy-Authorization: Basic` header from the CONNECT request is captured and base64-decoded to plaintext proxy credentials.
  - `https://` targets: TLS ClientHello (incl. SNI) is intercepted; TLS-encrypted content is not exposed. The attacker may send a TLS alert to terminate the connection (availability), or complete a MITM if the client has disabled TLS verification (`-k`).
- **Severity bound:** The C:H/I:H is fully realized for plaintext HTTP targets and for proxy-credential capture. For HTTPS targets the confidentiality impact is bounded to SNI/connection-metadata exposure (TLS content remains encrypted), and the availability impact is limited to connection termination. The attack requires the attacker to control the proxy or be a MITM; it does not grant the attacker any new network position they did not already hold, but it defeats proxy authentication — the mechanism intended to gate access to the proxy and to the upstream — and turns a proxy that would have rejected the unauthenticated CONNECT into one that silently exfiltrates the client's request and credentials.

title: SCP upload with --crlf sends more bytes than the size declared to the server (same class curl refused for IMAP CVE-2026-87864 and RTSP)
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

curl recently started REFUSING uploads that combine a size-declaring protocol with CRLF
conversion, because the LF->CRLF expansion makes the number of bytes actually sent differ
from the size declared to the server:

- IMAP APPEND — CVE-2026-87864, `lib/imap.c:885-886`:
  `if(data->set.crlf) failf(data, "Cannot APPEND with CRLF conversion making size unknown");`
- RTSP — commit e84f95a, `lib/rtsp.c:235-236`:
  `if(data->set.crlf) { failf(data, "Cannot do CRLF conversions on upload"); ... }`

SCP uploads do exactly the same thing and were not covered. The SCP code declares
`data->state.infilesize` to the server up front, then sends the body through the client
reader stack. When `CURLOPT_CRLF` / `--crlf` is set, the `cr_lc` reader turns every LF into
CRLF, so the body grows past the declared size. The SCP path has no "refuse CRLF conversion"
guard like IMAP/RTSP; it only rejects a negative size.

Exact source lines:

- Size declared to the peer (raw infilesize, not adjusted for CRLF growth):
  `lib/vssh/libssh2.c:2414-2416`
  `    sshc->ssh_channel = libssh2_scp_send64(sshc->ssh_session, sshp->path,`
  `                         (int)data->set.new_file_perms,`
  `                         (libssh2_int64_t)data->state.infilesize, 0, 0);`
  and `lib/vssh/libssh2.c:2438`  `data->req.size = data->state.infilesize;`

- The CRLF-expanding reader is inserted when `data->set.crlf` is set:
  `lib/sendf.c:1131-1149` (`do_init_reader_stack` adds `cr_lc`) and the lazy init in
  `Curl_client_read` (`lib/sendf.c:~1220`). `--crlf` maps to `CURLOPT_CRLF` at
  `src/config2setopts.c:1024`.

- SCP has NO crlf guard: `git grep -c crlf lib/vssh/libssh2.c` returns 0. It only checks
  `infilesize < 0` (`lib/vssh/libssh2.c:2771`). Size-declaring protocols that handle this
  correctly report an unknown length (`Curl_creader_total_length()` returns -1) when crlf is
  on; SCP instead declares the un-expanded size.

## Affected version

master @ 8e3722b7 (8.23.1-DEV), libssh2 backend. (The libssh backend
`lib/vssh/libssh.c:2155` declares the size the same way and should be checked too.)

## Steps To Reproduce

1. Make a local file with LF line endings whose content, after some bytes, contains an SCP
   control sequence, e.g. a NUL byte then:  `C0644 <n> evil\n<data>`
2. Upload it to an SCP server with CRLF conversion on:
   `curl --crlf -T ./payload scp://user@host/dir/goodfile`
3. curl declares size = original byte count but sends the longer CRLF-expanded stream. The
   bytes past the declared size are read by the remote `scp -t` sink as the next SCP protocol
   message.

Control: without `--crlf` the byte count matches the declared size (no issue). The IMAP/RTSP
equivalents are now rejected outright, which is curl's own confirmation that this combination
is unsafe.

The attached `verify.sh` proves the asymmetry against a fresh clone (IMAP and RTSP refuse
crlf uploads; SCP has no such check).

## Honest caveat for triage

Confirming that the overflow bytes actually reach the remote as a new SCP control message
(vs libssh2 truncating the write at the declared size) needs a local sshd capture — happy to
provide on request. The curl-side defect — feeding a stream whose length differs from the
size declared to the peer, with no refusal that the sibling protocols now enforce — is the
point of this report.

## Suggested fix

In the SCP upload path refuse the transfer (or recompute the declared size) when
`data->set.crlf` is set, mirroring the IMAP (`imap.c:885`) and RTSP (`rtsp.c:235`) fixes.

## Impact

## Summary

When an application uploads attacker-influenced content over SCP with CRLF conversion
enabled, the mismatch between the size curl declares to the server and the longer
CRLF-expanded stream it actually sends lets the trailing bytes be interpreted by the remote
SCP sink as a subsequent SCP control message — for example creating an additional file with
an attacker-chosen name, mode, and content under the upload directory.

This is the SCP sibling of the IMAP (CVE-2026-87864) and RTSP (commit e84f95a) upload issues
that curl already fixed by refusing CRLF conversion on size-declaring uploads; the SCP path
was missed.

Low severity: it requires the libssh2 backend, `--crlf` / `CURLOPT_CRLF` to be enabled, and
upload content that an attacker can influence.
