backends that support cached session resumption should be reviewed, but I have
not included them in the confirmed scope.

## Test environment

- Ubuntu 24.04.3 LTS, GCC 13.3.0
- OpenSSL 3.0.13 and GnuTLS 3.8.3
- `curl-8_23_0`: `3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273`
- `curl-8_12_0`: `34cf9d54a46598c44938aa7598820484d7af7133`
- `curl-8_11_1`: `75a2079d5c28debb2eaa848ca9430f1fe0d7844c`

## Root cause

`ssl_peer_key_build()` in `lib/vtls/vtls_scache.c` starts the cache key with:

```c
result = curlx_dyn_addf(&buf, "%s:%d:KEY-V2",
                        peer->origin->hostname, peer->origin->port);
```

It then adds transport, verification settings, TLS versions/options,
trust-store inputs, pins, client-auth fields, and the TLS implementation. It
never adds `peer->origin->scheme` or `peer->origin->scheme->family`.

Consequently, verified FTPS and HTTPS filters with the same host, port, and
TLS configuration construct the same key. `Curl_ssl_scache_take()` returns the
FTPS session to the HTTPS filter. OpenSSL applies it without an application
protocol check. GnuTLS also applies it when the cached ALPN is null, which is
the normal FTPS case.

ALPN does not contain this case. FTPS does not negotiate ALPN, so the cached
session has no ALPN. On resumption, the FTPS endpoint ignores the HTTP ALPN
offer, and curl falls back to HTTP/1.x. The reproducer confirms this behavior
with both OpenSSL and GnuTLS clients.

Before the rewrite, `Curl_ssl_getsessionid()` contained this comparison:

```c
strcasecompare(cf->conn->handler->scheme, check->scheme)
```

The rewrite removed `Curl_ssl_session.scheme` and did not put the scheme into
the replacement `ssl_peer_key`.

Relevant history:

- Prior Low finding: https://curl.se/docs/audit/cure53-curl-report-2016.pdf
- Prior fix: https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/1671d84b38ac61f0852e8ff2915fef3346dc53f7
- Regression commit: https://github.com/curl/curl/commit/fa0ccd9f1fbbbd77bf50b26e3ba231ea6c729474
- Pre-rewrite design discussion listing `scheme` as a cache discriminator:
  https://github.com/curl/curl/discussions/15684

## Attack sequence represented by the reproducer

1. curl starts `ftps://host:P/evil-file` and establishes FTPS control session
   `S` with full certificate verification.
2. The FTPS server advertises a passive data port. The MitM redirects curl's
   first connection to that port back to an FTPS control endpoint and holds it
   open. curl correctly resumes `S` there.
3. curl concurrently starts `https://host:P/good-file` using the same shared
   TLS session cache.
4. The MitM redirects that connection to the real FTPS data port.
5. Because the cache key does not distinguish FTPS from HTTPS, curl presents
   `S`. The data endpoint's session-association check succeeds.
6. The endpoint emits `evil-file`, whose raw bytes form an HTTP/1.1 response.
   curl reports successful HTTPS verification and returns the attacker's body.

The test server compares the TLS 1.2 session IDs. It releases
`ATTACKER-CONTROLLED-CONTENT` only when the HTTPS session ID exactly matches
the FTPS control session ID. It sends the raw HTTP-shaped file immediately
after that check, without interpreting the HTTP request; it only drains the
already-sent request afterward to make socket shutdown deterministic. A
generic malicious HTTPS server cannot satisfy the session-ID condition.

## Minimal reproducer

Attach the `cross-scheme-tls-session` directory and run:

```console
python3 run.py \
  --build /path/to/curl-8.23.0-build \
  --source /path/to/curl-8.23.0
```

Requirements are Python 3, a C compiler, pthreads, the OpenSSL CLI and
development libraries, and a CMake-style shared curl build. `run.py` compiles
`server.c` and `repro.c` in a temporary directory, generates a localhost
certificate, starts the server, and runs the client. It links the absolute
`libcurl.so` path from `--build` and fails if that library is absent.

The certificate is explicitly trusted with `CURLOPT_CAINFO`; neither
`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER` nor `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYHOST` is disabled. The client
uses the documented `CURL_LOCK_DATA_SSL_SESSION` share option and documented
lock callbacks.

Expected vulnerable output (abridged):

```text
ftps_result=0 (No error)
https_result=0 (No error)
https_verify_result=0
https_body=ATTACKER-CONTROLLED-CONTENT
attack_content_accepted=1
FTPS_FAKE_DATA_REUSED=1
FTPS_FAKE_DATA_MATCHES_CONTROL=1
HTTPS_CROSS_SCHEME_REUSED=1
HTTPS_SESSION_MATCHES_FTPS_CONTROL=1
ATTACK_RELEASED=1
client_exit=0
server_exit=0
```

I obtained this result in 10/10 consecutive runs against the `curl-8_23_0`
tag built in Release mode with OpenSSL.

This is a state-separation flaw rather than memory corruption, so an ASan
trace is not applicable. The equivalent direct evidence is the server-side
comparison of the TLS session IDs, together with the version and patch
controls below.

## Controls

### Pre-regression control

Running the same harness against curl 8.11.1 with `--expect-blocked` produces:

```text
ftps_result=0 (No error)
https_result=52 (Server returned nothing (no headers, no data))
attack_content_accepted=0
FTPS_FAKE_DATA_MATCHES_CONTROL=1
HTTPS_CROSS_SCHEME_REUSED=0
HTTPS_SESSION_MATCHES_FTPS_CONTROL=0
ATTACK_RELEASED=0
```

### Patched control

`fix.patch` adds the origin scheme to the peer key and a unit test. After
applying it and rebuilding:

```console
python3 run.py --expect-blocked \
  --build /path/to/patched-build \
  --source /path/to/patched-source
```

The patched current tree produces the same blocked outcome as 8.11.1. The
existing FTPS control-to-data reuse continues to work:

```text
FTPS_FAKE_DATA_REUSED=1
FTPS_FAKE_DATA_MATCHES_CONTROL=1
```

The proposed unit test (`unit3304`) also passes.

## Suggested fix

Restore scheme separation in `ssl_peer_key_build()`, for example:

```c
result = cf_ssl_peer_key_add_string(&buf, "SCHEME",
                                    peer->origin->scheme->name);
if(result)
  goto out;
```

The attached `fix.patch` contains this change and a regression test. If curl
wants to preserve session reuse between secure and STARTTLS variants of the
same application protocol, keying by `peer->origin->scheme->family` instead
would also stop the demonstrated FTP-to-HTTP crossing. Exact scheme matching
restores the invariant enforced from 2016 through 8.11.1.

## Suggested classification

- Severity: Low
- Impact: HTTPS response integrity violation under a constrained active-MitM
  scenario
- Possible CWE: CWE-345 (Insufficient Verification of Data Authenticity) or
  CWE-488 (Exposure of Data Element to Wrong Session)

## Impact

## Impact and attack prerequisites

The impact is substitution of attacker-chosen bytes for an HTTPS response
without disabling certificate or hostname verification.

The demonstrated attack requires all of the following:

1. The application lets the attacker cause an FTPS transfer and an HTTPS
   transfer to the same hostname and numeric port.
2. The two easy handles share a TLS session cache. This is a documented
   libcurl configuration; easy handles in one multi handle also share this
   cache by default.
3. The attacker has an active MitM position and can redirect TCP connections,
   but cannot forge certificates or decrypt TLS.
4. An FTPS service for that hostname uses TLS session reuse to associate its
   control and data connections.
5. The attacker can select or supply the downloaded FTP file. Its bytes begin
   with a syntactically valid HTTP response, which is necessary because modern
   curl rejects HTTP/0.9 by default.
6. The demonstrated path uses TLS 1.2 and requires concurrent transfers.

These constraints make Low appropriate. They do not eliminate the security
boundary: without the cross-scheme session reuse, the FTPS data endpoint
rejects the redirected HTTPS connection and releases no file.

title: CVE-2026-111953: GnuTLS SecTrust OCSP staple bypass
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
When curl is built with GnuTLS and Apple SecTrust, as MacPorts does for `curl +gnutls +sectrust`, a failed GnuTLS verification is handed to SecTrust, and if SecTrust accepts the chain the GnuTLS result is dropped (lib/vtls/gtls.c:1511-1521 in 8.23.0). SecTrust is called without the stapled OCSP response, so when GnuTLS failed because of the staple (revoked, bad signature, out of date), nothing looks at the staple again: 8.23.0 only checks that one was sent (gtls.c:1436-1451), and master reads the status code but assumes GnuTLS has already verified the signature and the time (gtls.c:1479-1483). As a result --cert-status accepts a correctly signed "revoked" staple on 8.23.0, and a staple with a forged signature or an expired one on 8.23.0 and on current master. The clearest way to see it, on 8.23.0 with a revoked staple: `curl --cacert root.pem --cert-status URL` fails with (60), the same command with `--ca-native` added returns HTTP 200, and so do default options, because SecTrust builds use the native store unless a CA file is given (lib/vtls/vtls_config.c:287-288). This is a separate code path from my report #4118610 (OpenSSL with SecTrust, CVE-2026-111484): its fix cd89b5178b passes `NULL, 0, FALSE` here on purpose ("We check OCSP separately"), and the GnuTLS fix 287df0b324 only added the status code check.

## Affected version
8.23.0 accepts revoked, forged and stale staples; master 629646d9b7 accepts forged and stale ones. 8.20.0 accepts forged and stale staples too (tested), and 8.18.0 to 8.20.x have the same code here. The fallback came with eefd03c572 (8.17.0), where it only ran for GNUTLS_CERT_SIGNER_NOT_FOUND, that is for roots GnuTLS does not have; 6aa8fa3fdf (8.18.0, "Do the same for GnuTLS") made it run for every GnuTLS failure, including failures caused by the staple. 8.22.0 rejected every intermediate-signed staple in my tests, good ones included, because of the be6c4ee7fa signature check that 8.21.0 also has (see curl PR 23311). That commit also reasoned that a bad staple cannot pass with peer verification on, because gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2() catches it; this fallback is the case that reasoning did not cover.

MacPorts builds `curl +gnutls +sectrust` with `--with-gnutls --with-ca-bundle=... --with-apple-sectrust`. The variant has existed since at least its 8.19.0 port (and +http3 requires +gnutls); the current 8.22.0 port is in the fail-closed window, 8.19.0 and 8.20.0 were affected, and 8.23.0 will be once the port is updated.

Tested on macOS 27.0.1 arm64, Homebrew GnuTLS 3.8.13, curl built from the curl-8_23_0, curl-8_22_0 and curl-8_20_0 tags and from master with `-DCURL_USE_GNUTLS=ON -DUSE_APPLE_SECTRUST=ON`, without a CA bundle, and for 8.23.0 and master also with one (MacPorts-style):

```
curl 8.23.0-DEV (Darwin) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV GnuTLS/3.8.13 zlib/1.2.12
curl 8.23.1-DEV (Darwin) libcurl/8.23.1-DEV GnuTLS/3.8.13 zlib/1.2.12   (master 629646d9b7)
Features: alt-svc AppleSecTrust AsynchDNS HSTS HTTPS-proxy IPv6 Largefile libz SSL threadsafe UnixSockets
```

## Steps To Reproduce:
All on 127.0.0.1, scripts in the attached zip under poc/ (same PKI generator as #4118610).

1. Build curl 8.23.0 or master with `-DCURL_USE_GNUTLS=ON -DUSE_APPLE_SECTRUST=ON`.
2. `python3 poc/mkpki2.py poc/pki2` creates root, intermediate and server "localhost", staples signed by the intermediate (good, unknown, revoked), one with a forged signature and a stale one.
3. `security add-trusted-cert -r trustRoot -k ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db poc/pki2/root.pem`
4. `openssl s_server -accept 127.0.0.1:23003 -cert poc/pki2/server.pem -key poc/pki2/server.key -cert_chain poc/pki2/chain.pem -status_file poc/pki2/ocsp-revoked.der -tls1_3 -www`
5. `curl --cacert poc/pki2/root.pem --cert-status https://localhost:23003/` fails with (60): GnuTLS rejects the revoked staple (verify status 34, INVALID and REVOKED).
6. `curl -v --cacert poc/pki2/root.pem --ca-native --cert-status https://localhost:23003/` logs "SSL certificate verified via Apple SecTrust." and returns HTTP 200 on 8.23.0. `curl --cert-status https://localhost:23003/` with default options returns 200 as well.
7. Restart the server with `ocsp-forged-good.der` or `ocsp-stale-good.der` and repeat 5 and 6: (60) for GnuTLS alone, 200 with SecTrust, on 8.23.0 and on master.
8. Clean up: `security delete-certificate -c "Verify Test Root CA" ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db`

poc/matrix.sh runs every staple. Keychain trust, no hooks of any kind, TLS 1.3 (TLS 1.2 gives the same). "GnuTLS alone" is `--cacert root.pem --cert-status`; "with SecTrust" is the same command plus `--ca-native`, or default options. Both give the results below, and default options give the same with a CA bundle compiled in (MacPorts-style):

| stapled response | 8.23.0 GnuTLS alone | 8.23.0 with SecTrust | master GnuTLS alone | master with SecTrust |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| none | (91) | (91) | (91) | (91) |
| good | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 |
| revoked | (60) | **200** | (60) | (91) |
| forged signature | (60) | **200** | (60) | **200** |
| stale | (60) | **200** | (60) | **200** |

The "unknown" staple is left out: 8.23.0 accepts it even with GnuTLS alone, which is the separate issue fixed by 287df0b324. Raw output: 01-keychain-trust-no-interposer.txt (every mode, with and without a CA bundle, TLS 1.3 and 1.2), 02-verbose-traces.txt (the pair above with -v, and `openssl ocsp` checks of each staple), 04-older-releases.txt (8.20.0 and 8.22.0).

## Fix
Hand the stapled response to SecTrust on this path and require a positive answer when verifystatus is set, as cd89b5178b does for OpenSSL. With that change on master (fix/gtls-sectrust-ocsp-fix.diff, 03-fix-check.txt) only the good staples pass, with default options and with --cacert plus --ca-native, on TLS 1.2 and 1.3, and nothing changes without --cert-status. Another option is to not let the fallback override a failure where GnuTLS set GNUTLS_CERT_REVOKED, GNUTLS_CERT_INVALID_OCSP_STATUS or GNUTLS_CERT_REVOCATION_DATA_SUPERSEDED; GnuTLS sets them even when it does not know the root (verify status 98, 1048642 and 4162 in 03-fix-check.txt).

AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant (Claude) for code review, test setup and drafting. I reproduced every result myself on curl built from the curl-8_23_0, curl-8_22_0 and curl-8_20_0 tags and from master; the attached logs are the raw output.

## Impact

--cert-status is documented to make the transfer fail when the stapled response is invalid or does not confirm the certificate. On GnuTLS builds with Apple SecTrust the staple stops being checked exactly when GnuTLS finds it bad, and this happens with default options. An attacker who holds the key of a revoked certificate and can intercept the connection passes --cert-status on 8.23.0 by stapling the CA's own current "revoked" response, and on 8.18.0 to 8.20.x and current master with an old or self-made "good" one, which is the attack OCSP stapling enforcement exists to stop. The conditions match CVE-2026-7009 and CVE-2026-111484 (both Medium) with GnuTLS in place of OpenSSL, in a configuration MacPorts ships as `curl +gnutls +sectrust`. libcurl applications that set CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS on such builds are affected the same way.

title: CVE-2026-111954: upload reader failed redirect UAF
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
Curl_req_hard_reset() (lib/request.c line 124 in curl-8_23_0) calls Curl_client_reset() while req->rewind_read may still be set, which keeps the client reader stack for a rewind (lib/sendf.c line 82), and only clears the flag at line 157, so the kept stack is never rewound or freed and is still installed when the next transfer on the same easy handle starts, since the hard reset runs at the start of every Curl_connect(). The flag is left set by http_perhapsrewind() when a server answers a request with a body with a redirect that then fails before Curl_http_follow() reaches its soft reset, for example a 307 with "Location: http://[::1" (CURLE_URL_MALFORMAT) or a 307 with a header line that has no colon (CURLE_WEIRD_SERVER_REPLY), both with CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION. The next upload on that handle over ftp, ftps, sftp, scp, file or tftp does not install a reader of its own and reads through Curl_client_read() with the old stack (file.c line 369, ftp.c line 561), so when the application has replaced the postfields in between, which frees libcurl's own COPYPOSTFIELDS copy (setopt.c line 2026), cr_buf_read() memcpy()s 65536 bytes per read from freed memory (sendf.c line 1334) and sends them to the upload destination. Reproduced on curl-8_23_0 built with ASAN: heap-use-after-free READ of size 65536 in cr_buf_read from file_do and from Curl_req_send_more (ftp), freed by curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS) and allocated by curl_easy_setopt(CURLOPT_COPYPOSTFIELDS); the plain debug build crashes with SIGSEGV in the same memcpy with a 1 MB body since glibc unmaps that chunk, and with a 100 KB body the read is silent and transfer 2 reports success. The ordering came with a93113b5b4 (8.16.0), master is unchanged, and calling curl_easy_reset() between the transfers avoids it. A six line fix in Curl_pretransfer() that drops a pending rewind at the start of a new transfer makes the reproduction clean and leaves the test suite unchanged (patch attached); AI tooling helped me with  the test programs, the reproduction and the numbers are mine.

## Affected version
curl 8.23.0 built from the curl-8_23_0 tag (3163ec0656), Linux x86_64, OpenSSL 3.6.4, clang with -fsanitize=address, and a plain gcc --enable-debug build. By the commit it is 8.16.0 through 8.23.0. curl -V: curl 8.23.0-DEV (x86_64-pc-linux-gnu) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.3.2 brotli/1.2.0 zstd/1.5.7 libidn2/2.3.8 libpsl/0.23.3 nghttp2/1.70.0 OpenLDAP/2.6.14

## Steps To Reproduce:
1. python3 http_307bad.py 8900 (attached: reads the request head and one body byte, answers "307" + "Location: http://[::1" + "Content-Length: 0", closes). For the second trigger run it with --badheader --location /ok.
2. Build reader_reuse.c (attached) against the ASAN libcurl. It uses one easy handle: a POST with CURLOPT_COPYPOSTFIELDS (BODY bytes) and CURLOPT_FOLLOWLOCATION, then without curl_easy_reset() it sets CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS to NULL, CURLOPT_UPLOAD, CURLOPT_READDATA to a FILE* and a second URL.
3. BODY=1000000 ./reader_reuse http://127.0.0.1:8900/post file:///tmp/out -> transfer 1 returns 3, then ASAN reports heap-use-after-free READ of size 65536 in cr_buf_read (sendf.c:1334) called from file_do (file.c:369), freed by setopt.c:2026, allocated by setopt.c:1811.
4. Same with ftp://127.0.0.1:PORT/x as the second URL against any FTP server that accepts STOR: the same report, now from Curl_req_send_more (request.c:468); on the non ASAN debug build the process dies with SIGSEGV in memcpy from cr_buf_read.
5. BODY=100000 (under the mmap threshold): no crash, transfer 2 returns 0 and the destination gets bytes from the freed buffer instead of the READDATA content.
6. Control: add --reset (curl_easy_reset between the transfers): transfer 2 uses the READDATA file as expected.
7. Apply fix-pretransfer-drop-stale-readers.patch, rebuild, repeat 3 and 4: clean, the real READDATA content is uploaded.

## Impact

## Summary:
A server that answers a redirect in a way curl cannot follow leaves libcurl with a reader stack that belongs to the previous request body, and the next upload on the same handle over one of the protocols that use the generic reader reads 64 KB blocks from memory libcurl already freed and sends them to wherever that upload goes, a remote FTP, SFTP or TFTP server included, or into a local file. The application only has to reuse its easy handle for more than one transfer, which is the documented and recommended way to use libcurl, replace the postfields, and not call curl_easy_reset() in between; the curl tool creates a new handle per transfer and is not affected, language bindings that keep one handle per object are. With a larger body the same read crashes the application.

title: CVE-2026-115529: Schannel TLS auto client session resumption
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:

In curl 8.23.0 with Schannel, TLS session resumption preserves an authenticated client certificate identity across a cross-origin redirect even after automatic client certificate selection is disabled.

This appears to be an incomplete fix for [CVE-2026-86415](https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2026-86415.html), where the original fix addressed authenticated connection reuse but did not prevent the same authentication state from being retained through TLS session resumption.

## Affected version
Reproduced with libcurl 8.23.0-DEV (Schannel) on a Windows Server 2022 GitHub Actions runner, using TLS 1.2.

## Steps To Reproduce:
1. Establish an mTLS connection to a localhost HTTPS server using `CURLSSLOPT_AUTO_CLIENT_CERT` and an ephemeral client certificate.
2. Close the physical connection while retaining the libcurl TLS session cache, then reuse the same easy handle to follow an HTTP redirect back to the HTTPS server.
3. With session caching enabled, the redirected connection resumes the authenticated TLS session over a new TCP connection, and the server reports the original client certificate identity in both TLS ticket and session-ID modes.
4. With session caching disabled, the redirected TLS handshake fails because no client certificate is provided.

## Impact

An application following an attacker-influenced redirect could unintentionally access an mTLS-protected endpoint under a previously authenticated client identity, potentially bypassing the intended redirect authentication boundary.

title: server filename with control characters printed to terminal (`-J`)

weakness.name: Improper Neutralization of Escape, Meta, or Control Sequences

vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
With `-OJ`, curl takes the filename from the server's `Content-Disposition` header. `parse_filename()` in `src/tool_cb_hdr.c` does not remove control characters such as ESC (0x1b). When a warning prints that name, the escape sequences reach the terminal.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Build curl from the source tree (`cmake` + `make -j8 curl`). The binary is `build/src/curl`.

2. Save as `srv.py` and run `python3 -I srv.py`:

   ```python
   import http.server

   class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
       def do_GET(self):
           self.send_response(200)
           self.send_header('Content-Disposition',
               'attachment; filename="ok\x1b[2J\x1b[31mPWNED.txt"'
               .encode('latin-1', 'replace').decode('latin-1'))
           self.send_header('Content-Length', '4')
           self.end_headers()
           self.wfile.write(b'data')

       def log_message(self, *a):
           pass

   http.server.HTTPServer(('127.0.0.1', 8765), H).serve_forever()
   ```

3. First download creates the file:

   ```
   mkdir t && cd t
   /path/to/build/src/curl -OJ http://127.0.0.1:8765/
   ```

4. Second download triggers the warning:

   ```
   /path/to/build/src/curl -OJ http://127.0.0.1:8765/ 2>&1 | cat -v
   ```

   Expected output includes:

   ```
   Warning: Failed to open the file ok^[[2J^[[31mPWNED.txt: File exists
   ```

   `^[` is the raw ESC byte.

## Root cause

1. **`parse_filename()` does not remove control characters.** In `src/tool_cb_hdr.c` (about lines 150–213), the function takes the name from `Content-Disposition` and:
   - strips quotes and anything after the closing quote,
   - keeps only the part after the last `/` or `\` (this blocks path traversal),
   - removes `\r` and `\n`.

   It does not remove other control characters, so ESC (0x1b), other bytes below 0x20, and 0x7f pass through. The Windows-only sanitizer (`sanitize_file_name`) would catch them, but it runs only under `_WIN32` or `MSDOS`, so on Linux and macOS the name is used as-is.

2. **`voutf()` writes its output without escaping.** In `src/tool_msgs.c`, `voutf()` sends the formatted message to stderr with `fputs` and does not check for non-printable bytes. When the warning `Failed to open the file %s` includes the server's name, the escape sequences reach the terminal.

The warning comes from `tool_create_output_file()` in `src/tool_cb_wrt.c`, which opens the file with `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`. The open fails when the name already exists, and the failure message includes the name.

Neither piece is wrong on its own. The bug is that a server-controlled name reaches a terminal-facing output without control characters being removed first.

## Impact

- A malicious server can make the terminal clear the screen, hide earlier output, or change colors.
- No code execution, no memory corruption, no file written outside the current directory, no data exposed.
- Needs `-J` (not the default), and the name must be printed (for example, a file with that name already exists).

title: Derived cookie Path aborts cookie jar loading in curl 8.23.0
Windows SSPI connection-pool probe can reuse a connection under the wrong user
20: HTAB before `Secure` attribute silently drops the Secure cookie flag
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

A `Set-Cookie` header using HTAB (horizontal tab) instead of SPACE before the `Secure` attribute — e.g. `Set-Cookie: sid=SECRET;\tSecure` — causes curl to store the cookie without its Secure flag. The cookie is then sent over plaintext HTTP on subsequent requests to the same host.

The space-separated form `Set-Cookie: sid=SECRET; Secure` works correctly.

## Affected versions

curl 8.13.0 through at least 8.21.0 (all versions containing commit `1aea05a6c26`, "cookie: convert to using strparse", 2025-02-18).

## Root cause

In `lib/cookie.c`, `parse_cookie_header()` uses a do/while loop that parses each cookie attribute:

```c
do {
    if(!curlx_str_cspn(&ptr, &name, ";\t\r\n=")) {
        // parse attribute
    }
} while(!curlx_str_single(&ptr, ';'));
```

After consuming the `;` separator, `ptr` points at the HTAB. Since `\t` is in the reject set of `curlx_str_cspn`, the function sees it as the first character, returns an empty match (failure), and the `if` block is skipped. Then `curlx_str_single(&ptr, ';')` fails because the current byte is `\t`, not `;`, so the loop exits. The `Secure` attribute is never parsed, but the cookie is still stored.

The previous parser (before `1aea05a6c26`) had `while(ISBLANK(*ptr)) ptr++;` before parsing each attribute, which correctly skipped HTAB. This blank-skipping was lost in the strparse conversion. The helper `curlx_str_passblanks()` exists in the codebase but is not called here.

## Reproduction

### Expected vs actual output

**Expected:** Neither cookie is sent over HTTP (both have `Secure`).

**Actual:**

```
HTAB  HTTP follow-up: sid=HTAB_SECRET      <-- leaked over HTTP
SPACE HTTP follow-up: <none>               <-- correctly withheld
HTAB  jar secure flag: FALSE               <-- wrong
SPACE jar secure flag: TRUE                <-- correct
```

## Impact

The `Secure` flag is a confidentiality boundary that prevents cookies from being sent over unencrypted connections. Silently dropping it means a session cookie intended to be HTTPS-only is exposed on any subsequent HTTP request to the same host. A network attacker observing that HTTP traffic can capture the cookie. All attributes at or after the HTAB position are similarly skipped (e.g. `HttpOnly`).

HTAB is valid optional whitespace per both RFC 6265 section 5.2 and the HTTP grammar (OWS). The old parser handled it correctly.

title: 14: HSTS cache import silently drops a longer-lived child beneath an includeSubDomains parent
vulnerability_information:
# HSTS cache import silently drops a longer-lived child beneath an includeSubDomains parent

## Summary

Loading an HSTS cache (file or `CURLOPT_HSTSREADFUNCTION` callback) can silently discard a child entry. When a live `includeSubDomains` parent is imported before a longer-lived `includeSubDomains` child, only the parent is retained. After the parent expires, the child's independently valid HSTS policy is gone and curl sends a plaintext HTTP request instead of upgrading to HTTPS. This violates the independent-policy model required by RFC 6797 §5.3.

## Affected versions

The file-load path regressed in commit `a94973805df96269bf3f3bf0a20ccb9887313316` (CVE-2024-9681 fix), first released in curl 8.11.0. The callback-load path inherited the same logic in commit `e65ba1bd349a7affb09275a442b6a0837df079d9`, released in curl 8.20.0. Verified at `c2676bf9e639e31e44b12a2cc82cf2046231b056`.

## Root cause

`hsts_add_host_expire()` in `lib/hsts.c` calls `hsts_check(h, host, hostlen, subdomain)` with `subdomain=TRUE` at line 464. `hsts_check()` performs hierarchical matching: if the parent `.example.test` is already loaded with `includeSubDomains`, it returns the parent as a match for `child.example.test`. The caller creates an entry only when no match exists, and its update branch runs only when the returned hostname exactly matches the imported hostname. An ancestor match therefore causes neither an update nor a creation — the child is silently dropped.

Network-learned `Strict-Transport-Security` processing does not have this problem because `Curl_hsts_parse()` uses exact-only lookup (`hsts_check(..., FALSE)`) at line 296.

## Security impact

When curl rewrites its HSTS cache after loading, the child entry is gone. After the parent expires, a request to `http://child.example.test` is no longer upgraded to HTTPS. An active network attacker can observe or modify traffic that should have been protected by HSTS.

The prerequisites limit practical severity: HSTS must be enabled; both entries must use `includeSubDomains`; the parent must be loaded first while still live; the child must outlive it; and the collapsed state must persist until after the parent expires. Reloading from an intact original source after parent expiry restores the child.

## Reproduction

1. Build an affected curl release, starting with 8.11.0, with HSTS support enabled.
2. Choose a parent hostname and one of its child hostnames, such as `example.test` and `child.example.test`.
3. Create an HSTS cache file containing two live entries. Place the parent first, mark both entries as `includeSubDomains`, and give the child a later expiration time than the parent.
4. Preserve an unchanged copy of this original cache for use as a control.
5. Make curl load the test cache and complete an unrelated HTTP transfer that does not return a `Strict-Transport-Security` header. This causes curl to rewrite the loaded cache without learning replacement HSTS state for either test hostname.
6. Inspect the rewritten cache. On an affected build, only the parent entry remains; the independently valid child entry has been silently discarded.
7. As an ordering control, repeat the import with the child listed before the parent. Confirm that both entries remain in the rewritten cache.
8. As a matching control, repeat the parent-first import with the child configured as an exact-host policy rather than `includeSubDomains`. Confirm that both entries remain.
9. Wait until the parent policy has expired while the child's original expiration time is still in the future. A debug build with a controlled clock may be used instead of waiting.
10. Start a plaintext HTTP server and map the child test hostname to that server.
11. Request an `http://` URL on the child hostname while using the collapsed, rewritten cache.
12. Observe the vulnerable result: curl retains the HTTP scheme and sends the request to the plaintext server because the parent has expired and the child policy was lost.
13. Repeat the same request using the preserved original cache in which the child entry is still present.
14. Observe the expected control result: curl upgrades the URL to HTTPS. If the test endpoint supports only plaintext HTTP, the TLS handshake fails instead of transmitting an HTTP request.
15. Confirm a fix by changing HSTS import deduplication to use exact-host matching while retaining hierarchical matching only for policy application. Repeat the parent-first test and verify that both entries persist and the later child request is upgraded to HTTPS.

### Expected result

Parent and child HSTS policies must be stored independently. Import order must not remove a child's longer-lived policy, and the child must continue to force HTTPS after the parent expires.

### Vulnerable result

The importer mistakes the already-loaded parent for a duplicate of the child and drops the child entry. Once the parent expires, curl sends a request to the child over plaintext HTTP.


## Suggested fix

Use exact-host lookup for import deduplication, as `Curl_hsts_parse()` already does for network-learned policies. Replace the `hsts_check()` call at line 464 with `subdomain=FALSE`:

```diff
-    e = hsts_check(h, host, hostlen, subdomain);
+    e = hsts_check(h, host, hostlen, FALSE);
```

This reserves hierarchical matching for deciding whether HSTS applies to a request, while import deduplication only matches on exact hostname.

## Impact

## Summary:
After the incorrectly retained parent HSTS policy expires, curl may send a child-domain request over plaintext HTTP even though the child’s own policy remains valid. An active network attacker can intercept or modify that request, potentially exposing credentials, authorization headers, request bodies, and response data that should have been protected by HTTPS.

title: FTP authentication options leak to a cross-origin FTP redirect with unrestricted auth disabled
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

libcurl 8.22.0 sends values configured with `CURLOPT_FTP_ACCOUNT` and `CURLOPT_FTP_ALTERNATIVE_TO_USER` to a different origin reached through an HTTP-to-FTP redirect even when unrestricted authentication is disabled. I reproduced this after a successful legitimate FTP download by reusing the same easy handle, which matches libcurl's documented handle-reuse and sticky-option behavior. The later HTTP response redirects from `http://localhost:<port>` to an attacker-controlled `ftp://127.0.0.1:<other-port>`, changing hostname, scheme, and port. Although `CURLOPT_UNRESTRICTED_AUTH` is explicitly `0L`, the new FTP origin receives the retained account value or alternative authentication command. Disabling redirect following or clearing the affected option before the HTTP transfer prevents disclosure. This affects libcurl applications; the curl command-line tool does not set these FTP-only options for this initial-HTTP flow.

## Affected version

Official curl/libcurl 8.22.0 release source, built locally on macOS with AddressSanitizer and UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer. The main test build reported:

```text
libcurl/8.22.0 OpenSSL/3.6.3 zlib/1.2.12 libidn2/2.3.8 nghttp2/1.68.1 OpenLDAP/2.4.28/Apple
```

The full result also reproduced on a separately configured 8.22.0 build with libpsl 0.21.5.

## Source location

- `lib/ftp.c:2957-2974` reads `STRING_FTP_ACCOUNT` after reply 332 and sends `ACCT <value>` without an origin check.
- `lib/ftp.c:2975-2994` reads `STRING_FTP_ALTERNATIVE_TO_USER` after failed USER/PASS authentication and sends it without an origin check.
- `lib/vauth/vauth.c:137-149` contains the existing initial-origin gate used for authentication, cookies, and other sensitive data.
- `lib/protocol.h:70-72` includes FTP and FTPS in the default redirect protocol set.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Build the official curl 8.22.0 release with HTTP and FTP support.
2. Compile the attached client against that build, for example:

   ```text
   cc -o ftp-auth-sticky-reuse-client ftp_auth_sticky_reuse_client.c $(/path/to/curl-8.22.0/bin/curl-config --cflags --libs)
   ```

3. Run the attached loopback-only probe:

   ```text
   python3 ftp_auth_sticky_reuse_probe.py ./ftp-auth-sticky-reuse-client
   ```

4. The probe first completes an authenticated FTP download, then reuses the same handle for HTTP and compares redirect-following, no-follow, and explicit-option-clear cases for both affected options.
5. The expected summaries are:

   ```text
   summary mode=account sticky_first_success=1 sticky_redirect_auth=1 nofollow_redirect_auth=0 cleared_redirect_auth=0 expected=1
   summary mode=alternative sticky_first_success=1 sticky_redirect_auth=1 nofollow_redirect_auth=0 cleared_redirect_auth=0 expected=1
   ```

The first FTP transfer returns `CURLE_OK` in every case. In the sticky-follow cases the redirected FTP peer receives `ACCT <SYNTHETIC_ACCOUNT_MARKER>` or `<SYNTHETIC_ALTERNATIVE_AUTH_COMMAND>`; the controls do not disclose either value. All traffic is loopback-only and all authentication-like values are synthetic.

## Expected result

FTP authentication values retained on a reused handle should not be sent after a redirect changes hostname, scheme, and port unless the caller explicitly enables unrestricted authentication.

## AI-use disclosure

AI assistance was used for source analysis and local test generation. I checked the claims against the curl 8.22.0 production source, reproduced both option paths on two independent sanitizer-enabled builds, and reviewed public curl issues and advisories for duplicates.

## Impact

An attacker who controls an HTTP response consumed by an affected libcurl application can redirect a reused easy handle to an attacker-operated FTP server and obtain FTP authentication material retained from an earlier legitimate FTP transfer. The attacker does not need access to the legitimate FTP server or to complete authentication at the redirected server. Depending on the application, the disclosed value can be an account or tenant identifier, token, or server-specific authentication command. I rate this Low because exploitation requires one of two specialized FTP options, cross-protocol handle reuse without clearing it, an attacker-influenced HTTP response, and a followed FTP redirect.

title: OpenSSL provider OSSL_LIB_CTX used after free via the connection shutdown list (CVE-2026-80229 fix incomplete)
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
The CVE-2026-80229 fix (7ea37abc6a, 8.22.0) only marks provider connections connclose(), but a closed TLS connection is handed to the multi handle's shutdown list (lib/conncache.c:242) and outlives its easy handle, while curl_easy_cleanup() frees the handle's OSSL_LIB_CTX (ossl_provider_cleanup(), lib/vtls/openssl.c:1747, via Curl_close() at lib/url.c:244) that the connection's SSL_CTX was created from (SSL_CTX_new_ex(), openssl.c:3748). When the shutdown list later reads from or destroys that connection, OpenSSL uses the freed context: SSL_read() handling a NewSessionTicket or KeyUpdate fetches algorithms through it, and SSL_CTX_free() in Curl_cshutdn_terminate() runs the provider teardown, which takes a lock stored inside it (a write lock with OpenSSL 3.6, a read lock with 3.0). With OpenSSL's shipped legacy provider, `curl -Z --engine legacy URL1 URL2` segfaults on every run in plain release builds of 8.23.0 on macOS and on Debian 12 (stock OpenSSL 3.0.22) and in Homebrew's 8.22.0 release, against a server that does nothing unusual, while the same command without --engine, or with a single URL, exits 0. Under AddressSanitizer the freed object is the OSSL_LIB_CTX allocated by ossl_set_provider() (openssl.c:1786) and freed by curl_easy_cleanup(), and both later accesses fault on the free-fill pattern. This is not the CVE-2026-80229 scenario, which needed a second easy handle to reuse the pooled connection: no reuse happens here, and the freed context is reached through the shutdown list that the 80229 fix now sends every provider connection to, in 8.22.0 and later, which that advisory lists as not affected.

## Affected version
8.22.0 through 8.23.0 and master (780405b584). Tested on release builds of the curl-8_23_0 tag on macOS 27.0.1 (OpenSSL 3.6.4) and Debian 12 (OpenSSL 3.0.22, in the official debian:bookworm image), an AddressSanitizer build of the same tag, and the Homebrew 8.22.0 release:

```
curl 8.23.0-DEV (Darwin) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.2.12
curl 8.23.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.22
curl 8.22.0 (aarch64-apple-darwin25.6.0) libcurl/8.22.0 OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.2.12 brotli/1.2.0 zstd/1.5.7 AppleIDN libpsl/0.23.3 libssh2/1.11.1 nghttp2/1.70.0 ngtcp2/1.25.0 nghttp3/1.18.0 mit-krb5/1.7-prerelease OpenLDAP/2.4.28/Apple
```

## Steps To Reproduce:
All on 127.0.0.1, sources in the attached zip under poc/.

1. `openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -nodes -days 7 -subj /CN=localhost -addext subjectAltName=DNS:localhost -keyout server.key -out server.crt`
2. `cc poc/tls_ku_server.c -lssl -lcrypto -o tls_ku_server` (a minimal OpenSSL TLS 1.3 HTTPS server that answers one request per connection)
3. `./tls_ku_server 22002 none 300 0 &`
4. `curl -Z --engine legacy --cacert server.crt https://localhost:22002/a https://localhost:22002/slow` ends with `Segmentation fault`, exit 139.
5. Controls: the same command without `--engine legacy`, or with only the first URL, exits 0.

Release-build backtrace, macOS (lldb); the Debian gdb trace in 04-linux-debian-bookworm.txt has the same curl frames:

```
EXC_BAD_ACCESS  pthread_rwlock_wrlock
  CRYPTO_THREAD_write_lock
  ossl_provider_deregister_child_cb
  OSSL_LIB_CTX_free
  legacy_teardown            (legacy.dylib)
  ossl_provider_free
  evp_cipher_free_int
  SSL_CTX_free
  ossl_close                 (curl)
  ssl_cf_destroy
  Curl_conn_cf_discard_all
  Curl_cshutdn_terminate
  cshutdn_perform
  curl_multi_perform
```

With `./tls_ku_server 22002 nst 300 0` (one NewSessionTicket 300 ms after the response) the fault moves to SSL_read() -> tls_process_new_session_ticket() -> evp_generic_fetch() in the shutdown read. The libcurl version (poc/poc_provider_shutdown.c, `PROV=legacy ./poc multi2 https://localhost:22002/`) does the usual remove and cleanup of the easy handle on CURLMSG_DONE and keeps driving the multi handle; calling curl_multi_cleanup() right after that crashes the same way. Scope: the multi interface, which includes curl -Z; the plain easy interface (curl_easy_perform() then curl_easy_cleanup()) does not reach it. Raw output: 01-release-curl-cli-segfault.txt, 02-release-backtrace.txt, 03-asan-freed-by-and-use.txt, 04-linux-debian-bookworm.txt (with gdb backtrace).

## Fix
Make the OSSL_LIB_CTX outlive every SSL_CTX and SSL created from it, for example by reference counting it and letting each connection hold a reference until its TLS filter is destroyed, or by tying it to the multi handle instead of the easy handle.

AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant (Claude) for code review, test setup and drafting. I reproduced every result myself on curl built from the curl-8_23_0 tag (macOS, and Debian 12 in Docker) and on the Homebrew 8.22.0 release; the attached logs are the raw output.

## Impact

A libcurl application that uses an OpenSSL 3 provider through CURLOPT_SSLENGINE with the multi interface, and the curl tool with --engine and -Z, uses freed memory every time a provider-backed connection is closed after its easy handle was cleaned up, which the CVE-2026-80229 fix makes every such connection. The freed context is reused by the allocator, and libcrypto reads it and takes a lock through a pointer stored in it (a write lock with OpenSSL 3.6) on the way to updating the provider bookkeeping it holds, so this is a use-after-free in live code paths rather than a plain crash. A TLS server can additionally drive the read path at a moment it chooses by sending a NewSessionTicket or KeyUpdate while curl waits for close_notify. Providers are how OpenSSL 3 exposes hardware keys (pkcs11, tpm2) and legacy algorithms, which is the documented purpose of CURLOPT_SSLENGINE on OpenSSL 3.

title: A disabled account's API key still works on BMO's Mojolicious /rest/ routes, including for security-group bugs filed after the disable

summaries.author: frida-k
summaries.content:
Mozilla's Bugzilla instance had two authentication implementations with inconsistent account status validation. The legacy REST API (rest.cgi) and web interface correctly refused disabled accounts, but the newer REST routes (/rest/search/*, /rest/component/*) authenticated API keys without checking if the account was still enabled.

The issue was fixed by adding proper account status validation to the REST API authentication flow.

summaries.author: timhaines
summaries.content:
BMO had two authentication paths, and only one of them checked whether an account was still enabled. The legacy stack (`rest.cgi` and the web UI) refused a disabled account. The Mojolicious `bugzilla.login` helper serving the native /rest/ V1 routes never called `is_enabled`.

Disabling an account deleted its login cookies but left its API keys and group memberships in place. So a key minted before the disable kept working on the native routes. Its owner could go on reading security-restricted bugs, including ones filed after the disable, and could still write through `PUT /rest/component`. Setting a component's triage owner or CC list that way handed restricted bugs to a second account that had never been in the security group. An account flagged to change its password, without being disabled, behaved the same way.

The people in that position are anyone whose account was shut off while they still held a key: offboarded staff, a banned user, or someone who closed their own account.

Mozilla fixed it in [mozilla-bteam/bmo#2757](https://github.com/mozilla-bteam/bmo/pull/2757), merged 2026-09-23 and shipped in `release-20260923.1`. The native login path now refuses disabled and password-reset accounts the way the legacy stack does. The affected code is BMO-specific. Upstream `bugzilla/bugzilla` has no Mojolicious login helper and isn't affected.

title: Cross-protocol redirect to imap:// or smtp:// uploads the -F/MIMEPOST form and the custom Authorization/Cookie headers to the redirect target
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
When a transfer that posts a multipart form (CURLOPT_MIMEPOST, the tool's `-F`) follows a redirect to an `imap://` URL, curl APPENDs the whole form to the mailbox on the redirect target and puts the application's CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER list into the mail headers, including custom `Authorization:` and `Cookie:` headers; CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER(3) states that since 7.58.0 and 7.64.0 libcurl "specifically prevents" these two "from being sent to other hosts than the first used one", and lib/http.c:1922-1927 enforces that for HTTP, but imap_perform_append() passes `data->set.headers` to curl_mime_headers() with no such check (lib/imap.c:876 in 8.23.0, :861 in master). It also happens on 301, 302 and 303, where HTTP itself sends no body at all: follow_switch_get() calls http_switch_to_get() for those three codes (http.c:1329, :1351, :1361), which sets `data->state.httpreq = HTTPREQ_GET` (:1171), but IMAP decides to APPEND from `IS_MIME_POST()` (imap.c:2080, :2018), which only tests that a MIME post is *configured* (urldata.h:1142), not what the current request is. The same mismatch means an application that reuses a handle after a MIME post and then sets CURLOPT_HTTPGET for an unrelated request uploads the earlier form, plus its Authorization header, to an IMAP URL that later request is redirected to: CURLOPT_HTTPGET(3) is documented for precisely that, to "get back to using GET" when "a POST, HEAD, PUT, etc has been used previously using the same curl handle", and promises that libcurl then "automatically sets CURLOPT_NOBODY(3) to 0 and CURLOPT_UPLOAD(3) to 0", but it does not clear the MIME post (setopt.c:473-481), so IS_MIME_POST() stays true and an application that followed that documentation still uploads. With the same commands a redirect to `http://` sends a plain GET with no body and neither header on 301/302/303, and on 307 sends the body but still withholds those two headers unless `--location-trusted` (CURLOPT_UNRESTRICTED_AUTH) is given, which is the opt-in the same documentation names; on the IMAP path that option changes nothing either way, because no such check is ever reached. lib/smtp.c has the identical code (:1008-1015, :1797) and leaks the same way once CURLOPT_MAIL_RCPT is set, which the attached run confirms.

## Affected version
Uploading the form on a 301/302/303 GET downgrade exists since IMAP MIME upload arrived in 7.56.0 (ce0881edee); the `Authorization:` leak dates from 7.58.0 and the `Cookie:` leak from 7.64.0, the releases that first withheld each of them cross-host. Up to 8.23.0 and master 59d2537b40 (imap.c:861, :2003, :2065 and urldata.h:1133 there). Both the curl tool and libcurl. Tested on macOS 27.0.1 arm64:
```
curl 8.23.0-DEV libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4   curl-8_23_0, tool and static libcurl
curl 8.23.1-DEV libcurl/8.23.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4   master 59d2537b40, tool and static libcurl
curl 8.22.0 ... AppleIDN ... (Homebrew, as shipped) tool and shared libcurl
curl 8.7.1 (SecureTransport) LibreSSL/3.3.6        macOS /usr/bin/curl, as shipped
```

## Steps To Reproduce:
Everything runs on 127.0.0.1 with Python 3 servers from the attached zip (`srv.py` redirects, `imapsink.py` and `smtpsink.py` are the attacker's mail servers and log what arrives, `sinksrv.py` is the HTTP control target); host names are mapped with `--resolve`. In the unzipped `poc/` directory, `./build.sh && ./run_tool.sh && ./run_lib.sh` does steps 1 to 3 against the curl on PATH and Homebrew's libcurl.
1. `CURL=/path/to/curl ./run_tool.sh` runs, for 301, 302, 303 and 307:
   `curl -L --proto-redir =http,imap -F file=@secret.txt -F note=hello -H 'Authorization: Bearer SECRET-TOKEN-123' -H 'Cookie: sid=SECRET-COOKIE-456' 'http://a.test:23201/x?code=<code>&loc=imap://b.test:23270/INBOX'`
   then the same command redirected to `http://b.test:23240/y` as the control, the SMTP twin (`--mail-rcpt`, 302 to `smtp://b.test:23280/`), a direct `imap://` upload as reference, and four OPT-IN CHECK runs repeating the HTTP and IMAP redirects with and without `--location-trusted`. Each case prints a `=>` line saying whether Authorization, Cookie and the file content arrived.
2. `./build.sh [curl build dir]` builds poc_mime_imap.c; without an argument it links Homebrew's libcurl.
3. `./run_lib.sh` runs it: `prior` does a CURLOPT_MIMEPOST to the application's own server with a custom Authorization header, then sets CURLOPT_HTTPGET=1 for another URL on the same handle which answers `302 Location: imap://b.test/INBOX`; `noprior` is the same without the earlier form.

Results (evidence/01 for 8.23.0, 02 for master, 03 for the reused handle, 05 for the stock binaries; all four builds above identical):
```
                                   301        302        303        307
-F form to imap://   APPENDed      yes        yes        yes        yes      Authorization + Cookie + file content
CONTROL, to http://  sent          GET only   GET only   GET only   body     no Authorization, no Cookie
SMTP twin (302, --mail-rcpt)       mail DATA with Authorization + Cookie + file content
libcurl reused handle, HTTPGET     APPEND of the earlier form + Authorization   (noprior control: LIST only)
REFERENCE direct imap:// upload    APPEND with its own -H headers (documented behaviour, unchanged)

OPT-IN CHECK                       default              --location-trusted
  http://b.test/ 307               no Authorization/Cookie   both sent      <- the documented switch works
  imap://b.test/ 302               both sent                 both sent      <- same either way: no check
```

## Fix
fix/imap-smtp-mime-on-redirect.diff (applies to master 59d2537b40 and to curl-8_23_0): IMAP and SMTP upload a MIME post only when the current request is one (`data->state.httpreq == HTTPREQ_POST_MIME`), and the mail headers taken from CURLOPT_HTTPHEADER leave out `Authorization:` and `Cookie:` when Curl_auth_allowed_to_host() is false — the helper curl documents as deciding whether authentication, cookies or other sensitive data "can be sent to the connection's origin" (lib/vauth/vauth.c:137-138), and which already honours CURLOPT_UNRESTRICTED_AUTH, so this applies curl's existing policy to IMAP and SMTP instead of inventing a new one. Built and re-run (evidence/04): 301/302/303 end with a `LIST` and no upload, 307 uploads the body without those two headers exactly as the HTTP control does, the SMTP case stops at `VRFY`, the reused handle uploads nothing, the direct `imap://` upload still carries its `-H` headers, and with `--location-trusted` the 307 upload carries them again, so the documented opt-in keeps working on IMAP just as it does on HTTP.

AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant (Claude) for code review, test setup and drafting. I reproduced every result myself with the attached scripts on the builds listed above; the logs in the zip are the raw output.

## Impact

A server that a user or application posts a form to, anyone who can answer its plaintext HTTP, or an open redirect on it, can collect the bearer token or session cookie carried in custom `Authorization:` or `Cookie:` headers together with every file and field of the form, by answering with a redirect to an IMAP or SMTP server it controls. Those two headers are the ones curl documents as never being sent to another host, and the form is uploaded even on 301, 302 and 303, where curl deliberately sends no body at all on an HTTP redirect, so a GET-downgrade redirect that an application author would reasonably treat as harmless becomes an upload of the form to the attacker. A libcurl application that reuses a handle, as the documentation recommends, sends an earlier and completely unrelated form the same way on a later plain GET. The precondition is the one CVE-2025-14524 (bearer token on a cross-protocol redirect to IMAP, LDAP, POP3 or SMTP) also required and which curl rated Low: the transfer must follow redirects and allow imap or smtp there, which is not the default for either the tool or libcurl, so this needs a user or application that opted into those redirect protocols — that advisory calls its own precondition "A highly unusual combination" and curl still assigned a CVE at Low; `--disallow-username-in-url` does not help here, since no userinfo is involved. Within that precondition nothing else is needed, no authentication options and no attacker-side validity: it affects the curl tool as well as libcurl, every version since 7.56.0 including macOS's and Homebrew's stock binaries, and the leak is exactly what CVE-2018-1000007 and CVE-2022-27776 fixed for HTTP.

title: OpenSSL+Apple SecTrust: SecTrust accepts certificates that the app's CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION trust store or verify callback rejected
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:
On OpenSSL builds with Apple SecTrust (USE_APPLE_SECTRUST, for example Homebrew's curl), libcurl runs the handshake with SSL_VERIFY_NONE, calls the application's CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION before it, and, if OpenSSL's verification fails, asks Apple SecTrust and accepts the server when SecTrust trusts it (lib/vtls/openssl.c:3946, :3979 and :4838-4847 in 8.23.0; :4868 in master). SecTrust is used by default unless CURLOPT_CAINFO, CURLOPT_CAPATH or CURLOPT_CAINFO_BLOB is set (lib/vtls/vtls_config.c:287-288), so when an application narrows trust in its SSL_CTX callback, by replacing the trust store with its own CA (as TAK's Commo library does, see Impact) or by rejecting the certificate in a cert verify callback (key pinning), SecTrust overrides that rejection for any certificate macOS trusts and CURLINFO_SSL_VERIFYRESULT reads 0. CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION(3) suggests using the callback "to add additional validation code for certificates", and curl published the same outcome for wolfSSL's CA cache as CVE-2026-82208 (Low): a certificate "rejected by the callback-selected store is then incorrectly accepted". The code comment anticipates that "the application intercepted the OpenSSL callback and installed its own" verification but skips SecTrust only when that verification succeeds, and 6aa8fa3fdf, which made SecTrust run after any OpenSSL failure, assumed that with a CAfile or CApath "the native store is disabled, so this does not affect use cases where users asks curl to use a specific set of trust anchors", which does not hold when the application sets its trust anchors or pin in the callback. The same binary rejects the server when the same CA is given with CURLOPT_CAINFO, an OpenSSL libcurl without SecTrust rejects in both cases, and an application that sets SSL_VERIFY_PEER itself aborts the handshake and is not affected.

## Affected version
The replaced-store case since 8.17.0, the first release with SecTrust (eefd03c572, which fell back only on X509_V_ERR_UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY); the verify-callback case since 8.18.0 (6aa8fa3fdf). Up to 8.23.0 and master 59d2537b40; libcurl only (the curl tool has no SSL_CTX callback). Tested on macOS 27.0.1 arm64 with OpenSSL 3.6.4:
```
libcurl/8.17.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.2.12     curl-8_17_0, -DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON -DUSE_APPLE_SECTRUST=ON
libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.2.12     curl-8_23_0, same options
libcurl/8.23.1-DEV OpenSSL/3.6.4 zlib/1.2.12     master 59d2537b40, same options
libcurl/8.22.0 OpenSSL/3.6.4 ... AppleIDN ...    Homebrew's curl as shipped (--with-apple-sectrust --with-ca-fallback)
```

## Steps To Reproduce:
The attached zip works against any public HTTPS site, so no keychain changes are needed. In its poc/ directory, `./mkpki.sh && ./build.sh && ./run_public.sh example.com` does steps 1 to 4 in one go.
1. `./mkpki.sh` creates pki/appca.pem (the only CA the application trusts) and pki/appsrv.pem (a certificate with an unrelated key).
2. `./build.sh` builds poc_ctx_store.c against Homebrew's libcurl, or `./build.sh <build dir>` against a curl build with `-DCURL_USE_OPENSSL=ON -DUSE_APPLE_SECTRUST=ON -DBUILD_STATIC_LIBS=ON`. It sets only CURLOPT_URL, a write callback and one of the two SSL_CTX callbacks in poc_ctx_store.c; verification options stay at their defaults.
3. `./poc https://example.com/ ctx pki/appca.pem`: the callback replaces the store with an X509_STORE holding only appca.pem. Expected (60); actual 0 and HTTP 200. With VERBOSE=1 curl logs `OpenSSL verify result: 14`, then `SSL certificate verified via Apple SecTrust.`
4. `./poc https://example.com/ pin pki/appsrv.pem`: the callback's SSL_CTX_set_cert_verify_callback() verifies the chain and then rejects because the key does not match (X509_V_ERR_APPLICATION_VERIFICATION). Expected (60); actual 0 and HTTP 200 (`OpenSSL verify result: 32`, then `verified via Apple SecTrust`).
5. Controls: `./poc https://example.com/ cainfo pki/appca.pem` gives (60) on the same binary; on a libcurl without SecTrust, steps 3 and 4 give (60) with verify results 20 and 50; pinning example.com's real key gives 200 everywhere.

```
                                      ctx (own CA only)   pin mismatch   cainfo (control)
8.17.0 OpenSSL+SecTrust               0, HTTP 200         60 (50)        60
8.23.0 OpenSSL+SecTrust               0, HTTP 200         0, HTTP 200    60
master 59d2537b40 OpenSSL+SecTrust    0, HTTP 200         0, HTTP 200    60
Homebrew curl 8.22.0                  0, HTTP 200         0, HTTP 200    60
master, OpenSSL without SecTrust      60                  60             60
```
The zip also has the same matrix against local servers, verbose logs, the code excerpts and a tested fix: in SecTrust builds, do not enable the native store by default when CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION is set (CURLSSLOPT_NATIVE_CA still enables it). With it, steps 3 and 4 fail with (60), pinning the right key still works, and transfers without a callback still verify via SecTrust. A narrower alternative is to skip the fallback only when the callback replaced the store or installed a verify callback.

AI disclosure: I used an AI assistant (Claude) for code review, test setup and drafting. I re-ran the PoC myself on every build in the table above with the attached scripts; the logs in the zip are the raw output.

## Impact

An application that limits which servers it trusts through CURLOPT_SSL_CTX_FUNCTION, to its own CA or to a pinned key, silently accepts every certificate macOS trusts when it runs on an OpenSSL libcurl built with Apple SecTrust, such as Homebrew's. An attacker who can intercept the connection and holds a certificate for the host from any CA the system trusts gets a normal transfer with CURLINFO_SSL_VERIFYRESULT 0; on managed Macs that includes the corporate or MDM-installed roots of TLS-inspection products, which are exactly what private-CA trust and pinning are used to keep out. Like CVE-2026-82208 this needs an application that narrows trust in the callback, and real code does: TAK's Commo library (github.com/TAK-Product-Center/atak-civ at 6cefd4c833, commoncommo/core/impl/urlrequestmanager.cpp:866-883 and :640-642) replaces the store with only the TAK server's CA, leaves CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYPEER on and sets no CURLOPT_CAINFO, and it has an iOS build that links a static OpenSSL libcurl, while curl offers USE_APPLE_SECTRUST on all Apple platforms. Such an application fails open without any error once its libcurl is built with SecTrust, nothing tells its author that CURLOPT_CAINFO must be set to keep SecTrust out, and the same application is safe with any libcurl built without SecTrust.

title: GnuTLS + Apple SecTrust discards authenticated OCSP failure
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

curl 8.23.0 and current master can accept a TLS certificate despite an explicit
`CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS=1` / `--cert-status` requirement when curl uses the
GnuTLS backend together with Apple SecTrust.

GnuTLS correctly marks an invalid or revoked stapled OCSP response as invalid.
Because a certificate trusted only by the Apple keychain is not trusted by
GnuTLS's file store, curl then invokes SecTrust. The GnuTLS caller passes no
OCSP response to SecTrust and does not require OCSP:

```c
Curl_vtls_apple_verify(cf, data, peer, chain->num_certs,
                       gtls_chain_get_der, chain, NULL, 0, FALSE);
```

If SecTrust accepts the certificate chain, curl clears GnuTLS's entire
verification result, including `GNUTLS_CERT_INVALID_OCSP_STATUS`.

- Released curl 8.23.0 subsequently checks only that a staple exists and
  therefore accepts an authentic `REVOKED` response.
- Current master parses the declared status but does not authenticate the OCSP
  responder or signature. It therefore accepts a matching `GOOD` response
  signed by an unrelated, self-signed certificate.

Peer and hostname verification remain enabled. `--insecure` is not used.

## Affected versions and configuration

Confirmed affected:

- curl 8.23.0 (`3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273`)
- master at `59d2537b40f9929fde00399be0f274001ad36aea`

Required configuration:

- an Apple operating system;
- curl built with GnuTLS and Apple SecTrust; and
- `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS=1` / `--cert-status` while native CA verification
  is active.

Apple SecTrust support began in 8.17.0. The bypass described here begins with
`5e727ca855429a684614a24646cb06fd965a1f7d`, which removed curl's independent
GnuTLS OCSP signature verification. That commit is in 8.23.0 but not 8.22.0.
Earlier affected configurations fail closed instead of accepting the bad
staple.

## Reproduction

The attached bundle contains a Linux harness so reviewers can deterministically
exercise curl's exact `USE_APPLE_SECTRUST` GnuTLS branch without changing a
macOS trust store. It replaces only `Curl_vtls_apple_verify()` with a narrow
stub that:

1. returns success, modeling SecTrust accepting a locally trusted chain; and
2. fails if the GnuTLS caller passes any OCSP bytes or asks SecTrust to require
   OCSP.

`lib/vtls/gtls.c`, the TLS handshake, GnuTLS verification, OCSP parser, HTTP
request, and response are unmodified. Thus this harness tests both the exact
fallback branch and its exact SecTrust arguments; it does not bypass or replace
the vulnerable OCSP decision.

Prerequisites are CMake, a C compiler, GnuTLS development headers, OpenSSL's
CLI, and `patch`.

For current master:

```sh
./reproduce-linux.sh /path/to/curl-current current
```

Observed:

```text
current unrelated-signer GOOD: exit=0
* SecTrust harness accepted the certificate-only check
* SSL certificate verified via Apple SecTrust.
< HTTP/1.0 200 ok

current signed REVOKED control: exit=91
* SecTrust harness accepted the certificate-only check
* SSL certificate verified via Apple SecTrust.
* peer certificate is revoked
```

For the 8.23.0 source tree:

```sh
./reproduce-linux.sh /path/to/curl-8.23.0 8.23.0
```

Observed:

```text
8.23.0 authentic REVOKED: exit=0
* SecTrust harness accepted the certificate-only check
* SSL certificate verified via Apple SecTrust.
< HTTP/1.0 200 ok
```

A control build without the SecTrust-success fallback rejects the same forged
`GOOD` staple with curl exit 60:

```text
SSL certificate verification failed: attached OCSP status response is invalid
```

All runs used ASan and UBSan and produced no sanitizer diagnostic. This is a
logical verification bypass, not a memory-safety issue.

### Direct macOS confirmation

1. Run `./generate-fixtures.sh`.
2. Build the target curl revision on macOS with GnuTLS and
   `USE_APPLE_SECTRUST=ON`.
3. Add `evidence/root.pem` as a trusted root in a disposable user keychain
   that SecTrust searches. Do not pass this root through `--cacert`; GnuTLS
   must lack the anchor so that the documented SecTrust fallback is exercised.
4. Serve the fixture leaf and staple:

```sh
openssl s_server -accept 24443 -www -tls1_2 \
  -cert evidence/leaf.pem -key evidence/leaf.key \
  -status_file evidence/forged-good.der
```

5. In another terminal, run:

```sh
curl --resolve tls.test:24443:127.0.0.1 \
  --cert-status https://tls.test:24443/
```

Current master returns 0 for `forged-good.der`. Curl 8.23.0 returns 0 even
when the server uses `signed-revoked.der`. A build given the root with
`--cacert evidence/root.pem` rejects the forged response because GnuTLS then
retains authority over its complete verification result.

The generated leaf deliberately has no AIA or CRL endpoint. SecTrust therefore
has no independent online revocation source; because the GnuTLS caller passes
`require_ocsp=false`, its best-effort revocation policy can accept the trusted
chain without authenticating the server's staple.

## Root cause

`gnutls_certificate_verify_peers2()` produces an invalid status containing
`GNUTLS_CERT_INVALID_OCSP_STATUS`. `gtls_verify_cert()` then treats successful
SecTrust chain validation as replacing that complete result:

```c
verified = !result;
if(verified) {
  *certverifyresult = 0;
}
```

However, the preceding SecTrust call received `NULL, 0, FALSE`, so SecTrust
never authenticated the stapled response.

Current `gtls_verify_ocsp_status()` imports the response, matches its
certificate ID, and reads its declared `GOOD`/`REVOKED` value. It never calls
`gnutls_ocsp_resp_verify()` or another signature-verification function. Its
comment assumes that GnuTLS's result is still authoritative, but that result
was just discarded by the SecTrust fallback.

## Why the recent fixes do not cover this

- PR #23420 / commit `287df0b324` added GnuTLS response parsing. It does not
  authenticate a response after the SecTrust fallback replaces GnuTLS's
  invalid result.
- PR #23430 / commit `cd89b5178b` passes the raw staple and
  `require_ocsp=true` from the OpenSSL caller. The GnuTLS caller explicitly
  passes `NULL, 0, FALSE` because the response is assumed to have been
  validated separately. That assumption fails precisely when SecTrust is the
  component that makes the chain acceptable.

## Suggested fix

When GnuTLS verification falls back to SecTrust and `verifystatus` is enabled:

1. retrieve the raw staple with `gnutls_ocsp_status_request_get()`;
2. pass those bytes to `Curl_vtls_apple_verify()` with `require_ocsp=true`;
3. retain the existing parser to require a `GOOD` entry matching the peer
   certificate.

Merely preserving `GNUTLS_CERT_INVALID_OCSP_STATUS` would make valid
native-only chains fail closed: GnuTLS cannot validate an OCSP signer whose
trust anchor exists only in Apple's store. The verifier that supplies the
missing trust anchor must authenticate the same stapled response.

`proposed-fix.patch` implements this plumbing against the tested master
commit. It compiles cleanly in the exact-branch harness; the harness then
rejects the forged response at the SecTrust boundary because OCSP bytes and
`require_ocsp=true` now reach it.

## Impact

An attacker who possesses the private key for a revoked but otherwise trusted
server certificate can defeat a caller's explicit OCSP-stapling requirement
and complete a TLS connection. This is an improper certificate-validation
issue (CWE-295).

The closest curl precedents were both rated **Medium**:

- CVE-2024-8096, "OCSP stapling bypass with GnuTLS"
- CVE-2026-7009, "OCSP stapling bypass with Apple SecTrust"

The latter advisory explicitly limits itself to OpenSSL-compatible backends.
This report concerns GnuTLS and code introduced after that advisory's fixed
range.

title: OpenSSL `--cert-status` accepts indefinitely stale GOOD OCSP staples
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

When curl uses its OpenSSL backend with `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS` (the
`--cert-status` tool option), a correctly signed OCSP response can be accepted
forever if its optional `nextUpdate` field is absent. curl passes `-1` as
OpenSSL's maximum permitted age for `thisUpdate`, explicitly disabling the
only remaining freshness bound:

```c
if(!OCSP_check_validity(thisupd, nextupd, 300L, -1L)) {
```

An attacker who has a revoked but otherwise unexpired server certificate and
its private key can replay an older, authentic `GOOD` staple that omitted
`nextUpdate`. curl accepts the TLS connection even though the application
explicitly requested revocation checking. This is a remote certificate
revocation bypass, not a malformed-input or memory-safety issue.

The attached end-to-end reproducer creates a CA and server certificate whose
validity started 60 days ago, signs four matching OCSP responses, starts a real
OpenSSL TLS server, and invokes the real curl tool. The attack response has a
30-day-old `thisUpdate`, no `nextUpdate`, a valid signature, and a matching
certificate ID.

## Affected configuration

- curl or libcurl built with the OpenSSL backend and OCSP support
- `CURLOPT_SSL_VERIFYSTATUS=1`, or the curl tool's `--cert-status`
- Any TLS-based protocol using this backend; the reproducer uses HTTPS

The vulnerable code was added by commit
`d1cf5d570663dac157740cb5e49d24614f185da7` and first released in curl
7.41.0. It remains present in the official curl 8.23.0 release and in current
master at the time of testing.

Tested directly:

- a fresh download of the official curl 8.23.0 `.tar.xz`, whose detached GPG
  signature validates against the release fingerprint published by curl;
  an ASan+UBSan binary built directly from this archive reproduces the issue
  and identifies itself as release `curl 8.23.0`, not a development build
- official `curl-8_23_0` tag, commit
  `3163ec065643ba20709f190111f42c3e1fe95273`
- official curl 8.23.0 archive, SHA-256
  `8dadd7d2536a314f982ad05a651b713f426bf7d02cc2c76cffb9796f2218e6c5`
- the archive and tag copies of `lib/vtls/openssl.c` are byte-identical,
  SHA-256 `973be1862430afef1bf15bd92e80eb8733d9fb62b9b32ed1a3063471e9c51331`
- OpenSSL 3.0.13 on Linux
- a separate curl 8.23.0 build using GnuTLS 3.8.3 rejected the attack control

OpenSSL-compatible forks share this source path, but only OpenSSL 3.0.13 was
tested and is claimed as directly demonstrated.

## Reproduction

Requirements: a C compiler, OpenSSL development headers and command-line
tool, Python 3 (only to reserve loopback ports), and the curl binary to test.

```sh
chmod +x reproduce.sh
CURL_BIN=/path/to/curl ./reproduce.sh
```

Observed with an ASan+UBSan build from the exact `curl-8_23_0` tag:

```text
curl 8.23.0-DEV (Linux) libcurl/8.23.0-DEV OpenSSL/3.0.13
fresh           curl_exit=0   expected=0
expired         curl_exit=91  expected=reject
revoked         curl_exit=91  expected=reject
stale-no-next   curl_exit=0   expected=0
VULNERABLE: a 30-day-old GOOD staple without nextUpdate was accepted.
```

The repository tag identifies itself as `8.23.0-DEV` in `curlver.h`; the
commit is the official annotated 8.23.0 tag, and the relevant file is
byte-identical to the released archive as recorded above.

The same four cases also reproduce with the system curl 8.5.0/OpenSSL 3.0.13.
No ASan, UBSan, or LeakSanitizer diagnostic was emitted.

The controls establish that curl reaches and enforces the normal verifier:

| Case | Signed status | `thisUpdate` | `nextUpdate` | Result |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Fresh control | GOOD | -1 hour | +24 hours | accepted (0) |
| Expiry control | GOOD | -30 days | -29 days | rejected (91) |
| Revocation control | REVOKED | -1 hour | +24 hours | rejected (91) |
| Attack | GOOD | -30 days | absent | **accepted (0)** |

The response signature and certificate ID are verified in every constructed
case. The attack differs from the expiry control only in omission of
`nextUpdate`. `fixture-times.log` also confirms that both the expiry control
and attack were signed 30 days ago (`producedAt` and `thisUpdate`), inside the
CA and leaf validity interval; this is a replay fixture, not a freshly signed
response carrying an artificial old status time.

## Root cause

`OCSP_resp_find_status()` returns `thisupd` and optional `nextupd`. curl then
calls:

```c
OCSP_check_validity(thisupd, nextupd, 300L, -1L)
```

OpenSSL applies the `nextUpdate` upper bound only when that field exists. Its
`maxsec` argument is the maximum age allowed for `thisUpdate`; a negative
value disables that check. Therefore:

1. future `thisUpdate` values are rejected;
2. expired present `nextUpdate` values are rejected;
3. an absent `nextUpdate` plus any past `thisUpdate` is accepted, regardless
   of age.

The curl source comment directly documents that `-1` means there is no limit.
OpenSSL's own `OCSP_resp_find_status` documentation warns about this exact
combination: because some responders omit `nextUpdate`, an ancient response
would otherwise be considered valid, and callers should use `maxsec` to limit
its permitted age. curl explicitly disables that safeguard.

## Why this is a security issue

RFC 6960 section 3.2 requires an OCSP client, before accepting a signed
response, to confirm that `thisUpdate` is sufficiently recent. Section
4.2.2.1 says omission of `nextUpdate` means newer revocation information is
available all the time; it does not mean the response never expires.

The current lightweight OCSP profile, RFC 9919 section 5 (which obsoletes RFC
5019), is stricter: clients must reject a response when `nextUpdate` is
absent. Its stated reason is specifically to prevent an out-of-date `GOOD`
response from masking a newer `REVOKED` response.

OCSP stapling does not use a request nonce, so time is the replay defense.
With both the `nextUpdate` bound absent and curl's `thisUpdate` maximum age
disabled, there is no replay lifetime other than the certificate's own
`notAfter` date. Revocation is intended to protect precisely the situation
where a certificate/private-key pair is no longer trustworthy before that
date.

## Suggested fix

The strict, one-line fail-closed fix is included as `proposed-fix.patch`:

```c
if(!nextupd || !OCSP_check_validity(thisupd, nextupd, 300L, -1L)) {
```

With that patch, the exact reproducer changes only the attack case:

```text
fresh           curl_exit=0   expected=0
expired         curl_exit=91  expected=reject
revoked         curl_exit=91  expected=reject
stale-no-next   curl_exit=91  expected=reject
FAIL-CLOSED: the stale staple without nextUpdate was rejected.
```

The run is selected with:

```sh
STALE_EXPECTED=reject CURL_BIN=/path/to/patched/curl ./reproduce.sh
```

If curl needs compatibility with general RFC 6960 responders that omit
`nextUpdate`, an alternative is to retain such responses but pass a finite,
documented maximum age as `maxsec`. Leaving both freshness bounds disabled is
the vulnerable condition. Strict rejection is preferable for the explicitly
fail-closed `--cert-status` option and matches RFC 9919.

## Duplicate analysis

- `git log --all -S'OCSP_check_validity'` finds only the 2014 introduction.
- `git log --all -S'300L, -1L' -- lib/vtls/openssl.c` likewise finds no fix.
- Public curl issue/PR searches for `nextUpdate`, `status age`, `stale OCSP`,
  and `OCSP freshness` found no curl report for this defect as of 2026-10-18.
- Public PR #23311 concerns GnuTLS signature and certificate-ID verification,
  not this OpenSSL freshness defect. Its checked fixtures all have a present
  `next_update`; its review comment points to the OpenSSL validity call without
  identifying the unbounded `maxsec=-1` plus missing-`nextUpdate` condition.
  The PR was closed without merge and neither it nor its proposed replacement
  changes `lib/vtls/openssl.c`.
- CVE-2020-8286 fixed certificate-ID matching in the same function, not
  response freshness; the `maxsec=-1` call remained unchanged.
- The Netty advisory concerns separate code and confirms the bug class; it is
  not a curl report.

Private reports are not searchable, so only the curl security team can make a
definitive duplicate determination.

## References

- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6960.html#section-3.2
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6960.html#section-4.2.2.1
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9919.html#section-5
- https://docs.openssl.org/3.0/man3/OCSP_resp_find_status/
- https://github.com/curl/curl/pull/23311
- https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2020-8286.html
- https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2024-8096.html
- https://curl.se/docs/CVE-2026-7009.html
- https://github.com/netty/netty/security/advisories/GHSA-jj3c-mwvr-9g52

## Impact

An attacker with a compromised, revoked, but unexpired server certificate and
its private key can impersonate the server to applications that explicitly
enable curl's OCSP-stapling verification. If the attacker retained a genuine
pre-revocation `GOOD` response without `nextUpdate`, curl accepts it
indefinitely and proceeds with the protected transfer. This can expose or
modify application data according to the protocol and request.

The prerequisite is meaningful but inherent to certificate-revocation threat
models: without the private key, the attacker cannot complete the TLS
handshake; without revocation checking, the compromised credential would
already work. The flaw defeats the control the caller enabled to contain that
compromise.

Suggested classification: **CWE-299, Improper Check for Certificate
Revocation**, **Moderate/Medium** severity.

The closest curl precedent is CVE-2020-8286, also introduced in the OpenSSL
`--cert-status` verifier and also allowing a breached TLS server to mask a
revoked certificate; curl rated it Medium. CVE-2024-8096 and CVE-2026-7009
are other curl OCSP bypasses rated Medium. Separately, Netty assigned
CVE-2026-93493/Moderate to the same unbounded-age condition for responses
without `nextUpdate` (with a different downstream failure mode).

title: wolfSSL TLS sessions retain native-CA trust after the application narrows trust
vulnerability_information:
## Summary

In curl 8.23.0 with the wolfSSL backend, a TLS session authenticated while the
build-default native CA store is active can be resumed after the application
changes the same easy handle to a policy that disables native trust. The
second transfer succeeds and exchanges HTTP data even though an otherwise
identical full handshake under the new policy rejects the peer.

The TLS session-cache key contains the raw `CURLOPT_SSL_OPTIONS` mask and CA
file/path/blob inputs, but not the resolved `native_ca_store` boolean. That
boolean can differ while every keyed field remains identical. wolfSSL then
applies the ineligible cached session and a resumed TLS 1.2 handshake does not
repeat certificate-chain authentication.
